I’m thrilled to start sharing some images of picture books from my collection! First up, a childhood favorite of mine: this stunning edition of Swan Lake, written by ballerina Margot Fonteyn and illustrated by the incomparable Trina Schart Hyman. Siegfried and Odette gaze serenely at each other on the front cover, while the owl magician Count von Rothbart stalks them on the back. Poring over this book with @ladyjaiduh many years ago (a youth decidedly well spent), I was simultaneously terrified and enthralled by von Rothbart’s eerie duality.

caption:
Here’s another childhood favorite of mine, this one quite well known: Rumpelstiltskin, retold and illustrated by the inordinately talented @paulozelinsky. A Caldecott honor book, this one was rightly celebrated upon its release for the rich detail and sheer grandeur of its art. For me, here is the definitive adaptation of the Grimms’ tale; whenever I tell Rumpelstiltskin aloud and affect the voice of the title character, it’s Zelinsky’s wildly expressive little imp with his bug eyes and razor-sharp nose who saunters irreverently into my mind and helps me get into character.

caption:
Now, here is one of my absolute favorite picture books of all time: Heckedy Peg, written and illustrated by @audreywoodauthor and Don Wood. The creative team (and married couple) achieves a true unity of word and image, the spare and elegant language complemented by the haunting beauty of the oil paintings. This story of a mother protecting her seven children from a menacing witch, though it reads like a classic fairy tale, is in fact an original narrative inspired by a sixteenth-century children’s game. The folkloric elements lend the book a striking and timeless quality that transports me straight back to my childhood as I hold it in my hands. Once read, never forgotten.

Today’s book is Count Silvernose, an Italian fairy tale adapted by Erik A. Kimmel and illustrated by @omarrayyanart. Unusually for a fairy tale, Kimmel depicts his heroine as large, physically powerful, hardworking, talented, and clever—but expressly not beautiful. Fascinatingly, Rayyan based his splendid paintings on art from a sixteenth-century Italian sketchbook. His choice to foreground this process by transitioning between line drawings and fully colored paintings within a single image induces the reader to view stately Renaissance imagery through a subtly postmodern lens.

A staple of my childhood: Snow-White and the Seven Dwarfs, by poet Randall Jarrell and illustrator Nancy Ekholm Burkert. caption:
For a thoroughly entertaining read, pick up a copy of S. T. Mendelson’s Stupid Emilien. While anthropomorphic rabbits populate this adaptation of a Russian folktale, their motivations and interactions are distinctly and outrageously human. Mendelson depicts both the beauty of the natural landscape and the ornate design of the architecture in a series of dazzling paintings that overflow with action, humor, and magic. The title, though it might come across as harsh, resounds with irony: the protagonist’s relaxed and unpretentious lifestyle reads to his judgmental community as stupidity, and he simply does not care to make a correction. Mendelson, of course, gently invites readers in on the joke.

Now this is a work of art: The Moon’s Revenge, written by Joan Aiken and illustrated by Alan Lee. For many years I hazily remembered my school librarian reading us this book, but I recalled neither title nor author nor illustrator—only brief flashes of plot. caption:
And now for something completely different: Masquerade, an elaborate puzzle of a book designed, written, and illustrated by @kitwilliamsartist. The absurdist text and cryptic art function together as a riddle with a single valid solution pointing to the location of a real physical treasure actually buried by the author in secret prior to the book’s publication. Having sparked the interest of amateur sleuths around the world, the mystery was solved after a few years had passed...though the first searcher to identify the correct location was later revealed to have cheated through insider knowledge. The success of the book inspired numerous public treasure hunts in the following decades, some of which remain unsolved to this day.

The book of the day is Rapunzel, retold from the Brothers Grimm and illustrated by Alix Berenzy. On each page Berenzy draws the reader further into a landscape of intoxicating detail through her vibrant use of color and her remarkable command of light and shadow. She achieves these distinctive visual textures through a singular combination of gouache painting and colored pencil drawing on black paper.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: in her text, Berenzy identifies the malevolent Mother Gothel as a “fairy”, a direct translation of the German word “Fee”, which the Grimms themselves used in the first edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen. The French-derived “Fee” hints at the work’s origin: the Grimms adapted it from a German translation of a French literary fairy tale. In later editions, they subtly cleansed the story of its roots by replacing “Fee” with the more appropriately Germanic “Zauberin”, or “sorceress”. Modern English-language adaptations typically give Mother Gothel the more familiar label “witch”.

caption:
How poetic, how meditative, how life-affirming, how hypnotically beautiful is this picture book version of The Hymn of the Sun by St. Francis of Assisi with illustrations by Tony Wright. Often called the Canticle of the Sun, or Laudes Creaturarum (“Praise of the Creatures”), the hymn is thought to have been written around the year 1224. St. Francis, who believed that commoners should be able to worship in a language they understood, composed it in his native Umbrian dialect of Italian. The text here comes from a 1927 English translation held in the Bodleian Library at Oxford. Wright’s watercolor paintings swirl and glow with a mystical energy, emphasizing the hymn’s lyrical and reverent celebration of the wonders of nature.

caption:
It’s a wild mix of fantasy, drama, loneliness, deceit, sorrow, and revenge you’ll encounter in The Blind Fairy by Brigitte Schär and Julia Gukova. The solemn tale, originally written in German and published in Switzerland, gives us a fairy protagonist trapped in a sinister hoax: blindness prevents her from noticing that her company of loyal servants has been driven out and replaced by a band of malicious dwarves. Impersonating her faithful retinue, the wicked creatures patronizingly assure her that all is well, even as their nightly revels send her mountaintop palace into squalor and disrepair. The fairy’s extended isolation amid the dwarves’ furtively contemptuous treatment might seem to make for entirely too gloomy a narrative, but Gukova’s illustrations add fascinating elements of scale and design, somewhat leavening the atmosphere of irony and despair. Schär, for her part, ultimately gifts her heroine with the necessary insight and resolve to confront her tormentors, and proceeds to end the story on perhaps the most brazen cliffhanger you’re ever likely to find in a picture book.

caption:
Here’s a book I remember fondly from my childhood: Goldilocks and the Three Bears by Jan Brett. This story ranks among the best-known fairy tales, and any of us could surely recount the plot from start to finish with little difficulty. Brett‘s bears dwell in a charming thatch-roofed cottage decorated with recurring motifs of flowers, berries, pine cones and other elements of nature. Her trademark borders, chock-full of textural detail, give readers a glimpse of the characters’ actions while they remain out of the narrative’s focus.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Brett cites Andrew Lang’s version of the tale from The Green Fairy Book (1892) as her source, and she retains much of Lang’s wording, though she has made several noteworthy character changes. In Lang’s story, the bears are described as a Little, Small, Wee Bear, a Middle-sized Bear, and a Great, Huge Bear. Brett, like many modern authors, assigns them family roles, depicting the smallest as a child, the middle as a mother, and the largest as a father. Readers may also be surprised to learn that one of Brett’s title characters fails to appear in the source material: Goldilocks herself. In Lang’s telling (itself adapted from Robert Southey’s original publication of the tale in 1837), the interloper is an old woman. Only in subsequent literary renditions of the story was the character replaced with a young girl, whose name was first given as Silver-Hair, then Golden Hair, then Goldenlocks, and finally the enduringly familiar Goldilocks.

It’s October, and the autumn night brings a chill both eerie and comfortingly familiar. I’ve decided to celebrate the week leading up to Halloween by posting a scary book each day. To begin, here’s Anthony Browne’s The Tunnel, in which a brother and sister, thrown out of the house for misbehavior, discover a mysterious passageway leading to...well, who knows where? The plot hinges upon their decision to crawl inside, the ominous tableau of the darkly gaping tunnel mouth a visual fulcrum for the narrative. Browne mines the visit to a frightening otherworld (whether real or imagined) for the progress it affords the siblings’ emotional relationship. His images pay homage to several iconic works from the Golden Age of Illustration, including Walter Crane’s Little Red Riding Hood and Kay Nielsen’s Hansel and Gretel.

caption:
Continuing with my series of seven scary books leading up to Halloween, we have The Soup Bone by Tony Johnston and Margot Tomes. An old woman, alone on Halloween, digs for a bone to add to her soup, but to her dismay she unearths a living skeleton. There ensues a madcap chase sequence, a tense standoff, and a hilarious reversal in which the undead specter truly meets its match. Moreover, the surprisingly touching coda celebrates the importance of mutual understanding and companionship without diminishing the value of a good scare. Johnston peppers the narration with irresistible onomatopoeias (“Clickety-click, clackety-clack”) and the dialogue with folksy, alliterative interjections (“Boogity-boo!” and “Skittle-skattle, skeleton!”), while Tomes‘s stark line and gloomy palette strike the perfect balance between grim fright and playful slapstick.

There’s only one more day until Halloween, a night on which we may contemplate the primordial fears unleashed by the darkness that obscures half our waking hours. To that end, let us examine Natalie Savage Carlson and Charles Robinson’s The Night the Scarecrow Walked. A young sister and brother, out after sundown on Halloween night, stop by a cornfield to show their jack-o’-lantern to a scarecrow that the sister imagines must be lonely. Here is an impressively tense thriller that, though it ends in safety, never fully dispels the creeping notion we all keep in the back of our minds: if you’re not careful, some still and harmless thing might come alive and shuffle toward you in the dark.

Halloween is here. On this night, when the specter of death looms large in the landscape of the human mind, I wish you warmth and safety in the arms of your loved ones. For the final book in this sequence of seven, I present hist whist, a poem by e. e. cummings with illustrations by Deborah Kogan Ray. I can scarcely imagine a selection that better captures the spirit of the holiday. In each stanza, cummings employs abstract language that coalesces into a playful evocation of the eerie sights and sounds of Halloween night: “little ghostthings/tip-toe/twinkle-toe”, “rustle and run and/hidehidehide”, “look out for the old woman/with the wart on her nose/what she’ll do to yer/nobody knows”. Ray’s darkly glowing, jewel-toned illustrations, inspired by glimpses of neighborhood trick-or-treaters, convey us to a shadowy demimonde where witches, goblins, and devils lurk, flocking together to whisper, to dance, to frighten...and to jubilantly unmask. Happy Halloween.

caption:
Today I’ve reached a milestone: my hundredth book review. Thanks to all of you who have liked my posts, followed my account, and left encouraging comments. It really means a lot, and I keep you all in my heart as I craft a new entry each day.

And now, the greatest picture book you’ve never heard of: Crackling Brat by Andrew Matthews and Tomek Bogacki. I found this one tucked away like hidden treasure in a dusty labyrinth of an old used bookstore and read it cover to cover on the spot. How could I not? Here was an original work that felt like a cross between a Norse myth and an American tall tale, brimming with magic and humor and rare depth of emotion. Crackling Brat is a human child...or is he? He certainly seems blessed with a raft of remarkable powers. He lives in our world...or does he? His home, it emerges, is situated in an extraordinary landscape filled with dangerous creatures. Something has happened to his father...or has it? He has indeed been missing for quite a while. It’s up to Crackling Brat to use his wits, his bravery, and his uncanny talents to defeat Snow Tiger, Night Bear, and Hunger Wolf and rescue his father from the clutches of Time itself. Matthews’ language sizzles and writhes and sings with explosive glee, choice phrases such as “I’m off out to see what’s what,” “his ears as careful as mice,” “louder than a forest full of birds singing down the sun,” and “his mouth open starving-wide” injecting the proceedings with electric flavor. Bogacki’s expressive illustrations convey the elemental ferocity of the monsters, the mischievous wildness of our hero as he goes toe to toe with each of them, and the indelible bond of affection between parent and child. With this book, you’re in for an unforgettable adventure.

caption:
Today I’m poring over this endlessly fascinating version of The Frog Prince or Iron Henry, translated from the German of the Brothers Grimm by Naomi Lewis and illustrated by Binette Schroeder. Lewis strikes a satisfying tone through her majestic narrative voice, while Schroeder’s eerily captivating illustrations frequently employ the clever technique of depicting action by staging a character in a sequence of poses within a single environment.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the Brothers Grimm originally titled this tale “Der Froschkönig oder der eiserne Heinrich”, which translates to “The Frog King or Iron Heinrich”. Fascinatingly, in the first edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen, the Grimms included a similar tale called “Der Froschprinz” (“The Frog Prince”). In his 1823 English-language edition (the first-ever translation of the Grimms’ fairy tales into English), Edgar Taylor kept “Der Froschkönig” but replaced its ending with that of “Der Froschprinz”, and combined the names of the stories, yielding the commonly used title that Lewis has selected for this adaptation.

caption:
Ready for your high fantasy fix? This is Elfwyn’s Saga by David Wisniewski, an original tale inspired by Icelandic tradition. The wicked curse of a bitter enemy causes the baby daughter of a noble house to be born blind. The young girl, Elfwyn, nevertheless grows up blessed by the ethereal Hidden Folk with preternatural agility and perception. If you’d like an epic clash between good and evil, may I suggest Joseph and Koza or the Sacrifice to the Vistula? In this religious tale originally written in Yiddish by Isaac Bashevis Singer (here translated by Singer and Elizabeth Shub), a village chieftain’s daughter is selected by a local witch as an offering to be drowned in the river. Hope arrives in the form of a young goldsmith from Jerusalem, who not only defends the young woman but also decries the tradition of human sacrifice. The confrontation between the pious craftsman (secure in his devotion to Judaism) and the devious witch (aided by goblins, devils, and none other than the fearsome Baba Yaga herself) comes to represent the tension between an ascendant faith in a single deity and a polytheistic tradition stretching back to a primeval epoch. Singer’s lyrical writing is enhanced by Symeon Shimin’s stark, expressive draft-style drawings in blacks, grays, and browns.

caption:
In Krystyna Turska’s The Magician of Cracow you’ll find an engaging tale of magic and trickery. The title character, a learned sorcerer renowned across Poland for his skill with the mystic arts, nourishes a single, burning wish—the ability to travel to the moon. He therefore makes a pact with the devil, signing away his own life in exchange for limitless wealth and power, but delays fulfilling his end of the bargain for years and years. When the fiend’s impatience boils over, the two engage in a battle of wits that leaves the magician trapped in limbo between freedom and captivity forever. Turska’s illustrations, filled with bright color and bustling detail, inject the narrative with a merry energy, while her ornate borders create an air of the antique.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this book is inspired not by a fairy tale but by a legend, which is a folk story that features characters believed to be real historical figures (such as Robin Hood or Mulan). This particular legend originates with the sixteenth-century Polish nobleman Pan Twardowski, a famous astronomer and alchemist believed by many to be endowed with supernatural powers.

There’s subtle humor and just a sliver of the celestial to be had in Hildilid’s Night by Cheli Durán Ryan and Arnold Lobel. This is a tale of insomnia writ large, of frustration, struggle, and eventual acceptance. Old Hildilid, in her hut in the hills near Hexham, is so averse to the dark of night that she endeavors to chase it away altogether. She tries sweeping it out with a broom, stuffing it in a sack, boiling it in a cauldron, binding it with vines, snipping it with shears, feeding it to her wolfhound, and a host of other whimsical tactics. Ryan observes the bizarre goings-on with a straight face, evincing wry sympathy for her ornery protagonist. Lobel (husband of illustrator Anita Lobel) employs meticulous hatching in his pen-and-ink drawings, crafting a ghostly landscape of black and white. Only on the last few pages does a gentle yellow glow creep over the horizon...just as Hildilid has finally fallen asleep.

Though it might seem like an outlandish scenario, this stroke of good fortune is just what befalls the lead character of Benjamin Elkin and Anita Lobel’s How the Tsar Drinks Tea. Elkin, who drew inspiration for this original tale from a Jewish folk song speculating about the lavish trappings of royalty, finds a common humanity in the genial interchange between the peasant and the tsar. caption:
Sinister indeed is the eponymous stranger of Robert Holden and Drahos Zak’s The Pied Piper of Hamelin. Based on an enigmatic German legend from the old town of Hamelin (also known as Hameln), the story tells of a town plagued by rats and a piper who frees them of the ruinous vermin by luring the animals out of town with his music. When the greedy people refuse to pay for his service, the piper takes revenge by playing his instrument once more—his siren call now ensnaring the town children, who follow him into the distance and are never seen again. Holden relates the tale in verse, adding a certain flavor of the antique. Zak’s art, studded throughout with disconcertingly colorless figures and objects, revels in distortion and unease: half-timbered houses jut upward in a crooked sprawl, the title character leers out at the reader with piercing, heavy-lidded eyes, and a human shadow stretches across the floor and up a wall to become an ominous, towering rat.

caption:
There must be a moment at some point in all children’s lives when they wish they could run away from their families and dwell in a fantasy paradise. In her idiosyncratic book The Parent Thief, Mitra Modaressi explores that very impulse and follows it to its logical conclusion. Jack Parsley, bored to tears on a family cruise, meets the mysterious Quinn, who whisks him away via bathtub-balloon-boat to an island where children live free of parental oversight. How to stave off Jack’s parents’ inevitable worry? Quinn volunteers to go back to the cruise ship in his place. But, Jack protests, Quinn looks nothing like him. Not to worry—Quinn will magically hypnotize the family so they perceive him as Jack. The disturbing implications of this power are made manifest when Quinn overstays his allotted time, and Jack must go and confront him to reclaim his rightful place in the Parsley family. Modaressi’s tone and illustrations leaven the frightening concept of alienation and replacement by an untrustworthy doppelgänger.

The newly fallen snow frosting tree limbs and blanketing the earth outside has put me in mind of an old classic: Owl Moon by Jane Yolen and John Schoenherr. One bright snowy night, a father and child go owling. They enter the woods and press on, taking care to remain silent; at last, the father’s practiced bird calls summon a Great Horned Owl. Yolen crafts an engrossing prose poem, interspersing sensory impressions of the winter walk with sage fragments of family wisdom passed down to the narrator from older siblings. Schoenherr achieves a tangible stillness with a muted palette of browns, grays, blues, and whites; his vividly rendered owl is an event unto itself.

An interesting bit of trivia: at this year’s Society of Children’s Book Writers and Illustrators Winter Conference, I attended a breakout session led by the talented and prolific author @heidieys, daughter of Jane Yolen, who revealed that she and her father were the inspiration for the characters in Owl Moon.

caption:
Here is an startlingly raw work that probes the human capacity for apathy and injustice: Libby Gleeson and Armin Greder’s The Great Bear. The animal of the title lives her life under the yoke of the circus, being made to dance for the entertainment of the masses who come to gawk at her in captivity. One day, she can take their jeering and prodding no longer. In a powerful extended sequence of wordless pages, she breaks free, walks past the terrified onlookers, climbs a pole, and somehow, magically, escapes into the sky. Is this ending real or imaginary? Does the bear truly ascend to the heavens, or are we presented with an externalization of her longing for freedom? It is up to the reader to decide. Notably, Gleeson and Greder collaborated on the structure and format of the story from the book’s inception, an unusual arrangement for an author and illustrator. Her short, unsentimental phrases and his gripping and expressive drawings come together to form a unique piece of art, at once an etiology for the constellation Ursa Major and a grim condemnation of animal cruelty throughout human history.

caption:
Let’s amble through the far-off climes of John Warren Stewig and K. Wendy Popp’s Princess Florecita and the Iron Shoes. Beckoned by the tale in the song of a bird outside her window, the daughter of a king and queen leaves the safety and comfort of her royal home and sets out in search of a prince lying in an enchanted slumber. She must traverse rough landscapes, listen for ethereal advice in the houses of the winds, and face a pair of fearsome gryphons, all while wearing out a pair of iron shoes. With pleasingly evocative language, Stewig adapts this tale with roots in the Spanish folk tradition; Popp’s smooth, hazy backgrounds contrast with her strikingly realistic character art to create an environment brimming with arcane allure.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: many people with a limited breadth of experience seem to believe that that all fairy tales feature strong, clever men who drive the story and passive women who wait to be acted upon. These readers (and writers) therefore applaud revisionist versions of such stories in which the genders are changed but all other plot details remain the same. The vast majority of gender-swapped fairy tales come across as heavy-handed and artificial. Moreover, they are entirely unnecessary, as authentic tales in which a female character performs the rescue and a male character is seen as a figure of gentle beauty already exist, naturally rooted in the folk tradition that produced them.

caption:
And so we have reached the Eve of the New Year. Now is a time for reflection, looking back and taking stock of what has come before. I started this series of posts five months ago, and set a few rules for myself: each day a new illustrator (that’s over one hundred fifty!), no repeated tale type (only one version of Cinderella, only one Rumpelstiltskin, et cetera), and feature classic work (that is, at least a decade old). I decided that I would challenge myself to stick to these rules for the duration of the calendar year, and then relax them a bit. Therefore, in 2021, you may see me post further work from illustrators I’ve covered before, new versions of fairy tales I’ve already discussed, and books by more current authors. I’m excited to be branching out in this way, and I hope you enjoy what’s to come! Finally, for those of you who have been reading and responding so kindly thus far: thank you from the bottom of my heart.

I am bidding farewell to 2020 with what I believe to be the ultimate achievement in the picture book form: Where the Wild Things Are by Maurice Sendak. Max, having misbehaved and quarreled with his mother, sails off to a faraway land where he tames and befriends a tribe of monsters. Then, in need of comfort, he sails home again to find the warm welcome of unconditional love. Sendak chooses his language masterfully, with not a wasted word in his quietly poetic text. The illustrations achieve shadow and depth through effective use of cross-hatching and color, with the images starting out tightly framed on the page and gradually expanding as we journey into a marvelous world that might exist alongside our own, in Max’s imagination, or perhaps both at once.

caption:
It is New Year’s Day. A time to celebrate new beginnings, to look ahead with hope for the future even as we maintain our joyful traditions. In recognition of the cyclical symbolism of the holiday, I am going all the way back to where I started and featuring the illustrator from my very first book review: this is Saint George and the Dragon by Margaret Hodges and Trina Schart Hyman. George, a valiant warrior known as the Red Cross Knight, journeys to a faraway land at the behest of the Queen of the Fairies to slay a fearsome dragon. Man and beast clash over and over on the battlefield, locked in a deadly struggle until the monster falls at last. Hodges employs sophisticated language and elegant imagery to create a tale of remarkable action and excitement. Hyman’s stunning art is divided into panels by crisscrossing brown strips resembling muntins, which also (on pages facing the illustrations) serve to frame the text in heraldic borders. The standout creation here is of course the glorious and ferociously beautiful dragon, its hide covered in thickly scaled armor, its membranous wings studded with hooked pinions, its flame breath choking the sky with billowing clouds of smoke. I wish you a joyful and prosperous New Year.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the medieval Christian legend of Saint George and the Dragon can be found in many sources, notably Legenda Aurea (“The Golden Legend”), a collection of hagiographies by thirteenth-century Genoese archbishop Jacobus de Varagine. Hodges adapts her text from Edmund Spenser’s expansion of the tale in his sixteenth-century epic poem The Faerie Queene.

caption:
In your younger days, did you wish you could fly? Perhaps you believed you could, knew it in your bones. The power of imagination and the wonder of flight come together in a riveting vignette of magic realism in @beatrizmartinvidal’s Bird. This wordless picture book juxtaposes two simple sequences, a bird high in the sky and a child donning a flight suit. As the child puts on a cap, goggles, and a pair of wings, the bird begins to take on a human shape and descend. Finally, the two sequences become one: the child stands on a board placed over a fulcrum just in time to be catapulted up into the air by the bird, who lands on the other end of the board entirely in human form, another child in a flight suit. The first child, soaring among the clouds, begins the transformation in reverse, shrinking, growing feathers, becoming a bird. The soft texture and nearly monochromatic color palette of Vidal’s art gives rise to an enigmatic beauty. Questions abound: Who are these children? Are they truly becoming birds, or are we witnessing pretend play rendered literally on the page? Different answers may speak to different readers, a testament to the poetic spirit of Vidal’s visual storytelling.

For today, a splendid visual feast: Dragon Feathers by husband-and-wife team Andrej Dugin and @duginart. In this adaptation of a folktale from Austria’s Ziller Valley, young Henry is obliged to pluck three golden feathers from a fearsome dragon sorcerer in order to win his sweetheart’s hand in marriage. Dugin and Dugina structure their masterfully detailed oil paintings in a palindromic sequence, such that each illustration of Henry’s path to the dragon’s house is paired with a mirrored image charting his path back home: the first page with the last, the second page with the second to last, and so on, leading inward to the center of the book, where the dragon’s marital bed (very much the narrative and visual fulcrum of the tale) is evenly split across a single page spread.

caption:
Any frequent reader of folklore knows that storytellers use the forest to represent magic, danger, and uncertainty. Heroes wandering among the trees must struggle against monsters and outwit villains who would do them harm. But what if the paradigm were shifted? Perhaps the good intentions of a cheery travelers can radiate outward and turn fear into safety, transform the unknown into the familiar. If this proposition sounds pleasing to you, then you just might enjoy Troll Wood by Kathryn Cave and Paul Hess. A family sets out into a dark forest where no one ever goes, deciding at every turn that they will push on though others have always turned back. At the end of their path they find a place that, with a little bit of work and love, feels like home. Cave structures the text as a simple call and response, with an omniscient narrator repeatedly asking if the family means to continue and the family resolutely responding, “We will.” Hess deliberately skews the perspective in his watercolor illustrations, depicting the wood as bizarre but not overtly menacing. He also makes the fascinating choice to place enormous trolls at the edges of many images, as though lurking just at the edge of the family’s sight—or perhaps in the corners of their imaginations.

caption:
Sometimes the title of a book just calls out to you, perfectly establishing the characters and setting and plot, and you know right away that you’re going to be entertained. To that end, here’s Robert D. San Souci and Alexi Natchev’s Peter and the Blue Witch Baby. See? Instantly, the curiosity is piqued. Who is Peter? A wide and good-natured Tsar. Who is the Blue Witch Baby? A wicked sorceress who tricks her way into the palace in the guise of a newborn girl. While the young king is away wooing the Little Sister of the Sun, the infant turns blue, swells to a gargantuan size, and devours everything in sight with her iron teeth. San Souci masterfully sustains the tension as Peter first confronts and then evades the enormous creature, whom Natchev portrays as an eerily cute monstrosity, the figure of a plump toddler perverted to a malevolent, lumbering nightmare.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: without citing a specific tale, the book’s front matter identifies this story as an adaptation of Russian folklore. San Souci’s source appears to be a tale from Narodnye Russkie Skazki, compiled by Aleksandr Afanas’ev, called “The Witch and the Sister of the Sun”, in which the horror is a bit subtler. Here, the antagonist is not a giant blue creature at all but the hero’s natural-born sister, a cannibal witch who devours their parents.

caption:
David Wiesner gives us a clever and visually delightful meditation on the creative process in his playful and surreal Art & Max. The story unfolds against a desert landscape suggesting the American southwest. Art, a haughty and grandiose horned lizard, attempts to complete a painting, but is constantly interrupted by Max, a collared lizard with a limitless supply of energy. With only a few carefully chosen lines of dialogue augmenting his masterful images, Wiesner employs the free-associative logic of a madcap cartoon, continually calling awareness to the medium of the illustrations. Art offers to let Max paint him, but Max takes him literally and splashes paint all over his body. Art becomes so frustrated that he swells up with fury, causing his beaded hide, which has thus far been rendered in acrylic paint, to shatter in all directions. Beneath is a smooth coat of pastel, which Max blows off with a fan, revealing a layer of watercolor. Art drinks a glass of water, which causes the watercolor to drip away, leaving only an India ink outline, which Max proceeds to unravel completely. Ultimately, Max reconstitutes his friend, and the two begin painting harmoniously side by side. Wiesner develops a subtle allegory for conflict and compromise between the formal rigor of planned composition and the joyous freedom of spontaneous experimentation. He cleverly extends this theme right into the names of the title characters: “Art” (nominally short for Arthur) implies a devotion to visual craft, and might “Max” (driven ever toward puckish excess) not stand for “maximum”?

caption:
Here’s a selection that always gives me a warm, cozy feeling: Antonia Barber and Nicola Bayley's The Mousehole Cat. In this original story inspired by a Cornish legend, an old fisherman named Tom and his faithful cat Mowzer live quietly together in a little village near a harbor called “The Mousehole” or “Mowzel”. When the Great Storm-Cat threatens to drown any who sail through the gap in the harbor wall, the villagers begin to run out of food. Tom must brave the Storm-Cat’s wrath and bring back enough fish to feed their community. Unlike on his other trips, Mowzer goes out on the water with him, and it is only by the sweetness of her voice that the mysterious beast is finally tamed. Barber weaves her tale with elegant, lyrical language, giving special prominence to her mouthwatering descriptions of Tom and Mowzer’s weekly menu: Mondays, morgy-broth; Tuesdays, baked hake with mashed potatoes; Wednesdays, kedgeree with smoked ling; Thursdays, grilled fairmaids; Fridays, fried launces with butter and lemon; Saturdays, soused scad with vinegar and onions; Sundays, star-gazy pie with pilchards in pastry. Bayley’s illustrations achieve a gripping intensity, particularly in her thrillingly dramatic presentation of the Storm-Cat, a darkly beautiful ocean ghost—perhaps a visual metaphor for Mowzer’s feline perception of the storm...or perhaps a very real elemental spirit of nature.

I am deeply moved by this gentle meditation on grief and healing: The Goblin and the Empty Chair by Mem Fox and Leo and Diane Dillon. A marvelous adaptation of a Greek myth tinged with grandeur and pathos is Jane Yolen and Dennis Nolan’s Wings, which recounts the life of the famed architect, sculptor, and inventor Daedalus, from his roots as an Athenian prince to his construction of a labyrinth to house the Minotaur on Crete to his imprisonment in a high tower and disastrous escape attempt by air with his son Icarus. caption:
Where are we? What has happened? Is anybody there? These are the questions that leap to mind at the start of The Story of Frog Belly Rat Bone by Timothy Basil Ering. A nameless boy exists alone in a blighted, junk-strewn expanse called Cementland, dearly wishing to find a treasure. One day he comes across a box filled with strange little specks, and in accordance with the accompanying written instructions buries them in the ground. However, he soon finds the pellets have been dug up and stolen away. To guard his efforts, he scavenges refuse and old clothing and erects a colossus, a trash golem, a bulbous green scarecrow whom he dubs Frog Belly Rat Bone. Why put the little beads into the earth? Just who are the sneak-thieves who dug them up? What lies ahead for Frog Belly Rat Bone and the boy? These are the questions that will be answered by the story’s end. Ering, with potent imagery, irresistible rhyme, and deliciously loose and kinetic line art, has created a dazzling world—lonely and grim, to be sure, but never so frightening as to snuff out the last ray of hope for positive change.

They label a single seed with the sign of a blue top hat, and then go to sleep in a bed out under a night of stars. Throughout the encounter, the bear’s presence remains gentle and comforting, despite the joyful wildness of each exotic display. With bright, solid colors and bold, thickly drawn ink lines, Nyeu’s silkscreened art beckons readers into a topsy-turvy domain that sits in the hazily liminal space between the dreaming and the waking.

Come sail away on the ocean, sail without a care, sail far and wide and free. This is The Maggie B. by Irene Haas. Young Margaret Barnstable looks out her window one night before bed and makes a wish upon a star. She asks for a boat of her very own, named after her and ready to sail for a day’s voyage. When she wakes up, she is already on the ship, and it is indeed named after her: The Maggie B. A little paradise of a vessel it is, for up on the deck is a farm with livestock and a fruit orchard. Best of all, Margaret’s baby brother James is there for company. After chores, cast-net fishing, a picnic lunch, a battering storm, a bath for James, seafood stew for dinner, and fiddle music and lullabies, the magical day is over. Margaret’s nautical adventure grants her access to a subtle blending of child and adult roles: she spends an entire day exploring her rich inner fantasy life while successfully acting in a guardianship role over her younger sibling. Curiously, the story ends with the children still adrift, though the language of the conclusion suggests that they will soon return to their familiar life. Haas crafts an atmosphere of high coziness through verse inspired by nursery rhymes and sea chanteys and her accompanying soft-textured paintings.

caption:
Every one of us surely has occasion now and then to consider the nature of existence on other worlds. In her gorgeous and ethereal Star Child, Claire A. Nivola turns this paradigm on its head and asks us to look at life on Earth through extraterrestrial eyes. A sentient wisp of vapor on a remote star in outer space asks his elders what it would be like to visit Earth. Their response details the path of a human life, vast in scope yet intimate in detail. The book’s suggestion that all humans are born as avatars of these heavenly visitors, and that we return to our sidereal state after our time here is at an end, can be read as a spiritual statement on the afterlife and the cycle of reincarnation, a literary metaphor for the scientific observation that we are all made of atoms forged in ancient stars, or perhaps both at once. Through the magic realism of her scenario and the richness of her color palette, Nivola explores the latitude and longitude of our journey through life as we transition from childhood to maturity to old age and reach outward to form true connections along the way.

caption:
For a Celtic tale fraught with monsters and dangerous magic, might I suggest Robert D. San Souci and Sally Wern Comport’s Brave Margaret? Our story begins in County Donegal, in the west of Ireland. Margaret, thoroughly bored of her simple life raising cattle, longs for escape and adventure. When Simon, the traveling son of a foreign king, sails ashore and asks to buy the herd, she agrees—but names passage aboard his ship as her only price. This bold choice whisks Margaret into a sprawling adventure of swordplay and enchantment, and she finds herself at the center of a mystic prophecy. San Souci renders his tale in elegant prose, matched by the rich color of Comport’s lushly expressive pastel art.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: San Souci, in adapting his narrative from the tale “Simon and Margaret”, found in West Irish Folk-Tales and Romances, makes several key changes. Rather than open with Simon’s voyage, he centers the beginning of the story on Margaret’s origins and experience. He heightens the degree of external threat to increase the dramatic stakes: an escape from a sea serpent becomes a slaying, an innocent old woman becomes a sinister hag, protecting the prince from a ferocious giant becomes avenging the prince’s death (and subsequently restoring him to life). Finally, he smooths over several wrinkles in the romantic storyline, omitting all mention of Simon’s first wife (an early victim of the giant) as well as the young man’s quickly aborted attempt to claim credit for the brute’s demise. Fascinatingly, where San Souci presents Margaret’s identity as the prophesied champion as a feminist revelation, the original folktale treats it as quite matter-of-fact, the presence of a female warrior no more shocking than that of a male.

caption:
This is a story of loneliness, courage, and the universal drive for companionship: Shy by @freedmanillustrates. The protagonist of this book is named Shy. But just who or what is Shy? It’s difficult to say: true to his name, Shy does not like to come out in the open. He hides in the gutter—that is, the seam that runs down the center of a book’s two page spread—where he cannot be seen by the reader. Shy loves to pass the time reading about birds. When a real bird with bright yellow feathers comes along (and all too quickly flies away), he is finally spurred to leave the comfort of his hiding place. As he travels far and wide across vast, colorful landscapes in search of the beautiful creature, Shy finally begins to experience the simple wonders that were around him all along—and takes what could be the first tentative steps towards mastering his overwhelming shyness. Freedman’s writing gives off an empathic warmth, inviting readers to consider the very real emotional conflict between the weight of isolation and the shock of exposure. On repeated readings, sharp-eyed viewers scanning the soft gradients of her pencil-and-watercolor environments may notice Shy subtly included among a diverse cohort of animals well before the ending’s unambiguous reveal of his identity.

caption:
What if your life suddenly got upended by the intrusion of a supernatural presence? Moreover, what if, instead of remaining with you only for a brief period of time, the otherworldly entity simply stayed and stayed and stayed until it became your new normal? You’ll ponder just such a predicament in My Life with the Wave, translated and adapted by Catherine Cowan (from a short story originally written in Spanish by Octavio Paz) and illustrated by Mark Buehner. A young boy playing at the seashore befriends a sentient wave, who follows him home and takes up residence with his family. While at first this bizarre scenario appears to bring nothing but delight, the capricious swell of water soon brings on dangerous weather and dredges up horrors from the deep. Buehner’s oil and acrylic paintings vividly capture the reflective surfaces and fluid dynamics of the swirling, frothing wave. Cowan preserves much of Paz’s lyrical language, but takes great liberties with the content of the story, changing the main character from an adult to a child, modifying his relationship with the aquatic being from one of sensual longing to one of innocent play, and excising a farcical episode in which an attempt to transport the salty water in a railway drinking fountain spirals into accusations of poisoning, an arrest, and a brief prison sentence.

caption:
It’s shocking to consider how much children’s role in our society has changed in the last few centuries, and especially in the last few decades. Both for better and for worse, the onset of independence has become a much more gradual process as our culture’s view of youth has shifted. Books are a window through which modern children may catch a glimpse of just how different their lives would have been in earlier times. To that end, here is Pelle’s New Suit, a classic work by Elsa Beskow. A young boy named Pelle performs a series of errands and working trades in order to obtain a new suit of clothes: First, he shears his beloved lamb. Then he weeds his grandmother’s carrot patch while she cards the wool. He tends his other grandmother’s cows as she spins the wool into yarn. He rows a boat to the local store and buys turpentine for a painter who lets him purchase dye with the change, and he dyes the yarn himself. He cares for his baby sister while his mother weaves the yarn into cloth. And he takes hay, feeds pigs, and carries wood for a tailor who sews him pants, a jacket, and a waistcoat. Finally, his new suit is ready. All of the adults Pelle encounters treat him as an equal, respecting him as a group member fully capable of performing labor in exchange for their own. With straightforward language and soft, colorful illustrations, Beskow depicts the effort, thought, and care that goes into the tradition of textile craft and demonstrates the power of mutualistic support to create the bonds of a tight-knit community.

caption:
If exploring the gentle subtleties of a child’s realistically drawn emotions against the backdrop of a cryptic metaphysical dimension sounds like your cup of tea, then have a look at La La La by Kate DiCamillo and @jaimekimmy. A little girl paces back and forth, alone in a stark white space. “La,” she sings to herself, and “La La La”.. All at once, maple leaves begin to drift in through a mysterious portal, which leads her to an outside world as lush and verdant as the blank void was barren. Sadly, there are no people out there, no human beings for companionship. However, the call of a mysterious voice soon leads her to make a connection of a most unexpected and otherworldly nature. Is this a wordless picture book? Well, no and yes. Strictly speaking, it’s not wordless, because it does in fact feature words. And yet it functions like a wordless picture book, because the words are restricted to dialogue, and that dialogue is abstract and impressionistic, consisting only of “La” and various elongations and repetitions thereof. The narrative is conveyed not through text but through illustration. It’s something in between, then: perhaps semi-wordless. Collaborations between an author and an illustrator on a book with so little text are quite unusual. Kim’s scintillating visual interpretation of DiCamillo’s pensive story draws on her own childhood memories of the pangs of solitude and the joy of togetherness.

caption:
Enjoy this delicate fable of opulence and modesty, of avarice and temperance: Michael Catchpool and @alisonjay17’s The Cloud Spinner. A young boy lives alone in a little house atop a hill. To pass the time, he spins thread from passing clouds overhead and weaves it into exquisite cloth, a gift his mother taught him long ago. When a pompous king learns of this extraordinary talent, he conscripts the boy into his service, demanding garment after garment to appease his own vanity. When the supply of clouds dwindles and the sky is left barren, only an act of kindness and generosity can save the land and the people from environmental ruin. Catchpool chooses his words with subtlety and care. The story’s refrain, “Enough is enough and not one stitch more,” serves as a powerful call for moderation without ever becoming distractingly moralistic. The repeated mentions of the boy’s mother in the past tense (coupled with her stark absence in the present storyline) leave readers to draw their own conclusions. Jay’s signature technique (warm shades of alkyd paint on thick cartridge paper, with a crackle varnish applied to the finished composition) produces a fascinating contrast with her modern character design, establishing a visual style simultaneously classic and contemporary.

There’s a deceptive depth of philosophically thought-provoking material bundled into Pezzetino by Leo Lionni. The book presents us with an abstract geometric universe in which motley organisms composed of brightly colored square tiles roam around a barren landscape of marbled rock. Each is named for its characteristic behavior or environment: the one-who-runs, the strong-one, the swimming-one, the one-on-the-mountain, the flying-one, the wise-one. Far different is Pezzetino (Italian for “little piece”), a single orange square who concludes from his diminutive size that he must be a mislaid fragment of one of his larger compatriots. Seeing Pezzetino’s distress, the wise-one sends him on a quest to the Island of Wham, where he discovers the unexpected truth of his inner nature. Lionni’s clear, expressive writing style and his favored medium of variegated collage blend to form a satisfying meditation on existential questions of identity and belonging.

If you live your life completely alone, you may convince yourself that you don’t need companionship. But what if you realize that you’re lying to yourself? After all, humans are social creatures. In Mr. Brown's Fantastic Hat, Ayano Imai explores this very situation, though her protagonist is some sort of anthropomorphic mammal. A bear? A fox? A capybara? Difficult to say. The text simply refers to him as Mr. Brown, a perennial loner of whom others appear to be frightened. One day, to his dismay, a woodpecker makes its home in his hat. As more birds arrive, the hat magically grows taller to accommodate them, and Mr. Brown soon becomes fond of the birds and their beautiful song. However, when the weather grows colder, they fly south in search of a warmer climate. Now lonelier than ever, Mr. Brown settles in to hibernate for the winter. He awakens to find that his bird friends have returned and a marvelous transformation has taken hold of his hat, mirroring the transformation within his heart. Imai’s empathic writing voice and muted color palette sensitively render a personal journey from loneliness to community.

caption:
Here’s a clever and engaging adaptation of an indigenous Australian folktale: Rainbow Bird by Eric Maddern and Adrienne Kennaway. The story opens at the beginning of the world, in the Time of Dreams, where among the animals dwells the ferocious Crocodile Man, the only creature endowed with the gift of fire. He breathes it out as might a dragon, playing with the flames and jealously guarding them from all who dare come near. Bird Woman remonstrates with Crocodile Man, urging him to share fire with the other animals, but he will not hear of it. When the reptile lets his guard down for a yawn, the bird snatches a burning branch, flies away, and imbues the whole forest with combustibility. Bird Woman absorbs the flaming color into her tail, and Crocodile Man sinks down into the swamp in dismay. Maddern’s expressive language and Kennaway’s vivid illustrations honor the spirit of a folktale that provides an etiology for the phenomenon of fire, the colorful plumage of birds, and the habitat of crocodiles.

I am gazing through the window at a world lying quiet and still under a thick blanket of snow. The soft, white expanse suggests a blank canvas, a realm of endless possibility. This theme, the paradigm of freshly fallen snow as fertile ground for imaginative inspiration lies at the core of Deirdre Gill’s Outside. A boy rushes to put on his winter clothes so that he can play in the snow. He flops backward down the front steps, lands in a snow bank, and makes a snow angel; then he begins to build in earnest. After repeatedly trying and failing to get the attention of his older brother, who prefers to remain indoors in front of a computer screen, he creates a towering snow giant. The colossal being soon comes to life and accompanies the boy as he erects a snow palace and rides on the back of a snow dragon. By the day’s end, the stream of creativity proves so appealing that the older brother reconsiders his decision to stay in. Fortunately, there’s still a little bit of time before bed, and the two siblings begin to sculpt, pack, and build. Through minimal text and soft, expressive illustrations, Gill crafts a winning paean to the power of play.

caption:
There is a startling blend of misfortune, poverty, greed, violence, malady, and death in Master Snickup’s Cloak by Alexander Theroux and Brian Froud. A good-hearted pauper in the medieval Dutch town of Sleutel falls into gloom and despair when his new bride is lured away by a wealthy boor with the gift of gold and the promise of social standing. Wrapped only in his blue cloak (a wedding gift from his estranged sweetheart), he wanders away and maroons himself on a saltswept sea stack, where he remains in constant prayer. The young man’s immense piety attracts a host of vicious devils who hex his body with disease and infest his cloak with vermin. After he dies, a rat flea from his cloak takes wing and returns to the mainland, where its virulence soon spreads to become the Black Death itself. Theroux’s writing reveals itself in layers: a veneer of wry comedy, then a band of grim horror, and finally a fundament of unflinching truth, all laced with arcane wordplay and biting irony. With a muted color palette, Froud cheerfully depicts cruelty both supernatural and all too human. You may well perceive the story’s treatment of its subject matter as rather bleak, particularly for the picture book medium. I quite agree. But for mature and prepared readers there is a searing social and historical honesty at the heart of this work, waiting to be confronted, digested, and remembered.

There’s a powerful distillation of innocence and imagination throughout The Story of James by David McPhail. James pulls his younger brother in a wagon down to a nearby stream. Soon, to his confusion, he realizes that the wagon is empty, except for a note—waterlogged and illegible. Where could his brother have gone? An unexpected twist provides the relief of a happy ending, but subtly calls the entire preceding sequence of events into question. Through delicately humorous writing and softly shaded art, McPhail expertly guides his readers through the shifting grounds of childhood fantasy and emotion.

caption:
What a tour de force is The Book of Mistakes by @corinnaluyken. An unseen artist sketches a girl (beginning with the face and then adding a body and clothing) and then draws other characters and details of the surrounding environment. Each successive page of the book provides a snapshot of the work in progress. Several times, the fictional artist makes a mistake—that is, puts an unintentional mark to the paper or inaccurately renders an anatomical feature. However, each seeming error inspires an inventive solution or modification: stray smudges transform into leaves, an obtrusive splotch becomes a hat. Has Luyken extracted the elegant form of her story from its intriguing content? Or perhaps the other way around? It’s difficult to adduce directionality in such an original and well-balanced pairing. Through her restricted color palette (isolated patches of soft green, warm yellow, and pale pink on an ink-black line art landscape), she visually foregrounds the cyclical process of creation and revision. Her pensive and philosophically rich text cleverly directs the reader’s focus to the emerging art rather than to the identity of the artist. In the book’s final pages, however, the perspective begins to pull back—gradually at first, and then by orders of magnitude. Finally, the world of the drawing is revealed as part of a larger whole, and an astonishingly profound metafictional dimension emerges. Here is a lyrical study of the vital link between creator and creation and of the compelling search for joy in the unexpected.

caption:
For a tale of light fantasy with a sobering undercurrent of folly and woe, check out The Stars in the Sky, an English fairy tale collected by folklorist Joseph Jacobs and illustrated by Airdrie Amtmann. A young girl nurtures a deep longing to play with the stars themselves. Consumed by this wild dream, she leaves home and embarks on a fanciful search; along her path she encounters a mill-dam, a brooklet, the mystical Good Folk, and the elliptically named “Four Feet” (who turns out to be a horse) and “No Feet at all” (a large fish). Sadly, the path leading up to the stars proves impossible to climb, and she finds herself falling until she awakens on the floor of her home, back where she started. This abrupt ending establishes the entire adventure as a rudely truncated dream, and therefore something of a shaggy dog story. However, the girl’s transition from discontent to determination to despair are rendered with touching simplicity and poignance. Rather than adapt Jacobs’ text (originally published in More English Fairy Tales), Amtmann imports it directly, changing only a single word and altering the spelling of two others. The pen-and-ink illustrations convey a subdued blend of peculiar magic and cold reality.

You may have read the beloved picture book classic The Rainbow Goblins, but were you aware that there was a sequel? Well, here it is: The White Goblin by Ul de Rico. This story deals with the eighth member of the Rainbow Goblins clan, banished long ago to the frozen north by his polychromatic brethren. He descends into the earth and marshals a race of subterranean Cave Goblins, who spread to the surface, lustily consume the colors all around them, and soon begin to industrialize. Sadly, their civilization devolves all too quickly into chaos and ruin. The pollution of their cities and factories chokes the atmosphere with smog, and the violence of their military clashes rends the very crust of the earth, triggering horrendous global cataclysm. Only an enlightened group of survivors and their shared memory of nature’s glory can restore peace and balance to the world. Through eloquent world-building and dazzling oil paintings, de Rico has created a worthy successor to his original work.

Clarke once said, “Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.” In his update of Goethe’s poem The Sorcerer’s Apprentice, Ted Dewan explores this blurred boundary by swapping out the enchantment of fantasy for the machinery of science fiction. The Sorcerer here is an inventor, the Apprentice a robot he builds to tidy his cluttered workshop. Fascinatingly, the process through which the robots are granted sentience appears to rely on phonographic records, a conceit Dewan underscores by integrating musical staff notation into the robots’ schematics.
The language of this retelling incorporates lively energy and madcap humor while maintaining the drama and stakes of the original plot.

caption:
There’s an impenetrable enigma at the heart of Zilpha Keatley Snyder and Charles Mikolaycak’s The Changing Maze. A young shepherd boy named Hugh listens to his grandmother’s oft-told tale of the wizard-king of the Ragged Lands, of his bewitched greenthorn maze, of its sinister, ever-shifting pathways, of the many travelers who entered in search of royal gold and found themselves subtly transformed from within. When his beloved black lamb wanders off, Hugh follows it and discovers that it has stumbled into the maze from his grandmother’s story. But can he rescue his lamb and emerge unscathed? And just what sort of treasure lies within the treacherous hedge? Mikolaycak’s moody pencil and watercolor illustrations capture expression, body language, and a wealth of intriguing environmental detail. Snyder shows masterful command of language throughout the book. The very title contains a double meaning: “changing” can be parsed as intransitive (“the maze is changing”) or transitive (“the maze is changing those who walk within”). Moreover, spotting the hidden pairs of rhyming words on every page reveals a prose-poem structure as ornate and protean as the labyrinth itself.

Humor can bubble up from the simple act of viewing a familiar situation from an unusual perspective. In David LaRochelle and Richard Egielski’s The End, the comical story unfolds in reverse, starting with the happy ending. What led to the knight and the princess falling in love? Well, she poured a bowl of lemonade onto his head. But why did she pour the lemonade on his head? His curly red beard was on fire, of course. And why was his beard on fire? Because, naturally, he’d been tickling a great green dragon. And so goes the backwards tale, winding its way past rabbits, giants, and an enormous rolling tomato, from effect to cause to effect to cause until we reach the event at the root of it all, which ties the entire chain into a surprisingly neat circle. LaRochelle’s lighthearted high-concept slapstick and Egielski’s brightly colored cartoon-style art meld into a deliciously topsy-turvy fantasy farce. The illustrations’ subtle inclusion of a character not mentioned in the text suggests a trace of divine intervention at play.

Lamm uses flowing lines of lyrical prose poetry to achieve a hopeful and humanistic tone in her far-reaching portrait of the human race. caption:
Just try not to enjoy yourself while reading Ingrid and Dieter Schubert’s The Magic Bubble Trip. James loves frogs and dearly wishes his parents would let him keep them as pets. One day, he blows a soap bubble that inexplicably grows larger and larger, envelopes him, and carries him out the window. James floats off to a bizarre meadow filled with mounds of grass-covered frogs and enjoys an afternoon of merriment before seeking the help of the eccentric Mr. Odds-and-Ends to return home. The married author-illustrators’ collaboration results in a charmingly offbeat adventure with entertaining and cheerfully loopy illustrations. Fascinatingly, the original Dutch title, “Helemaal verkikkerd” (“totally in love”) derives from the word “kikker” (“frog”). A literal translation might therefore read: “Completely befrogged”.

caption:
What do we wait for in life? How does waiting make us feel? Sometimes waiting can be the most frustrating thing in the world. However, if we perceive something as being worth the wait, perhaps we do not mind quite so much. But what if we don’t even know what we’re waiting for? If you seek a peaceful and beautifully philosophical meditation on these ideas, then allow me to present Waiting by Kevin Henkes, a book that explores the lives of inanimate objects in the absence of human attention. Five toys sit on a windowsill, all waiting, but each for something different—the owl waiting for the moon, the pig waiting for the rain, the bear waiting for the wind, the puppy waiting for the snow, and the rabbit simply waiting. Some familiar toys leave and return, some novel ones fall to the ground and break, and finally an unexpected newcomer makes a surprising and permanent addition to the little waiting family. Henkes allows his illustrations, done in brown ink, watercolors, and colored pencils, to convey the literal, objective plot; in his text, he explores the emotional landscape of the characters’ lives. Here is a particularly strong example of the shift in modern picture books toward a minimalist aesthetic, in which (rather than pictures illustrating words and words describing pictures) writing and art complement each other to form a cohesive story. Case in point: nowhere in his text does Henkes tell us that the five animals are toys perched on a ledge. Instead, he simply shows us, and lets our imaginations do the rest.

caption:
I can hardly believe I’ve reached my two-hundredth book review! Many thanks for your likes, follows, and kind comments. You make it all worthwhile!

Today’s book is a special one: Precious and the Boo Hag, written by Patricia C. McKissack and Onawumi Jean Moss and illustrated by Kyrsten Brooker. Precious, afflicted with a stomachache, stays home while her family heads out to harvest crops. Before leaving, her brother warns her of Pruella the Boo Hag, a shapeshifting ogress who haunts the prairies. Sure enough, once Precious is alone, the wicked creature appears and attempts—through a combination of intimidation, guile, and deceit—to gain entry into her house. The clever girl must keep her wits about her and defend her home against incursion. This book possesses an inexplicable allure. Simply put, children love it. They adore the potent mix of humor and danger as a series of visitors proves one by one to be the Boo Hag in disguise. McKissack and Moss know when to play up the fear—leaving to the imagination Pruella’s sinister motives for coming inside, heightening the paranoia of familiar faces acting as untrustworthy masks—and when to snap the tension as Precious accosts and banishes the hag with a raucously chanted refrain. Brooker’s mixed-media art, with collages of natural textures and expressionistic character design, strikes a perfect middle ground between funny and scary.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the figure of the boo hag originates in the Gullah culture of the southeastern United States. This book has considerably toned down her bizarre and disturbing traditional appearance, as the folkloric boo hag climbs astride her victims at night, sucks out their breath, and strips them of their skin to cover the raw, red flesh of her body.

caption:
Rarely is a nonfiction picture book on physics presented as gorgeously as You Are Stardust by Elin Kelsey and @soyeonis. Inspired by the poetic but scientifically sound observation that atoms from old stars can be found everywhere, even within our bodies, Kelsey weaves an extended complex of metaphors and similes to liken aspects of human anatomy and physiology to elements of nature. A fetus occupies an amniotic sac as fish swim in the salty ocean, we learn to speak as as birds learn to sing, we breathe as the wind blows pollen, electricity crackles through our brains like lightning, our hair sheds like autumn leaves. Kim illustrates these powerful concepts with stunning dioramas that comprise drawing, painting, collage, stitching, dyeing, and assemblage of natural materials.

caption:
The book of the day is @vic_turnbull’s Pandora, a tale of loneliness, connection, and healing. The plot opens in a barren, junk-choked wasteland (subtly hinted by both the text and the art to be a post-apocalyptic zone). Pandora, an anthropomorphic fox, lives in a little house held up above the refuse by tall wooden stilts. She spends her days scavenging in the vast mountains of refuse, collecting tokens and trinkets to mend as best she can. One day, a bird plummets out of the sky. She takes the poor creature in and lets it build a nest in an old cardboard box. This simple act of care sets off a series of events that will soon upend Pandora’s daily experience and utterly transform the face of the world around her. Turnbull pairs an elegantly spare writing style, marked by short, well-chosen phrases, with softly shaded, finely detailed illustrations in colored pencil and watercolor. The combination gives rise to an exquisitely restrained study in character and emotion.

caption:
Here is a fairy tale replete with grandeur and delight: Claire Martin and Gennady Spirin’s Boots and the Glass Mountain. Heedless of his older brothers’ taunts, a young man tames three magical horses, dons three fine suits of armor, and rides three times up a perilously smooth slope of glass to win a princess’s hand in marriage. Martin renders the plot in engaging, straightforward prose, while Spirin’s characteristically resplendent paintings lend the proceedings an air of old-world grandeur.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this book was adapted from “The Maiden on the Glass Mountain”, a tale in Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe’s Norske Folkeeventyr. The plot remains quite faithful to the original story, with the notable addition of a pack of trolls to serve as antagonists. In the Norwegian text, the hero is named “Askeladd” or “Askeladden” (literally “Ash Lad”), a male counterpart to Cinderella who appears throughout Norse folklore. The widespread English-language rendering of “Askeladd” as “Boots” (used here by Martin) was coined by nineteenth-century writer George Webbe Dasent, the original translator of Norske Folkeeventyr, who chose the name to evoke the English tradition of the youngest family member performing menial household chores.

caption:
I’ve decided to try something new. Whereas in 2020 I featured only one version of each tale type (only one Snow White, only one Jack and the Beanstalk), I will spend this entire week reviewing seven different book versions of the same fairy tale. And this week’s tale shall be none other than that most widespread and beloved of stories: Cinderella.

First up is Marcia Brown’s classic adaptation. The text, described as “a free translation from the French of Charles Perrault”, retains much of the wording and flavor of its source material, including the stepsisters’ fine outfits (one wears lace-trimmed red velvet, the other a gold cloak and a diamond headpiece) and the fairy godmother’s transformation of a pumpkin into a carriage, mice into horses, a rat into a coachman, lizards into footmen, and Cinderella’s rags into a gown of rare beauty. Also preserved is the little-known detail that only the younger stepsister uses the name “Cendrillon” (“Cinderella”), while the rest of the family call her “Culcendron” (literally “Cinder-Ass”, which Brown euphemistically renders as “Cinderseat”). Through loose, energetic line art and pale washes of color, the illustrations convey a light and jovial fairy tale atmosphere.

caption:
Second in my weeklong project of featuring a new version of Cinderella each day, we have a lovely edition adapted and illustrated by @ruthsandersonart. This iteration foregrounds Cinderella’s loneliness and despair at the start of the plot, giving way to a pleasingly magic-tinged conclusion. Both the elegant text and the stately oil paintings contribute to an air of refinement and grandeur throughout the book.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Sanderson bases her retelling on Charles Perrault’s 1697 narrative from Histoires ou Contes du Temps Passé. To this foundation she adds a lovely tree and a helpful bird, elements from the Brothers Grimm’s 1812 variant of the tale from Kinder- und Hausmärchen (with some notably macabre scenes of mutilation judiciously excised). Fascinatingly, she introduces the Grimm-derived section of the plot with the motif of Cinderella’s father asking each daughter what gift they would like him to bring back from his travels, a motif borrowed from Beauty and the Beast.

caption:
For the next entry in my Cinderella series, it’s this version by Laura Francesca Filippucci. The setting features dainty half-timbered houses and handsome castle towers, while the characters are depicted with well-rendered facial expressions and body language.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Filippucci bases her retelling wholly on Aschenputtel, the variant collected by the Brothers Grimm in Kinder- und Hausmärchen—even including the grisly detail of the stepmother convincing the stepsisters to cut off parts of their feet in order to fit into the glass slipper. Unsurprisingly, though, the final gory indignity, the stepsisters’ eyes being pecked out by birds (added by the Grimms in the second edition of their work in 1819), remains absent.

Here at the halfway point in my weeklong exploration of Cinderella picture books we have a collaboration between author Amy Ehrlich and illustrator Susan Jeffers. Here’s the final post in my week of Cinderella books! This has been a delightful experiment, and I would love to repeat it in the near future with another tale type.

This last version comes from illustrator Kinuko Y. Craft, whose lyrical writing voice delves deeply and sensitively into her heroine’s emotional life. An array of truly sumptuous paintings rendered in oil over watercolor produce an atmosphere of gilded, shimmering fantasy.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the front matter lists as sources the renditions of “Cinderella” in The Arthur Rackham Fairy Book and Andrew Lang’s The Blue Fairy Book. Both texts are in fact relatively close translations of Perrault’s French original. Craft departs from tradition with a chance encounter between Cinderella and the prince in the forest at the start of the story. She also weaves threads of tantalizing mystery into her distinctive portrayal of the fairy godmother, who initially appears in the form of a bird, and whose drop-waist gown and beaded headpiece, in contrast to the surrounding early modern French fashion, give off a subtly futuristic sensibility.

Friendship comes in all shapes and sizes, often informing the pleasures of a cherished ritual. But what happens when a pattern is disrupted, when connections are severed and must be reforged along new pathways? These questions inform the gentle aura of A Sick Day for Amos McGee, written by Philip C. Stead and illustrated by Erin E. Stead (whose shared account can be found @number5bus). A kindly zookeeper savors his daily routine visiting and caring for the animals in their habitats. One morning, he wakes up feeling ill, and the animals show their concern by taking the bus to visit him at home and reciprocate his warmth and kindness. The married collaborators establish an inviting aesthetic; Philip Stead’s elegantly simple prose conveys the amiable relationship between Amos and his friends, while Erin Stead’s inviting art, a combination of pencil drawing and woodblock printing, evokes subtle shades of emotion in the animals’ faces while maintaining a thoughtful realism in their anatomy.

caption:
Imagine having to leave everything behind and strike out into the unknown, traveling without company, without guidance, without clear hope of survival. Come explore the muted mystery of @_beckyoung_ and @mattottleyart’s Teacup. A boy climbs into a boat and rows across the sea. At the mercy of the elements, he carefully guards a single precious possession: a teacup full of earth. This lone reminder of the land of his origin both anchors him to the severed roots of his past and propels him toward a glimmer of hope on the horizon of his future. Young’s delicate minimalist text achieves a remarkable feat of worldbuilding, never directly addressing the cause of the boy’s displacement, but obliquely alluding to his family, their whereabouts now uncertain. Ottley’s oil paintings place the reader squarely in the center of the action through grippingly cinematic composition, arresting use of impasto, and unforgettable imagery of magic realism.

caption:
What if you opened what appeared to be a nondescript informational manual and discovered a philosophical treatise suffused with artistic beauty? This unorthodox premise may well have inspired How to Paint the Portrait of a Bird. The text of the book, originally a 1945 poem by Jacques Prévert “Pour Faire le Portrait d’un Oiseau”, is here translated from the French and illustrated by Mordicai Gerstein. A series of instructions details the imaginative process of painting a bird, the act of capturing the bird’s image represented by magically capturing the bird itself on canvas. Gerstein renders the poem’s lush imagery with great sensitivity, creating a young painter protagonist to ground the emotional journey. The translation is largely faithful, with two notable departures. Prévert’s uncompromising passage, “Si l’oiseau ne chante pas/C’est mauvais signe/Signe que le tableau est mauvais” (“If the bird doesn’t sing, it’s a bad sign, a sign that the painting is bad”) is softened by Gerstein to “If it doesn’t sing, don’t be sad. You did your best.” And an extra line at the story’s close (“Tomorrow you can paint another one”) opens up tantalizing possibilities for new inspiration to come.

caption:
The book of the day is @claudeclementauteure and @fredericlement’s The Painter and the Wild Swans. In this original tale, a renowned Japanese artist named Teiji encounters a flock of migrating swans. Captivated by their movement and song, he develops an all-consuming desire to track them down and again experience their ethereal beauty and grace. When his quest is derailed by the harsh realities of nature, the painter achieves an epiphany that alters not only his perception but the very fabric of his being as well. The author and illustrator (unrelated, though they coincidentally share a surname) display a strong unity of vision and purpose. For her haunting text (translated from French by Robert Levine), Claude Clément drew inspiration from Swans, an art book by Japanese photographer Teiji Saga, after whom she named her protagonist, and to whom the story is dedicated. On delicately desaturated landscapes evoking traditional Japanese art, Frédéric Clément depicts lightly surreal transitions: a bird’s tail feathers become a sweeping brushstroke, a flock of swans becomes a hazy cloud bank, a mountain lake becomes a comforting cup of tea. Interspersed with the images are elegant lines of Japanese calligraphy, revealed at the end to be a poem told from a mysterious transhuman perspective.

caption:
There’s something at once spooky and reassuring about Hedgehog in the Fog, written by Sergey Kozlov and Yuri Norstein and illustrated by Francesca Yarbusova. Hedgehog makes his way through fields, groves, and thick fog to his friend Bear’s house to share raspberry jam and juniper tea. Along the way he encounters a number of mysterious animals, including a pale horse, a helpful dog, and a menacing owl. He ponders his surroundings and contemplates his own identity. Finally, he reaches his destination unscathed, but his mind continues to linger on the eerie sights from his journey. The genesis of this book is a fascinating one: in 1975, Norstein, an acclaimed animator, directed an animated film called Hedgehog in the Fog from a screenplay by Kozlov, a distinguished children’s author and poet. This adaptation of the film bears a text (translated into English by Luba Golburt) whose slow and methodical plot emphasizes tone and atmosphere. Yarbusova, Norstein’s wife and collaborator, based her soothing, richly textured illustrations on sketches she created for the film.

Spirituality can be the thorn in an author’s side. How to write with a reverence for the divine while maintaining a human scope and sensibility? The text (originally a poem written by Gaiman for singer/songwriter Tori Amos’s unborn child) takes the form of an incantation, an arcane hymn invoking a cadre of goddesses and female spirits, adjuring them to grant a bevy of natural gifts and talents to an unborn girl—and, by extension, to girls everywhere. Gaiman’s effortless rolling verse crackles with language and imagery that celebrates both the specificity and universality of womanhood. Vess’s illustrations intertwine celestial figures with humans, animals, and elements of nature, amplifying the sacred beauty within them all.

Have you ever tried to capture that elusive moment on the brink of sleep when your eyelids grow heavy and your mind drifts off into the fog? Even if that threshold crossing remains forever beyond our grasp, the next best thing may be the whimsical warmth of Helme Heine’s The Marvelous Journey Through the Night. Peace reigns until morning, and then the journey is done...until the next night.
