Both the triumph of individuality and the value of community are celebrated in Richard Lee Vaughan and Lee Christiansen’s Eagle Boy. In this Native American tale from the Pacific Northwest, an orphan irks his elders by continuing to offer a share of salmon from his daily catch to the eagles that wheel in the air above him. Vaughan’s straightforward retelling and Christiansen’s cinematically framed illustrations complement each other well and allow the emotional themes of the narrative to shine.

caption:
For a fantasy quest with a gentle message at its heart, try Dyan Sheldon and Gary Blythe’s The Moon Dragons. A king receives a visitor who tells him a strange tale. According to the wandering guest, the moon dragons, long thought to be extinct, still survive on a cloud-bounded mountaintop. The greedy king, wishing to capture one of the elusive beasts for himself, offers a lavish reward in exchange for their exact whereabouts. Though many embark on the quest for their hidden sanctuary, none can reach it. Then, much to the amusement of the court, a humble peasant girl responds to the royal decree. She is then faced with a choice: prove her doubters wrong by revealing the dragons’ hideaway or swallow her pride and preserve the secret of the exquisite creatures’ existence. I’m chuckling at the conceit behind Sea Creatures from the Sky by @rmcortes, a parody of alien abduction accounts from the perspective of an anthropomorphic denizen of the deep. In charmingly earnest rhyming couplets, a shark describes being captured by unrecognizable beings, taken aboard a mysterious vessel, probed and measured with bizarre instruments, and suddenly released. Our recognition of the visitors and our comprehension of their prosaic motives may help us conceptualize the prospect of benign, space-faring scientists, advanced far beyond our ken, idly conducting innocuous experiments on us. Cortés underscores this comparison by juxtaposing views of the deep ocean, the far reaches of outer space, and the horizon where the separate worlds of sky and water meet, all with a bright color palette, varied textures, and a series of dynamic perspectives.

caption:
If you’re searching for a fairy tale replete with danger, deception, and dark magic, I’ve got just the thing: The Enchanted Book by Janina Porazińska and Jan Brett, a Polish story that prizes intelligence, education, and hard work above all things. A miller’s three daughters each have the chance to learn from an extraordinarily educated old woman who visits their mill. The eldest and middle girls fritter away their opportunity, but the youngest learns to read with facility. This handy skill enables her to decipher a book of arcane spells and save her sisters from the grip of a wily enchanter. Porazińska’s text, translated by Bożena Smith, sings with expressive phrasing and sharp dialogue. Brett executes her vivid watercolor art in a graceful classic style that evokes the grand tradition of the golden age of fairy tale illustration. She shows restraint in framing each image with folk-art-inspired patterns, rather than following her usual practice of inserting small vignettes into the borders, which might distract from the potency of the main story.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This tale was originally published in Za Górami...Za Lasami... a 1954 Polish folklore collection whose title translates to “Beyond the Mountains...Beyond the Woods...”, a common opening phrase in traditional Polish oral storytelling. The plot is a clear example of the “Maiden Rescues Her Sisters” type, best known by the Brothers Grimm variant “Fitcher’s Bird”.

caption:
Enter a quirky and fanciful world in the pages of The Book No One Ever Read by @cornelia.funke.official Here, books are sentient creatures harboring strong opinions about the humans who rifle through them. Morry, having spent his short life on a lonely, untouched shelf surrounded by older, stuffier volumes, understands without a doubt that to be read and known is to be loved. The neighboring books, fearful of tears, creases, and smudges, counsel conformity. Despite their withering disapproval, Morry strikes out on his own, in search of his ultimate purpose: a reader. Funke’s snappy dialogue and engaging illustrations deliver an irresistible story that celebrates reading both as an emotional necessity and as a sensory delight. Easter eggs abound: Funke names and draws a number of books that share either the given name or the surname of a famous author, including Victor, Jane, and Beatrix. Stronger and stronger clues throughout the story will allow sharp-eyed readers to discern the author namesake of the protagonist, Morry himself.

caption:
There’s insight, humor, and irrepressible joy in @peterbrownstudio’s Mr. Tiger Goes Wild. Our story opens in a world of animals who walk about on their hind legs wearing human clothing, their animal instincts long since cast off. Prim, demure, and buttoned-down, they mind their manners and abhor uncouth behavior. Mr. Tiger cannot stand this stifling mode of existence, and he begins reverting to his animalistic ways: he walks on all fours, roars for all to hear, and eventually removes his clothing. His neighbors, scandalized, send him off into the jungle, where he has plenty of room to move and breathe free. But after a while, missing life with his friends in the city, he sets out to rejoin his community and find a happy medium. Brown’s inspired color palette reinforces the narrative’s central themes by portraying Mr. Tiger as a lone burst of bright orange among the other anthropomorphic mammals, who nearly fade into the background of grays and sepias. Only when Mr. Tiger reaches the lush jungle do we see notes of vibrant green, cyan, and pink: the visual world of the book itself has gone wild. In the text, Brown allows his short, punchy sentences to land with maximum impact, and they nimbly convey the emotional beats of the plot. His animal characters may have something to teach us humans; after all, behind our manners, beneath our veneer of propriety, we all have a little spark of wildness just waiting to burst free.

caption:
I recently conducted a delightful experiment: an entire week featuring a different picture book version of Cinderella each day. Since it was such an enjoyable experience, I’ve decided to do it again—this time with a different fairy tale. I’m very excited to announce the start of Jack and the Beanstalk Week!

First up is this classic version by Kay Brown and Gerry Embleton. Brown’s writing crafts an engaging atmosphere befitting the action and suspense of the narrative. Embleton’s illustrations insert a number of appealing details, including an anthropomorphic hedgehog and a tiny insect farmer that lives in a mushroom. The giant house in the clouds bears a forbidding skull and crossbones on one of the towers and several ominous faces carved into the walls, rafters, and furniture.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Brown’s retelling preserves much of the linguistic flavor of Joseph Jacobs’ rendition of the story in English Fairy Tales, including the mysterious old man’s question, “How many beans make five?” (Jack’s snappy answer: “Two in each hand and one in your mouth.”) and the famous “Fee fi fo fum” rhyme. Small changes include the cow’s name (“Milky-White” has become “Buttercup”) and the species of the antagonist (the text initially refers to him as an ogre, as in Jacobs’ original, but thereafter calls him a giant, the term familiar to most modern readers).

Here is the second entry in my Jack and the Beanstalk series, a lighthearted version by John Cech and Robert Mackenzie. Cech takes certain liberties with the plot, most notably allowing the giant to live (his rage at being trapped in the clouds providing an etiological explanation for thunder) while his amiable wife escapes to live a peaceful life as the best friend of Jack’s mother. caption:
Jack and the Beanstalk is the theme of the week, and you should absolutely check out this fine work by Ann Keay Beneduce and Gennady Spirin. Beneduce employs an eloquent writing style and engaging character details to evoke an aura of romance and classic adventure. Spirin’s masterful paintings, executed in watercolor and tempera, brim with glowing detail. Text-only pages are elevated by the presence of ornate borders in alternating designs—one shows images of the marvelous objects in the story, another holds coiled vines bearing bean plants, while the third contains a sumptuous banquet fit for a giant.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Beneduce adapts her story not from the Joseph Jacobs variant but from the iteration in the 1881 collection The Children’s Book. Here, Jack is given a motivation—indeed, an excuse—for his repeated theft. A fairy conveniently reveals that long ago the giant (posing as a friend) killed Jack’s father and purloined his marvelous treasures. Jack is therefore not stealing so much as reclaiming his birthright. Though plot devices like this are nothing new, it’s worth pointing out that they weaken the potency of the tale, inserted as they are by writers and editors afraid to celebrate Jack’s seemingly unjustified crimes. Moreover, this revisionist approach misses a deep truth about the structure of folktales and the function of their characters: the human Jack exists as purely good, the giant as purely evil. In the fight against a monstrous foe, a fairy tale hero needs no further justification.

caption:
At the midpoint of Jack and the Beanstalk Week, I’ve landed on a strikingly literary adaptation by E. Nesbit, illustrated by @tavaresbooks. Nesbit’s tale, written in 1908, delights with whimsical asides detailing Jack’s fickle train of thought, his relationship with his mother, and his exploits atop the beanstalk. Tavares, working nearly a century later, has taken a compelling approach to the visual side of the story, framing the action and emotional beats with cinematic flair. His pencil-and-watercolor illustrations sharply delineate between the two spatial planes of the story: the mundane world’s golden wheat fields are bathed in warm, saturated tones, while the barren, blighted road of the giant’s country—studded with bleached bones and withered trees—is permeated by deathly pale grays and browns.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Nesbit includes the (arguably unnecessary) motif of the fairy who reveals that the giant’s treasures are actually Jack’s stolen birthright.

caption:
Continuing with my week of Jack and the Beanstalk posts, I’m excited to include this entertaining version with rigorous analytical underpinnings, written and illustrated by Albert Lorenz with collaborating artist Joy Schleh. In an Author’s Note, Lorenz details the process of his design for the book, in which he determined the height of the giant and then proportionally scaled up the castle and its contents. He follows this concept through to its logical conclusion, fully immersing the young hero in an environment designed for beings whose thimble he can use as a drinking cup. Both Lorenz’s text and art inject an impressive degree of engineering detail into Jack’s abscondence with the ill-gotten goods. The boy continually raids the giant woman’s sewing kit, from which kitchen string serves as rope, knitting needles as sturdy rods, buttons as both wheels for carts and and pulleys in a block and tackle. Lorenz also outlines his unconventional working relationship with Schleh, who consults with him on each project, contributing preliminary sketches and refining details throughout. The partnership here results in a remarkable degree of mathematical precision, best exemplified in the architectural spreads that present the gargantuan castle alternately in worm’s-eye, section, and plan perspective.

caption:
Another Jack and the Beanstalk entry of interest is this oddball adaptation by Anthea Bell and Aljoscha Blau. Bell provides a straightforward and respectful adaptation of Joseph Jacobs’ telling, sprinkling a few well-chosen bits of original phrasing throughout the traditional dialogue and story beats. It is in Blau’s illustrations, however, that a unique and engrossing vision arises. Strangeness abounds on every page. Jack rides to the market on a penny-farthing, towing his cow in an oversized basket, only to meet the mysterious bean-giving stranger driving a steampunk jalopy with a miniature boiler for an engine and a tufted armchair seat. Up at the top of the beanstalk, the ogre resembles a lethargic man in pants and an undershirt, while his wife sports the inordinately disturbing combination of an uncanny doll mask over her face and a boning knife hanging from her apron pocket. The couple keeps a peculiar pair of small pets with animal bodies and human faces, and their entire homestead appears to be located on a parallel plane with its gravity opposed to our own.

caption:
Let’s take a walk through a world that might appear perfectly ordinary...until you peer just a little bit closer. This is On Bird Hill by Jane Yolen and Bob Marstall, released by the Cornell Lab Publishing Group to benefit educational and community programs sponsored by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. Yolen constructs a simple yet elegant rhyme (based on the Appalachian cumulative folk song “The Green Grass Grew All Around”) that leads from the narrator to a tree, to a trunk, to a limb, to a twig, to a nest, to a bird, to an egg, to a chick, and finally back to the narrator. Perhaps taking this circularity as his cue, Marstall produces a countryside containing a handful of ever-so-slightly peculiar details. The narrator sets out from a little hilltop house, a pool of water still reflecting the stars of the early morning sky. The trees feature rope-like helical trunks, curling tendrils, and little red berries, an unexplained cutout in the earth revealing a tangled network of roots far below. Once the chick emerges, a miniature replica of the narrator’s house can be seen within the cracked egg, complete with a starry sky on the inside of the shell. Finally, all roads seem to lead through the grassy fields to a pool of water that (despite the bright daylight) reflects the stars of early morning—or is it perhaps a hole looking down into a pit of midnight below?

caption:
Does your group of friends have an odd member out? Someone just a little bit stranger than the others? Maybe it’s you! Or, perhaps, does each group member feel like the weird one? After all, everybody has something that makes them unique. In Three Ladies Beside the Sea by Rhoda Levine and Edward Gorey, one woman’s foibles provoke the curiosity of her closest friends. Edith of Ecstasy, Catherine of Compromise, and Alice of Hazard live together by the sea. Edith and Catherine cannot help but wonder at Alice’s strange habit of spending hour after hour up in a tree. When they finally ask for an explanation, she reveals that she is keeping watch for a bird whose song enchanted her as it flew by long ago. Nothing will dissuade Alice, not even the loan of Edith and Catherine’s own birds, which simply remind her of the bird she once encountered. Eventually, the ending suggests, Alice’s friends accept her as she is. Levine tells her story in rhyming quatrains, the rollicking beat of common meter enhancing the whimsicality of the plot. Gorey employs his signature spare black and white line art with judicious use of hatching, and adds a leitmotivic color scheme, yellow representing Edith and green representing Catherine (Alice stands out once again in perpetual black and white).

caption:
Sometimes the treasure at the end of the road isn’t quite as important as the wisdom one might glean along the way. This is certainly the case in Ivan Gantschev’s Moon Lake, a call for humility and temperance in the face of desire. Deep in the mountains lies a bright, sparkling lake, its shores littered with gleaming silver stones. These mystical gems (scattered, according to local lore, by the moon itself) are highly sought after, but no one knows the route to this secret spot except an old shepherd who lives in a cottage nearby. After his death, his grandson Peter stumbles upon the lake, and learns from a talking fox that anyone who fails to leave by sunrise will be blinded by the dazzling light. When Peter innocently takes a few stones to the market to sell, a greedy king demands to be taken to the lake. However, he ignores Peter’s earnest warnings...to his grave misfortune. Gantschev’s illustrations recall folk art in their gentle simplicity. Added for the English-language edition (translated from German by Marianne Martens) are shiny patches of foil stamping on the moon and the ethereal lakeside stones.

caption:
Relationships are truly life’s most precious resources. They nourish us, comfort us, and endow our existence with meaning and purpose. What happens to the connection between two people when one of them is no longer living? Some say that remnants of a loved one’s presence can be powerfully felt even in their absence, and it is the texture of this enduring affection that @mossmontmomery and @david_c_litchfield explore superbly in The Building Boy. Grandma, a retired architect of great renown, tells her grandson time and again of the special house she will build for the two of them, far away on a hill by the sea. After her death, the boy, now alone, channels his sorrow into a project. He sets to work building a statue of his beloved Grandma, a motley effigy all beams and rivets and glass and shingles. To his amazement, the handcrafted colossus comes to life and carries him far away, across the sea, to where the promised house sits atop a little hill. However, the structure is unfinished—there is a hole in the middle, just waiting to be filled. The manner of the house’s completion serves as a metaphor for the nature of relationships and the ways loss can transform our lives forever. Montgomery engineers his tale in simple but affecting language, ably capturing both the physical journey over land and sea and the emotional journey through grief towards acceptance. Litchfield renders his environments with gleaming color and delicate contrast between light and dark; he constructs remarkable depth of character in the interactions between the boy and the grandmother (both in her human body and in her refabricated frame).

caption:
The book of the day is Kate Westerlund and Robert Ingpen’s If You Wish, a dainty and dreamlike adventure. Mired in boredom, a young girl named Willow encounters a friendly being named Tally, who guides her through the process of transporting herself to another world. A carousel suddenly appears, and Linnet the horse springs to life, ready to carry Willow over a marvelous landscape of villages, fairies, castles, and dragons. Westerlund has fun with her premise, scattering clues here and there that this entire escapade may in fact be taking place within Willow’s capacious imagination. Ingpen’s richly detailed art simultaneously conveys far-off wonder and a gentle, reassuring warmth.

Curiously, a character named Tally also appears in a picture book called The Dream Keeper, published three years before his one. Similar to the figure in this story, he is short and mystical, and he sports an enormous white beard. The Dream Keeper was both written and illustrated by Robert Ingpen. Whether this connection is intentional or simply an enormous coincidence I cannot say.

caption:
Where does our food come from? This simple question has many answers, and the pursuit of those answers can often enrich our minds as the food itself nourishes our bodies. @nikkimcclure’s To Market, to Market explores this topic in engrossing detail. On a visit to the local farmer’s market, a child observes the inviting sights, sounds, and smells all around. Alternating pages dive deeply into the process of each farmer and make. It’s not simply the goods for sale that receive focus in McClure’s detailed text, but also the humans doing the work that makes it all possible: their lives, attitudes, and experiences. We learn about Michael’s apple orchard, Steve’s salmon smoker, Benjamin’s beehives, Yukie’s fabric dyeing tubs, and many other centers of productivity. McClure’s illustrations, meticulously cut from black paper and digitally colored, highlight each item with a strong hue that stands out starkly from the black and white environment.

A personal anecdote: several years ago, I was lucky enough to have Nikki McClure come visit my preschool classroom (graciously arranged by the wonderful @heatherrossinsta). My students were enthralled as she demonstrated her process, nimbly cutting a sheet of paper into a finished image with practiced strokes of her craft knife right before our eyes.

caption:
We’ve all imagined ourselves on marvelous adventures in search of hidden treasure. But what if the object of your quest were invisible, intangible? What tools are needed to navigate a voyage of the heart? This question fuels the spiritual journey of Colin Thompson’s Looking for Atlantis. A young boy’s grandfather returns from a lifetime of ocean exploits. Now old and infirm, he leaves his chest of riches to his grandson, and tells the boy to find Atlantis—which, he cryptically hints, can be found anywhere and everywhere, as long as you know how to look. But Atlantis proves elusive indeed, and perhaps wholly out of reach. With careful and sensitive wording, Thompson aligns the literal with the metaphorical, delicately blurring the line between physical search and emotional introspection. His exquisitely detailed illustrations present a nearly overwhelming array of nooks and crannies, each of which holds a new and tantalizing secret. Ultimately, Thompson uses the idea of a treasure hunt as a metaphor for processing grief and loss, the mythical city itself a symbol for enduring love and lasting legacy.

What if vestiges of the past could somehow cling to a specific location, truly forgotten but waiting to be rediscovered? The Old Banjo by Dennis Haseley and Stephen Gammell imagines just such a paranormal phenomenon and imbues it with quiet meaning and gentle power. A boy and his father, working on their farm, hear a banjo, a trombone, a piano, a violin, a trumpet, and a clarinet mysteriously playing by themselves, echoing the sounds they once made in the hands of a family band. They bring as many of the dusty old instruments as possible outside, where the music rings out in the night like the inscrutable words of an ancient tongue, a song of days gone by. Haseley’s writing takes the form of a sensory tone poem, replete with evocative imagery and well-chosen line breaks. Gammell’s illustrations in black, white, and gray hold an eerie beauty, the misty landscapes and shadowy interiors lending the proceedings an aura of ghostly calm.

caption:
Today I have for you The Enchanted Nightingale, Bernadette Watts’s adaptation of the Brothers Grimm tale “Jorinda and Joringel”. Two young sweethearts wander too close to the castle of a malevolent witch and fall under the sway of her power: the man is paralyzed and left to watch as the woman is turned into a nightingale and imprisoned. Aided by a clairvoyant dream, the youth locates a magic flower with which he undoes the old hag’s terrible enchantment. Watts presents the tale with graceful turns of phrase and fully realized emotional depth. She composes her illustrations with beautiful contrasting colors to achieve rich textures of light and shadow.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Watts has created a faithful adaptation of the Grimm’s plot. She preserves much of their vocabulary and phrasing, and only alters a few details (changing the flower from red to purple, muting a few references to death, explicitly noting that the witch’s other victims are freed at the end). Her original German-language edition of the book even retained the Grimms’ original title; the new title was selected for the English translation.

caption:
There’s always a certain mysterious quality to the night—plans can be quietly carried out and concealed in the darkness, later to be revealed in the light of day. Though many associate this atmosphere with danger, there’s no reason that one can’t use the opportunity to create something beautiful in secret. And, if making one beautiful thing, why not another? What about a whole slew of them? Just such a lovely sequence of events occurs in The Night Gardener, co-written and co-illustrated by @terryfanillustration and @ericfanillustration, also known as @thefanbrothers. William and his neighbors on Grimloch Lane notice that someone has begun to cut the foliage into topiary animals under cover of night. Each morning, a new work appears, to the locals’ growing delight. Finally, William spots the creator of the wonderful art and joins him in transforming the local park into a verdant menagerie. The rich detail of their digitally colored graphite illustrations complementing the spare, contemplative voice of their writing, the Fan Brothers display a mastery of the picture book form. The style and content of the images communicate subtle bits of information not present in the text. The gardener receives inspiration for his sculptural pieces first from William’s drawing of an owl and then from a pack of feral cats. William himself is shown to live in the Grimloch Orphanage, a lone photograph of a man and a woman sitting on his windowsill. Moreover, while at first the topiary animals appear as isolated patches of color in an otherwise desaturated grayscale environment, the neighborhood and its residents boast a widening range of hues as the art brightens the spirits of the entire community.

caption:
Loneliness can weigh heavily on the human heart. We are, after all, social creatures, in need of companions, of connection. For a powerful exploration of solitude’s quiet chill and friendship’s soothing balm, look no further than The Uncorker of Ocean Bottles, written by @pgreenboat and illustrated by @erinestead. The title character spends his days fishing glass bottles out of the sea and delivering the letters inside. Carrying each message to its addressee gives the Uncorker a sense of purpose and fulfillment. More than anything else, he longs to open a letter just for him, but he is convinced this will never happen—for who would write him one? When he discovers a lost party invitation, he goes from door to door hoping to find the intended recipient. Little does he realize the inadvertent connections he is building along the way, and the impact those connections will have on his own life. Cuevas employs lush prose poetry, constructing shades of character and emotion through simile (“loneliness as sharp as fish scales”) and metaphor (“a quill dipped in sadness”). Stead’s art, a combination of woodblock prints, oil pastels, and pencil, apply soft washes of color to the quiet emotions of the seaside community.

caption:
In the pages of Celia by Christelle Vallat and @stephanie_augusseau (originally published in Belgium as “Zélie”), we encounter a character who truly changes the world around her for the better. The members of a small community amass worries and fears over the course of each week. Then, every Sunday, they go to Celia’s house. Celia provides a vital service: each visitor may approach her and quietly whisper their troubles. As they spill out their hearts, they grow more relaxed, more content. The people pay her in seeds, which Celia spends the rest of the week miraculously transforming into balloons, apples, flowers, and stars, to the delight of all nearby. When a young boy loses his seed and cannot pay for a turn to express his sorrows, Celia patiently works with him until he feels safe and comfortable again. Vallat’s metaphorical tale contains deep insight into the nature of anxiety and the value of a sympathetic, nonjudgmental ear. Augusseau establishes a minimalistic landscape in black, white, and gray, reserving bright colors for the wonderful seeds and, subtly, for the flush of happiness in a contented cheek.

caption:
This week will be my third exploration of multiple picture book retellings of the same fairy tale, and I’ve selected Little Red Riding Hood!

We begin with a version by Beni Monstresor, who takes a playfully scary approach to the material: while the anthropomorphic wolf at first appears quite dapper in his smart double-breasted suit and bowler hat, he later reveals his bestial nature by swallowing Little Red Riding Hood head-first.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Montresor follows Charles Perrault’s variant of the tale from the 1697 collection Histoires ou Contes du Temps Passé, avec des Moralités (Stories or Tales of Times Past, with Morals), also known as Contes de ma Mère l’Oye (“Tales of Mother Goose”). He includes Perrault’s ending, in which the young girl is simply swallowed up by the wolf, and that is that. However, his final illustration contains a silhouette of the huntsman (a character included in the German variant recorded by the Brothers Grimm over a century after Perrault), suggesting that all may yet turn out right. The composition of Montresor’s cover image is clearly borrowed from Gustave Doré’s engraving of Little Red Riding Hood climbing into bed with the wolf, one of several illustrations the artist made for an 1867 edition of Perrault’s tales.

It’s Little Red Riding Hood Week, and today I have for you a classic version by Trina Schart Hyman. The details here are drawn faithfully from the Brothers Grimm variant of the tale, with the slight addition of a specific given name (“Elisabeth”) that precedes the heroine’s well-known nickname, and with the notable omission of the more gruesome details of the wolf’s demise. caption:
With Little Red Riding Hood Week in full swing, I’m excited to share this outlandish version by Francesca Cosanti. The text bears a noticeably relaxed and colloquial tone, and the climactic slaying of the wolf is elided with the euphemistic phrase, “he hit the wolf steadily,” the results left to our imagination. A few pages are starkly framed by the wolf’s negative-space silhouette, and each tree in the forest, in a masterstroke of visual synecdoche, is represented by a single gargantuan leaf.

caption:
Here’s yet another Little Red Riding Hood picture book, this one by Christopher Coady, who mines the tale for its aura of slowly creeping menace. The text establishes a chilling atmosphere and builds tension through a strong economy of language (“As she walked into the darkening wood, Red Riding Hood felt two eyes on her.”). It is raining when the young girl sets out for her journey, perhaps an omen of looming danger. The painterly illustrations, executed in vivid, mismatched brushstrokes, bear a moody color palette replete with warm lights and heavy shadows.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: here is the rare version of Little Red Riding Hood that faithfully adheres to the Charles Perrault rendition of the tale by having the wolf eat the girl and simply ending the story then and there. Unwilling to cushion the blow, Coady leaves us with the striking image of the red cloak strewn forlornly on the bed. As an epilogue, he includes a loose translation of Perrault’s moral, an admonition against trusting the cunning and deceptive “wolves” in everyday life.

caption:
Our expectations of reality can shape our appearance, mold our perception. Given enough time, whispered rumor becomes common legend, ingrained in cultural memory. For a shining example of this phenomenon wrapped in an irresistibly entertaining package, see Denise Doyen and @wheelerstudio’s The Pomegranate Witch. An enterprising gang of children longs to taste the pomegranates growing on a tree in the yard of the old house on the outskirts of town. However, in order to obtain the sweet-tart fruit, they must do battle with the tree’s owner, the fabled Pomegranate Witch. The conflict stretches on for weeks, months, years—long enough to pass into neighborhood lore. However, each Halloween a Kindly Lady opens the gate of the old house’s front yard and welcomes the children to share a drink of delicious cider, the frightening witch nowhere to be seen. In ornate rhyming couplets of iambic alexandrine, Doyen combines evocative imagery, poetic word-painting, and rhythmic repetition, hinting all the while at a connection between the Witch and the Lady that the children may not yet understand. Wheeler’s art, executed in India ink with dip pens and watercolors, portrays a touching community tradition of imaginative play that lasts for multiple generations.

caption:
Life’s greatest and most enduring mysteries can often be succinctly expressed in the form of questions, powerful queries whose answers may elude us forever. The subtle yet deeply affecting narrative of Questions Asked by Jostein Gaarder and Akin Düzakin unfolds as a series of musings on themes universal to the human condition. A young boy wanders out into nature, quietly reflecting on his own existence. The text (translated from Gaarder’s original Norwegian by Don Bartlett) comes only in the form of his inner monologue, with no further narration. “Where does the world come from?” he asks himself. “Can anyone know what I think?” “What do I fear losing most?” “What is time?” “Can I be sure all my memories really happened?” “Why am I alive?” “Why do I dream?” “What happens when I die?” “What shall I do with my life?” Potent philosophical material indeed. Though any one of these ideas might serve as the basis of a lengthy treatise or dialectic, the chaotic jumble of their passage truly captures the raw wonder of a child’s imagination. Each of Düzakin’s images depicts a thematic moment appropriate to the accompanying question. In black and white flashbacks, the boy shares his experiences with a twin. In the illustrations of the present, this brother is nowhere to be seen, but a pale, enigmatic specter trails the boy like a lost loved one at the edge of his memory. These components hint at an unfathomably tragic backstory, though the ultimate truth, like the answers to the ethereal questions, is left for the reader to determine.

caption:
Is ignorance truly bliss? As this clever and compelling book suggests, sometimes uncertainty can be so excruciating that even delusion might be preferable. In Jean-François Chabas and @davidsala.illustration’s The Enchanted Chest, a haughty emperor comes into possession of a mysterious metal box that cannot be opened, no matter who tries. The captain of the guards, the emperor himself, the locksmith, the strongman, the magician, the alchemist...all apply their most trusted tools and techniques, and all utterly fail. Finally, the emperor captures a wild lynx, said to be capable of seeing through all things, and asks the wild beast to describe the contents of the chest. The lynx’s discovery and her report to the emperor provide the reader with startlingly deep insight into human behavior and motivation. Chabas, his work here translated from French, creates an original parable with elegant phrasing and subtle beats of humor. Sala flattens his images to create exaggerated two-dimensional scenes replete with glittering metallic colors arrayed in delicate patterns and textures.

Here is another Puss in Boots book for your viewing pleasure, this one adapted by Carolyn Magner and Judith Cheng. Magner conveys the story succinctly with a few tweaks here and there; notably, she replaces the fearsome ogre with a sorcerer, human in appearance but still possessed of magical shapeshifting ability. The warm palette and soft textures of Cheng’s cheery illustrations lend a lighthearted tone to the proceedings.

caption:
Puss in Boots Week is half done, but I’ve got plenty of treats in store! Today’s book comes to us from John Cech and Bernhard Oberdieck. The two complement each other’s styles well, with Oberdieck’s merry, bright-hued illustrations in watercolor, pen, and ink (particularly the cheekily winking cat) enhancing the jocund tone of Cech’s writing voice. The typical denouement, in which the cat eats the ogre-turned-mouse, is softened to the villain’s irreversible confinement in rodent form.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the back matter compiles a far-ranging history of the Puss in Boots tale type, as well as the image of cats in world traditions. This section includes mention of the literary fairy tale “Costantino Fortunato”, believed to be the first published iteration of Puss in Boots (hailing from Giovanni Francesco Straparola’s 1550 collection Le Piacevoli Notti), and more than likely Cech’s own inspiration for replacing the hero’s usual French pseudonym (“The Marquis of Carabas”) with the moniker “Lord Fortunato”.

caption:
This next Puss in Boots, written by Joy Cowley and illustrated by Sam-hyeon Kim, takes a light and playful approach to the material. Cowley cultivates an economy of language, keeping her sentences compact and effective. The title “Marquis of Carabas” is here given as “Lord Carabas”, while the traditional ogre is now a giant. The references to violence in the original text are toned down or omitted, with the Puss’s threat to grind peasants into sausage meat changed to a warning that he will bite or scratch them; the young man’s thought to eat his cat and make a muff of the hide is nowhere to be found. Kim’s quirky sensibility infuses each page with an charming energy, from the young man’s listless body language to the giant’s oversized head and hookah.

Fascinatingly, this particular book appears to have been originally published in Korean, with Cowley’s English-language text for the American edition replacing (as opposed to translating) the work of original author Gyeong-hwa Kim.

caption:
Here’s a tale that explores the subtle inner conflict between the lofty ideal of honor and the immediate pull of moral duty. In Ann Tompert and Doug Keith’s The Errant Knight, a proud warrior receives a summons from his king. Insisting that he will not be an errant knight who strays from his path, he sets out promptly for the royal castle. However, on the way, he is delayed by a series of people in need, and—against his better judgment—he stops to help each one. In this way, many years pass, and the knight grows old and feeble. When he finally reaches the castle, the king puts forth a more flexible interpretation of his noble calling, and the grizzled paladin realizes that he may not have been a knight errant after all. Tompert conveys her worthy moral with grand and flowing language, accompanied by richly colored, expressive oil paintings from Keith.

When you were growing up, did you have a special relative that you always thought might secretly know magic? One whose gifts you treasured forever, believing they contained mysterious secrets? The narrator of Eve Bunting and Dennis Nolan’s Thunder Horse receives a tiny horse from her enigmatic Aunt Aldora, who tells her the creature will grow and change. Bunting’s first-person narrative mines true emotional depth from a scenario of magic realism. Nolan’s illustrations, drawn in colored pencil over watercolor washes on watercolor paper, employ lush, hazy color, delicate texture, and marvelously detailed equine anatomy.

caption:
This is a character study of quiet loneliness. This is a supernatural story of inexplicable connection across vast distance. This is Boat of Dreams, a wordless book by @rogerio_coelho_illustration. An old man dwells in a house by the ocean with his seagull companion. When a bottle washes up on shore with a blank piece of paper inside, the man sketches a wondrous ship, places his design in the bottle, and sends it back out to sea. Elsewhere, a boy and his cat live alone in a quiet city. The boy discovers an envelope left on his doorstep, opens it, and finds the old man’s drawing. Intrigued, he adds to the illustration, placing himself and his cat aboard the ship, and tapes the page to the headboard of his bed. The enigmatic encounter that follows may be magic, or a dream, or perhaps simply a metaphorical experience, but it holds powerful significance for the two characters who otherwise never meet. Coelho’s angular art establishes the pelagic setting of the old man’s house through sepia-toned full-bleed illustrations before shifting suddenly to tighter images in cool blues and grays, bound by wide margins. This stark difference in visual language suggests a gulf between the two worlds—but the nature of the divide is left to the reader’s imagination.

caption:
What if you couldn’t see the sun? Looking up at a sky perpetually obscured by clouds and rain, where would you imagine light comes from? That’s just the problem that occurs to Kate, the thoughtful heroine of Uwe-Michael Gutzschhahn and Thomas Docherty’s The Lighthouse Under a Clouds. The lighthouse-keeper on an island below a sky that never clears, she theorizes that there must be a giant lighthouse above the clouds whose light filters down to earth during the day. Her friend Tom sketches the plan for a giant tower built of old boats, and together they begin construction. Though their neighbors regard their work with skepticism, the endeavor permanently transforms the community and its understanding of the natural world. Gutzschhahn creates a compelling work of lightly speculative fiction, while Docherty’s loose and energetic illustrations balance the weather phenomena with the emotional experiences of the characters.

caption:
The comfort of normalcy can scarcely be overstated. We live our lives within a framework of prescribed patterns, and any deviation can be cause for alarm—let alone a seeming violation of the laws of physics. Dr. Seuss explores the ramifications of just such a paranormal phenomenon disrupting a commoner’s typical display of fealty to a monarch in The 500 Hats of Bartholomew Cubbins. The story opens in the kingdom of Didd, ruled over by the proud King Derwin. Bartholomew Cubbins, a young peasant boy very much the social (and geographical) opposite of the king, finds himself unable to demonstrate the proper respect for the passing of the royal carriage—each time he removes his hat, an identical one appears in its place. Before the day is done, Bartholomew and King Derwin are swept up into series of farcical attempts to dispel the weird occurrence, escalating to the point of threatening the boy’s life. Seuss applies his usual inimitable style to the whimsical original tale (written in prose, instead of his typical rhyming verse). He makes the bold choice of executing the illustrations in thickly shaded black and white—all except for the brilliant scarlet of the hats themselves.

caption:
The comfort of normalcy can scarcely be overstated, but there’s a fine line between normalcy and monotony. The tedium of repetition can make people long for surprise, excitement, variety—although a drastic change might have unforeseen and devastating consequences. Dr. Seuss follows this idea to its logical conclusion in Bartholomew and the Oobleck. A direct sequel to The 500 Hats of Bartholomew Cubbins, the story opens with young Bartholomew in service as a page boy to King Derwin, who has developed an all-consuming vexation with the cyclical nature of his kingdom’s weather: spring rain, summer sun, autumn fog, winter snow. The exasperated king calls on his magicians to create a new form of precipitation. In response, the mystical guild concocts a viscous green substance called oobleck. At first, the goo descends from the clouds in tiny specks, but it quickly begins hailing down in droplets, then large pellets, and finally enormous blobs. Wherever it lands, the oobleck mires objects, animals, and people in a terrifying, inescapable sludge. With the entire kingdom facing ruin, Bartholomew must devise a plan to end the cataclysmic storm. In keeping with the previous volume, Seuss writes in eloquent, engaging prose and restricts his color palette to black and white—save for the sinister green of the oobleck itself.

Were you ever blamed as a child for something you didn’t do? Perhaps you’d garnered a reputation for misbehavior and, the one time you weren’t to blame, no one would believe you. Through minimal text, Castillo plumbs true emotional depth, giving her main character real human flaws and a subtle but critical breakthrough of empathic understanding. Her illustrations, alternating between brightly colored images and stark silhouettes, let the reader in on the identity of the mysterious kleptomaniac long before the characters cotton on. A final thought: the title of the book contains a pleasing ambiguity, applicable as it is to both the spirited young boy and the sneak-thief.

caption:
Fear of the dark gives way to thoughtful understanding in The Dark, written by @authordanielhandler (under his well-known pen name Lemony Snicket) and illustrated by @jonklassen. Laszlo has an uneasy peace with the dark, which seems to occupy his house as a sentient force. He greets it from the top of the basement steps every morning, hoping against hope that it will stay below. One night, however, the dark creeps up into Laszlo’s room and speaks to him, beckoning him down the stairs and into the basement. What does it want? A helpful discovery soon brings on the realization that Laszlo’s fears may have been misplaced, that the dark might not be such a sinister presence after all. Snicket applies his trademark authorial sensibility, dry and understated wit peeking out from behind a mask of grim austerity. Klassen’s illustrations, a combination of gouache paintings and digital technique, convey an aura of mystery. No parents, siblings, or other characters of any kind appear—if Laszlo has any human company in the house, we do not see it. The dark is never fully anthropomorphized, never rendered as a discrete entity. Rather, the intentional placement of text on large patches of black imply that the dark is everywhere at once and nowhere at all.

caption:
There’s a delicate joy that winds through The Pattaconk Brook, James Stevenson’s loving ode to nature and friendship. While transcribing the sounds of the rushing stream, Sidney the frog meets Sherry the snail. Curious to hear the sounds the water might make farther downstream, the two ride a branch downstream to where the water flows into the sea, the frog carrying the snail under one arm. They experience new sights, new sounds, new smells, as they explore the unfamiliar environment of the seashore. Sidney’s curiosity is satisfied, and he wishes to return upstream; Sherry elects to remain near the ocean where gastropods gather. The two bid a solemn goodbye and part ways. Stevenson constructs blank verse in amphibrachic tetrameter, omitting the final syllable of every other line for a decisive downbeat, and revels in playful onomatopoeia for the brook sounds (“thub cada bup”, “we dee oh picka”, “ooba du globum”). His trademark loose line drawings in black pen, filled in with watercolor paints, lend a gentle energy to the emotional arc of the story.

caption:
The fairy tale theme week is back, and this time I’ll be delving into seven different versions of Rapunzel.

We begin with a version translated from the German of the Brothers Grimm by Anthea Bell and illustrated by @majadusikova. Soft washes of color create a lush and pleasant landscape; Rapunzel’s tower rises high from among the trees, resembling a half-timbered cottage with shingled roof.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Bell, working from the seventh edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen, includes the detail of Rapunzel’s plan to weave a ladder out of silk so that she might escape from the tower. She translates “zauberin” as “witch” (instead of the more accurate “sorceress”). Following the Grimms’ bowdlerization of their own earlier material, Bell gives Rapunzel the thoughtless line, “Tell me, Godmother, how is it that you seem so much heavier than the young prince when you climb up?” In the first edition of the fairy tale, the maiden betrays herself with an innocent observation about the tightness of her clothes, unaware of the biological significance of her burgeoning belly.

caption:
We’re halfway through Rapunzel week, which brings us to a graceful retelling with pictures drawn on stone by Felix Hoffmann. The witch here is a squat, wizened figure who carries the baby Rapunzel away under one arm. The prince, in his scarlet tunic, stands out from the muted environment of blues, greens, and browns. In a touching visual detail, Rapunzel emerges from the forest at the close of the tale (in an illustration replicated on the book’s cover) with the remains of her hair crowned in a wreath of autumn foliage.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Hoffmann makes a number of distinctive changes that lend the story extra flavor. After hearing about the wife’s pregnancy cravings, the witch, in an unusual show of leniency, offers the husband one last chance to leave her garden scot-free; however, the wife insists he return to steal the tempting salad greens once more, thus triggering the punishing condition that they give up their baby. Later, rather than simply confront the prince and shock him into jumping from the tower, the witch actively cuts Rapunzel’s shorn-off braid, causing him to fall. This spiteful tactic, however, proves her undoing: without the hair, she cannot climb down. Trapped in the tower room, she shrinks to the size of a shrivelled apple and is carried away by a huge bird. This epilogue, an original invention of Hoffmann’s, stands out as a rare example of the witch being punished at the end of a Rapunzel story.

caption:
Another Rapunzel unveiled: this time, an elegant adaptation by Barbara Rogasky and Trina Schart Hyman. The glowing watercolor scenes, surrounded by narrow, decorative borders, brim with energy, replete as they are with a rich and inviting clutter. The gaunt, piercing-eyed Mother Gothel receives a corvine motif, suggested by her cadre of crow familiars and bird skull necklace. The tower is a tumbledown spire in the depths of a sprawling birch wood. Hyman makes the fascinating choice of including a door at the base, initially operational but later boarded up, answering the perennial question of how Mother Gothel transports Rapunzel to the top of the tower to begin with.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Rogasky remains faithful to the text of the Brothers Grimm, with a few subtle alterations. Rather than make a blanket demand, Mother Gothel expresses a gender preference, stipulating that the child must be given to her “if it is a daughter”. In the original tale, Rapunzel believes the prince loves her more than her possessive stepmother does, whereas here she notes first that he is “better looking” (as well as kinder) than the witch. Finally, instead of deliberately throwing himself off the tower, the prince backs away from Mother Gothel in fright and inadvertently falls out the window.

caption:
Rapunzel refracts through an altogether different lens in the eclectic vision of Dorothée Duntze. While the wondrous garden and the mother’s craving for leafy greens already accords the Grimms’ tale a strong horticultural theme, the design of the characters and environment here foregrounds flora’s influence on the plot. The mother’s skirt and petticoats resemble a the petals of a pink flower; Rapunzel’s dress, bulbous and green, gives off the appearance of a brussels sprout; the witch’s voluminous gown—shot through with veins, covered with snail and slugs, sporting an ever-present puddle with a frog on a lily pad—recalls a head of cabbage. Strangeness abounds: the wall of the witch’s garden seems to be capped with a row of giant human teeth, the tower takes the form of a monumentally tall circus tent, and at the top Rapunzel reclines on a large pear and sleeps on an enormous, puffy snail.

caption:
Finally we reach the end of Rapunzel week, and what better version to cap off the sequence than this glorious work by @paulozelinsky? Sumptuous oil paintings evoke the glory and wonder of a heightened fairy tale past. Zelinsky recreates architectural and design of the Italian Renaissance, particularly notable in his tower, which resembles an ornate campanile. Uncommon depth of emotion arises in the characters’ facial expressions and body language, particularly those of the sorceress—wild rage at the husband’s theft, shocked dismay at the discovery of Rapunzel's deception, and simmering fury as she shears off the flowing, red-gold tresses.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Zelinsky’s adaptation remains true to the text of the Brothers Grimm in several unique ways. Zelinsky refers to the antagonist of his tale as a sorceress, respecting the direct translation of the German word “zauberin” from the seventh edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen. Moreover, the moment in which Rapunzel’s trysts with the prince are discovered truly stands out. Unlike other authors, who follow the Grimms’ bowdlerization of their original work (having Rapunzel absentmindedly ask, “Frau Gothel, tell me why it is that you are more difficult to pull up than is the young prince, who will be arriving any moment now?”), Zelinsky returns to the very first edition of the text, in which the maiden innocently inquires, “Frau Gothel, tell me why it is that my clothes are all too tight. They no longer want to fit me,” an oblique reference to pregnancy which exposes Rapunzel’s loss of virginity.

While climbing up to reach a honey pot on the mantel, three young bears named Dash, Charlie, and Theo accidentally knock their mother’s special blue seashell to the floor, breaking it to smithereens. caption:
Readers of Barbara Cooney’s Miss Rumphius will surely come away with a deepened love of the environment and a heightened appreciation for the values of humanist thought. The book’s narrator relates the life of her great-aunt Alice Rumphius, whose life is depicted as one long flashback, a story within a story. Young Alice dreams of emulating her grandfather, traveling the world and settling down in a house by the sea. But, says Alice’s grandfather, there is a third thing she must do with her life: she must find a way to make the world more beautiful. Alice (or Miss Rumphius, as she is called as an adult), does indeed travel far and wide, and she does indeed buy a little cottage overlooking the ocean. For a time, she casts about for a way to make the world a better place. Eventually, she takes inspiration from the wind’s dispersal of her favorite flower, the lupine, and begins scattering seeds everywhere she goes. Lupines soon spread over the countryside, transforming the landscape and endearing Miss Rumphius to her community. Cooney’s clear, attractive prose and her soft-textured illustrations (colored-pencil-accented acrylic paintings on gesso-coated fabric) give us a longitudinal view of a life well lived, of meaning made and long-held dreams achieved.

caption:
Here’s an ode to those moments when somnolence hangs thick and silent over all: So Sleepy Story by Uri Shulevitz. In the middle of the night, a house lies filled with sleeping objects. Strange music floats in through the window, and everything—chairs, dishes, cabinets—gradually wakes up and begins to dance. Then, the music fades away and the house drifts back into slumber. Shulevitz uses the simplicity of the story as an exercise in linguistic experimentation, the repetition of the word “sleepy” (and of the reduplicative phrase “sleepy sleepy”) taking on a lulling, rhythmic quality. He externalizes the sleepiness of the house, playfully illustrating the inanimate objects with sleeping faces, which naturally turn wakeful when the unexplained music makes its entrance.

caption:
Human connection can occur in many forms. While it’s perhaps more typical to find friends with whom we’re quite similar, sometimes opposites do attract. So it is for the title characters of The Full House and the Empty House, a quirky meditation on mutually fulfilling relationships by @lkjamz. Two sentient houses spend their days together, basking in each other’s company; one contains a multitude of objects, while the other has practically nothing at all inside. Though this stark dichotomy suggests the potential for bad feeling, each of these beings sees the best in the other—the empty house rejoices in the rattling noise the full house makes when it dances, and the full house exults in the great soaring heights the empty house achieves when thrown into the air. The visually bizarre premise, bolstered by James’s stylized hand-drawn ink art, serves as the unexpected vehicle for a simple and refreshingly healthy message about taking pleasure in appreciation of another’s differences.

caption:
We’ve all had moments when we sensed we were a bit out of place. Now imagine this feeling writ large. What would it mean to lack true community? We would undoubtedly set off in search of the place where we belonged. And the young boy at the heart of Lane Smith’s There Is a Tribe of Kids does just that. He wanders from place to place, along the way passing through a multitude of habitats and environments, rendered in a variety of eye-popping textures in Smith’s acrylic-sprayed oil paintings augmented with colored pencil, graphite, collage, and digital techniques. Despite the boy’s best efforts, he never quite seems to fit in. Whether he is living in prehistoric times or simply traversing a wilderness far from civilization is a question readers must answer for themselves. Smith adopts a precise and minimalistic writing style; though he conveys the story through a simple list of collective names for various animals and elements of nature, the emotional whole is far greater than the sum of its parts. At the story’s appealing conclusion, the boy finds a group with whom he truly belongs—and the book’s title, seemingly an innocuous reference to the events of the opening pages, takes on a different significance altogether.

caption:
How does the thought strike you that, despite our amassing of information, we can never truly know every inch of the world? Some may find it comforting to believe that there will always be another adventure waiting around the corner for those who look hard enough. Others might consider it ominous to think about the unknown phenomena eluding our ken. Both camps may find pleasure in the eerie twists and turns of The Wretched Stone by Chris Van Allsburg. Captain Hope and the crew of the merchant vessel Rita Anne dock at an uncharted island, where they discover a mysterious rock set with a smooth glass panel that gives off an unearthly light. After bringing the item aboard the ship, the men develop a fascination with it and begin visiting it below deck every day. Perturbed by the sailors’ mounting obsession with the glowing stone, the captain resolves to throw it overboard, but the crew locks him out of the hold. The true effect of the paranormal artifact cannot be explained...but can it be reversed? Van Allsburg makes a distinctive storytelling choice by setting the narrative in the format of an epistolary novel, the text consisting entirely of the captain’s entries in the ship’s log. His illustrations view the characters from odd angles and distant perspectives, until the climax, when the insidious transformation of the crew is revealed in a moment of surreal horror. Any intent on Van Allsburg’s part to construct a deliberate metaphor for the hypnotic effect of a glowing screen upon suggestible masses can only be inferred.

caption:
Imagine making a discovery that you’re convinced will bring you fame and success. Now imagine that some unknown entity has crept into your life to stymie that success. What would you do to outwit your foe? This is the very question faced by the protagonist of Sybil Wettasinghe’s The Umbrella Thief. Kiri Mama leaves his small Sri Lankan village and takes a bus trip to the big city, where he discovers umbrellas. Realizing these items will be popular with his neighbors, who typically hold banana leaves over their heads in the rain, he purchases one. However, when he stops for a meal at a coffee shop on the way home, the umbrella vanishes from its hiding spot outside. Dispirited, he returns the next day for a new umbrella, but he stops at the coffee shop again and this umbrella too is taken from the exact same place. The cycle repeats, with Kiri Mama buying and losing umbrella after umbrella. He finally hits upon a solution that allows him to locate his missing wares and, having amassed so many, he opens an umbrella shop. But just who—or what—is the mysterious umbrella thief? Told with a mixture of engaging prose and bright, thickly lined art, Wettasinghe’s gentle story (originally published in Japan as “Kasa Doroboh”) saves its cheery surprise for the very last page.

caption:
Today is the day of my three-hundredth book review. I can’t believe it’s been so long since I began this little project of mine—the time’s just flown by. Thank you for your kind feedback and support along the way!

Here is a unique tale, by turns softly meditative, warmly comforting, and utterly terrifying—Brinton Turkle’s Do Not Open. Miss Moody dwells at the edge of the ocean with her cat, a foundling known as Captain Kidd. The day after a cataclysmic storm, she sets off down the beach in search of treasure and finds a bottle buried in the sand. Scratched on the dark purple vessel is the ominous message: “DO NOT OPEN”. Moved by a plaintive voice emerging from the bottle, Miss Moody pulls the stopper, and out pours the stuff of nightmares. An enormous smoke cloud trickles from the bottle, dissipating to reveal a colossal monster with glowing eyes and glistening fangs. Turkle’s chilling art elevates the scenario to a vignette of pure horror as the shapeshifting creature grows larger and more hideous with the turn of each page. His unflinching prose sets up the demonic entity not only as a direct foe for his protagonist but also as a threat to the entire human race. With a direct question to the reader (“Should she open the bottle?”) he prompts us to consider what we might do in Miss Moody’s place. The scratched warning, the disembodied voice—what clearer warning signs could one ask for? Surely, we may scoff, we would detect the danger and leave the bottle alone. However, we must never underestimate the all-consuming power of curiosity. May we all have the presence of mind Miss Moody displays in the face of danger...and may we all have such a devoted companion at our side as the trusty Captain Kidd.

caption:
In honor of the beloved Eric Carle, here’s a look at his delightful story Papa, Please Get the Moon for Me. Looking out into the night, Monica becomes enamored of the moon and asks her father to retrieve it. Papa fetches a very long ladder, puts it on top of a very high mountain, and fetches the moon during its crescent phase. Delighted, Monica dances with the moon, hugs it, and throws it into the air. The moon, however, wanes until it disappears completely, only to reappear shortly thereafter, back in its proper place in the sky. With delicately simple language and his signature painted collage illustrations on large-scale fold-out pages, Carle frames Monica’s journey neither as a triumphant celebration of success nor as a cautionary tale of excess but simply as a quiet moment in a child’s experience. Desiring, obtaining, and losing—all parts of the universal human journey. In the end, Monica sees the new moon and drops calmly off to sleep. May we all find the same tranquility in our lives. Rest in peace, Mr. Carle.

All who see color begin to assign it significance, dreams and treasured memories linking to specific tints and shades. In her lush and introspective prose poem They Say Blue, @jilliantamaki explores the personal meaning color can accrue over the years of a complex human life. The narrator, a young girl taking in the chromatic richness of the world around her, reflects on each hue she encounters and its association with her life experiences. Her aura radiates outward, orange on the side where she holds an egg, red on the side of her heart; she rides a boat over fields of golden grass; she stretches her arms up and becomes a tree, standing still with the passing of seasons; she looks out the window to see the blackness of her hair echoed in the feathers of crows. Tamaki’s lyrical writing draws the reader in with well-chosen phrases and powerfully tactile imagery. Her stunning art, a mix of acrylic painting on watercolor paper and digital technique, employs strong line and vivid color, imbuing the meditative story with a strong sense of forward motion.

caption:
Art is an expression of the human spirit. We that well assume that artists who return over and over to a specific theme or subject do so out of love or fascination. But what if one creates art based on fear? This scenario fuels the philosophically rich story of Demi’s The Boy Who Painted Dragons. The dragons of heaven look down through a hole in the clouds and cast their gaze to earth. They notice a boy named Ping painting dragons just like them. Though he tells his friends that he loves and admires dragons, the young artist is in fact afraid of the great beasts, and he paints them in an attempt to conquer his fear. When the Heavenly Dragon visits earth and discovers what truly lies in Ping’s heart, he gifts the boy three pearls of celestial advice: “Seek your truth”, “Find your truth”, and “Dare to be true”. Ping embarks on a quest to visit the dragons of water, fire, earth, and wind, each of whom recognizes his courage and grants him a new form of wisdom. Demi’s vibrant art, created with paint, ink, and Chinese silk brocade, illuminate the emotional themes of her compelling and insightful text.

caption:
In honor of the wonderful Lois Ehlert, here’s a peek at her marvelous book Leaf Man. The title character is simply the narrator’s perception of a face arising from a collection of leaves. But this transient being blows away on the wind, passing over land and water as it goes. The art is a triumph, integrated perfectly into the book’s construction. The turning of the pages recapitulates the movement of Leaf Man over the landscape; the die-cut top edges suggest fields, meadows, hills, forests, and mountains. Animals, crops, and other items along the way are collaged from color copies of leaves, which Ehlert complements with saturated earth tones, lending a natural beauty to the story. The text may appear simple at first blush but reveals itself upon close reading to be quite complex, particularly in the thought-provoking refrain, “A Leaf Man’s got to go where the wind blows.” The personification of Leaf Man allows for a poetic examination of the passing of time and the delicate impermanence of our surroundings. Perhaps we might all do well to slow down and watch for a Leaf Man blowing by, dancing on the breeze on his way to nowhere in particular. When our time comes, may we all be borne away on such a serene and gentle wind. Rest in peace, Ms. Ehlert.

caption:
Family typically serves as a support system, as a network of trust, as a guide to becoming a citizen of the wide world. Imagine, then, a life in which the only family you know is an oppressor, a smothering figure who cares far more about keeping you close than about granting you any sort of independence. This shocking scenario is our entry point into The Enchanter’s Daughter by Antonia Barber and Errol Le Cain. The story opens in a lofty castle at the top of the world, far away from all human contact. In this lonely place, a powerful enchanter and his daughter live together, their relationship as jailer and captive: he will not let her leave, and the verdant lands surrounding the palace are ringed by icy mountains. Slowly but surely, the maiden develops curiosity about her past and begins to long for the lands beyond her father’s domain. Despite the enchanter’s best efforts to keep her docile and contained, his daughter concocts a daring plan for escape. Barber’s high fantasy setting and eloquent writing create a gripping story, elevated by the sinuous tendrils and curls of Le Cain’s eldritch art.

caption:
It takes a very specific gift to create a reliably funny picture book. Witness, then, the talents of Jules Feiffer in his hilarious Bark, George. A young dog continues to flummox his mother with his bizarre behavior. Each time she instructs him to bark, he emits an animal noise quite unbefitting a dog: “Meow”, “Quack-quack”, “Oink”, “Moo”. George’s mother takes him to a veterinarian, who proceeds to reach deep (deep, deep) down inside George and pull out a series of animals—a cat, a duck, a pig, and finally a cow—ostensibly the source of the unusual sounds. Writing with a deadpan narrative style and augmenting his instantly recognizable loose line art with bright, solid colors, Feiffer mines the silliness of the premise for its full comedic potential. He leaves the question of how the animals got inside George in the first place utterly aside, as any possible answer would only detract from the humor. The twist ending, on the other hand, ratchets up the absurdity as high as it can go.

caption:
It’s always fascinating to consider the origin of old wives’ tales. Did they all start purely as folkloric entertainment? Did any of them perhaps form around a kernel of truth? Here’s an eerie bit of invented lore that can’t possibly have a basis in reality...or can it? In Joanne Robertson and László Gál’s Sea Witches, a young boy recalls his Scottish grandmother’s peculiar warning to crumble his eggshells into tiny pieces when he has finished eating. This admonition evidently serves to thwart the plans of witches, who prowl around looking for eggshell halves, which they can transform into seafaring vessels. Once on the water, purely for their own foul amusement, they conjure up storms that sink ships and drown sailors. All this witchcraft unfurls as a story within a story, an extended quotation of a bit of folk wisdom. Despite the grandmother’s Scottish roots, Robertson makes the distinctive choice to structure her text as a series of haiku, a poetic form of Japanese origin. Gál’s witches are truly monstrous, clustering together in a fell swarm as they slaver for mischief and bloodsport. Perhaps the utility of such a story for adults is simply the old-world tactic of frightening children into compliance. There certainly isn’t a bit of truth to such superstition, we worldly adults tell ourselves. Or is there? After all, though we may be confident there’s nothing there in the dark, every now and then we still find ourselves glancing over our shoulders...just to be sure.

caption:
It’s high time I kicked off another fairy tale theme week, and this time I’ll be journeying through seven versions of Rumpelstiltskin!

To begin, an adaptation translated Anthea Bell and illustrated by Bernadette Watts. The text remains faithful to the original Grimm story, while the soft-colored and -textured illustrations achieve an idyllic sweetness. Rumpelstiltskin himself, with his long white beard, cherry-red nose and cheeks, and green hose, tunic, and cap, resembles a whimsical gnome.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Bell’s translation includes the ending of the story in which Rumpelstiltskin, apoplectic with rage at the queen’s discovery of his secret name, stamps one leg into the ground, grabs his other leg, and pulls on it so hard that he tears himself in half. In the original 1812 edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen, the little man simply runs away in anger. The colorful moment of extreme gore was added by the Brothers Grimm in later revisions of the text, a moralistic punishment for the man’s threat to take the queen’s child. Watts, having perhaps concluded that this disturbing image might prove too much for children to witness even in illustrated form, tones down the violence by depicting Rumpelstiltskin a moment beforehand, as he begins his fateful stamping.

caption:
Today’s version of Rumpelstiltskin comes to us from Paul Galdone, who illustrates the tale with detailed scenes in thick, loosely drawn lines and bright hues. With many bales of straw, the finished spools of gold, and the cascading blonde hair of the heroine, yellow dominates the color palette of almost every page. To the traditional cast of characters Galdone adds a court jester who hovers near the king, leering and smirking at the miller and his daughter. The little fool bears an uncertain significance in the story, prominent in the art but unmentioned in the text. Curiously, with his diminutive stature, long, pointed noise, heavy-lidded eyes, and hairy brows, he sports more than a passing resemblance to Rumpelstiltskin himself. A closer inspection reveals that the jester even seems to be wearing Rumpelstiltskin’s gold-buttoned blue jacket at the royal wedding. Has Galdone slyly inserted the antagonist of the tale into parts of the story where he does not belong? That may be up to readers to decide—but note that the two bizarre little men never appear together on the same page.

caption:
Rumpelstiltskin Week is half gone, but I’m only just getting warmed up! Take a look at this masterful adaptation by Alison Sage and Gennady Spirin. Sage provides a motivation for the miller’s otherwise thoughtless lie: his wife convinces him that earning the king’s favor will pull them out of financial difficulty. Hence, he claims that his daughter (here named Rose) can spin straw into gold. Realizing too late the terrible penalty she will face if she cannot fulfill his rash boast, the father actually admits to his falsehood, but his pleas are ignored. Spirin’s illustrations evoke the world of classical art, not simply in the environments, objects, and fashion but in the formalistic grandeur of the visual style. He borders each page with gold or silver spinning wheel components. A long gray beard and mustache give his Rumpelstiltskin a lightly comical air.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Sage’s choice to have the king overhear Rumpelstiltskin’s name and convey it to Rose draws from the first edition of Grimm, who did not introduce the character of the queen’s trusty servant until later.

caption:
This Rumpelstiltskin adaptation features luminous illustrations by none other than Kinuko Y. Craft. The text hews quite closely to the original language of the Brothers Grimm. The characters, with their elongated limbs and angular poses, appear quite at home in the glimmering, eldritch environments. Executed quite early in Craft’s career, the art is quite fascinating to consider from an extradiegetic perspective. Much flatter and more graphic than the painterly style typical of her later oeuvre, they bear the visual influence of Hilary Knight, who himself incorporated elements of the work of Kay Nielsen, who was in turn greatly inspired by the technique of Aubrey Beardsley, who drew from the potent imagery of Japanese printmaking.

caption:
Rumpelstiltskin Week concludes with Christopher Noël and @peter.sis.art‘s whimsical and wonderfully bizarre vision of the tale. Noël maintains the Grimms’ structure, while making distinctive narrative choices of his own. The little man appears in the chambers of straw from a different entry point each day: a trapdoor in the ceiling, and loose stone in the wall, a crack in the floor. Rather than sending a servant out on her behalf, the queen takes a hands-on approach and sets off on her own (baby in tow) to discover the name she so desperately needs. As in other adaptations, Rumpelstiltskin stamps his foot into the floor when finally confronted with the secret knowledge; however, here he spins like a tornado, drilling into the earth until he disappears. Sís employs his familiar detailed style to create an ever-so-slightly eldritch visual landscape where the king’s castle perches atop a hill looking like a staring human face. Behold Rumpelstiltskin—a mad jester with a red coxcomb and a white ruff and Venetian plague doctor mask. The wicked dwarf’s popping eyes, bared teeth, and inhuman claws make him a sinister figure indeed, a disturbing monster clown waiting to pounce on anyone who falls afoul of his twisted game.

caption:
For a vibrant celebration of music, energy, and individuality, check out Ben’s Trumpet by Rachel Isadora. The story is set during the ascendancy of jazz in the landscape of popular music—and popular culture. Young Ben listens awestruck to the artistry of the players at his local jazz club. He hears them each day as he walks by on his way home from school, and he can still hear them while sitting out on his fire escape at night. He admires the pianist, the saxophonist, the trombonist, and the drummer, but his favorite is the trumpeter. Inspired by the player’s lively energy and skill, Ben begins to play an imaginary trumpet of his own everywhere he goes. Sadly, no one seems to take much notice of his budding musical interest—except the one person who might matter most of all. With evocative slang (“Ben thinks the trumpeter is the cat’s meow”, “practicing a red hot piece”) and expressionistic black-and-white illustrations that combine Art Deco elements with a Cubist slang, Isadora conjures an irresistible visual representation of the thrill of jazz.

caption:
There’s a deceptively mind-bending architecture visible within the confines of @emily_gravett’s spare, dramatic, and pleasingly spooky Wolves. Rabbit takes out a book on wolves from the library (aptly and perhaps ominously titled “WOLVES”) and sets off, reading while walking. Employing a range of mixed-media techniques, Gravett constructs the story with a postmodernist bent, blurring the boundary between Rabbit’s trip home and the large overlaid images of the fictional book-within-a-book. Rabbit seems to inadvertently cross into the dangerous landscape of the wolf book itself, even as the wolves within appear to step out into Rabbit’s reality. Inevitably, just after finding out what sort of furry animals wolves love to eat, Rabbit is unceremoniously devoured (or, at least, so it would appear from the dreadful claw marks on the library book’s cover). But, in a metafictional postscript dripping with wicked irony, Gravett offers a revised ending—a collage in which the wolf and the rabbit are altered to look as though they are enjoying an innocent jam sandwich. This subtle critique of sanitized storytelling serves as a defiant exclamation point on the refreshingly grisly narrative. To cap it all off, Gravett obscures the line between the universe of the book and our own external world with quotes from favorable reviews by fictional rabbit-run publications.

caption:
For some people, bedtime poses no trouble—it may even be a welcome event. For others, it’s quite a different story—they toss and turn restlessly for hours before slipping off into slumber. The protagonist of @imageblockstudio’s Dreamland may well belong to this latter group, but it’s refreshing to view the frustration of insomnia from her playful perspective. Amelie experiences each night as a journey through a hazy world where wakeful sensations are represented as physical elements of the topography. She drifts high and low across a surreal, uncertain landscape, images refracted and sounds distorted through the lens of somnolence. At last, she finds her way to her own bed, at once the farthest and the nearest points in her excursion, and drops into cozy sleep. Klocek welcomes a warm ambiguity in both his soothing text and his cool-hued digital art: each well-chosen phrase and carefully composed image furthers the hypnagogic duality of the book’s central extended metaphor.
