Every night, the children’s sleep is disturbed by a masked gnome who extracts the happy dreams from their minds and replaces them with nightmares. Bartholomew, the affable town librarian, sets off with young siblings Michael and Gabby McDool to seek out the thief's lair in an eerie swamp and return the dreams to their rightful owners. Cosgrove’s scenario crackles with fantasy and excitement, and he sprinkles his dialogue with humor and heart. Heyer’s illustrations give us a land of alluring mystery, all darkness and rainbows and flickering flames.

caption:
Sometimes a persistently terrible environment can force one to acclimate, to become desensitized to the wrongness of the world. Not so the eponymous heroine of David Lucas’s Nutmeg, who grows ever more frustrated with the bizarre, junk-strewn wasteland where she lives with only her Uncle Nicodemus and Cousin Nesbitt for company. The three spend their days doing little to nothing at all, consigned to eating cardboard for breakfast, string for lunch, and sawdust for supper. One day, something unexpected happens: Nutmeg finds a bottle floating in the polluted water and releases a genie, who grants her three wishes. Weary of her monotonous routine, she requests something different for each meal of the day, and the genie provides her with a sentient spoon that prepares food all by itself. But the spoon has a mind of its own, and proceeds to stir and stir so vigorously that everything in the kitchen, in the house, in the entire world is soon caught up in a cosmic vortex. Where Nutmeg will land next is anybody’s guess, but she has certainly left her dull existence behind her. Lucas’s writing, replete with expressively italicized words, demands an animated reading voice, while his eye-popping cartoon-style illustrations offer a plethora of bright and merry details.

caption:
Once again we embark upon a fairy tale sequence…come and join me for Hansel and Gretel Week!

First, a version written and illustrated by Holly Hobbie. In a detailed Artist’s Note, Hobbie explains her childhood obsession with the Great Gildersleeve’s audio record of the fairy tale. She adapted the text of this book from Ralph Manheim’s translation of the Brothers Grimm. Her illustrations, created with transparent watercolor, pen and ink, and gouache on watercolor paper, feature characters and objects clustered in the center, with stark, lonely space at the edges. In contrast to the bleak tone of the beginning of the book, the witch appears flamboyant, garish, and almost disturbingly cheerful, sporting a black hat and brooch outdoors and a preposterous chef’s jacket and toque hat while serving dinner. In a more frightening moment, she sharpens a knife on a grindstone as the children look on, surrounded by the bones of her previous victims.

caption:
To continue, here is a Hansel and Gretel illustrated by Sandy Ann Nightingale, who peppers her images with absorbing details: a cat glancing down in shock at its empty saucer, a cookbook open to the ominously titled recipe “Baked Boy”, a chair tipping over as a happy father jumps to his feet. As she puts the children to bed by candlelight, the witch (who with her long nose and pointed ears resembles a goblin) casts a stark shadow on the wall, recalling imagery from German Expressionist cinema.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this version of Hansel and Gretel, like many adaptations, refers to the woodcutter’s wife as the stepmother, following later editions of Kinder- und Hausmärchen by the Brothers Grimm. In the first edition, published in 1812, the woman is explicitly identified as the mother. As the Grimms had become aware of their tales’ popularity with children, their alteration perhaps reflects a belief that fictional abuse and neglect would be more traumatizing if committed by a biological parent. The text of this adaptation furthermore changes the death of the woodcutter’s wife to an unexplained departure.

caption:
Here we are at the center of Hansel and Gretel Week, examining a stunning adaptation by Rika Lesser and @paulozelinsky. Lesser’s quietly elegant writing style, with its straightforward language and unflinching depiction of cruelty and despair, honors the tradition of the Brothers Grimm. Zelinsky fills his haunting oil paintings with tantalizing elements that elucidate themes and character connections. Hansel’s outfit (brown jacket, white shirt, blue breeches, white stockings) greatly resembles that of his father, while Gretel’s clothing (blue dress, white shift, white apron, white bonnet) closely matches that of her mother…and of the witch. The house in the forest presents the familiar exterior of candy and baked goods. However, a view from behind reveals the sweets as nothing more than a facade, a false veneer applied over stone walls and a thatched roof. Scattered inside and out are a variety of arcane paraphernalia: a broom, occult symbols and diagrams (including pentagrams and the Planetary Seal of Saturn), various frogs and lizards, an hourglass, and a hand of glory.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: unusually, Lesser bases her retelling on the first edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen. Thus, the woodcutter’s wife is referred to as the children’s biological mother, and Gretel slides the witch into the oven on a bread board (before slamming and barring the door).

caption:
Moving right along through the week, we come to a Hansel & Gretel by Will Moses, whose detailed oil paintings draw on the tradition of folk art passed down to him by his grandfather. The text is interspersed with vignettes and spot illustrations, with several two-page spreads depicting seeping aerial views of critical plot points.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this is one of the rare adaptations to include one of the darker details from the Grimms’ text. As Hansel and Gretel wait for woodcutter and his wife in the forest, they think they can hear the sound of an ax chopping wood. However, when they go to investigate, they discover that they were in fact hearing the rhythmic clatter of an old branch that their father had tied to a dead tree. Imagine the siblings’ nasty shock of disappointment at suddenly finding themselves abandoned, combined with the horrific realization that their guardians would go to such lengths to coldly deceive them, and understand the despair closing in on the two young protagonists. Moses chooses to have the stepmother play the wicked trick on the children, absolving the father of his active role in the cruelty.

caption:
To finish Hansel and Gretel Week, here is a version translated from German by Elizabeth D. Crawford and illustrated by Austrian artist Lisbeth Zwerger. Crawford’s translation remains deeply faithful to the text of the Brothers Grimm, right down to the last detail—present are the stepmother’s harsh remark about preparing four coffins in light of the famine, the branch tied to a dead tree, the morbid description of the witch’s evil nature, the witch’s sadistic taunting of Gretel, and the white duck that carries the children across the lake. On pages alternating with the text are Zwerger’s pictures, spare and moody with muted washes of color. Her witch displays a number of frog-like qualities: her pallid green skin, her squat, bulbous body, her hunched-over pose when recording the caged Hansel. However, in her mortal panic while being pushed into the oven by Gretel, her pupils momentarily lengthen into vertical slits like those of a cat.

caption:
Have you ever been convinced that just one little change to the world around you would make everything better? Perhaps you were right. And so, it seems, is the protagonist of Catching the Moon by @myla_goldberg and @chrissheban. When an old Fisherwoman begins casting her line off the pier each night, all who notice wonder why she chooses to fish in the dark. As curious as any of them is the Man in the Moon, who begins visiting her in disguise each month, tempting her with ethereal delicacies like sea cucumber sandwiches and moon pie. Eventually, he learns of the Fisherwoman’s unusual motive: she means to reel in the moon itself to stop the ocean from wearing away at the houses and docks at the water’s edge. Eventually, with the application of some miraculous moon paint, the tide ebbs and a new equilibrium is reached. Goldberg unfurls her whimsical tale with eloquent prose, while Sheban’s soft watercolor-and-pencil artwork brings a warm, hazy glow to the proceedings.

Even when one is surrounded by opportunities, one can still be bored. Even when one is all alone, one can still create entire universes of wonder. caption:
Here is a look at @paulowenlewis’s compelling and enigmatic Storm Boy. A boy is swept out of his fishing boat by a storm and finds himself in an unknown land where a tribe of giant people welcomes him with food, warmth, and shelter. They teach him the steps of their dances, and he in turn teaches them the songs and dances of his own people. The true nature of these otherworldly beings can be inferred from the hints Lewis scatters throughout both the text and the art, and can finally be plainly seen during the boy’s journey back to his own land (for which he has his eyes closed). When he returns to his family, he is shocked to discover that, in the space of what he perceived as only a few hours, an entire year has slipped by. Written under the guidance of a cultural advisor, and with a portion of its proceeds having been donated to the Haida Gwaii Rediscovery program for tribal youth, the story combines folkloric motifs from the Haida, Tlingit, and other native tribes of the Pacific Northwest and draws inspiration from Joseph Campbell’s template of the “hero’s journey”. Lewis’s illustrations honor the tradition of Pacific Northwest art in their depiction of both the mundane and the supernatural.

caption:
Will the search for information yield valuable wisdom or mortal danger? In Crocodile’s Tears by @alexbeardstudio, it’s both. Stopping at the river for a drink, Rhino and Tickbird begin to wonder why Crocodile appears to be crying. They set off across the land in an attempt to discover the cause of Crocodile’s tears. Each animal they encounter suggests another animal who might answer their question, and their journey takes them to the mountains where Golden Eagle perches, to the plains where Elephant trumpets, to the forest where Tree Frog sings, to the meadow where Brenton Blue Butterfly flutters, to the savanna where Maasai Giraffe roams, and to the grasslands where Cheetah runs. Finally, Rhino breaks down and asks Crocodile himself. The great reptile replies that the tears are not a sign of sadness but a mechanism to keep his eyes moist. This explanation given, his Crocodile nature takes over, and Rhino is in for a nasty shock. Beard uses his engaging narrative and thick-lined illustrations both to entertain and to educate: both the story proper and a glossary at the end draw attention to the vanishing habitats of these animals in countries across Africa. Moreover, a share of the book’s proceeds go to the Shompole Community Trust, a land and animal reserve overseen by the Maasai people in Kenya.

caption:
There’s often an inexorable quality to a scary story. Though we wish we could warn the main character of the danger, into the danger they must go, for otherwise there would be no story at all. And so it is in @diterlizzi’s adaption of Mary Howitt’s classic poem The Spider and the Fly. The art, executed in gouache, colored pencil, and graphite combined with digital techniques, presents a black and white world of refined Victorian interiors lit with soft chiaroscuro. The monochromatic color scheme and the presentation of several lines as white intertitles on cobwebbed black backgrounds evoke the visual conventions of silent film. DiTerlizzi extends the period setting into the design and costumes of the characters: the Fly is unmistakably a flapper girl with her loose, straight-cut, sleeveless dress, her opera gloves, and her bobbed hair tucked under a cloche hat, while the Spider is an unctuous cad, transitioning from a fez and smoking jacket indoors to a stovepipe hat and ulster outside. Moreover, the Victorian mansion that serves as the spider’s home harks back to Edward Hopper’s famous painting House by the Railroad—which served as the inspiration for the house in Alfred Hitchcock’s Psycho.

caption:
It may well be impossible to know the internal experience of someone who is injured, unconscious, and fighting for their life. Can they hear us as we sit next to them and call their name? Can they exert their will—their spirit—their life force—from within and make the journey to recovery? Perhaps all we can do while we wait is wonder, and from just such a wondering as this springs Adam’s Smile by David McPhail. A young boy lies in bed, convalescing from an injury he received when a car struck his bicycle. Suddenly, a band of supernatural beings lassoes his bed and whisks him away into the night, a winged horse towing him through the sky to their otherworldly den. Their leader explains that the encroaching forces of darkness can only be repelled by the boy’s smile, whose light must be captured and preserved in a little box. Then the boy returns (from a dream? from an ethereal night land? from within himself?) to his room, awake and on the mend. McPhail depicts a nocturnal adventure of soft colors and surreal imagery in service to a touching story that was inspired by a true event from his life: a young boy he knew was hit by a car while riding his bicycle and lay in a coma for months. This book served its author as a way to process and make sense of the accident, and perhaps it can do the same for others in times of dire need and despair. McPhail’s personal case ends on a happy note: the boy made a full recovery.

caption:
There’s a truly heartwarming relationship anchoring @authorstrator’s wordless companion to The Boy and the Airplane, The Girl and the Bicycle. While out on a walk with her little brother, a girl sees a bicycle in a store window. When she cannot scrounge up enough money around the house for the purchase, she decides to work for it. A kindly neighbor employs her over a period of months for a variety of tasks: raking leaves, cleaning the house, shoveling snow, planting the garden, trimming the hedge. She finally saves enough money, but when she returns to the store she finds that the bicycle is gone. In that moment, she makes a decision with her hard-earned cash—one that shows true selflessness. Pett’s pencil-and-watercolor artwork beautifully portrays the growing connection between the girl and her neighbor, which provides the story with a quietly lovely denouement.

A subtle and delightful Easter egg: while the girl and her neighbor are cleaning out the garage, the neighbor gazes at a photograph of the protagonist of Pett’s earlier The Boy and the Airplane (suggesting that she may be his wife, or his sister, or even his daughter) just as the girl stands a few feet away from the eponymous toy plane itself.

caption:
Warning—this story is not for the faint of heart, for it gazes unflinchingly into the experience of a child at the mercy of a cold and apathetic world. Carly by Annegert Fuchshuber is a difficult but vitally important work of fiction. Harrowing from the very beginning, the plot follows a little girl as she flees from the fiery devastation of an unspecified conflict or disaster. No family, no friends, she searches high and low for shelter and comfort, with little success. In the land of the Stone-eaters, she cannot consume the food. In the land of the Silk-tails, she cannot blend in. In the land of the Smoky-crows, she cannot adjust to the habitat. In the land of the Greedy-managers, she cannot even garner a shred of sympathy. The tale ends on an uncertain but optimistic note as Carly encounters kindness and support from an unlikely source: a Fool. Originally published in German as “Karlinchen”, the gripping text has been translated into English by Florence Howe and Heidi Kirk. Fuchshuber’s illustrations depict the sobering sequence of events in a style that is fanciful yet unsentimental.

caption:
There’s a refined and understated humor to be found in The Crows of Pearblossom, a picture book version of a children’s story by Aldous Huxley, illustrated by @sophieblackall. Mrs. Crow is puzzled to find that the egg she lays each day goes missing when she leaves the cottonwood tree to shop for groceries. When she identifies the culprit as the wicked Mr. Snake, who lives in a hole at the bottom of the tree, she informs Mr. Crow, who enlists the wise Old Man Owl for help. Old Man Owl shapes a few eggs out of clay, bakes them, and paints them to look just like the ones laid by Mrs. Crow. When Mr. Snake consumes the decoy eggs, he receives his just comeuppance, and from then on Mrs. Crow hatches eggs to her heart’s content. With soft-textured illustrations executed in ink and watercolor, Blackall depicts the world of Huxley’s scenario, rendering quirky details from the text (Mrs. Crow’s groceries, Old Man Owl shaving) and making charming additions of her own (Mr. Snake’s fang dentures and seven-day pill organizer, an edition of Nest magazine on the Crows’ bed).

caption:
There’s a stunning blend of scientific information and aesthetic beauty in My Light, Molly Bang’s exploration of the many ways we harness energy for use in our society. Bang writes from the perspective of the sun as it gazes down on the earth and remarks on our technology. Her luminous art depicts light as tiny particles radiating from the sun and aligning themselves into waves. She illustrates myriad components of the energy grid, including hydroelectric dams, power lines, wind turbines, coal-fired plants, and solar panels. She explores plant life, the water cycle, and other elements of the natural world that feed on the sun’s energy just as humans do. Finally, a wealth of back matter provides further information on the making of the book, the details of the pictures, and further steps readers can take to consume energy responsibly as citizens of our planet.

caption:
Come explore the thought-provoking tale of The King and the Magician, written by @jorgebucayofficial and illustrated @gusti.rosemffet. You’ll find both story and illustrations by turns rich, clever, and compelling. A King who rules his subjects with an iron fist hears of a wise Magician who can foretell the future. Threatened by the thought of a greater power than his own, he invites the old man to a feast and gives him a simple but perilous challenge: “Tell me the exact date of your own death.” No matter the man’s answer, the sovereign plans to kill him on the spot. The Magician replies simply that he will die on the exact same day as the King. These words strike fear into the ruler’s heart. What if the old sage is telling the truth? He begs the man to stay at the palace, offering the pretext of seeking the Magician’s advice in matters of state but in reality desperate to protect him from harm and stave off their apparently intertwined fate. Many years pass, and jealousy and fear give way to understanding, the two men attaining a deep friendship. Finally, the King confesses his murderous intentions, and the Magician admits that he fabricated the prediction about their deaths. They embrace one another as brothers and equals. Bucay’s text, translated from the original Spanish, contains true insight into the psychology and emotional depth of human relationships. In his art, filled with motley textures and hues, Gusti employs a two-dimensional perspective, creating the look of a sophisticated diorama or puppet show. He inserts a subtle detail (unmentioned in the text), a clue to the monarch’s underlying benevolence: a morose-looking royal teddy bear. In a touching gesture, the King offers this bear to a group of peasants who have presented him with gifts.

caption:
Let’s dive back into the world of fairy tales with another themed week of exploration—this time around, it’s Beauty and the Beast!

To begin, we have a version by former spouses Marianna and Mercer Mayer. Her elegant text and his lush illustrations combine to form a rich and ethereal setting filled with enticing details. The beast’s palace contains subtle but unmistakable imagery drawn from ancient Egyptian art: pharaonic columns, carved hieroglyphs in cartouches, jackals, falcons, serpents, bulls, scarabs, and a large stone sphinx. The beast himself resembles a ferocious, digitigrade otter.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Beauty and the Beast was originally a novella-length story (of about one hundred pages) written by Gabrielle-Suzanne Barbot de Villeneuve in her 1740 collection La Jeune Américaine et Les Contes Marins. In 1756, the tale was substantially abridged by Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont in Magasin des Enfants. Marianna Mayer has used the structure of de Beaumont’s adaptation as the basis for her story, but reintroduced a subplot from de Villeneuve’s original, in which Beauty receives visits from a mysterious young man in her dreams.

caption:
Beauty and the Beast Week now brings us to this fascinating version by Etienne Delessert, who uses the the tale’s supernatural details as jumping-off points for his bizarre imagination. Humans, animals, and objects appear in his trademark grotesque style. Whimsical details include a large, hanging spider with flashlight eyes, a flock of birds playing dominoes, and a Beast in the shape of a large eagle with paws and a fanged beak.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this edition incorrectly attributes the source material to French writer Marie-Catherine Le Jumel de Barneville, Baroness d’Aulnoy. The true author of the original tale is Gabrielle-Suzanne Barbot de Villeneuve. Madame d’Aulnoy, who died many years before the story’s publication in 1740, did, however, write numerous literary fairy tales using folkloric motifs present in Madame Villeneuve’s later work (both authors were likely inspired by the tale of Cupid and Psyche from Roman philosopher Apuleius’s book the The Golden Ass, written in the second century of the Common Era).

caption:
There’s a delicate sweetness and magic to @jeankim_illustration’s Rabbit Moon. Every night, the residents of Earth (here a cadre of anthropomorphic animals) write down their dearest wishes on sheets of paper, which they fold into airplanes. These airplanes are sent soaring up to the moon, where the sole inhabitant, Rabbit, collects them in a mortar, pounds them into stars, and flings them into the night sky. One day, Rabbit puffs a star full of air, inflating it like a balloon, and rides it down to earth. After a crash landing, an encounter with the local animals, and hours of exuberant play, it is time to return to the moon and resume the transformation of wishes into stars. However, the animals have one last package to deliver to Rabbit, which ensures their connection will never be truly lost. Kim unfolds her story in spare text, bolstered by slant rhyme and a loose, playful meter. Her illustrations, executed in pencil and colored digitally, are presented in a comic-strip layout; we view the endearing characters and their peaceful environments from a variety of dynamic perspectives.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: in a prefatory author’s note, Kim explains that she drew inspiration for her story from her native Korean folk tradition, which interprets the markings on the face of the moon as a mystical rabbit pounding rice into rice cakes.

caption:
As we transition from childhood to adulthood, we all eventually muster our confidence in our burgeoning skills and begin to take on responsibility, to discover our place in the world. For some of us it’s a gradual shift, but for others there’s a single point of transformation. In Pearl, written and illustrated by @mollyidle, the eponymous character (a wide-eyed, eager young mermaid) witnesses those around her caring for the undersea flora and fauna and dearly wishes to join in. Her mother gives her a seemingly insignificant grain of sand and explains that “Even the smallest of things can make a great difference.” Soon, to Pearl’s surprise, the little speck becomes a tiny pearl, which grows larger and larger until it floats up into the sky as a shimmering full moon, penetrating the surface of the water with its light and illuminating the realm below. Idle’s thoughtful and poetic text sparkles with powerful oceanic imagery and metaphor, following Pearl’s emotional journey from tender hope to deep disappointment to new awakening to tranquil understanding. Her luminous art achieves a sense of warmth and familiarity in its depiction of a fantastical marine world. The mermaids’ hair and tails mirror the aspects of the sea they are assigned to preserve: stony coral, seahorse fins, stalks of seaweed, squid tentacles, and (in the case of Pearl and her mother) seashells.

Today’s book celebrates the deep kindness and generosity of the human spirit: The Falling Stars, translated from German of the Brothers Grimm by Rosemary Lanning and illustrated by Eugen Sopko. A young girl, orphaned and homeless, sets out into the world with only a crust of bread and the clothes on her back, all of which she soon gives away to those in even greater need. Finally, when she is left with nothing at all, stars rain down from the sky and turn into gold coins, thus providing her with a fortune. Lanning’s appealing translation honors the Grimms’ language, while Sopko’s pictures, done in a naïve art style, ameliorate the profound sadness of the story’s setting.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the Brothers Grimm titled their original tale “Die Sterntaler” (“The Star Thalers”), as they specify that the miraculous money falls from the heavens as Joachimsthalers, a sixteenth-century Bohemian coin.

The book of the day is Meghan Collins and László Gál’s The Willow Maiden. Lost in the Whispering Woods, Denis discovers the hidden world of the Willow People. There, he encounters Lisane, daughter of the Willow King, who professes her love for him and protects him against the dangers of the mysterious fairy troupe. caption:
What happens to a person when they have wronged so many that their misdeeds begin to define their character? While society may view them as wholly immoral, do they see themselves that way? Once deemed a criminal and shunned by others, what must they do to repair their relationship with the community? And who determines when such a reconciliation can begin—or whether it can be made at all? These are the powerful and uneasy questions raised by @squeaknbanana’s The Outlaw. A brigand menaces a settlement in the Old West, gaining a fearsome reputation. After a time, he disappears, and no one seems particularly bothered to be rid of him. Years go by, and a stranger rides into town. Of his own volition, he begins to make small repairs wherever he sees a need. Suddenly, the citizens recognize the stranger as none other than the Outlaw himself. They begin to upbraid him, venting their frustration at his past wrongs, until a young boy steps protectively in front of him and tells the assembled crowd: “Leave him alone! He’s trying.” At this simple but powerful rebuke, the throng disperses, and the Outlaw resumes his quest to make amends. With spare text and a largely monochromatic color palette, Vo presents a thought-provoking parable of morality, atonement, and compassion.

Connection to nature is a soothing balm, a vital component of a healthy human life. Conversely, the absence of such a link may lead to an empty daily experience, as can be glimpsed in The Hidden Jungle, a timely cautionary tale by Simon Henwood. The view from Mr. Pinn’s apartment window reveals a depressing urban clutter—not a bit of green in sight. That is, until he brings home a potted plant to brighten things up. He gently waters it and cares for it, but despite his good intentions it begins to droop and wither. Ultimately, he is obliged to bring the plant to the city garden, revealed in a series of wordless spreads to be in the center of the vast stretch of metal and stone. Finally, Mr. Pinn is left alone, as grim and morose as before. Henwood’s cheerily colorful illustrations blunt the sharp sting of his urgent message and the shock of his startlingly bleak ending.

caption:
Today is a personal milestone: this is my three hundred sixty-fifth book review. That’s right; I’ve been at this, once a day, for an entire year. I can’t thank you all enough for reading along with me! Every time you Follow my account, every time you Like one of my posts, every time you leave an encouraging comment, you’re bringing a smile to my face. Thank you all so very much.

To round out my first full year of book reviews, here’s a work that deserves to be hailed as a modern classic: Hungry Jim by @ohmylorelei and @c.groenink. Have you ever woken up on the wrong side of the bed? One morning, young Jim opens his eyes and discovers that he has somehow become a lion. His monstrous appetite provokes him to devour a long succession of characters, beginning with his own mother downstairs in the kitchen and ending with a bear out in the wilderness. Jim finally tames his beastly impulses, regurgitates all those he has consumed, and transforms back into a boy. However, with the bear still standing menacingly before him…he eats it again. Snyder dances masterfully back and forth between the literal and the figurative: has Jim truly undergone some strange magical transformation? Or are we experiencing his imagination as a visual metaphor for a child succumbing to his powerful emotions? In Jim’s frustrated inner monologue, Snyder bravely incorporates raw, powerful phrases such as, “Shut up,” and “I hate you,” language often forbidden in modern picture books but absolutely vital to the construction of her protagonist’s voice. With a mix of pencil and digital technique, Groenink employs detailed line art and a warm color palette to create a landscape of ferocious beauty.

In a tender closing note, both author and artist dedicate their work to their spiritual influence: Maurice Sendak.

Among other bewitching details, note the cadre of enchanted princes sitting around the table in the mysterious castle’s grand hall: some feature bizarre appendages growing from their body (one has leafy branches on his head, one has grown deer antlers, one has sprouted a unicorn horn, one has iridescent butterfly wings) while others have been partially transformed into animals (one has the head of a blue jay, one the head of a swan, one the head of a frog).

caption:
Did you go to the beach as a child? Was it a sandy beach or a rocky beach? Was the water warm or cold? Were the waves low or high? Did you enter gradually or plunge in all at once? All of these questions and more are synthesized in the striking visual world of the wordless Wave by @suzyleebooks. A young girl visits the beach with her mother. As a flock of curious seagulls looks on, she inches up to the water’s edge, scampers back from an oncoming wave, ventures forward again, and finally begins to dance and splash in the shallows. Finally, a colossal breaker rises up and crashes over her. Dazed, she sits on the wet sand for a moment but soon amuses herself by gathering shells, sea stars, and other things washed ashore by the mighty surf. All too soon, it is time to leave. The girl departs with her mother; as she looks back over her shoulder at the ocean, she smiles and gives one final wave. Lee carefully crafts each design element of the book to support her visual storytelling. The girl and the sea serve as two main characters engaged in an animated back-and-forth confrontation, the lolling waves suggesting a staunch force opposing the girl’s defiant, boisterous energy. The wide horizontal layout of the book enhances this stark contrast. The gutter (or the vertical seam between the two open pages) represents both a physical barrier (the water’s edge) and an emotional barrier (her own anxiety) for the girl to traverse. Eventually, she crosses to the ocean’s side, and the ocean crosses to her side, drenching everything. From then on, the water’s deep, rich cyan (the only hue present in the book’s otherwise greyscale landscape) can be found in the girl’s dress, the marine life, and the sky itself. The opposites are integrated (emotionally, spatially, and chromatically) and harmony is achieved.

caption:
Have you ever been blamed for something you didn’t do? Alternatively, have you ever convinced yourself that you weren’t really to blame but later looked back and realized you were? The tension between these possibilities informs @levi_pinfold’s merrily insightful The Django. Jean leads a peaceful existence traveling, working, and making music with his Roma family and community. One day, he begins receiving visits from the Django, a bizarre little creature who routinely triggers bouts of mischief and then promptly vanishes, leaving Jean to take the blame. After finally losing his temper and banishing the tiny imp, the boy finds that he misses its playful nature and feels guilty for speaking to it so harshly. The book, with its playfully conversational narrative voice, slew of invented words (“cozzler”, “smunch”, “grotsnobbler”), and rich, engaging watercolor illustrations, can be read on multiple levels. The story functions both as a freely imaginative celebration of the life of legendary Jazz musician Jean “Django” Reinhardt and as an account of visitation by an entity that may be either a supernatural creature or a child’s invention to buck responsibility for trouble he himself has in fact caused.

caption:
Home is a concept that holds many meanings. To some it is a place of birth, growth, life, and death. To some it is the relief of warmth, safety, and physical comfort. To some it is the promise of love and acceptance, a joyous and welcoming community. To some it is a reflection of identity, family, and culture. Some tableaux reflect snapshots of modern life, some contain echoes of bygone eras, and some evoke visual motifs of fantasy, folklore, and raw imagination. With a lively writing style and appealing gouache and ink illustrations, Ellis honors the nature and function of home and its meaning across time and space.

caption:
Sharks, so frequently depicted in popular media as malevolent, bestial killing machines, receive a sympathetic and even respectful portrayal worthy of their honored place in Hawaiian culture in Rafe Martin and @nodavid2018’s The Shark God. Two siblings rescue a shark tangled in a fishing line—evidence of their kind and caring nature. But a short while later they carelessly violate the law of their land by tapping on the drum of the king, who promptly locks them up and sentences them to death. Their frantic mother and father venture into the cavern of Kauhuhu the Shark God, who is moved by the children’s plight and their parents’ plea. He sends a great tidal wave and a massive shark to destroy the king’s palace and free the children; the family safely escapes and makes their way across the sea to a new island. Martin’s text includes Hawaiian words and phrases throughout: “mano” (“shark”), “kapu” (“sacred” or “forbidden”), “lele ka hoaka” (“the spirit has flown”). The rich, saturated colors of Shannon’s art heighten the beauty and spectacle of the story.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Martin explains in a detailed author’s note his history with this traditional Hawaiian tale. He encountered it first in Padraic Colum’s Legends of Hawaii, then became inspired to conduct deeper research after being invited to Hawaii’s Talking Island Storytelling Festival, and found a more complete rendition of the story (titled “Kauhuhu, the Shark God of Molokai”) in William Drake Westervelt’s Hawaiian Legends of Ghosts and Ghost-Gods. Martin’s adaptation alters numerous plot details of the source text, adding and removing characters and changing the ending to add a note of optimism, likely intended to appeal to younger readers. Both Martin and Shannon visited the Bishop Museum on Oahu to conduct cultural research in preparation for this book.

caption:
Loneliness—true, utter loneliness—is a prison. While escape may be difficult, all it takes is a single moment of possibility. For a touching example, take The House of Lost and Found by @martin.widmark and @emilia.dziubak. Niles lives alone. His wife has died and his children have moved. His house has fallen into disrepair. Even his cat has run away. All he has are his memories. One day, a neighbor boy knocks at the door; he and his family are about to leave for a vacation, and he wants Niles to take care of his potted plant, which has not yet sprouted. Unexpectedly, the plant’s presence sparks a new vitality in the old man, and he sets about cleaning and fixing up his house. His cat returns and his spirits brighten. By the time the boy returns, Niles is ready for friendship. Widmark’s prose, translated from Swedish by Polly Lawson, tells a story both tender and uplifting, bolstered by Dziubak’s rich, vivid colored-pencil artwork.

caption:
Opposites hold powerful sway in the minds of children—and in the mind of adults. We enjoy considering the relationship and connections between two contrasting characters, objects, or qualities. To that end, come browse through @annemargotramstein and @matthiasaregui’s Inside Outside. Each two-page spread shows a pair of illustrations depicting an enclosure from two perspectives: the interior and the exterior. The authors’ wordless digital art makes a strong graphic statement as we see the inside and outside of a duck egg, a cave of quartz crystals, a maiden’s castle prison, an aviary, an anthill, a fishing pond, a storm-tossed sailboat, a submarine, a beehive, a ski lodge, a transport truck driving through the desert, and an art museum that has just been burgled. Some of the spreads reveal startling events and illuminating juxtapositions: the apple a young woman is about to bite into has been tunneled through by a worm, a whale has swallowed a castaway on a raft, a dog occupies so much of the interior of its doghouse that it would be a giant if the house were blown up to human size, the heart in the body of a bungee jumper is beating uncontrollably, a castle that appears to be outdoors is in fact inside a snow globe, and a house that looks just like all the others in its suburban sprawl contains the eclectic decorations and souvenirs of an old man’s long and exciting life.

caption:
The book of the day is The Prince and the Mermaid, a magical tale by Ian Deuchar. After her clan shelters in a forest stream for the winter, a mermaid remains behind in the spring. When she sees a prince visiting the woods, she falls in love with him from afar and one day recites an incantation to transform herself into a human like him. When the young man brings his mysterious new bride to court, his childhood sweetheart grows bitter and vengeful; in her rage and despair, she employs the dark powers of a witch to sow doubt in the prince’s heart and sunder his happy relationship. With eloquent prose and appealing art, Deuchar spins a grand tale of joy, envy, and loss. Though the eponymous lovers are forever separated, the mermaid returns each month at the full moon to watch over her beautiful sleeping son.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the book’s front matter names as the source a story by thirteenth-century German writer Gottfried Von Strassburg, and also cites as an influence the earlier French folktale Mélusine and the Prince.

What would you do if a lifelong friend began to slip away from you and spend time with someone else? If they experienced heartbreak in their new relationship, would you be prepared to comfort them? Little Moon Dog by Helen Ward and Wayne Anderson turns on just such a compassionate decision. Originally published in the United Kingdom as simply “Moon Dog”, this book tells the tale of the Man in the Moon, whose peace is disrupted each year by the arrival of a rogue band of mysterious winged tourists. caption:
Another Fairy Tale Collection now commences—it’s time for Firebird Week! This sequence will be a little different from the ones that came before, as it is centered not on an specific plot but on a mythical beast. Firebirds appear not just in one tale type but in a number of different stories from Russia (replaced by analogous supernatural birds in variant tales from other cultures). I will therefore cover picture books adapted from several different Firebird stories throughout the week.

First, here is The Tale of the Firebird by Gennady Spirin. Tsarevich Ivan must journey throughout the land in search of the mysterious Firebird, helped along the way by a good-natured Baba Yaga (the wild witch of the forest in Russian folklore) and hindered by the villainous Koshchei the Deathless. Spirin’s resplendent illustrations capture the glory and adventure of the heightened fairy-tale setting.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this book is adapted from “Tsarevich Ivan, the Firebird, and the Gray Wolf”, a tale collected by Aleksandr Afanas’ev in Narodnye Russkie Skazki. Spirin takes the liberty of adding Baba Yaga and Koshchei, who do not appear in the original text—though they are included in many other well-known Russian tales.

Continuing into a new phase of Firebird Week, let us examine The Firebird by Robert D. San Souci and @kriswaldherr. Waldherr illustrates the narrative with a series of oil paintings executed over golden acrylic underpaintings on stretched, gessoed, and sanded paper. A note for folklore enthusiasts: this book retells the plot of the 1910 Russian ballet The Firebird, for which choreographer Mikhail Fokin and artist Alexandre Benois combined elements of several traditional tales to form a story honoring the breadth of Russian folk culture. Fokin and Benois may have taken their inspiration from “A Child’s Verse”, an 1844 poem by Yakov Polonsky containing references to both the Firebird and Koshchei.

caption:
A cleverly crafted verbal and visual experience is Henri’s Walk to Paris, written by Leonore Klein and illustrated by graphic designer Saul Bass. Henri lives in Reboul, a small city in France. One day, eager to experience city life in all its abundance, he sets out on foot for Paris. On the way, he lies down to take a nap and lays down a pencil with its tip pointing onward to remind him which way he was walking. While he is asleep, a bird picks up the pencil, carries it into the air, and drops it so that it lands pointing precisely backwards. When Henri wakes up, he follows the pencil’s direction, inadvertently retracing his steps. Arriving back in Reboul, he marvels at the similarities between his home town and what he believes to be Paris. Klein’s story rings with gentle humor and warmth. Bass interprets the story in a modern style with graphic shapes, strong patterns, and bold block colors.

If you have an elderly friend or relative whom you truly cherish, you know just how important even small acts of kindness can be. @ingridchabbert and @guridi___ know this too, and show us in their contemplative and moving book A Drop of the Sea. Ali lives at the edge of the desert with his great-grandmother, who is beginning to feel the pains of old age. One day, he asks her whether all her dreams in life have come true, and she reveals that she has always wished to see the ocean. Inspired, Ali undertakes the four-day round trip on foot to bring back a pail of seawater. By the time he reaches home, most of the water has evaporated, and only a few drops remain…but those are enough to lift the spirits of Ali’s great-grandmother and fulfill her dream at long last. caption:
What if you were completely and utterly alone, viewed as hopelessly obsolete? What if a companion suddenly came into your life and you were the only one who could help them? How much would you give to ensure your new friend’s survival? These are the daunting questions asked in The Robot and the Bluebird by David Lucas. The story opens in a futuristic and highly mechanized society. A robot, broken beyond repair, is tossed out and consigned to an enormous junk heap. There he sits, friendless and downcast, until the day company arrives: a bluebird, exhausted from its journey south to escape cold weather. The robot welcomes the poor bird into the hollow space where its heart ought to be, and even musters the last of its strength to carry the bird as far south as it needs to go. Just as it reaches a warmer climate, the robot wears down completely and comes to a standstill. The bird, in memory of its electronic friend’s extraordinary sacrifice, makes its home inside the cavity of the robot’s chest forever after. With touching language and warm cartoon-style illustrations, Lucas spins a captivating tale of sadness and hope.

A young woman named Ava pines for Marcello, but despairs of ever catching his attention. Vincent, Ava’s suitor, vows that he can give her the moon as a symbol of his love. Sure enough, he retrieves the moon, pulling it down to Ava’s window on a long string. The moon proceeds to carry Vincent and Ava up into the sky. Marcello grows despondent in Ava’s absence, and his sadness moves Ava to tears. One of her tears falls to earth, causing a seed to sprout into a miraculous tree overnight. Marcello carves this tree into an instrument resembling an oversized violin, which captivates everyone with its sonorous timbre. The birds begin to chirp Marcello’s name, but the listeners only hear “cello…cello…” giving rise to a new name for the string instrument. Galliez, whose text was translated from French by Susan Allen Maurin, uses ethereal romantic fantasy as the backdrop for a playful etiology of the violoncello (as noted in a brief foreword on the title page), while Delanssay provides luminous illustrations replete with blooming flowers and twinkling stars

caption:
The book of the day is an evocative wordless dream sequence: Damon Lehrer’s Rocket Boy. A young child sits in his room, sketching a rocket. To his surprise, the rocket comes to life, lifts off the page, and blasts out the window. Testing the limits of his newfound artistic powers, the boy draws a convertible car and a giant ramp leading out his window. He drives down the ramp, performed a jump off its upturned end, and flies into the mouth of an enormous pipe leading to another world. There, a mysterious girl shows him where his rocket has made a crash-landing. After executing a portrait of the girl, the boy attaches the rocket to the side of his car and drives back out of the pipe, through the night sky, into his house (whose roof miraculously opens on hinges to welcome him in), and directly back into a sheet of blank paper waiting on his bedroom floor. Suddenly, the boy awakens in his bed to discover that his entire adventure was merely a dream…or was it? Lehrer’s striking grayscale drawings represent the action of this strange nocturnal outing in powerful black and white.

caption:
One of the most fundamental psychological needs is to know oneself, to find one’s place in the world. Though it may be tempting to seek answers from others, true understanding must come from within. And so it goes in siblings Grace and Chong Chang’s Jin Jin the Dragon. After hatching out of a thousand-year-old egg, a golden creature begins to wonder just what sort of a being it is. A few nearby animals name the newborn creature Jin Jin, but a name is not enough to reveal its true identity, and so it sets off on a quest for self-discovery. Several beasts it encounters note hatchling’s similarity to themselves: Jin Jin has scales like the fish, talons like the eagle, a sinewy body like the snake, green eyes like the hare, pointed ears like the water buffalo, antlers like the deer, a tail like the lion, and a face like the camel. When a farmer seeks aid for his village, which is experiencing a drought, Jin Jin instinctively rises into the air and breathes an enormous plume of water over the village’s rice paddy. Thereafter, he has no doubt: he is most certainly a water dragon. Grace Chang weaves elements of Chinese culture, mythology, and writing into her endearing original tale; Chong Chang has used soft washes of Chinese watercolor to create his illustrations. The book contains an author’s note detailing the direct inspiration for the story, as well as notes on dragons in Chinese culture and on the history of the Chinese alphabet.

caption:
Today brings my four-hundredth book review! I’m thrilled to have had all of you as readers and commenters along the way. To mark the occasion, here is a look at something dark, delicious, frightening, and funny: The Tooth Gnashing Witch by Tina Meroto and Maurizio A. C. Quarello. Three brothers disobey their mother’s warning of a cannibalistic witch and stray into the woods. As the hour grows late, the boys arrive at a house, and an old woman invites them inside for supper. The oldest and middle brothers declare that she can’t be the witch, but the youngest realizes that everything feels a bit off. And just why is there a cage in the corner? Meroto’s text, based on a traditional tale and translated from Spanish by Mark. W Heslop, creates excitement and suspense with a grim scenario. After placing her characters in grave danger, she allows the youngest boy to rescue his older brothers with wit and humor, fooling the witch with cleverly feigned innocence. Quarello’s character design embraces exaggeration and distortion. His witch is a magnetically grotesque figure, her unsettling features revealed gradually over the course of numerous pages. Her stark hair, nose, and chin all stretch out into thorny spikes. Her breasts hang pendulously downwards. Her metal teeth are pointed like those of a shark. Hair sprouts from her upper lip and nostrils. Her house, too, holds weird and sinister contents, from magical objects to eldritch creatures to a pile of her victims’ bones.

caption:
For an appealing bit of historical fiction with more truth than meets the eye, pick up Blueberries for the Queen, written by husband and wife John and Katherine Paterson and illustrated by Susan Jeffers. William, a child living in Massachusetts during World War II, dearly wishes he were old enough to contribute to the war effort. When he learns that Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands has brought her family to America for safety and rented a nearby estate for the summer, he resolves to meet her. After gathering a basket of blueberries from his family’s field, he brings it to the grand house and presents it to the queen—an act he terms “peace work”. Jeffers renders William’s view of the world by depicting his extraordinary dreams, his moments of imagination, and his view of real events through a fantasy lens. The good will and earnest nature of a child in the face of wartime anxiety serve as the themes of this semi-autobiographical story, inspired by author John Paterson, who as a child really did bring blueberries to Queen Wilhelmina in the summer of 1942.

caption:
This week, I’ll be delving into an old German legend that has inspired fear and curiosity for generations: The Pied Piper of Hamelin.

To begin, let us consider a version originally written in German by Renate Raecke and illustrated by Lisbeth Zwerger. The people in the old German town of Hamelin have been overrun by rats. A man in pied, or multicolored, robes appears and offers to remove the rats in exchange for a large sum of money. The bargain is struck, and the rat-catcher plays a tune on a pipe that lures the rats out of the town and into the River Weser to drown. The people rejoice at being rid of the pests, but suddenly balk at paying the promised fee. In revenge, the Pied Piper begins to play a different tune on his pipe, a mysterious song that bewitches the children of the town, who follow him into a nearby mountain and are never seen again. Raecke retells this traditional tale with compelling language, accompanied by Zwerger’s haunting art, which depicts the events of the story with dramatic lighting and angles.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the most familiar telling of this legend comes from Kinder- und Hausmärchen by the Brothers Grimm, who state with striking specificity that the strange occurrence took place on June 26th, 1284.

There’s an even mix of cozy humor and starlit mystery permeating the pages of Maurice Sendak’s In the Night Kitchen. Mickey tumbles out of his bed and into an otherworldly plane rimmed by a skyline of buildings formed from everyday food objects, where a trio of bakers is busy preparing bread in a large oven. caption:
There’s a gently meditative quality to be found in Grandmother Thorn by @kidlitlove and @rebecca__hahn. This original tale opens in the fictional Shizuka village, a place of natural beauty and tranquility. Outside her house, Grandmother Thorn maintains a dry landscape garden, working diligently to rake the gravel and clip the trees and harshly rebuking anyone who disturbs her. Only one person meets with her approval: an old man known as Ojiisan (which translates to “grandfather”), who often brings sweets from the village and sits down with her to share a cup of tea. When a careless merchant drops a stray berry into Grandmother Thorn’s garden, a stubborn plant begins to sprout; no matter how hard she tries, she cannot rip it from the earth. As much from frustration as exhaustion, she falls ill. After a long rest, she returns to find that Ojiisan has cared for the garden in her absence. He presents her with the fruit of the little seedling, and Grandmother Thorn accepts it as a symbol of both his love and the value of serenity. Howes creates a distinctive parable, centered as it is on the quiet relationship between two elderly characters—a rarity in modern picture books. Hahn’s soothing hand-painted and -sewn collage art neatly and respectfully evokes the Japanese cultural setting of the work.

caption:
In the mood for a clever and thought-provoking character study? Voices in the Park by Anthony Browne just might hit the spot. The story’s distinctive structure depicts the events of a single afternoon in first-person narration from the utterly different perspectives of four characters, rendered in the illustrations as anthropomorphic apes. Charles and his mother leave their opulent home to walk their dog Victoria in the park. At the same time, Smudge and her father travel through their crowded urban neighborhood to bring their dog Albert to the very same park. The dogs immediately begin playing together, and the children soon find each other and spend an enjoyable afternoon together. Browne deliberately selects a nondescript slice of time in order to let his characters’ voices take center stage. The tone of his writing changes significantly with the shift from one narrator to the next. Charles’s patrician mother focuses on the trappings of wealth and status, while Smudge’s father is drained and dejected from a fruitless job search. Timid, lonely Charles recedes in the face of his mother’s haughty indifference, while Smudge exudes merriment and good cheer. The style of the art morphs to represent each character’s attitude toward the world around them, accompanied by subtle extra-textual details such as the typeface and illustration borders.

caption:
There’s a flavorful blend of fantasy, danger, and humor in Salt, a Russian folktale retold by Jane Langton from a translation by Alice Plume and illustrated by Ilse Plume. Ivan is regarded as a fool by all those around him—not least his merchant father, who provides Ivan’s two older brothers with valuable goods to sell abroad but sends Ivan off with only a boatload of wooden spoons. After discovering a marvelous mountain of salt on an island in the middle of the ocean, the young man successfully trades with a foreign tsar for great riches and the hand of his daughter in marriage. However, when his envious brothers betray him, he must enlist the aid of an enormous giant to reach home and reclaim both his fortune and his bride. Langton’s narrative voice and Plume’s jocund watercolor drawings pair delightfully in service of a compelling and enjoyable adventure.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: on the title page, the author lists the source of this tale as Narodnye Russkie Skazki by Aleksandr Afanas’ev.

Elsie Times Eight, an original tale written and illustrated by Natalie Babbitt, blends fantasy and farce in equal measure. The giddy machinations of her hard-of-hearing fairy godmother cause young Elsie to be multiplied into eight identical versions of herself, much to her Mama and Papa’s consternation. Babbitt accompanies her madcap plotline with lighthearted illustrations that foreground the comedy and sheer absurdity of the situation.

caption:
The book of the day is @evanturkart’s The Storyteller, an original narrative replete with wisdom and heart. In the ancient Kingdom of Morocco, the fountains have run dry and the storytellers have lost their place in the hearts of the people. A thirsty young boy encounters an old storyteller who over the course of several days unfolds a mysterious and recursive tale: the old man tells the boy of a girl, a blind woman, and a marvelous bird; the blind woman tells the girl of a weaver, an enigmatic stranger, and a skein of fantastical yarn; the stranger tells the weaver of her odyssey in the desert as a young runaway bride. Each time the old man finishes speaking for the day, the boy’s cup has miraculously filled with water. When the kingdom is threatened by an enormous sandstorm incarnated as a fearsome djinn, the boy uses the power of the old man’s story to return water to the fountains and save the people from ruin. Turk’s language dances and sparkles, rich imagery and captivatingly tactile similes enlivening his unique story-within-a-story-within-a-story structure. His avant-garde illustrations create expressionistic tableaux through lively contour drawings, eye-popping geometric designs, and myriad other techniques.

caption:
Let’s have another theme week, shall we? It’s time to begin exploring an ancient tale of magic and marvels: Sleeping Beauty.

To begin, here is an adaptation retold and illustrated by Trina Schart Hyman. The language sings with a clear and elegant phrasing. The illustrations flow with a delicate movement, particularly in strands of hair, folds of fabric, and wisps of candle smoke. The fairies are an ethereal bunch, adorned with head scarves, wreaths, and butterfly wings. The oldest fairy, however, sports a sinister hooded cloak, a snarl of occult necklaces, and a tall wooden cane. The book’s most frightening tableau is surely the briar hedge surrounding the sleeping castle, filled with the countless skeletons of would-be heroes who have become ensnared and starved to death.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Hyman mixes and matches details from versions of “Dornröschen” (“Little Thorn-Rose”) appearing in multiple editions of the Grimms’ Kinder- und Hausmärchen. The magical invitees to the royal feast are “fairies”, a translation of the German “Feen”, a word that only appears in the original 1812 publication (in the second edition the Grimms replaced it with “weisen Frauen”, or “wise women”, in an effort to remove perceived French influence from their stories). However, the animal that predicts the queen’s coming pregnancy in Hyman’s book is a frog, which did not appear until the third edition of 1837 (in the first two editions the clairvoyant creature is a crab).

caption:
Continuing with Sleeping Beauty Week, I’m looking through this appealing version by Margaret Early, whose dramatic text and illustrations (executed in oils on synthetic canvas and augmented with gold paint) create an air of antique refinement. The wicked fairy, with her sharp claws, snaggletooth, warty nose, and lazy eye, stands in grotesque contrast to her dainty sistren (though she shares their diaphanous wings).

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Early has based her retelling on “La Belle au Bois Dormant” (“The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood”) from Charles Perrault’s Histoires ou Contes du Temps Passé, published in 1697. Notably, the number of fairies here is seven, with the wicked fairy making eight (in the Grimms’ variant, they are twelve with the wicked fairy making thirteen). As reference for her illustrations of the royal castle, she cites the Château d’Ussé in the Loire Valley, the very building from which Charles Perrault is said to have drawn inspiration for the castle in his immortal fairy tale.

caption:
Sleeping Beauty Week moves steadily ahead, and next up is a version by Jane Yolen and Ruth Sanderson. Yolen’s graceful prose draws readers irresistibly through the enchantment and dark drama of the story. Sanderson’s oil paintings, created from reference photos of costumed models, shine with rich colors and a striking contrast between light and shadow.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Yolen has adapted the plot from the Brothers Grimm, keeping the heroine’s name Briar Rose and the number of fairies at the royal feast thirteen. The messenger who informs the queen that she is with child, instead of a crab or frog, is a fairy as well. Notably, upon seeing that the princess has pricked her finger, the old spinning woman gives “a high wicked laugh”, suggesting that she is in fact the thirteenth fairy in disguise—a detail not present in the original tale but invented by  Pyotr Ilych Tchaikovsky for his 1890 ballet Sleeping Beauty.

caption:
Here we lie at the center of Sleeping Beauty Week, and for your enjoyment I’ve got a sumptuous adaptation written by husband-and-wife team Mahlon F. and Kinuko Y. Craft. Both text and illustrations shine with a stately elegance. Mahlon Craft’s language captures the charm, grandeur, and wonder of the antique fairy tale setting. Kinuko Craft’s marvelous paintings, achieved through an application of oil over watercolor on illustration board, glow with jewel-bright color; of particular note is her depiction of the wicked fairy, who appears in the grand palace hall as a menacing, smoke-black wraith and advances on the king and queen like an unholy storm cloud.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the source of this book’s text is identifiably the Brothers Grimm, based on the frog foretelling the queen’s pregnancy and the thirteen fairies. However, several elements signal the influence of the Tchaikovsky ballet. The old spinning woman is explicitly identified as the wicked fairy lying in wait to ensnare the princess, a dramatic beat first used by Tchaikovsky. Moreover, the princess herself is called Aurora, a name not found in any version of the tale prior to Tchaikovsky—except in Charles Perrault’s 1697 text in which Aurora is the name the princess gives to the daughter born to her after she awakens from her slumber.

caption:
Onward we press through Sleeping Beauty Week, though examining and contrasting this many versions of a single story can feel as difficult as struggling through a snarl of thorny briars. Today we have a handsome adaptation by @adelegeras and Christian Birmingham. Geras adds a good deal of flavor and intrigue to the traditional tale, fleshing out the plot with lyrical descriptive language to create her own singular vision, while Birmingham’s dazzling art brings a lush visual drama to the proceedings.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the wicked fairy takes a place of unusual prominence in this version, with Geras bestowing on her the original name Skura. Here she keeps bats, ravens, and wolves as familiars, and she appears to possess the power to turn into a little gray cat. While she fulfills the villainous role demanded by the fairy tale plot, she receives a good deal of focus and characterization, enough perhaps to be viewed by some readers as the story’s protagonist.

caption:
Just as all dreams melt away with morning’s light, so must the enchantment of Sleeping Beauty Week come to an end. But here is one last morsel of magic for you, in the form of an adaptation illustrated by John Collier. The text is taken directly from the French of Charles Perrault, while the scratched lines and muted colors of Collier’s illustrations accord the tale a stark, quiet severity.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This version, unique among Sleeping Beauty picture books, preserves the second half of Charles Perrault’s 1697 fairy tale “La Belle au Bois Dormant” (“The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood”), usually excised from retellings for its startling content. After the princess awakens, journeys to the prince’s castle, and bears him two children, the queen mother (an ogress) begins to reveal a sinister, cannibalistic appetite. While the prince is away at war, she demands that the royal cook slaughter first the daughter, then the son, and finally Sleeping Beauty herself and serve them to her for dinner; only through the cook’s kindness and bravery are the three innocents hidden away and spared. After discovering the deception, the ogress queen condemns her daughter-in-law and grandchildren to die in a vat of toads and vipers. However, the prince arrives at home just in time, and his mother, enraged at being thwarted yet again, throws herself into the deadly tub and is devoured.

caption:
Have you read Elsa and the Night by @jonsmellgren? If not, now’s your chance. What would you do if you discovered a physical incarnation of darkness lurking in your home? Though such a situation might sound frightening, Elsa takes it in stride, shutting the Night up in a tin and hiding it in the boiler room. However, once she realizes that the world is trapped in permanent daylight, she has a change of heart and lets the little blob out again. She tells the creature of her time working in the galley of a boat, of the shipwreck that stranded her on a remote island with only an elephant named Olaf for company, and of her years operating the island’s lighthouse, which left her afflicted with insomnia. The two go for a walk, the Night growing bigger with every step, until it is able to carry Elsa, who, after unburdening herself, can finally rest. Mellgren’s text (originally published in Swedish as “Sigrid och Natten” and translated into English by Anita Shenoi) provides exposition through gentle observations and subtle details, most notably Elsa’s subdued grief for her long-dead elephant friend. The illustrations accompanying this whimsically introspective tale feature graphic art in bold, block colors, warm yellows and oranges contrasting with cool blues and purples against blank white backgrounds.

caption:
If you’re looking for a lighthearted and unpredictable adventure, Chris Van Allsburg’s Probuditi! is an irresistible tale that explores the perils of tampering with forces beyond one’s understanding and control. For his birthday present, Calvin’s mother gives him two tickets to a magic show. He and his best friend Rodney sit amazed as Lomax the Magnificent hypnotizes a volunteer from the audience and makes her behave like a chicken. Inspired, the boys assemble a homemade mesmerism device to implant the suggestion into Calvin’s younger sister Trudy that she is a dog. Too late do they recall that the magician ended the hypnotic spell with a specific mysterious word. Having forgotten this word, the two friends must figure out an alternate method of bringing Trudy out of her canine trance. With engaging prose and vivid, sepia-toned art, Van Allsburg tells an entertaining story whose twist ending may leave readers turning back to reexamine and reevaluate the character dynamics from start to finish.

caption:
Here’s a tale that warns of the peril of rushing to judgment and celebrates the virtue of loyalty and devotion: Lynn Cullen and Laurel Long’s The Mightiest Heart. Llewelyn, prince of the Welsh region of Snowdonia, spends the days of his youth with Gelert, a faithful dog who remains constantly at his side. Years pass, and the monarch grows up, marries, and has a son. One night, Llewelyn discovers Gelert in the nursery with blood on his muzzle; believing for a terrible instant that the dog has killed his child, he drives his pet away in rage. Though he soon finds the baby alive and realizes that Gelert fought off a hungry wolf, it is too late: the noble hound is gone. Much time goes by before the two friends meet again in a brief but tender reunion. Though it is too late for Llewelyn and Gelert to regain the friendship they once shared, the king now possesses hard-won wisdom to pass on to his growing son. Cullen crafts a tender and emotionally affecting story, while Long provides oil paintings whose regal beauty perfectly suit the medieval setting.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Cullen has adapted her tale from an old legend of Llewelyn ab Iorwerth (also known as Llewelyn the Great), a thirteenth-century ruler of Wales. In the traditional story, rather than driving Gelert away, Llewelyn kills him outright. Once he realizes his mistake, the king buries his dog with great honor and ceremony. To this day, a burial mound stands as a tourist attraction in the village of Beddgelert (the name meaning “Gelert’s grave”).

caption:
Can you recall the feeing of being a child trapped inside on a rainy day? Perhaps you grew bored. Perhaps you stared out the window, fearing you’d be trapped inside forever. Perhaps your mind began to wander and you discovered something unexpected, something secret, something delightful. This experience forms the essence of Barbara Lehman’s Rainstorm. A young boy in a grand house by the sea, eager to pass the time until the weather clears up, discovers a key. With it, he unlocks a chest concealing a hole in the floor, climbs down a ladder, and finds himself in a secret tunnel under the earth. He follows the passage to its end, climbs a spiral staircase, and finds himself atop a lighthouse on an island near the coast. He meets a group of children who live on the island, leading to a day of carefree wonder and the beginnings of a lasting friendship. In her wordless narrative, Lehman employs watercolor, gouache, and ink to craft a comic-style story that merges slice-of-life vignettes with quiet hints of intrigue and mystery.

caption:
What a resoundingly lovely book is Abiyoyo, a Bantu folktale and lullaby retold by Pete Seeger and illustrated Michael Hays. A father and son unwisely provoke the ire of their neighbors. The boy constantly plays the ukulele, irritating the adults around him. The father owns a magic wand with which he can cause things to vanish into thin air, but he uses his incredible power to play obnoxious practical jokes, relieving acquaintances of their tools, furniture, and food. At their wits’ end, the people finally expel the father and son from their village. However, soon afterward, a giant named Abiyoyo, long thought to be a figment of lore, appears and starts devouring every living thing in his path. As the rest of the town cowers in fear, it is up to the two outcasts to tire the monster out with an irresistible ukukele tune and make him disappear with a flick of the wand. Now hailed as heroes, they happily rejoin their community. Seeger’s language, deeply respectful of the South African source material, shines with the potency of oral storytelling, his lively sentences marked by magnetic phrases such as, “One day, one day, the sun rose blood red over the hill.” Hays sets the tale in a world seemingly out of time, with the town populated by people of all races and ethnicities dressed in the fashion of many disparate regions and periods, from saris to kimonos, from Stetsons to yarmulkes. Contrasting with this colorful bunch is the grotesque appearance of the eponymous giant himself, squat, craggy, lumbering, and disheveled. Together, the two artists craft a remarkable story that celebrates magic, danger, and the loving bond between father and son.

When a soothsayer predicts his reign over the Land of the Seven Caves will be undone by a Painted Fan, Lord Shang commands all fans in the realm to be burned. caption:
As you read Anthea Bell’s translation of the Brothers Grimm tale The Six Servants, illustrated by Sergei Goloshapov. A wicked enchantress queen assigns impossible tasks to any suitors who seek the hand of her beautiful daughter in marriage; when the men inevitably fail, she gleefully beheads them. One young prince decides to try his luck and sets out for the queen’s city. On his way, he encounters an enormous man with an insatiable appetite, a man with giant ears that allow him to hear anything in the world, a man with inordinately long legs, a man whose powerful stare can shatter anything before him, a man who experiences heat as cold and cold as heat, and a man with sharp eyes that can see across huge distances. Each of these six men agrees to be the prince’s servant, and each has a crucial role to play in fulfilling the evil queen’s three befuddling tasks: retrieve a ring she once dropped in the Red Sea, consume three hundred oxen (skin, bone, hair, horns, and all) and three hundred barrels of wine in a night, and keep watch over the princess despite a sleeping spell. Bell sticks closely to the Grimms’ language and phrasing, while Goloshapov represents the marvelous servants’ anatomic irregularities with charmingly grotesque distortion in his watercolor, gouache, and ink art.

caption:
There’s a quiet comfort to the atmosphere of @juliefogliano and @erinestead’s If You Want to See a Whale. The book comprises a set of instructions for whale watching, replete with warnings to avoid distractions from various animals and objects nearby. Of course, these competing elements offer their own distinct tactile pleasures, and only after running through them all is the question of spotting a whale finally addressed. Fogliano’s delicate prose poetry shines with the effortless application of rhetorical devices such as repetition (“and time for waiting/and time for looking/and time for wondering”), alliteration (“sleeping eyes can’t watch for whales/and whales won’t wait for watching”), and chiasmus (“things that are smaller than most small things”). Stead’s art accentuates the pensive quality of the text with its soft, faded colors and freely drawn lines.

caption:
Each time I read @audreywoodauthor and Don Wood’s The Napping House, I’m struck by the skillful craftsmanship of the married co-creators’ verbal and visual storytelling. Audrey Wood’s delightfully engaging text emulates the form of a cumulative nursery rhyme, each page introducing a new object or character—first the eponymous napping house itself, then a cozy bed, then a snoring granny, then a dreaming child, then a dozing dog, then a snoozing cat, then a slumbering mouse. Each one climbs on top of the last, creating a large, somnolent pile. Finally, a wakeful flea (which sharp-eyed readers may spot in advance) bites the mouse, setting off a raucous chain reaction in which each character jostles, disturbs, or agitates the one below and they all go flying giddily around the room. Don Wood’s art brilliantly draws form from the content of the writing. The bedroom starts out in a muted palate of soft blues as the rain patters down outside the window, but gradually shifts to bright, saturated yellows as the characters wake up and sunlight streams in. Mirroring the shift in weather, the inanimate objects take on a certain personality, wooden chair and bed drooping with sleepy energy. Moreover, with each page turn the perspective of the illustrations subtly shifts upward from a side view of the room, to almost a bird’s-eye view at the moment of the flea’s climactic bite, and then back again. Here is a book perfect for going to sleep with, for waking up to, and for all moments in between.

caption:
Take a gander at @paulowenlewis’s mysterious and captivating Frog Girl, a companion to his earlier work Storm Boy. A chief’s young daughter ventures beneath a lake to a land of sentient, humanoid frogs. The leader of the community is bemoaning the loss of her brood, captured and taken away by human boys. The wrath of Grandmother Frog ignites a volcano, whose eruption sparks a forest fire that threatens to burn down the girl’s village. However, after the girl finds the stolen frogs and returns them to their home under the lake, the rains put out the fires, the village is saved, and the girl tells her people of her newfound kinship with their amphibian neighbors. Written under the guidance of a cultural advisor, and with a portion of its proceeds having been donated to the Haida Gwaii Rediscovery program for tribal youth, the story combines folkloric motifs from the Haida, Tlingit, and other native tribes of the Pacific Northwest and draws inspiration from Joseph Campbell’s template of the “hero’s journey”. Lewis’s illustrations honor the tradition of Pacific Northwest art in their depiction of both the mundane and the supernatural.

caption:
For a touching story that encapsulates the beauty of play, the sting of misfortune, and the consoling relief of family, look no further than Float by @danielmiyaresdoodles. After a family member makes him a paper boat out of folded newspaper, a young boy heads outside to play. Raindrops begin to fall, but he has come prepared with a bright yellow rain slicker, and he delights himself jumping in puddles and exploring rivulets. When he lets the paper vessel drift too far, however, it rushes away in the current, falls into a storm drain, and is washed out into a nearby river. The boy trudges home dejectedly, his spirits as damp and drooping as his beloved boat. However, a family member—no doubt the same one who fashioned the little craft in the first place—is waiting with a healing embrace, a mug of hot chocolate, and another newspaper ready to fold. In his wordless narrative, Miyares skillfully conveys action, tone, and palpable emotion. Against a backdrop of subtle grayscale, his digital illustrations employ only three colors: soft cyan and faded pink, for images visible amid the print of the newspaper, and bright yellow for the raincoat. As the boy heads out once more in the book’s final pages, clutching his newly folded paper airplane, the rain is gone and the yellow has migrated outward to fill the joyfully glowing sky.

Come and rediscover your sense of enchantment and delight with @angelamcallisterbooks and Grahame Baker-Smith’s Leon and the Place Between. Leon and his siblings sit in a tent at a traveling carnival, waiting to be amazed by a magic show. After a troupe of jugglers and a pack of mechanical toys, out steps the magician Abdul Kazam, who performs a suite of miracles. The master conjured asks for a member of the audience to step into a mysterious box, and Leon volunteers. Once through the door, he finds himself in the Place Between, an eldritch zone that serves as a nexus where the people, animals, and objects made to disappear by all stage magicians linger until they are recalled to the ordinary world. Leon returns safe and sound, but with his eyes opened to a new dimension of reality. McAllister’s language soars with wonder and excitement, and Baker-Smith’s digital montage illustrations create a fitting air of circus theatricality.
