caption:
Let’s flip through the effortlessly charming and insightful I’m Not Bobby by Jules Feiffer. Bobby is getting called by his mother. But Bobby doesn’t want to go. The text of the book consists of his inner monologue as he scurries impishly away from his family and his home, imagining himself alternatively as various creatures too fearsome to confront and vehicles too swift to catch. At the same time, hand lettering in the illustrations themselves conveys his mother’s mounting exasperation as she shouts at Bobby, gives up in disgust and shuts the door. Finally, once Bobby has a chance to catch his breath, he realizes he is hungry and returns to the house, but on his own terms: as a lion pretending to be Bobby. With striking accuracy and a wicked sense of humor, Feiffer deftly captures children’s use of fantasy play for comfort, escape, and power, as well as their ability to step back and forth between the pretend role and their own mundane identity. His zany art, characterized by loose, energetic line, explores the broad strokes and fine shades of Bobby’s emotions throughout.

caption:
The book of the day is The Fifth and Final Sun, an Aztec creation myth adapted and illustrated by C. Shana Greger. In a primordial time, the earth is dim, lit only by the White Evening Star God until she bursts after a pointed insult from Tezcatlipoca, The God of the Night. After that, Tezcatlipoca himself becomes the first sun, followed by a succession of gods: Quetzalcoatl, God of the Wind, then Tlalloc, God of Rain, Thunder, and Lightning, then Tlalloc’s wife Chalchihuitlicue, Goddess of the Waters, and finally the humble Nanautzin, known as the Scabby-Pimply one. Greger’s retelling conveys the scale and spectacle of the clashes of the gods, and her art dazzles with dynamic composition and glowing, saturated color.

Humble Pie, written by Jennifer Donnelly and illustrated by Stephen Gammell is a jocular and fanciful look at the depths of one child’s insolence and the lengths to which one family member will go to transform his attitude. Theo’s grows up in a family with loving parents who give him everything his heart desires. However, unappreciative of their doting and fawning, he develops into an obstreperously behaved child. One day, his grandmother chants a magic spell and traps him into an enormous pie. Theo rolls this way and that, but nobody can understand his pleas for assistance. He finally escapes and returns home a contrite and dutiful son, having eaten “humble pie”. Donnelly’s merry wit makes for a thoroughly entertaining read, with Gammell contributing frenetically speckled and splattered illustrations.

caption:
In honor of the amazing @jerrypinkneystudio, let’s explore his work in collaboration with author Patricia C. McKissack in Mirandy and Brother Wind. It is spring, and the community of Ridgetop prepares to hold its traditional cakewalk dance. Mirandy, powerfully excited to attend, wishes she could bring Brother Wind as her partner. When her Ma Dear relates an old saying that whoever catches the wind can make him do their bidding, Mirandy sets out to do just that. She receives tidbits of advice from various acquaintances around the county, including a good-natured local boy named Ezel, whose reputation for clumsiness has made him an unlikely candidate to dance with anyone at all. Finally, quite by chance, Mirandy successfully traps Brother Wind in her barn and prepares to summon him as her partner at the cakewalk. However, when she hears Ezel being mocked behind his back, she has a change of heart, and chooses to dance with him instead. Whether their preternaturally light and graceful steps are the result of their own effort or the mystical influence of Brother Wind is left for the reader to decide. McKissack’s winning narrative in African-American dialect makes for an delightful read. Pinkney’s illustrations are a triumph, with each full-page spread chock full of energy and expressive emotion. Particularly enchanting is his lively depiction of Brother Wind as an elegant, jovial spirit in transparent blue, cyan, and gray. May we all dance with such magic in our step. Rest in peace, Mr. Pinkney.

caption:
The Legend of the Persian Carpet by Tomie dePaola and Claire Ewart provides wisdom and delight in equal measure. Of all his precious possessions, King Balash of Persia most prizes an enormous diamond that refracts light into dazzling rainbows. The overly trusting ruler leaves the jewel unguarded and open for public viewing. One day, tragedy strikes: a thief steals the diamond. While riding away on horseback, he accidentally drops it and shatters it into a thousand fragments. Without the diamond’s light, the palace is filled with somber shadows. When a young apprentice weaver named Payam discovers the shards lying on the rocky plane, the king resolves to abandon his royal duties and spend his days sitting and gazing at the twinkling pile. In an effort to pull him out of his stupor, the enterprising boy organizes his fellow textile workers to create a vast carpet that replicates the chromatic beauty of the wondrous gem, and the monarch’s spirits are finally lifted. DePaola, in his first collaboration with an illustrator, adapts a Persian legend associated with a famed sixteenth-century Mamluk carpet. In preparation for her warmly colored illustrations, Ewart spent time studying Persian miniaturists and traveled to witness and gain an understanding of traditional Persian architecture and textile production.

caption:
What does it mean to be a small part of a larger whole? Though we often feel like the protagonists of our own stories, it can be humbling to remember that countless others out there are having experiences both similar to and different from our own at any given time. Here and Now by @juliadenos and @ebgoodale explores the universality of such an instant, detailing all of the phenomena constantly taking place around the world. Denos’s text unfolds in elegantly simple vignettes, moving deftly from one observation to another. Along the way, she gently examines everyday contrasts (the tiny work of ants and the great motion of planets) and comparisons (the growth of muscles and the growth of figures). Goodale’s illustrations, made with ink, watercolor, monoprinting, and digital collage, incorporate engaging visual devices: cutaway drawings reveal underground activity, outlines placed within a landscape suggest the spirituality of human presence, and a book-within-a-book creates “mise en abyme” (a recursive sequence in which an image contains a smaller copy of itself which in turn contains an even smaller copy, shrinking towards infinity). Though each page depicts a mundane event, the cumulative effect of their presentation invites us to slow down and mindfully regard them as interconnected pieces of a wondrous cosmic snapshot.

caption:
Once again October has cast its delightfully dark shadow upon the landscape of my imagination. As I did last year, I’ll be counting down the seven days leading up to Halloween with a sequence of scary picture books. This first one, Eve Bunting and Susan Meddaugh’s In the Haunted House, begins with an austere Victorian home surrounded by a grove of barren trees. Bunting’s energetic rhyming couplets beckon us inside to meet a delightful cadre of fearsome creatures: ghosts, witches, bats, a mummy, a skeleton, a vampire, a werewolf, Frankenstein’s monster, and other ghouls and creepy-crawlies. Meddaugh’s spooky pencil-and-watercolor art depicts only the feet of the two humans taking their tour of the eerie house. In brief interludes throughout, the adult comforts the child and offers to leave early. In a wordless sequence at the conclusion, however, it emerges that the parent was the one frightened all along—while the child is ready to go back for more.

Here’s the second entry in my seven days of Halloween: There’s a Nightmare in My Closet by Mercer Mayer. A young boy’s bedtime is plagued by a persistent nightmare. However, this nightmare is not a somnolent experience but rather an oversized, wrinkly, spotted goblin. One night, the boy catches the grotesque creature tiptoeing toward him across the room and switches on his bedside lamp. In the glare of the light, the nightmare instantly becomes passive and doleful, bursting into tears at a well-timed blast from a toy pop gun. The boy then takes pity on the nightmare and welcomes it into his bed to calm down and go to sleep. But what’s that peeking out of the closet now? With short, punchy sentences and merry cross-hatched drawings, Mayer creates a whimsical and emotionally layered guide to facing and accepting nighttime fears.

This horror-themed counting book presents one scarecrow, two toads, three jack-o-lanterns, four owls, five bats, six witches, seven ghosts, eight cats, nine skeletons, and ten mice. caption:
Halfway through Halloween Week, my excitement for the day itself continues to grow. Lest we fall prey to our eagerness and rush too quickly ahead, have a look at Susan Hill and Angela Barrett’s quietly chilling Beware Beware. As her mother prepares food at the hearth, a young girl peers out of the window at the nearby woods, wondering what hides among the trees. Soon, the lure of the unknown proves too great and she slips unnoticed out the door and treads over the freshly fallen snow towards the forest. Though at first she marvels at her experience in nature, her wonder soon turns to dread as she perceives dangerous and evil creatures lurking in the shadows. She flees home to her mother’s warm embrace, but a shard of curiosity still remains. In place of a traditional narrative, Hill unfolds the plot in impressionistic verse, rhythmic lines of dimeter following the girl’s stream of consciousness. Barrett’s alluring pencil-and-watercolor art pulls us from the cozy hearth out into the dark, wild unknown before returning us safely home.

caption:
As Halloween inches closer, spooky scenarios steal into my imagination. For example, have you ever been convinced of impending doom but been unable to persuade those around you? What would be worse? Being wrong…or being right? Moreover, what to do when the bell tolls and disaster strikes? Just ask the young protagonist of @neilhimself and @davemckeanhourglass’s The Wolves in the Walls. Lucy begins to hear strange noises around her house. Strange and inexplicable noises. Noises that start to convince her that there are wolves in the walls. She tries to tell her mother, her father, and her brother, but no one (other than her trusty pig puppet) seems to believe her—though they all casually refer to the sinister adage, “If the wolves come let of the walls, it’s all over,” without elaborating. And then, one day, the wolves do indeed come out of the walls, forcing the family to flee into the garden. Though the other three are perfectly happy to take up residence elsewhere, Lucy leads them on a charge to take back their home and oust the lupine invaders. Gaiman’s writing strikes a balance between humor and fear, mining deeply bizarre energy from the heightened premise. McKean’s mixed-media collages, a combination of hand drawing, photography, and digital technique, create a wildly expressionistic tone that aptly complements the darkly quirky text.

caption:
With Halloween nearly upon us, I’m reveling in the grotesque horror of Wee Winnie Witch’s Skinny by Virginia Hamilton and Barry Moser. James Lee knows enough about witch lore to know that his Uncle Big Anthony, who lives next door, is the target of a witch—or, as his Mama Jo puts it, a Wee Winnie. Each night, the fell creature hangs up her skin on the wall, bridles the helpless man, and rides him in an eerie gallop through the sky. She even snatches James Lee out of his house and carries him right along with her. Fortunately, Uncle Big Anthony’s mother-in-law, Mama Granny, comes to the rescue by sprinkling her homemade spice-hot pepper witch-be-gone potion into the hanging skin. When Wee Winnie slips her skin back on, the potion causes her to shrivel up and crack into pieces, which Mama Jo and Mama Granny summarily burn in the hearth. James Lee, though he was certainly afraid of the witch, looks back on his mysterious ride with unabashed pleasure. Hamilton’s writing beautifully conveys the characters’ voices and emphasizes the eldritch terror of the ordeal, particularly in this chilling passage: “The Wee Winnie slowly turned and looked over at James Lee. She must’ve heard him. She took off her bald head and swung it from side to side in Uncle Big Anthony’s window! Her eyes glowed, like the triangles in a candlelit pumpkin.” Moser’s bold, dramatic wood engravings capture both the familiar and the uncanny in the narrative.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: for her original narrative, Hamilton drew inspiration from an array of folk beliefs across the African diaspora about witches removing their skin and riding victims at night.

caption:
And, just like that, Halloween is upon us. Come celebrate with me as I relax and enjoy this picture book adaptation of Harry Behn’s classic children’s poem Halloween, with illustrations by Greg Couch. Three rollicking stanzas detail the devilish doings of strange creatures making merry in the dark. Behn’s language employs internal rhyme (“Tonight is the night/When dead leaves fly/Like witches on switches/Across the sky”) and iambic rhythm (“When ghoul and ghost/And goblin host/Dance round their queen./It’s Halloween!”) to draw the reader into a world of mischief and magic. Behn’s accompanying pastel-textured art presents three child characters in costume as a devil, a witch, and a skeleton encountering the horde of monsters, befriending them with an exchange of candy, and joining them in a raucous supernatural bacchanal. Happy Halloween.

caption:
On each page of If… by Sarah Perry you’ll find pensive prompts for strange and otherworldly hypotheticals. Each page gives an image that juxtaposes two unlikely objects or concepts, ranging from concretely peculiarities “If worms had wheels…” to abstract philosophy “If ugly were beautiful…” Perry’s art brings these wild, impossible moments to life, her soft textures and bright colors affording them a gently natural quality.

caption:
In @movingbookpress’s Palazzo Inverso you’ll find engaging tribute to the work of famed Dutch graphic artist Maurits Cornelis Escher. Mauk, apprentice to a master builder, hastens to work. Everything seems to be going wrong on the construction of the grand palazzo—workers falling, water spilling upward, towers built upside-down..or is it downside-up? Only when Mauk (who is not allowed to draw, only to sharpen pencils) reveals that he turned the palazzo’s architectural plans around while his master was napping are the mysteries revealed. The boy then scampers cheekily away away, using his knowledge of the building’s odd geometry to evade capture. Johnson’s playful text and grayscale mixed-media illustrations draw inspiration from the content of Escher’s celebrated lithographs, woodcuts, and mezzotints. The book’s clever design (the last page instructs the reader to rotate the book and follow upside-down text back toward the beginning) allows the images to be recontextualized in new dimensions, much like the gripping mathematical strangeness of Escher’s art. Even the protagonist serves as a symbol: his peaked cap and spritely gait echo the figure from Escher’s 1938 print “Cycle”, and his name is taken from Escher’s nickname in life: Mauk.

To top it all off, the boy sneaks his beloved cloud companion home in his overcoat. In Wiesner’s remarkable wordless narrative, the comic-book-style panel sequences convey dynamic action and gentle humor, while the full-page spreads radiate both a cinematic scale and a deeply human warmth.

caption:
Let me entertain you with The Fisherman & His Wife, a Brothers Grimm adaptation with art by John Howe. An old married couple lives in a tiny hut by the sea. One day the man, fishing for supper, catches a flounder and finds to his surprise that it can talk. Awed by the creature’s miraculous ability, he returns it to the water. His wife, however, angrily orders him to take advantage of the situation by returning to the water and asking the magical creature to change their hut into a cottage. The flounder obliges, and the wife proceeds to issue a series of increasingly outlandish demands: she wants to live in a castle, then she wants to be king, then emperor, then pope. Finally, she insists on becoming a god, with power over the rising of the sun and moon. With that as the last straw, the fish strips the couple of all their marvelous possessions and leaves them sitting in the hut where they started. With sweeping tableaux and dramatic compositions, Howe creates a sense of grandeur in his illustrations. He playfully depicts the fisherman as growing smaller and smaller in the face of his domineering wife, who in turn looms larger and larger with all the power she amasses.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this edition, like most English translations of the tale, tastefully labels the initial dwelling a “hut”. However, the German term used by the Brothers Grimm, “pisputt”, would be directly calqued as the memorably earthy “piss pot”.

caption:
Can we ever truly understand someone else’s perspective when we lack the context of their experiences? And, if we can successfully see through the eyes of another, will we be enlightened, our consciousness expanded, or will we merely grow frustrated at what we glimpse but cannot touch? Leo Lionni’s classic story Fish Is Fish just might hold an answer within. A minnow and a tadpole live together in a pond, sharing a close friendship. Eventually, they grow into a fish and a frog. The frog, using its legs, clambers up out of the water and returns with tales of birds, cows, and humans. The fish listens to the extraordinary tale, picturing each land denizen with piscine characteristics, and later decides to leap onto the bank and experience life above. The poor creature of course cannot breathe outside the lake and is rescued only by the timely arrival of the amphibious frog. Lionni’s straightforward writing style and cheerily colorful art celebrate the values of friendship, imagination, and self-understanding.

She rehearses an act with the master and his goose, cat, and sow, and after many months the troupe enters the circus. As they begin their performance, Kashtanka hears the excited shouts of her former owners in the audience. Reunited, dog and humans leave together in happiness. Spirin’s elegant treatment of the story brings beauty and lively energy to the proceedings.

caption:
Here is a breathtaking meditation on time and the human condition: @j.patricklewis and Roberto Innocenti’s The House. A house built in 1656, long since abandoned and fallen into disrepair, is rediscovered and renovated at the turn of the twentieth century. Over the course of a hundred years, it stands silent witness to community, toil, joy, war, grief, hope, love, death, and the passage of generations. Lewis organizes his poetic narrative into elegant quatrains in iambic pentameter, alternating between an AABB and an ABBA rhyme scheme. Innocenti accompanies each stanza with an illustration of the eponymous house from exactly the same perspective, a choice that results in a captivating time-lapse effect.

caption:
If you’re searching for an unforgettably raucous and spirited heroine, look no further than Robin Muller’s adaptation of the Norwegian fairy tale Tatterhood. A queen who desires children encounters a kindly witch who advises her to spill water under her bed, which will cause two flowers to grow. The beautiful flower is to be eaten, the ugly one to be left alone. The queen, however, cannot control herself and eats both. From the queen’s impulsive consumption of the strange blossom is born an equally strange child, for nine months later out pops Tatterhood, a girl who wears rags, rides a goat, and wields a wooden spoon. Another girl, Belinda, is later born as a result of the queen having eaten the beautiful flower. Years later, Tatterhood defends the castle from a pack of unruly witches, but one of them swaps her sister’s head with that of a calf. After a wild journey to reclaim the stolen head, the two princesses encounter two princes and make plans to be married. Tatterhood’s husband-to-be treats her with kindness and respect, and she in turn reveals that there is far more to her than meets the undiscerning eye. Muller’s text, bolstered by a collection of dynamic illustrations, conveys excitement and high adventure. His protagonist is a triumph, an impish young woman all pouts, grimaces, smirks, scowls, and cackles.

caption:
The Jewel Heart by Barbara Helen Berger is a book woven of pure magic. An ethereal forested landscape is revealed to the reader framed by grand red drapes, suggesting a stage. The action occurs between two human figures: Gemino, a voiceless violinist in a Pierrot costume with a red jewel for a heart, and Pavette, a dainty ballerina. The young musician loves nothing more than to play music that inspires his companion to perform her beautiful dances. One day, disaster strikes: Gemino takes a terrible fall and lies broken on the ground. Pavette, aided by whispers from ethereal beings known only as shadows, repairs her friend as well as she can. But Gemino is not quite as he was before: his white clothing has become a motley suit of shadows, his short black hair is now wisps of dandelion down, and his lost jewel heart is replaced by a seed, which blooms into a wonderful flower heart. Berger’s text instills a dreamy atmosphere with delicate metaphor (“His face was a fallen moon,” later echoed: “His face was a rising moon.”) In her soft acrylic-paint-and-colored-pencil illustrations, the shadows take the form of ordinary woodland creatures. At the start of the book, these animals gather in front of a decorative red curtain, as audience members patiently awaiting a performance. On subsequent pages, they peer in at the action from a seemingly nondiegetic outside border, their bodies now tinted pale blue and cyan. Who are these animal “shadows”? Why do they watch Gemino and Pavette? What is the nature of this strange dualistic realm? We the audience are left to wonder, imagine, and marvel.

caption:
It’s been far too long since I’ve done a Fairy Tale Theme Week. The onset of the twelfth month of the year has me reflecting on the magical significance of the number twelve, which recurs in myriad tale types and motifs across the folklore canon. Take, for a prime example, the theme of this week’s exploration: The Twelve Dancing Princesses.

This first version comes to us from @ruthsandersonart, whose oil paintings on canvas set the story in a medieval landscape of great splendor and beauty. She applies a deep formalism and keen eye for detail in her representation of period architecture, decor, and costume.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: though this tale type has many variants occurring across cultures, the most famous version comes from the Brothers Grimm, who published it in Kinder- und Hausmärchen as “Die Zertanzten Schuhe” (“The Danced-Out Shoes”). In the source material, the main character is an old soldier who ultimately takes to wife the oldest princess. Sanderson’s hero, Michael, a good deal younger than in the Grimms’ tale, falls in love with the youngest princess.

caption:
Twelve Dancing Princesses Week is half over, and today I present you with Dorothée Duntze’s pleasingly quirky version. The writing remains thoroughly faithful to the original text of the Brothers Grimm, right down to the old soldier’s appropriate choice of the firstborn princess as his bride. These tantalizing (and perhaps contradictory) asides leave the reader to puzzle out the origin and precise rules of the arcane spell.

caption:
Let @suzyleebooks take you on a riveting emotional journey in her wordless picture book Mirror. A young girl sitting alone in a bare white void spots an identical child sitting across from her. They rise to their feet and begin to dance, the centerfold an unwavering line of symmetry between them. Streaks of color bloom between them as they leap and twirl in harmony. Then disaster strikes: the girls drift out of synchrony, begin moving independently, and grow angry with one another. The girl on the left reaches over towards the middle and pushes. Suddenly, the entire right-hand side of the expanse tilts backwards like a pane of glass, falls, and shatters. The remaining girl is left as lonely as downcast as when she started. The narrative raises more questions than it answers: What is the nature of this strange, empty place? Who is the girl crouching all by herself? Is she truly looking at her own reflection or interacting with a mysterious doppelgänger? These questions remain unresolved, and the tale ends on an unusual note of sadness, encouraging contemplation without offering satisfaction. Lee captures an impressive depth of feeling in her sequence of stark, powerful drawings in black, white, and yellow, supported by the ingenious core visual conceit of the gutter representing the mirror.

caption:
Oh my goodness. This post marks my five-hundredth book review. Can it really be that many? Thank you to everyone out there who has made this daily project such a rewarding endeavor!

In celebration, I’m revisiting one of my childhood favorites: Marilee Heyer’s gripping, unforgettable The Forbidden Door. On a distant star in the valley of the Bao-Bickle tree, deep in a network of caves live Reena and her parents, the last surviving members of a subterranean community. Reena dreams of seeing the outside world, but her parents insist that to leave the caves is forbidden. One day, concealed behind an ancient tapestry, the young girl discovers a door that leads out into the bright sunlight of the valley. Immediately, she runs afoul of the Okira, a monstrous creature who long ago preyed upon many of Reena’s ancestors and drove the rest into hiding. With the help of the birdlike valley denizens, led by the wise elder Nimar, Reena must outwit the Okira and free her parents from their subjugation underground. The powerful spell of Heyer’s original high fantasy adventure plot is enhanced by her lush, detailed, dazzlingly cinematic art. Come and make your way through this forbidden door…if you dare.

caption:
The book of the day is Reynard the Fox, a rollicking medieval tale by Selina Hastings and Graham Percy. The animal citizens gather at court to petition the Lion King for redress of grievances. Reynard the Fox, a notorious and unrepentant scoundrel, has long engaged in murder, robbery, and all manner of deceit. Sympathetic to their complaints, the sovereign commands that the fox be brought to justice. The nimble trickster outwits Bruin the Bear and Tibert the Cat, each sent to collect him from his estate, he flatters the King himself into a royal pardon, and he even slips the grasp of Isegrim the Wolf, who challenges him to mortal combat. At the end of the whole ordeal, he knows he must finally change his ways…but temptation will always lurk in his heart. Hastings retells this traditional story with charm and great brio, while Percy’s illustrations depict the animal characters with a winning depth of emotion.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Reynard the Fox comes to us from a literary cycle of Dutch, French, English, and German fables originating in the late twelfth century. These folktales contain an allegorical dimension, with the fox himself said to represent the bourgeoisie, the lion as the monarchy, the bear as landowners, the wolf as knights, the donkey as clerics, and other small animals as the peasantry.

caption:
Have you ever lived with the feeling that you were meant to be somewhere else? Have you ever read a fabulous story and wondered whether it could possibly be true? In his delightful A Small Tall Tale from the Far Far North, @peter.sis.art traces the life of Jan Welzl, a Moravian Czech explorer whose biography blurs the line between fact and fiction, truth and tall tale, history and legend. Welzl, so the stories go, travels north to the Arctic where he is sheltered by the indigenous tribes, learning from them and sharing his knowledge in kind. Some historical sources identify these tales as entirely true; others believe them to be sensationalized narratives fabricated by Czech journalists; still others believe Welzl was real but may have exaggerated or embellished details of his own exploits. With illustrations executed in colored inks, watercolors, acrylic gold, and rubber stamps on aquarelle paper and dried before an oven, Sís honors the spirit of his native folk hero.

Helldorfer and Yvonne Gilbert. A young boy named Finder lives with his mother and siblings, his father lost to a recent war. He puts on his father’s cloak and sets out into the snow, taking with him a golden ring bearing the king’s insignia, a symbol of his father’s faithful service. After the hunter wounds the majestic beast, an outraged Finder smears the blood on the old man’s face, which miraculously restores his sight. Finally, the boy reaches the castle and the old hunter reveals himself as the king and promises not only to tend to the needs of Finder’s family but to heal the kingdom from its wartime suffering. Inspired by the medieval legend of St. Eustace and by Chaucer’s Book of the Duchess, Helldorfer plumbs true depth of emotion with his eloquent writing. Gilbert’s exquisitely detailed illustrations celebrate love and warmth amid the bleak of winter white. May safety and tranquility be yours this Christmas Eve.

caption:
Christmas Day is here. Allow me to add a little bit of warmth and cheer to your celebration with The Wish Tree by @kyomaclear and @turnhamator. One bright, clear day in winter, Charles decides to go out in search of something he calls a “wish tree”. Heedless of his older brother and sister’s skepticism, he treks into the snowy woods with Boggan, his faithful and supportive (if a bit taciturn) toboggan companion along for company. Though at first they find no wish tree, they stop now and then to help the woodland creatures with their tasks: squirrel is collecting hazelnuts, beaver is gathering birch branches, fox is stockpiling berries. As the hour grows late, Charles begins losing his strength. Finally, he falls asleep and the forest animals come to his aid, pulling him along on Boggan. When he awakens, there is the wish tree, standing silent and white in a twilit glade. After writing his wish on a slip of paper and tying it to one of the tree’s branches, he sits down to a night feast at a table laid by the kindly animals, replete with hazelnut soufflé, birch tea, and berry biscuits. Ultimately, Maclear keeps Charles’s wish a secret from the reader, shifting focus from the specifics of the plot to the soothingly contemplative atmosphere and a beautiful economy of language. With glowing digital illustrations, Turnham renders the narrative in a soft, attractive palette of pink and purple, blue and brown. The author and artist achieve an unexpected air of magic realism, particularly in their inspired quasi-animate portrayal of Boggan. Maclear accords the toy subtle snippets of whispered dialogue, while Turnham depicts its dangling rope handle as a perennial smile. My wish for you today is happiness, light, and the love of family and friends. Merry Christmas.

caption:
Come follow along with me as I work my way down through the numerical world of Ten Birds by @cybeleyoung. This clever counting-down book opens in a barren landscape with ten odd sculptures standing by the side of a wide river. A flock of blackbirds arrives and wishes to cross to the other side. One by one, each bird approaches a different sculpture, detaches one physical piece, fashions it into a transportation device, and nimbly traverses the river. In a clever design choice, the birds’ removal of the structural components transforms the sequence of sculptures into numerals in descending order from ten to one. Most humorously of all, the final bird simply walks in a circle (leaving a ring of footprints to represent zero) and then crosses the river using a method available to the entire flock from the very beginning: a bridge.

caption:
You’ll find wisdom and wonder in equal measure when you read The Fourth Question, a Chinese tale retold by Rosalind C. Wang and illustrated by Ju-Hong Chen
Yee-Lee wonders why he is poor despite his hard work, and resolves to seek the counsel of the Wise Man of Kun-lun Mountain. On his way he meets several people with questions of their own. An old woman asks why her daughter is mute; a farmer asks why his fields lie barren; a dragon asks why he cannot ascend to heaven. Yee-Lee agrees to obtain the answers to these questions as well. But, when he reaches Kun-lun Mountain, the Wise Man tells him of an unexpected rule: visitors may only ask questions in odd numbers. Thus, he must give up one of his four questions and only ask three. After thinking it over, he selflessly decides abandon his original quest in order to keep his promises. Wang’s straightforward text and Chen’s smudge-textured art create a beautifully satisfying journey.

There the princess dwells in isolation until she and a passing prince fall for each other from afar. caption:
Imagine a terrible threat looming on the horizon. Imagine the only member of your family leaves to face this threat. Imagine they do not come back, and you have no one to turn to. Now imagine that you yourself must venture forth to confront the deadly danger, and you will put yourself in the place of the brave heroine of Anna Höglund’s The Stone Giant, originally published in Swedish as Förvandlingen (“The Transformation”). A knight departs from his island home to battle a giant whose ferocious gaze turns humans to stone. His daughter, left alone, waits day after day, but he does not return. One night, her candle burns out and all is dark. Taking only a knife and a mirror, the child swims off the island and sets out to rescue her father. An old woman gives her an umbrella, which she uses to shield herself from the giant’s baleful stare. Then, she cuts a hole in the umbrella with her knife. When the giant peers down through the hole, she meets her own eyes in the child’s mirror and she turns herself to stone. Immediately, all the giant’s victims come to life again, and the child is happily reunited with her father. Höglund’s spare text, and translated into English by Julia Marshall, echoes with mythic power, particularly in the totemic symbolism of the supplies the child takes on her journey. The art, rendered in copper plate etchings and watercolors, presents an eerie, barren landscape in somber shades of gray.

caption:
New Year’s Eve—a time of rest, reflection, finality. On this night, we may wish to take stock of all that has gone on in the year before and consider the course of our lives. While pondering such weighty matters, I am digesting a book filled with a powerful sorrow and loneliness: The Fairy Tale of the World by Jürg Amann and Käthi Bhend. A child, abandoned and alone, must leave the earth to seek solace in the heavens. But the moon turns out to be a piece of rotting wood, the sun a wilted flower, the stars a scattering of dead flies. Even the earth now seems to be an old, upturned kettle, and the child is left to weep, friendless and unloved, forever. The startlingly unhappy original text comes from a tale told by an old grandmother in the play Woyzeck, written by German playwright Georg Büchner. Amann has expanded upon the story, adding descriptive imagery to Büchner’s hauntingly bleak narrative. In Bhend’s rapturously beautiful illustrations, however, there appears a note of warmth and hope, for she has taken the radical approach of resisting the grim despair of the text. The final page contains an illustration of the child’s family peering back in through open doors, perhaps never truly having left in the first place. On this last day of the old year, I wish you serenity, strength, and resilience of spirit.

Good endures and evil meets its comeuppance in The Stepsister by Naomi Lewis and Allison Reed. Rose, a kind young woman, lives with her stepmother and with her stepsister, who coincidentally is also named Rose. However, the stepsister’s rudeness to the community earns her the nickname “Rose-Grumpety”. When Rose  by chance meets and marries a handsome prince, Rose-Grumpety and the stepmother hatch a wicked plan to spoil her newfound happiness. But, no matter how many times they attempt to destroy her, Rose returns—as a bird, as a tree, as a carven lute. With the help of Rose’s talking cat Bonamy, the prince succeeds in restoring the girl to her own form once again. Lewis imbues her writing with clarity and warmth; Reed’s quietly atmospheric art bears an etched, tactile quality.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the front jacket flap identifies the story as an adaptation of an ancient Chinese folktale. Though Lewis cites no specific source, the general plot is recognizably indebted to the Beauty and Pock Face, a Chinese story combining motifs of the Persecuted Heroine (Cinderella) and the Kind and the Unkind Girls. Unusually, the back jacket flap credits Reed, the artist (rather than Lewis, the author), as the discoverer of the tale.

Magic and marvels abound in The Sea-King’s Daughter by Aaron Shepard and Gennady Spirin. Young musician Sadko is renowned in the port city of Novgorod for the merry music of his twelve-string gusli. caption:
Dancing is unquestionably a vital component of human cultures all over the world. To dance together is to share an moment of true delight, and asking someone else to dance is often the key to initiating the entire experience. With these ideas in mind I am reading Keisuke Tsutsui and Chihiro Iwasaki’s Invitation to the Dance. Outside a large manor house, a young boy watches the wealthy guests arrive for a ball. The gatekeeper angrily chases him away, and he flees, only to find himself on an expansive lawn where he meets a young girl and asks her to dance. They are joined in their reverie by sentient flowers, butterflies, and fish. A bizarre apparition of the gardener looms before them, but they escape and safely bid each other farewell. Tsutsui’s text, translated into English by Ann King Herring, sets up a diverting landscape of imaginary wonder. Iwasaki’s art conveys a delicate watercolor world of shimmering beauty.

A word about the source: Invitation to the Dance is an 1819 piano composition by Karl Maria von Weber. A concert waltz (that is, a waltz meant for listening rather than dancing), the piece tells the story of a man asking a woman to dance at a ball. Tsutsui has transformed the characters to children in a fantasy setting, while maintaining the spirit of Weber’s original work.

caption:
Negative emotions can make us deeply uncomfortable. Adults often send children the message, whether implicit or explicit, that being angry is wrong. While it is of course important to practice constructive forms of expression, the internal feeling of anger is a universal experience, to be acknowledged and understood rather than denied. To that end, it is with true awe and delight that I am reading When I See Red by @britta_teckentrup. A young girl narrates the course of her wrath as it emerges, builds to a thunderous crescendo, and then recedes. The rush of fury evolves through physical symbols: storms, oceans, monsters, wild beasts. Teckentrup’s powerful language flows, twists, and soars throughout the book, an evolving series of gerunds serving as a bold prose poetry refrain. The compositions of the art employ strong motion and vivid color in the externalization of the girl’s rage, her ability to emerge once more into a state of calm, and, crucially, her discovery of the limitless possibilities that follow.

caption:
Here is an enchanting story shot through with dark magic: Little Parsley, retold and illustrated by Enzo Giannini. When a pregnant woman cannot resist tasting parsley from the garden next door, the witches who own it demand ownership over her unborn daughter. Little Parsley, as she is named, is taken by the old hags several years later, forced to live in their house and obey their orders. With each seemingly impossible task, the witches’ cousin Nino agrees to help Little Parsley, and the two are eventual able to vanquish the wicked crones once and for all. Giannini’s text and art brighten the mood of the otherworldly proceedings.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Giannini has adapted this story from “La Prezzemolina” (Little Parsley), a folktale collected by Vittorio Imbriani in La Novellaja Fiorentina (1877). The plot combines elements of multiple tale types. The theft of the garden plant by the pregnant woman recalls the opening of The Maiden in the Tower (whose best known variant is Rapunzel), while the rest of the tale features a heroine laboring under an evil taskmaster, a structure perhaps most famously used by the Roman writer Apuleius in the tale of Cupid and Psyche.

For a diverting tale with plenty of action and historical intrigue, have Margaret Early’s Robin Hood. Each page chronicles a further chapter in the life story of the legendary outlaw, including the beginning of his exploits, his first encounters with Little John and the Merry Men, his love of Maid Marian, his conflicts with the Sheriff of Nottingham, and his eventual death. Early’s writing faithfully follows the well-known stories with clear and engaging language, while the bright colors and flattened perspective of her illustrations call to mind medieval art.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Robin Hood has long stood as an iconic figure in medieval English folklore. The historicity of his legend, a matter of extensive debate, may never be settled, not least because of the prevalence of the names “Robin” (a diminutive of “Robert”) and “Hood” (thought by some to be descended from “Wood”).

In the warm and whimsical Zilla Sasparilla and the Mud Baby, Judith Gorog and Amanda Harvey use a dash of magical realism to explore the ins and outs of parenthood. It has been raining all week by the Little Muddy River. While walking home along the river bank, Zilla Sasparilla gets her foot stuck in the mud. She reaches in to retrieve her shoe and pulls out a baby. On the advice of her Granny Vi, she bathes the mud baby, first in milk, then in water. She names him Cinnamon and raises him as her own son. As the boy grows up and becomes more independent, Zilla remains plagued by the fear that he will one day wash away in the Little Muddy River. Determined to protect her child, she plans to move house. But, when Zilla herself accidentally falls into the river, Cinnamon bravely dives in to rescue her—dispelling his mother’s fears once and for all. Gorog’s inviting and lightly humorous narrative peers through an oddball lens at the joys and fears of raising a baby. Harvey’s cheery watercolor and pencil illustrations convey a pleasingly humanistic spirit.

caption:
Let us consider Why Mosquitoes Buzz in People’s Ears—not simply the question, but the book by Verna Aardema and Leo and Diane Dillon. An unlikely concatenation of events begins one morning at a waterhole. A boastful mosquito begins to annoy an iguana, who plugs his ears with sticks and departs. A python, interpreting the lizard’s bizarre behavior as hostile, creeps into a rabbit hole. The rabbit flees in fear, which leads a crow to sound the alarm, causing a monkey to fall into the an owl’s nest, mortally wounding an owlet. Mother Owl, in her grief, cannot bring herself to wake the sun, and so the forest is trapped in eternal darkness. King Lion presides over an inquest, and each animal in the chain blames its predecessor for the disturbance. When the unlikely sequence is traced back to its source, the mosquito is finally identified as the culprit, but she evades capture, and her descendants constantly approach the ears of human beings to ask whether the grudge remains. Aardema peppers her expressive text with distinctive onomatopoeias such as “mek, mek, mek, mek” (the iguana’s footsteps), “wasawusu, wasawusu, wasawusu” (the snake slithering), and “nge, nge, nge” (the lion’s laughter). Husband-and-wife illustrators the Dillons employ a vibrant, eye-popping mixed-media technique, with watercolors airbrushed in both fine spray and large spatter, pastels rubbed on by hand, and india ink.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this West African tale is an etiology, or an explanation for the origin of an object or aspect of nature.

David Lucas gives us a look at an unorthodox approach to social anxiety in his entertaining and heartfelt Halibut Jackson. The eponymous protagonist is so shy that he does his best to blend into the background at all times. He is so skilled at tailoring that he is able to design clothes that allow him to do just that: suits to blend in at the park, at the shops, at the library. One day, he receives an invitation to a birthday party for the queen. He promptly sets to work making a gleaming suit of silver, gold, and jewels in order to camouflage himself in the royal palace. When he arrives at the event, however, he discovers to his chagrin that it is a garden party. Out in the middle of the lawn, there is nowhere for him to hide. Just what will become of Halibut Jackson once everyone can see him for who he truly is? With a gentle, knowing author’s voice and merrily cluttered drawings, Lucas honors the wallflowers, those whom society might otherwise overlook, and asks what gifts they might have to contribute if we are willing to open our hearts and listen.

Michael Moniz explores a complex emotional dynamic through the interactions of a flock of birds in The Cardinal and the Crow. The story opens on the edge of a small forest where discord thrives among the birds. The crow is an outcast, an object of derision for the other birds, who taunt him and call him ugly. The ringleader, a bright red cardinal, seems to take particular delight in the bullying. The crow, for his part, takes to squawking loudly in order to drive off the other birds. One day, after the cardinal is captured by a cat and about to be eaten, the crow uses cunning flattery to convince the cat to let out a victory roar, and the cardinal is able to make a hasty escape. From then on, no one bothers the crow, and all the birds live in harmony. With a narrative inspired by Aesop’s fables and soft, muted washes of black, red, brown, and gray, Moniz creates a stunning parable of exclusion, forgiveness, and understanding.

caption:
What would you do when confronted by a fearsome supernatural entity? Perhaps you might display your great strength? Your indomitable courage? Your dazzling wit? The protagonist of Valerie Scho Carey and Johanna Westerman’s Maggie Mab and the Bogie Beast gets by on nothing but her genuine, unflagging positivity. A poor old woman on her way home one evening comes across an iron pot full of gold coins in the road. Delighted, she wraps it in her shawl and begins to drag it home, but soon looks again and sees that the pot has changed to a lump of silver. Still pleased, she continues down the road. Her prize mysteriously transforms again and again (to a lump of iron and then to a large stone), and each time she responds with enthusiasm and good cheer. Finally, the thing reveals its true nature—it is a bogey beast, a shapeshifting spirit resembling a large, spectral donkey. The ghostly apparition carries her over land and sea, but still not a word of complaint does she utter. As a reward, the bogey beast leaves her with three gold coins before departing for good. Carey retells this English folktale with verve and charm, while Westerman’s dynamic, cool-hued illustrations add a bevy of mischievous fairies lurking at ankle height, entirely unmentioned in the text.

Let’s take a stroll together along the lanes of imagination: here is @macbarnett and @jonklassen’s Extra Yarn. Annabelle’s town lies under a thick blanket of snow. One day, she comes across a box filled with yarn of every color. She knits herself a sweater, and finds herself with some yarn left over. She knits a sweater for her dog and still has some left. She knits for more and more people—family, friends, neighbors, local animals, and even the town buildings—but never seems to run out of yarn. Word spreads of Annabelle’s talent, and a wealthy archduke sails from across the sea to meet her. But, rather than commission a sweater, the archduke offers to buy the box of yarn itself. When she refuses, the haughty lord hires three robbers to steal the box from her house. However, when he opens the box, it is entirely empty. He hurls it out the window and into the sea in a rage, whereupon it finds its way back to its rightful owner. Barnett deftly navigates the faint magical realism of the plot with a tone of elegantly restrained humor. Klassen provides his trademark flat-style illustrations with light pinks, yellows, and greens against earthy browns.

caption:
How formidable even the the gentlest corners of the world must appear from the perspective of the protagonist of today’s book, The Adventures of Tom Thumb by Marianna Mayer and Kinuko Y. Craft. Tall Tim of the Mountains and his wife Kate dearly wish for a child. Tim seeks out Merlin the wizard and declares that he would be happy even with a baby no bigger than his thumb. caption:
I’m engrossed by the allegorical power of drama and pathos in Everyman for Every Child by Werner Thuswaldner and Julian Crouch. The story explores such universal concepts as greed, fear, love, and death. A rich miser known as Everyman is stalked by death incarnate as punishment for his pride and avarice. Only by reconnecting with the good deeds of his past can he shield his soul from the devil and achieve peace. The text, translated into English by Pamela and Gregor Thuswaldner, presents the deeply philosophical story in starkly simple terms for a young audience, while Crouch’s art depicts the proceedings as a production on a grand operatic stage.

A note on the text: The book is adapted from Hugo von Hofmannsthal’s 1911 German-language play Jedermann. Das Spiel vom Sterben des reichen Mannes (“Everyman. The play of the rich man’s death”), which in turn draws from sources such as the fifteenth-century Dutch morality play Elckerlijc and its sixteenth-century English adaptation the Somonyng of Everyman.

caption:
Have you ever felt as though you stood out from everyone around you? To be different can be an isolating experience…but what if embracing your unique qualities is exactly what allows you to fit in and be celebrated by your community? Here is a look at just such a case in Elmer by David McKee. In the jungle lives a group of elephants. All of them are gray…except Elmer. His hide is a rainbow patchwork, a bizarre hodgepodge of hues. With a personality as colorful as his skin, he keeps his friends entertained all day long with games and jokes. However, he secretly harbors feelings of self-consciousness and one day he sets off on his own. Out in the wilderness, Elmer comes across a bush of elephant-colored berries. He rolls in the berries and rubs their juices all over himself until he turns gray, just like his fellow pachyderms. Back at home, he blends in with the herd and chooses just the right moment to break a tedious silence with a good scare. Still, no one recognizes him until a rainstorm washes away his disguise. The other elephants are so tickled with Elmer’s good-natured prank that they resolve to commemorate the occasion with a yearly holiday on which they decorate themselves with all sorts of zany colors and patterns, while Elmer stands out in plain gray. McKee pairs his good-natured and goofy story with eye-poppingly chromatic illustrations.

For children, found objects carry a distinct meaning, a subtle power that we all too often forget by the time we reach adulthood. Come and jog your memory with the wordless Sidewalk Flowers by JonArno Lawson and @sydneydraws. On the walk home from grocery shopping, a girl stops to pick flowers she notices growing here and there in little cracks and crevices of the urban environment. Eventually, she amasses a small, variegated bouquet. Though she enjoys her collection, she then begins leaving the flowers as gifts and offerings for those she passes: a dead bird, a man sleeping on a park bench, a dog on a leash, and finally her mother and younger siblings. The gentle, introspective story, conceived by Lawson, explores the meaning of childhood rituals and celebrates beauty for beauty’s sake. Smith’s art, created in pen and ink with watercolor and digitally edited, underscores these deeply humanistic themes with a color palette that begins in grayscale and slowly but surely introduces a breadth of soft, delicate hues.

The book of the day is Greyling by Jane Yolen and William Stobbs. A fisherman rescues a seal pup stranded on a sand bar. When he brings it home to his wife, they find it has transformed into a baby boy with grey eyes and grey hair. They name him Greyling and raise him as their own son. Fifteen years later, a terrible ocean storm swallows the family’s hut, and the fisherman is nearly drowned offshore. Greyling, in reality a selchie or seal spirit, selflessly dives into the water, reverts to his aquatic form, and rescues his father. He then vanishes from his parents’ lives, returning only for a brief visit one night out of each year. Yolen’s arresting prose injects this tradisitonal Shetland Islands tale with poetic language and high drama. Stobbs beautifully conjures the antique atmosphere of the seaside town with soft lines and a dark color palette.

A quirky and mysterious little world unfolds in Yendor by Graham Smith and Rodney Matthews. Strange plants and animals of all colors populate a bizarre fantasy landscape. Tucked away in a little house live Yendor and his parents. The boy, tired of his uneventful daily existence and vexed at being so often called “the small one in the middle”, sneaks away from home one night in search of adventure in the wild country. He does battle with a flying Killwing, matches wits with a great muddy Grumposaur, unknowingly avoids a poisonous Grabsting, and finally receives a lift home from a giant riding on a winged Snawk. Come, gather your nerves and open up Anthea Bell and Keiko Kaichi’s adaptation of the Brothers Grimm’s The Wolf & the Seven Kids. A mother, preparing to leave the house in search of food, bids her seven kids goodbye. Before she departs, however, she warns the children about the hungry wolf that wants to get inside. Sure enough, as soon as she is gone, the wicked beast begins knocking at the door. When the kids refuse to let him in, the wolf employs all his cunning to disguise the telltale signs that distinguish him from the mother goat: he eats a lump of chalk to make his voice soft and coats his paws in floured dough to make them white. Finally, the seven young goats let him in and all but one are swallowed whole. Fortunately, the mother goat bravely tracks down the sleeping wolf, cuts open his belly, pulls out her children, and replaces them with stones, whereupon the terrible predator falls into a deep well and is never seen again. Bell faithfully translates the Grimms’ thrilling tale, and Kaichi provides exaggerated character design that heightens the contrast between the adorable young kids and the ghastly wolf.

Today I’ve got a stunningly executed realistic fiction adventure for you: @sophieblackall’s Hello Lighthouse. The book begins with a tiny island on the edge of the world. On this island stands a lighthouse. When the old lighthouse keeper’s service comes to an end, a new keeper arrives to take his place. Deftly weaving together text and illustrations, Blackall finds subtle ways to communicate the passing of time, detailing natural phenomena (storms, fog, ice, migrating whales, aurora borealis) and major life events (the arrival of the keeper’s wife, the keeper’s serious illness, the birth of their baby, the baby’s growth into a young child). Through it all, the story is punctuated by the lyrical refrain, “Hello!/…Hello!/…Hello!” Finally, the lighthouse is automated and the keeper’s family is able to return to life on the mainland, where they can still look out across the water and view their old island home from their front door.

caption:
At the middle of my second Cinderella Theme Week, I’m turning my sights in a different direction. Thus far, I’ve focused on the best-known Western iterations of the tale (by Charles Perrault and the Brothers Grimm) and presented interpretations by numerous artists. For the remainder of the week, however, I’m going to branch out and explore books based on variants of the story from other cultures around the world.

Today I have Jude Daly’s adaptation of Fair, Brown & Trembling, an Irish Cinderella. Three sisters of wealth and status in the kingdom of Erin (Ireland) wish to go to church. Fair and Brown, the elder two, put on their finest dresses every week and set off—but, envying the beauty of their younger sister Trembling, they force her to stay home and cook for them. One day the local henwife takes pity on the girl. She throws on her cloak of darkness and uses her mystical powers to procure wonderful garments for Trembling: first a white dress, the next week a black gown, and the week after that a red skirt with a white bodice, green cloak, white cap, and blue slippers. Each week Trembling rushes away the moment the Mass is over, so no one can discover her identity. On the third week, the Prince of Emania attempts to hinder her, but only succeeds in retrieving her blue slipper. There follows the plot of the search for the slipper’s owner, the happy union of Trembling and the Prince, and the just punishment of Fair and Brown. Daly’s illustrations employ a jewel-toned color palette and enchantingly elongated character design.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this story comes from Jeremiah Curtin’s Myths and Folk-Lore of Ireland. Daly’s pragmatic adaptation omits a final episode in which Fair and Brown return to take revenge on their sister but are thwarted one last time.

caption:
Here is a variant of Cinderella hailing from the Native American oral tradition: The Rough-Face Girl by Rafe Martin and @nodavid2018. At the center of a village on the shores of Lake Ontario stands a large, beautifully painted wigwam, home to the rich and powerful Invisible Being. There he remains, hidden to all except his sister, who declares that he will only marry a maiden who can see his face. Elsewhere in the village lives a young woman whose older sisters force her to tend the fire day after day until her skin is charred and her hair is singed. Her resulting appearance earns her the nickname “Rough-Face Girl”. One day, the vain sisters dress up in all their finery and ask to marry the Invisible Being, but cannot answer the obligatory questions proving they have seen him. The Rough-Face Girl, in simple, handmade attire, ventures to the great wigwam and correctly answers the questions. The Invisible Being’s sister tells her to bathe herself in a nearby lake, which magically heals her body and restores her beauty. She and the Invisible Being are married and spend the rest of their days in happiness. Martin’s expressive writing neatly evokes the voice of an oral storyteller. Shannon’s rich illustrations celebrate the beauty of nature and the triumph of humility over arrogance.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Martin cites the source for the story as Algonquin. A similar narrative appears in Cyrus Macmillan’s collection Canadian Wonder Tales, containing a few earthier details. Notably, the heroine’s envious sisters, rather than forcing her to tend the fire, actively burn her with coals to disfigure her. At the story’s end, they are turned into aspen trees as punishment.

caption:
The next of my Sequel Cinderellas is a special one indeed, for this is one of the oldest known variants of the tale: Yeh Shen, retold by Ai-Ling Louie and illustrated by Ed Young. A cave chief in ancient China takes two wives, each of whom in turn bears him a daughter. One wife takes ill and dies, and soon afterward the chief too passes away. Their child, Yeh-Shen, grows up with her father’s widow and other daughter. Her stepfamily treats her cruelly, and her only pleasure comes from feeding a fish in a nearby pond. When the stepmother discovers her pet, she kills it and cooks it for dinner. A mysterious old man soon appears before the grieving girl and tells her that the fish’s bones will grant her every wish. Some time later, Yeh-Shen uses the bones to conjure a marvelous blue gown and golden-soled shoes to wear to the spring festival. Fearful of being recognized, she flees and leaves behind one shoe. When the king seeks out the shoe’s owner, he discovers Yeh-Shen and marries her. He does not, however, invite her stepfamily to live in his palace, and one day, in the cave where they have always dwelled, they are crushed by falling rocks. Louie’s graceful writing and Young’s splendid art breathe vibrant energy into this ancient Cinderella narrative.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the story of Yeh-Shien (also transliterated “Yè Xiàn”) first appears in Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang, a book written by Tang Dynasty poet Duan Chengshi in the ninth century of the Common Era.

caption:
The book of the day is Night Wall by @duncan_weller—a story that mixes the uncanny and the comforting in equal measure. Young Sarah and her older cousin Julie go for a vacation in the woods north of their urban home. Feeling nervous out in the wilderness, Julie hires a contractor to build a wall around their cabin. However, as soon as the wall is complete, disturbing monsters begin to creep over from the other side. It is not until the construction crew returns and knocks down the wall that the weird apparitions vanish. After that, Sarah and Julie take a walk in the woods and discover the odd beasts as miniature figurines in a buried chest. Just what are the monsters? Why do they leave when the wall is taken down? Do they have their own independent existence or are they a physical manifestation of Julie’s anxiety. In his straightforward text and eerie illustrations, Weller carefully leaves the intriguing central questions of his work unanswered.

The book of the day is Nancy Ekholm Burkert’s Valentine & Orson. Twin brothers are separated at birth. Valentine grows up in the royal court of King Pepin of France while Orson is raised in the forest by bears. When they meet in adulthood, they start as enemies but quickly become friends. Here is a peek at The Son of the Sun and the Daughter of the Moon, a Saami folktale retold by Holly Young Huth and Anna Vojtech. High in the sky, the sun goes about his business supplying the earth’s light and warmth. One day, he approaches Mother Moon on behalf of his son Solvake and proposes marriage between their two children, but the moon refuses. Known as Vanishia because of her uncanny ability to disappear without a trace, the girl grows into a lovely and otherworldly young woman. She eventually marries Luminias, one of the rowdy Brothers of the Northern Lights. Unfortunately, when the sun learns of their union, he murders Luminias with a flaming arrow. Enraged by Vanishia’s continued defiance, he flings her away into the sky where she lands in her mother’s waiting embrace. Huth’s straightforward language and Vojtech’s luminous watercolor paintings meld for a lush, thrilling dramatic presentation.

caption:
Do you fear for the future? It’s hard not to worry when confronted with humanity’s ongoing voracious consumption and the vast quantities of ensuing waste. Chris Van Allsburg’s Just a Dream hooks into these sobering concepts, to be sure, but also provides the hopeful blueprint for a solution. Young Walter demonstrates little care for the environment as he tosses empty bags to the ground and takes out the garbage without sorting it. Though he blissfully imagines that the future will hold all sorts of conveniences and technological marvels, a prophetic dream soon warns otherwise. His bed travels from one Kafkaesque nightmare scenario to another: a neighborhood buried in mountains of refuse, a forest cut down to produce toothpicks, a colossal factory producing medicine for the very symptoms caused by its own pollution, a luxury hotel marring the natural beauty of Mount Everest, fisherman reduced to scrounging for small fry, a snarled highway with an endless traffic jam, the Grand Canyon obscured by smog, birds flying for days in search of their natural habitat. When he awakens, Walter resolves to become a steward of the earth, picking up his trash, sorting his family’s garbage, and purchasing a tree to plant for his birthday present. His next dream is far more pleasant: a vision of a low-technology future in which his tree and another planted by his neighbor have grown to a towering size. Van Allsburg’s moral, as timely as ever, benefits from clear writing and engrossingly cinematic renditions of the apocalyptic tableaux.

caption:
If it’s a modern take on love and power in a fairy tale idiom you’re after, look no further: here is The King’s Equal, written by Katherine Paterson and illustrated by Vladimir Vagin. With his father near death, Prince Raphael stands to inherit the throne and rule his country. However, the old king makes an unexpected final decree: the prince may not wear the royal crown until he marries a woman his equal in beauty, intelligence, and wealth. Try as they might, the royal councilors cannot produce a bride that the haughty Raphael deems worthy.  Meanwhile, the young man initiates a selfish and tyrannical reign, caring little for his people’s wellbeing. Far away, across the kingdom, a poor farmer’s daughter named Rosamund ekes out a meager living in an old goatherd’s shack. One day she encounters a sentient wolf who gives her a magic circlet and bids her go to the capital city and present herself as a candidate to be the new queen. After passing the required tests of beauty, intelligence, and wealth, she boldly observes that she has outshone the king—if a wedding is to take place, he must now prove himself her equal. In a stunning reversal, Raphael journeys to Rosamund’s old home in the mountains and learns honest work and compassion from the wolf, while Rosamund remains in the capital and works to undo the damage of Raphael’s wanton cruelty. At the end of one year’s time, the two are reunited and accept each other as wise and loving equals. In a light fantasy setting, Paterson’s insightful text and Vagin’s stately art combine for a quietly radical treatment of court politics and gender relationships.

caption:
Today marks the occasion of my six-hundredth book review! As always, I am supremely grateful for your continued reading and kind feedback. Now then…

Come journey with me into the bizarre, enchanting, and utterly unforgettable world of Holly Grant and @kgcampbellauthor’s Wee Sister Strange. The tale opens at sundown. A mysterious young girl wanders out of her rickety old shack and into the woods, where she seems oddly at home among the plants and animals in the gathering dusk. Up the trees she climbs, into the bog she dives, through the brambles she creeps, in a ceaseless hunt for some unspecified quarry. Finally, in a wild metafictional twist, she peeks through the window of a house and sees you, the reader, nestled in bed with a book. Moreover, the book appears to be this very book, Wee Sister Strange, suggesting a path of infinite recursion. At last, the girl has come to the end of her search, for what she wanted all along was a bedtime story. Satisfied to curl up outside and listen, she drifts off to sleep, a strange presence in a strange world. Grant’s language crackles with offbeat, vibrant energy, producing such eye-opening imagery as: “She drinks up the moon/Like a cat drinking cream./She drinks up the dark/Like it’s tea with the queen.” The poetic form proves as protean and unpredictable as its protagonist: some quatrains contain rhyme, some feature slant rhyme, and some do not rhyme at all. In his watercolor-and-colored-pencil illustrations, Campbell realizes the eldritch world of the night forest in a palette dominated by slate blue, cloudy gray, and yellow ochre. Just who or what is Wee Sister Strange? Where does she come from? Why is she here now? There may be no satisfying answers, but the tantalizing questions make for a uniquely delicious experience.

caption:
An eerie tale of menace and wrath is contained in The Hobyahs, an old English tale retold by Robert D. San Souci and illustrated by Alexi Natchev. An orphan girl lives with an old man and an old woman in a little hemp-stalk hut on the edge of the woods along with five dogs named Turpie, Topie, Tippy, Tarry, and Teeny. Over the course of five nights, sinister beasts called the Hobyahs emerge from the forest and begin slinking toward the house. The dogs bark loudly enough to scare the creatures off, but the old man and woman, ignorant of the danger, punish their faithful pets for the disturbance—over the pleas of the girl, they whip the poor animals and abandon them in the woods. Now defenseless, the elderly couple is quickly devoured on the sixth night, but the girl is rescued by the loyal dogs, who gobble up the Hobyahs. San Souci’s dramatic language and Natchev’s eerie art create an atmosphere of ghostly suspense.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: The original tale, published by Joseph Jacobs in his 1894 volume More English Fairy Tales, contains only one dog, Turpie. This animal suffers a much more grisly fate than those in San Souci’s softened adaptation—to punish him for barking on the five nights, the old man cuts off each of his four legs and then his head.

For today, how about a gently humorous etiological narrative? Here’s a look at How Thunder and Lightning Came to Be, a Choctaw tale adapted by Beatrice Orcutt Harrell and illustrated by Susan L. Roth. Long ago, in the early days of the world, The Great Sun Father prepares to send wind and rain down to earth. To warn the Choctaw people that they must take shelter, he enlists the help of two rather silly birds. The speedy but clumsy Melatha bungles his first few attempts to spread the message. The rumbling sound they make as they roll away across the clouds and the great streak of sparks caused by yet another comical misstep as Melatha chases them serve as the very first instance of thunder and lightning, warning of the oncoming harsh weather. Harrell’s amusing text and Roth’s handcrafted collages match well in this whimsical origin story.

The Red String, conceived by Margot Blair and illustrated by Greg Colson, makes me smile. To see why, you need only open it up. caption:
Come and enjoy yourself by flipping through The Queen Bee, a Brothers Grimm tale translated into English by Elizabeth James and illustrated by Iassen Ghiuselev. Two princes decide to abandon their desire for adventure and lead a wanton, unruly life. Their younger brother, saddled with the rude nickname Dimwit, seeks them out and joins them on their travels. He stops his cruel older siblings from destroying an anthill for pleasure, catching ducks to roast, and smoking bees out of a hive for the honey. When the three arrive at an enchanted castle, they are challenged to complete three tasks in order to break the spell. The two older brothers are soon turned to stone, but Dimwit succeeds with the help of the animals to whom he showed kindness: the ants help gather scattered crystals, the ducks retrieve a key from the bottom of a deep lake, and the queen bee herself distinguishes a princess from her sisters by sniffing out the honey on her lips from a bedtime snack. James’s adaptation is well served by the medieval period details of Ghiuselev’s smooth-textured art.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: in the original text from Grimm, the youngest brother is set apart from the others not by a perceived lack of intelligence but by dwarfism.

This tale drawn from Arthurian lore takes place at the dawn of the New Year. The Knights of the Round Table and the court of Camelot is interrupted during a feast by the arrival of a knight with green skin, green hair, green clothing, green horse, and all manner of green accoutrements. The strange visitor challenges any man present to strike a blow at him with the axe—provided the same man will allow himself to be dealt a blow in return one year and one day later. Sir Gawain, youngest of the knights, swings the axe and severs the green man’s head from his shoulders, but the green man’s body simply picks up the head and departs. So begins an adventure of high magic and chivalry that gravely tests Gawain’s spirit, mettle, and honor. Hastings employs elegant and refined language in her retelling, while Wijngaard provides art in brilliant, saturated color.

caption:
Selina Hastings and Juan Wijngaard present a parable of supernatural romance in Sir Gawain and the Loathly Lady, companion to their earlier work Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. The story opens in the England of medieval legend. King Arthur is attacked by the wicked Black Knight, who gives the monarch three days to save his life by answering the question, “What is it that women most desire?” A hideous old hag provides the answer, “What all women most desire is to have their own way,” but in return extracts the promise that she may marry a Knight of the Round Table. The loyal and selfless Sir Gawain volunteers to marry the ancient crone, treating her with kindness and respect as they prepare for the wedding. Once the two are alone the bridal chamber, the woman reveals that she is in fact a fair young maiden under a spell. She tells her husband that he must decide—will she remain ugly by day and beautiful by night? Or will she be ugly at night and beautiful during the day? Readers who have been paying close attention to the story may correctly predict Sir Gawain’s choice. Hastings and Wingaard imbue the text and illustrations with a lush, refined beauty.

caption:
If a tale that mixes folkloric menace with a healthy dose of comedic slapstick violence is what you’re after, just wait until you get your hands on Ed Young’s The Terrible Nung-Gwama. A woman sets out to journey to her parents and bring them some cakes. On the road, she is confronted by a Nung Gwama, a ferocious monster with the body of a bull, sharp teeth and claws, and fat, floppy feet. When she refuses to hand over her cakes, the Nung Gwama informs her that he will come to her house that night and devour her. Fearing the creature’s reputation for messily devouring his prey, the woman begins to cry. Sympathetic passersby donate helpful objects to construct traps: a peddler gives her needles, a farmer gives her manure, a snake seller gives her poisonous snakes, a fish seller gives her biting fish, an egg seller gives her eggs, and a millstone seller gives her a heavy millstone and an iron bar. Incredibly, the Nung Gwama falls afoul of every single hazard exactly as planned and loses his life in the process. Young’s illustrations contrast the stoic body language of the woman with the exaggerated movements and outrageous expressions of the wicked beast.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this tale was originally collected and recorded as “The Nung-guama” in Chinese Folk and Fairy Tales by Leslie Bonnet.

We’ve all felt the discomfort of surrounding ourselves with technology and severing our relationship with nature. But what might be the reaction of a purely technological being upon experiencing nature for the very first time? This is the question asked—and satisfyingly answered—in Unplugged by @mrsteveantony. A power cable connects a small robot named Blip to a large computer, which keeps her constantly informed and entertained. caption:
Have a look at John Ruskin’s classic tale The King of the Golden River, illustrated by Sandro Nardini. The story opens in a pleasant land nicknamed the Treasure Valley, owned by three brothers. Schwartz and Hans, the elder two, are ugly, cruel, and miserly; Gluck, the youngest, is fair, kind, and generous. The sudden arrival of a mysterious old man turns disastrous when the older brothers treat him quite shabbily. caption:
If you’ve ever wondered whether your surroundings could be improved by small yet heartfelt acts of goodness, you’ll find your answer in The Curious Garden by @peterbrownstudio. Liam lives in a city choked in pollution. One day, he discovers a patch of plant life struggling to grow on the tracks of a derelict elevated railroad line. Liam diligently tends the plants, watering them, pruning them, and even singing to them. The garden begins to push outward, extending down the length of the railway track. After a cold winter, the greenery resumes its forward creep, extending first to nearby rooftops and then to old cars, signposts, and fire hydrants. Other people soon begin to notice and care for the plants in their vicinity. Years later, the garden has spread out to transform the entire city into a lush, verdant landscape. Brown marries a simple yet effective text with acrylic and gouache art to produce a stirring celebration of nature’s resilience and the human drive to effect positive change.

The crossing of a subtle geographical boarder leads to a gentle, appealing adventure in Barbara Lehman’s Trainstop. A young girl waits in an underground subway station with her family. They board the train, and she watches out the window as the view shifts from dreary city to dark tunnel to bright countryside. In her wordless narrative, Lehman imbues the light fantasy with an enchanting air of delicate emotional realism.

Have you read The Cloud Princess by @khoa.le.artwork? I’ve been leafing through it today and smiling at its colorful aesthetic of sweet tranquility. The Cloud Princess lives high in the sky with only Miss Sun and Miss Moon for company. The book of the day is Bearskin, written by Howard Pyle and illustrated by Trina Schart Hyman. When a cruel king learns that a certain baby is prophesied to marry his daughter, he commands the infant be put to death. Instead, thanks to the compassion of a forester, the child is instead set adrift in a basket on a river and raised by a great she-bear. As an adult, the foundling comes to be known as Bearskin, after the hide he wears wrapped around his shoulders. With the help of his foster mother the bear, he slays a dragon and thwarts the wicked plot of a faithless steward in order to fulfill his destiny. Pyle writes with wit and flair, while Hyman’s ink-and-acrylic art depicts a utopian medieval kingdom shared by citizens of many ethnic backgrounds.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: though Pyle’s text is an original composition, devotees of the folktale canon will recognize many familiar motifs, including the foundling rescued from the murderous monarch and the dragon-slayer stymied by the conniving attendant.
