caption:
Do you enjoy the bizarre combination of humor and frustration in the comic letdown of a shaggy dog story? Well, here’s something of a shaggy cat story: The Porcelain Cat, written by Michael Patrick Hearn and illustrated by Leo and Diane Dillon. When an old Sorcerer detects a rat infestation, he decides to take action. In order to concoct a potion that will bring his porcelain statue of a cat to life, he sends his apprentice Nickon to collect a vial of basilisk blood from the Witch Beneath the Hill. As payment, the witch demands a magical salve from the Undine of the Brook. The Undine requests that Nickon forage for a certain delectable mushroom, but the mushrooms are guarded by the Centaur of the Wood, who requires that the boy pluck him fruit from the surrounding trees. Hearn’s fanciful cumulative tale ends with an abrupt ironic twist—the Sorcerer successfully animates the porcelain cat, who immediately sees a rat, leaps off the table, and shatters on the floor. The Dillons contribute lush, jewel-toned illustrations that accentuate the beauty of the fantasy setting.

caption:
A trip outside inspires philosophical questions and a profound reverence for nature in Wonder Walkers by @michaarcherart. Two children relax on the couch, the weather outside sunny and calm. After looking out the window, they decide to go on what they refer to as a “wonder walk”, evidently an established tradition. Freely and without adult supervision, they wander out the door, over a bridge, past mountains, across meadows, though forests, and all the way down to the seashore before returning home for the evening. The sights they see along the way generate such potent questions as, “Is fog the river’s blanket?”, “Are trees the sky’s legs?”, “Are shells the shore’s necklace?”, and “Is the wind the world breathing?” Such ideas demand no verbal response, dealing as they do in the poetic, rather than the scientific. Archer accompanies her lyrical text with intricate collages using ink, tissue paper, and homemade stamps.

caption:
In honor of the delightful David McKee, check out his deceptively anarchic Not Now, Bernard. The communication skills of the family at the center of the satirical story leave something to be desired. The young son’s attempts to engage with his mother and father are routinely met with the dismissive response, “Not now, Bernard.” Having failed to convince his parents that there is a monster in the backyard, Bernard wanders outside and is promptly devoured. The monster then enters the house and proceeds to wreak low-level havoc but is met with the refrain: “Not now, Bernard,” the parents having apparently failed to notice the difference between their son and a squat, surly imp. But wait…just what is McKee up to? Is this a satire on adult distraction and apathy? Or is Bernard perhaps alive and well, his replacement by the monster a metaphor for rowdy childhood behavior? The cheeky cartoon-style illustrations offer no definitive answer. The subtle ambiguity of the plot’s key event and the irresistible energy of the presentation make for an uproarious, unforgettable read. Rest in peace, Mr. McKee.

Through a subversive art practice, one woman’s irrepressible vitality radiates outward and alters the course of her neighbors’ lives in Pockets by Jennifer Armstrong and @marygrandpre. Mood lifted, they slowly but surely transform their ascetic surroundings into a bright, joyful community. caption:
In Sonia Levitin and @jerrypinkneystudio’s The Man Who Kept His Heart in a Bucket, magical realism gives way to a sweet story of loneliness, warmth, and friendship. Jack lives in a little village, earning a living by crafting goods out of metal. While he does procure a satisfactory wage, he seems unable to enjoy himself or feel positive emotions, for he keeps his heart in a bucket—in order to protect himself from heartbreak. One day, a fish transforms itself into a mysterious maiden before Jack’s eyes, snatches his heart away, and challenges him to solve a riddle. As Jack puzzles out the answer, he slips closer and closer to forming positive connections with those around him. Levitin finds humanistic joy in her light fantasy setting, while Pinkey celebrates the movement and lively energy of the goings-on.

caption:
Once again it is Fairy Tale Theme Week. I’m very excited to explore several variants of a fascinating type in which a maiden must break a terrible spell that has been laid upon her family. Here, for your viewing pleasure, is the Week of the Brothers Turned into Birds.

For our first example, here is a version of The Six Swans, translated from German by Anthea Bell and illustrated by @gerdaraidt. In order to break the curse keeping her brothers in swan form, a young woman must sew each one a shirt made of starflowers. She is forbidden to make a sound until she finishes the task—a process that takes several years, during which time she marries a king and gives birth to several children. But the queen mother’s jealous temper threatens to end the maiden’s life and destroy her family forever. The story is set in an early modern European country, with soldiers sporting bayonets and half-timbered houses lining the town square. Raidt’s soft colors and angular character design complement Bell’s expressive writing.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: The Six Swans was originally published in 1812, in the first edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen by the Brothers Grimm. The most notable changes in this adaptation are the omission of the queen mother’s evil trick (smearing blood around the young woman’s mouth and accusing her of devouring her children) and the softening of her execution to imprisonment.

caption:
Another version of the Brothers Turned into Birds arrives in this adaptation of The Six Swans, translated by Anthea Bell and illustrated by Dorothée Duntze. Duntze’s alluring illustrations reveal a wealth of fascinating details, including the use of fox imagery on the witch’s daughter and the furtive reappearance of the witch herself in miniature form in the young king’s garden.

A note about the text: Bell’s translation for this edition was later reillustrated in a version by Gerda Raidt, which was the first book I featured during this very theme week. A side-by-side comparison reveals the text of the two books to be identical, with two glaring exceptions—this earlier version includes the queen mother’s false accusation of cannibalism, which Raidt’s later version softens to killing, and her eventual fate of being burned at the stake, which the later version changes to life imprisonment.

caption:
The Week of the Brothers Turned into Birds has woven its winged spell, and to conclude I present Hans Christian Andersen’s The Wild Swans, retold by Amy Ehrlich and illustrated by Susan Jeffers. Ehrlich’s eloquent writing honors the language of Andersen’s original text. Jeffers creates entrancing, detailed art by first laying down a pencil drawing, then applying fine-line pen, adding color with inks and dyes, and finally erasing the original pencil lines. She achieves shading and texture in her compositions through the use of shading, cross-hatching, and an intricate pebbled texture.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this tale was originally written by Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen and published in 1838 in Eventyr, fortalte for Børn. Ny Samling. Første Hefte (Fairy Tales Told for Children. New Collection. First Booklet). In developing this literary variant of the well-known tale type, Andersen drew inspiration most directly from “The Eleven Swans”, a folktale collected by Mathias Winther in 1823.

caption:
For some good-natured, witch-flavored adventure, try Margaret Hodges and Amanda Harvey’s Up the Chimney. When their bag of money is stolen, a family falls on hard times. Two sisters set out one at a time, hoping to earn a little money for their parents, and enter the service of a witch. Though ordered not to look up the chimney, each succumbs to temptation and discovers a bag of money suspiciously like the one stolen from their family. However, because of the kindnesses she has shown to others, the first sister is able to hide from the witch and escape; the second, apathetic and self-absorbed, is caught and beat with a broom. Hodges tells the story with wit and warmth, while Harvey illustrates with a lively energy.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this tale is adapted from “The Old Witch”, a tale collected by Joseph Jacobs in his 1894 work More English Fairy Tales. Hodges makes one key change to the text that radically shifts the heroine’s characterization. In the original, the money bag rightfully belongs to the witch, and the girl is not retrieving it for her family—she is simply stealing it.

caption:
Were you fascinated by light and dark as a child? Did you marvel at the interplay between them? Did you imagine them as two worlds straddling an ethereal border? If so, @suzyleebooks will show you an aspect of yourself in her powerfully alluring Shadow. A young girl explores the landscape of her pretend play in her family’s storage room. The light casts shadows onto the floor, and soon a silhouetted jungle landscape takes form. When a menacing wolf creature threatens the girl, she joins forces with the other shadows to create an enormous monster. Truly frightened, the wolf accepts an invitation to join the gleeful, harmonious dance. Finally, the girl is called to dinner, and all the marvelous shadows revert to mundane shapes. However, once the girl departs, the mysterious shadow game continues in her absence. In this nearly-wordless book, Lee employs her trademark use of the gutter between the two pages as a boundary between two diegetic spaces—its function here as the border of a shadowy underworld demands that the entire book be held sideways, the pages flipped upward to progress. Stark black, white, and gray represent the reality at the beginning of the story, while warm, brilliant yellow begins to creep in as a visual representation of the force of the girl’s imagination.

caption:
Have a look at Little Johnny Buttermilk, an English tale retold by Jan Wahl and illustrated Jennifer Mazzucco. A young boy selling buttermilk at the town market for his family is menaced by a witch, who sees him as a tasty treat. Each day, she stuffs him into her sack and drags him off toward her house, and each day he must outwit her by escaping the sack and replacing himself with something else—thistles and thorns, large stones, and finally the witch’s own fine china. caption:
This is a touching tale of loneliness, regret, and lost love: Kathleen and Michael Hague’s The Legend of the Veery Bird. The story is set on the edge of a forest full of fairies and ancient magic. A young boy named Veery has great difficulty communicating, as he speaks with a stutter. As he grows, he becomes deeply self-conscious and prefers to spend his time among the trees, away from people. When his father dies, he feels unable to express his sadness, even to his beloved mother. Soon afterward, the boy meets a being known as the Keeper of the Forest, who gifts him with the power of song, but makes him promise to sing only for her. Veery is able to keep his oath for a long time, but after many years, as he sits by the side of his dying mother, he grants her final request and sings her to rest. Thereafter, Veery can no longer find the Keeper of the Forest, with whom he has fallen in love. The force of his grief transforms him into a bird, and he soars through the night sky. When the morning comes, the Keeper of the Forest welcomes him back into her embrace, and leaves a little bird in his place. Wife Kathleen Hague’s eloquent prose and husband Michael Hague’s rich watercolor and gouache paintings combine for a dramatic original etiological fairy tale.

caption:
Warning: there’s no happy ending here, only a grim and sobering look at history in Gary Crew and @shauncytan’s The Viewer. Tristan, a curious young boy with his head in the clouds, often wanders away from home to explore, much to the consternation of his parents. He develops a particular affinity for the town garbage dump, with its heaps and heaps of hidden treasures. One day, he comes across a box filled with binoculars, magnifying glasses, sextants, and other devices for viewing and measuring. Most fascinating of all is a stereoscope, equipped with discs containing rings of images. Through it, he gets an unvarnished glimpse at humanity’s time on earth: the chaos of the prehistoric era, the tumult of early civilizations, the discord of the Middle Ages, the cruelty of imperialism, the hazards of industrialization, and the horrors of planetary devastation. The more he looks, the more mesmerized Tristan becomes. Ultimately, he is drawn involuntarily into the strange machine and vanishes entirely. Crew weaves a haunting tale that, absent a clear moral, forces the reader to contemplate the dark saga of human brutality. Tan heightens this effect by featuring closeups of discs as the book’s central images, encoding multilayered historical symbolism within the silent, sinister visual narrative.

For a wickedly comedic caper, try The Devil & Mother Crump by Valerie Scho Carey and Arnold Lobel. An ill-tempered old baker woman named Mother Crump treats all around her with deep hostility. To assuage Mother Crump, he grants her three wishes. She asks for the power to trap anyone who touches her flour barrel, her bread dough, or her birch tree. Carey constructs a merry text full of slapstick misadventures; Lobel gives us devils and imps with equal parts humor and menace.

caption:
Here is a peek at a lovely version of Goldilocks and the Three Bears by Jim Aylesworth and @barbaramcclintockart. The book opens from the perspective of Goldilocks, who skips through the woods to the bears’ quaint stone house covered in ivy. Aylesworth presents a sweet and gentle retelling, while McClintock provides warm-toned art in watercolor, sepia ink, and gouache. Close examination of the opening illustration reveals the young girl to be reading Aylesworth and McClintock’s adaptation of The Gingerbread Man.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: In the book’s front matter, Aylesworth cites Robert Southey’s 1837 publication of the tale. In Southey’s text, the bears are described as a Little, Small, Wee Bear, a Middle-sized Bear, and a Great, Huge Bear. Aylesworth, like many modern authors, assigns them family roles, depicting the smallest as a child, the middle as a mother, and the largest as a father. Readers may also be surprised to learn that one of Aylewsorth’s title characters fails to appear in the source material: Goldilocks herself. Southey’s interloper is an old woman. Only in subsequent literary renditions of the story was the character replaced with a young girl, whose name was first given as Silver-Hair, then Golden Hair, then Goldenlocks, and finally the enduringly familiar Goldilocks.

caption:
What does your name mean to you and your family? That simple but eternally relevant question informs the spirit of Knots on a Counting Rope, written by Bill Martin Jr. and John Archambault and illustrated by Ted Rand. A boy begs his grandfather for a story—the story of the boy’s own birth, of the inspiration behind his name, of meeting and training his very own horse, and of a subsequent horse race. When the story is done, the grandfather ties yet another knot on the counting rope, which, when full, will indicate that the boy knows the story by heart and can tell it himself. Martin and Archambault’s vivid back-and-forth dialogue without surrounding narration provides a thoughtful treatment of the boy’s experience with blindness, as well as his patience and strength. Rand’s rich-hued illustrations create a powerful sense of place, emotion, and tradition.

caption:
Shudders and gasps invariably arise from an audience for this next book: Mirra Ginsburg and Jos. A. Smith’s Clay Boy. Don’t let the charming cover art fool you—a horror story lies within. An old man and an old woman make a boy out of clay and bake him in the oven. Soon he emerges, sentient and hungry. The old couple try to assuage his craving for food, but he is insatiable. The clay boy devours the farm animals, the pets, and the old man and the old woman themselves. Then, grown large and terrible, he moves on to the rest of the people in the village. The only one to defy the creature is an ornery goat, who tricks him into standing still and then leaps from a high hill, smashing him to smithereens. Ginsburg presents the drama of this old tale with serious and straightforward language, but it’s in Smith’s square like and gouache paintings that the events of the story truly become a nightmare. The clay boy grows and grows, body swelling along with his monstrous appetite. As he transforms from a sweet little imp to a demanding glutton to a lumbering behemoth, his face morphs into a bestial snarl. Here is the Gingerbread Man’s dark and twisted twin—readers, be warned.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: In the book’s front matter, Ginsburg mentions that the story of Clay Boy can be found in many cultures, and that she used Russian sources as inspiration for her retelling.

caption:
The Blue Stone: A Journey Through Life by Jimmy Liao mines surprisingly subtle shades of emotion from an inanimate object. The story spans years, hundreds of years, thousands of years. A large blue rock is discovered in the forest and continually chiseled into various statues and sculptures for visual consumption. Liao accords the stone a measure of consciousness; each time it recalls its home among the trees, it crumbles out of sadness and lies in pieces until another stoneworker arrives to transform it yet again. An elephant in a public square, a bird in a garden, a fish by a wharf, a moon in a gallery, a cat in an orphanage…the blue stone experiences these and many other forms until finally only a few specks of rock are left to drift on the wind back to the forest where they began as a solid whole. Liao’s poignant text (translated from Chinese by Sarah L. Thomson) and engaging illustrations combine for a simultaneously intimate and epic narrative of poetic realism.

caption:
When you were a child, did you ever just start digging, convinced that buried treasure lay somewhere beneath your feet? Perhaps you think that now you’re all grown up and you know better. But perhaps you had the right idea from the beginning. Here’s the gently amusing, faintly mysterious Sam & Dave Dig a Hole, written by @macbarnett and illustrated by @jonklassen. Two boys decide to start digging a hole, eager to find something spectacular. They move through the earth, traveling down, sideways, diagonally, and then down again. Unfortunately, in every direction they narrowly miss a series of large, brilliant gemstones—unseen by them but blatantly obvious to the reader. Ultimately, they fall through a hole and plummet into a mysterious abyss, which leads down, down, down, until they land right back in the spot where they started. Or do they? The landscape seems subtly different. Their original hole is nowhere to be seen, and a number of subtle environmental changes are visible: a pear tree stands in place of their apple tree, a blue daisy has replaced a red tulip in the flowerpot, their cat has a blue collar instead of a red one, and their house has a duck weathervane instead of a chicken. What is going on? Have the boys dropped into an alternate universe? That determination is left to the reader. Barnett’s straightforward text and Klassen’s understated illustrations (a blend of colored pencil and digital technique) combine for an atmosphere of deadpan humor and metaphysical enigma.

For a time, they receive daily visits from a mysterious sentient bear, whom they grow to care for a great deal. Later, they begin to encounter an ill-tempered dwarf who repeatedly needs rescuing from dangerous situations but offers only insults and abuse in place of gratitude. Finally, a secret connection between the bear and the dwarf is revealed, a curse lifted, and a happy ending earned. Topor’s expressive art makes use of loose cross-hatching and deep, saturated color.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: The source material for this story is the fairy tale “Snow-White and Rose-Red”, originally published by the Brothers Grimm in 1837 in the third edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen. The Grimms themselves appear to have adapted “The Ungrateful Dwarf”, an originally tale by Caroline Stahl published in 1818.

caption:
Today brings my total number of book reviews to seven hundred. I’m delighted to have come this far, and I’m not done yet! Thanks as always for reading these posts and leaving friendly comments along the way.

To mark the occasion, here’s a book that sank its claws into me when I was young: Verna Aardema and Susan Meddaugh’s Bimwili & the Zimwi. At the beach, a young girl finds an enormous, beautiful seashell. On the way home, she realizes she has forgotten the shell, but her older sisters refuse to turn around, so she returns to the beach alone. The shell has been found by a zimwi, a wrinkled old ogre who lures Bimwili closer and closer until he snatches her up. He stuffs her into a large drum, lugs her from village to village, and commands her to sing. One day, Bimwili hears familiar voices and discovers that the zimwi has reached her very own community. She cleverly modifies the lyrics of her song to alert her relatives, who sneak her out of the drum to safety. In a closing episode, Bimwili and her sisters again escape from the zimwi, who has transformed into an enormous pumpkin. Aardema retells this chilling tale with a compelling voice, including onomatopoeias for sound effects such as laughter, scuttling crab legs, and magical transformations. Meddaugh’s illustrations create a cheerful landscape of village, jungle, and ocean. The pitted face of the sickly green zimwi, all sinister smiles and furious frowns, serves as a sharp deviation from the peaceful surroundings.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Aardema here adapts her own story “Little Sister and the Zimwi” (published in her 1969 book Tales for the Third Ear), itself a retelling of the tale “Watoto na Zimwi” (“The Children and the Zimwi”), published by Henri Junod in Kibaraka: Swahili Stories in 1896.

caption:
When you were young, did your parents respond to conflict by issuing threats? Assuming the threats were effective, did you look back later in life and realize your parents would have been unlikely to carry them out? Readers can witness the fallout from one child’s decision to call his father’s bluff in Jules Feiffer’s By the Side of the Road. The story begins in that pressure cooker of sibling tension: the back seat of the family car. Richard and his younger brother Rudy pass the time by getting into physical fights, headless of their parents’ reprimands. After one too many squabbles, their father declares that he will pull the car over and leave anyone still fighting to stand and wait until the car returns. Richard, undaunted, accepts and steps out onto the shoulder of the highway. Since neither he nor his father is willing to apologize, he stays there—for days, weeks, months, years. He makes friends, builds a house, digs a series of underground tunnels, gets married, starts a family…and eventually reconciles with his parents. Feiffer takes a clever premise and exaggerates it to ridiculous proportions, with a charming first-person narrative and expressive, loose-lined black and white art.

If you, like me, are regularly in the mood for a tale of grandeur, romance, and dark magic, Lisbeth Zwerger’s version of Swan Lake should do nicely. Out for a moonlit hunt, young prince encounters a maiden bewitched by an evil sorcerer to take the form of a swan each day from sunrise to midnight. The two of them declare their love for each other, and the young man resolves to break the spell. After he is tricked into pledging himself to an impostor, the prince must defeat the sorcerer and save the swan maiden once and for all. Zwerger’s text, translated from German by Marianne Martens, brims with energy and wonder. Her illustrations employ quiet symbolism to externalize the traits of various characters: the maidens’ bodies always contain swanlike features and the sorcerer enters the grand ballroom with a dark lighting cloud overhead. Facing each illustration is a grand staff containing a musical passage from Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s immortal ballet.

caption:
@pgreenboat and @catia_chien’s The Town of Turtle is many things: A story of introspection and transformation. A celebration of optimism and creativity. An ode to friendship and community. Turtle, all alone with his shadow, decides to make some upgrades to his surroundings. He paints, builds, landscapes, and engineers until he creates a small town, perched marvelously atop his shell. Enticed by this wondrous new locality, a host of workers and artists migrates from afar to populate the houses. Where Turtle was once all alone, he now enjoys an abundance of friends. Cuevas sprinkles her quirkily fascinating tale with potent similes (“as empty as a bird’s nest in December,” “as dark as the underside of a bell”), creative metaphors (“he slept the sleep of a broken pocket watch.”), and delightful personification (“The dream, feeling brave, ventured out into the world,” “laughter moved into the houses”). Chien’s colorful artwork, a combination of acrylic, pencil, and paper collage, reflects the magic and vibrancy of the story.

caption:
Here’s the merry tale of a misfit who is not afraid to make his own fortune: @katecoombs13 and @johnnickleart’s Hans My Hedgehog. A wealthy farmer and his wife deeply long for a baby. The man, in despair, declares that he would want a son even if the boy were half hedgehog. Soon enough, the woman does indeed give birth to a human-hedgehog hybrid. The child, known as Hans-My-Hedgehog, shows talent for tending pigs and playing the fiddle. In time, he decides to fly off on the back of a rooster and live in the forest. On two separate occasions, he encounters kings who are lost and cannot find the road. In exchange for help, the two kings agree to give Hans the first thing they meet when they return to their palaces—and for each king the one who greets him at the gate is his own daughter. The first king reneges on the deal, and Hans plunders his royal fortune in revenge. The second king keeps his word, leading to a happy union and a miraculous transformation. Coombs crafts a narrative full of wit and warmth, while Nickle supplies inviting, smooth-textured acrylic paintings.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: in adapting the narrative from the original tale by the Brothers Grimm, Coombs has lightened the tone considerably. In the Grimms’ story, rather than show Hans love and support, his parents resent him for the strange form of his body and wish him dead. Hans himself plays the bagpipes, slaughters his pigs, attacks and wounds the first princess, and turns fully human when his hedgehog skin is burned in a fire.

Have you ever been searching for a spot to complete a difficult task—or simply to relax—and wished that everyone would just go away for a while? So too does the long-suffering protagonist of @verabee’s wry and faintly metaphysical Leave Me Alone! A grandmother attempting to finish her knitting is constantly thwarted by her hordes of pesky grandchildren. If she is to complete her work in a timely fashion, she will need some peace and quiet. She therefore leaves home and sets off into the wilderness. She stops in a quiet forest, but is immediately annoyed by a towering bear. She sits on a frosty mountaintop, but a herd of goats begins to crowd her. Farther and farther she goes, so desperate for solitude that she begins to play fast and loose with the laws of reality. She marches effortlessly onto the moon, but a vexing collective of little green aliens instantly throngs around her. Finally, she steps into a wormhole and finds herself in a pitch-black void. There, outside the bounds of spacetime, she can knit uninterrupted. Once she is done, she makes her way back home without a care in the world. Brosgol’s tongue-in-cheek narration is perfectly matched by her whimsical cartoon-style art.

When I was young, I imagined I might one day escape the drudgery of daily life and slip away to a hidden world. Perhaps you did as well. But what if there was already someone waiting for you when you arrived…or something? If this premise intrigues you, then Steven Kellogg’s The Island of the Skog is just the book for you. A plucky troupe of mice decides to flee from the dogs and cats that predate upon them in their home town. They set sail in a little ship and voyage to an island whose population, according to their guidebook, consists of one Skog. Just what is a Skog? When the mice discover enormous footprints, they hatch a plan to combat the mysterious creature. Their foe soon presents itself as a rumpled, shadowy specter...but, it soon emerges, there is more to the Skog than meets the eye. Just who ought to be afraid of whom? The rodent crew and their new neighbor finally realize they have far more in common than they had thought. Kellogg’s oddball story, accentuated with wit and suspense, comes alive in energetic, cross-hatched illustrations.

caption:
Fear of the dark is quite common in childhood. Sometimes, though, all it takes to overcome a long-held fear is to look at things from a new viewpoint. To that end, here is Switch On the Night by Ray Bradbury and Leo and Diane Dillon. A young boy afraid of the dark spends his time in the illuminated rooms of his home, even going as far as keeping the light on in his room at bedtime. One night, when he has all the lights turned on in the entire house, he hears a knocking from outside. There stands a girl named Dark who promises to introduce the boy to the Night. She teaches him about all the things that can only be perceived when the lights switches are flicked off: frogs, crickets, stars, and the moon. From then on, the boy is pleased to take part in the daily ritual of switching on the night. Bradbury’s lyrical writing underscores the poignancy of the gentle story, while married collaborators the Dillons emphasize the tale’s subtly cosmic nature with Escher-inspired illustrations that play with perspective and dimensionality.

caption:
Deep in the heart of summer, nature has come alive with the thrum of energy and mystical possibility. Wandering the shady woods at a time like this, one might expect to encounter fairies around every bend in the path. It is with this thought in mind that I present a new theme week, inspired by an ancient folk ballad: today commences seven adaptations of the tale of Tam Lin.

Let us begin with a version written by Jane Yolen and illustrated by Charles Mikolaycak. Jennet MacKenzie, a fearless and headstrong young woman, pays a visit to her family’s ancestral home of Carterhaugh, despite warnings that the derelict castle is haunted. There, amid the lonely ruins, she meets Tam Lin, a handsome youth kidnapped by the mysterious Fair Folk and kept in a state of eternal youth in the land of the Ever-Fair, the kingdom inside the green hill. The two of them quickly fall in love, and Jennet boldly rescues Tam Lin from an unearthly procession of Faerie riders on Hallow’s Eve. But hers is no easy task, for she must then cling tightly to her beloved’s body as the haughty Queen of the Fey turns him into a ferocious lion, a constricting serpent, and a burning firebrand. In the end, Jennet’s determination overcomes the power of the fairies, and Tam Lin is released to a mortal life once more. Yolen’s powerful voice gives rise to a thrilling and richly descriptive text, accompanied by Mikolaycak’s dynamic and captivating illustrations.

Next in our week of Tam Lin adaptations comes a version written by Susan Cooper and illustrated by Warwick Hutton. Margaret, a bold and independent-minded king’s daughter, is warned never to wander near the enchanted wood of Carterhays, for fear of the Elfin knight Tam Lin. Naturally, that is just where she goes. She does indeed encounter Tam Lin, and spends a day with the charming young man. However, when she returns to her castle, the household informs her that she has been missing for an entire week. Margaret returns to see Tam Lin and learns that he will be sacrificed to the Devil unless she rescues him from the Elfin procession on Midsummer’s Eve. As she clings tightly to his body, the furious Elfin Queen transforms him into a snarling wolf, a venomous snake, a wild deer, and a red hot iron bar. Once Margaret drops the iron bar into a nearby well, the Elfin folk flee and Tam Lin is released from his bondage. Cooper’s elegant text is well complemented by the pale colors of Hutton’s art.

caption:
Here we stand in the very heart of our Week of Tam Lin, and I’m transfixed at this version by Robin Muller, titled The Nightwood. Elaine, daughter of the Earl of March, grows up in wealth and happiness. Her old nurse warns her to stay away from the Nightwood, a nearby forest in the mystical grip of the Elfin Queen. If she goes near, she might just vanish like the son of the Earl of Roxborough, who strayed too near the trees long ago. When her father throws a ball but forbids her to attend, Elaine retaliates by running straight to the Nightwood, where an Elfin knight called Tamlynne welcomes her. Each month at the full moon, she returns to dance with the Elfin throng. Finally, she learns that Tamlynne is none other than the long-lost son of the Earl of Roxborough, a mortal trapped among the supernatural band. On All Hallow’s Eve, she boldly saves him by pulling him off his horse and holding him tightly to her, though the Elfin Queen in her wrath changes him into a snarling bear, a fluttering dove, a coiling serpent, and a fiery brand. With respect for the original Scottish ballad, Muller presents an ornate story and elegant, brightly colored illustrations.

caption:
Even when surrounded by warmth and comfort, it’s all to easy to feel trapped by social isolation. A sense of belonging may develop over time, but wouldn’t it be lovely if something came along to break the ice in the most extraordinary way possible? @danielmiyaresdoodles gives us just such a tale in his imaginative and alluring Night Out. The protagonist is a young boy attending a dignified boarding school in a stately country manor house. While the other children seem to have made friends, he eats alone at the table and lies sadly awake in bed after lights out. Beckoned by the appearance of a mysterious invitation and map, he sneaks out the window and rides into the night on his bicycle. An enormous turtle carries him across dark waters to a cave, where a bear, an owl, a rabbit, a goose, and a fox are hosting a tea party and a lively dance. Is all of this a dream? As possible clues, the midnight adventure contains several visual links to the mundane world of the school. The giant turtle seems to be a larger version of the boy’s own tiny pet (seen crawling out of its bowl early in the night and back in at dawn), the cave resembles the rock in the turtle’s habitat, and the chair at the party is identical to those seen in the school dining room and dormitory. Whether dream, truth, or a creative bit of fiction, the story serves its social purpose: by entertaining his schoolmates, the boy is quickly welcomed into the group. Miyares employs a structure somewhere between a traditional story and a wordless picture book, the narrative propelled by strongly evocative illustrations occasionally accompanied by brief snippets of dialogue or short phrases hinting at the boy’s internal thoughts. The art, a glowing combination of gouache and colored pencil, establishes a world anchored in reality with currents of magic trickling in at the edges.

caption:
Margaret Hodges and Aki Sogabe create an appealing presentation of a Japanese legend in The Boy Who Drew Cats. The story begins with a child in a small village whose parents take him to the local temple so that he may learn to be a priest. However, his training is derailed by his compulsive habit of drawing cats at all possible times and on all possible surfaces—in books, on walls, on delicate paper screens. Finally, the miffed priest banishes him permanently. Despondent, the boy hopes to resume his studies at a large temple in the neighboring village. However, this temple has been taken over by a frightful goblin. Luckily, the young artist draws cats all over the walls before going to sleep. In the middle of the night, these cats come to life and kill the goblin, who has taken the shape of an enormous rat. The big grows up to be an artist, respected and admired by all who know his work. Hodges writes with compelling language, while Sogabe contributes dramatic illustrations made from a combination of cut-paper collage, watercolor, and airbrushing.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: in the back matter, Hodges details the lineage of her source material. The boy in the story is based on legends of Sesshū Tōyō, a renowned fifteenth-century Zen-Shu priest and sumi-e artist. Though this particular story was first published in a pamphlet in Tokyo by Takejiro Hasegawa, Hodges works from a version in Japanese Fairy Tales (1918) by Lafcadio Hearn.

If you’d like to immerse yourself in the world of early New England, read Island Boy, a classic work of realistic fiction by Barbara Cooney. The Tibbets family lives on a little island of the coast of Maine. Matthais, the youngest of twelve children, grows up fishing, hunting, and working on the family farm. He works aboard a merchant ship, rising from cabin boy all the way to captain. As an adult, he spends his life back home on Tibbets Island, first with his wife and daughters, and later with his youngest daughter and her son, also named Matthais. Finally, he drowns while out at sea and is buried on the island that he called home. With the charming details of her text and the pale colors of her artwork, Cooney paints a tender portrait of a simple life, happy and well-lived.

caption:
Imagine yourself surrounded by cold, empty wilderness, no one to brighten your life of drudgery. What would it take to change your world for the better? Helen Ward and Wayne Anderson assemble a marvelous world of magic realism and heartfelt connection to answer this very question in The Tin Forest. At the center of an enormous wasteland covered with junk and garbage lives an old man. Alone and dejected, he dreams nightly of lush greenery growing all around him. These thrilling visions inspire him to construct a scrap metal forest populated with plant and animal sculptures. One day, unexpectedly, a living thing arrives: a bird, perching on a tin tree branch. Soon, more birds come, carrying seeds, which take root and begin to sprout. Real plants and trees creep upward, attracting more and more animals. The tin forest transforms into a real one, the old man’s wonderful dream finally come true. Beginning with the striking line, “There was once a wide, windswept place, near nowhere and close to forgotten,” Ward’s spare, poetic text employs powerful imagery and gentle strokes of emotion from start to finish. Anderson’s dramatic illustrations instill a strong sense of place, shifting from barren gray to glowing yellow and green as the environment slowly comes to life.

Changes by Anthony Browne uses visual metaphor to explore this very thought process. Joseph Kaye is home alone. His father, before going out to pick up his mother, mentioned that things were going to change. Browne renders the wild possibilities suggested by Joseph’s confused imagination literally on the page, setting up normal scenarios through his limited text and unleashing their oddball potential in his delightfully surreal art.

caption:
I have now written seven hundred thirty of these daily book reviews, which means I’ve been posting for exactly two years! I’m excited to have come this far, and I’ve still got a whole lot more that I’m excited to share with you all. Many thanks for reading and responding!

To conclude my second year, let us immerse ourselves in a little-known but absolutely incredible book: Lionheart by Richard Collingridge. The story traverses the boundary between waking and dreaming, between real life and the world of imagination, with a fluid ease. Young Richard, alone but for his beloved stuffed toy Lionheart, is deeply afraid. He cannot stay in his room, for he is being menaced by a terrifying monster, a sinister dragon-snake that haunts him like a slithery nightmare. Richard runs from his home out into the night, stalked at every turn by the shadow creature, accidentally dropping Lionheart in his anxiety. He finds his way into a strange jungle populated by a host of animals. Oh and on he goes until suddenly Lionheart appears before him as a fully grown lion. Together, boy and beast take a stand and banish the dark, looming serpent with a ferocious roar, joined by all the animals of the jungle. Having conquered his fears, Richard finds himself back in his bedroom, morning light streaming through the windows, Lionheart a stuffed toy once more. With gentle text and truly epic illustrations, Collingridge creates a stunning portrait of childhood emotion, equal parts high fantasy grandeur and tender picture book intimacy.

Acamar hurtles down to earth as a flesh-and-blood human, while Eridani ascends into space as a celestial being. She masterfully vivifies the glowing spectacle of her alternate history setting with mixed-media art executed in watercolor, India ink, salt, graphite, pastels, and digital paint.

Do you need some respite from the summer heat? Perhaps you’re dreaming of frozen lands far away? Let me take you there with The Ice Palace by @angelamcallisterbooks and Angela Barrett. Anna’s family lives in a hot, dry land near a grand palace, where her father works in the kitchens. One day, the young girl falls ill and must rest in bed. Her father has been tasked with a secret project for the grand banquet table, for which he continually visits the palace’s ice house, just across from Anna’s bedroom window. Though he will not reveal the secret, he tells her stories of the North Wind rushing through icy halls among snow-white mountains, of a princess in an ice palace in a land where snowflakes always fall, of white bears and ice ships and snowbirds. Night after night, Anna dreams herself in all of these wondrous scenarios. Finally, her father reveals the surprise: he has meticulously carved an intricate ship of ice. McAllister’s text masterfully conjures imagery of sweltering heat and shivering cold. Barrett’s illustrations neatly weave back and forth between the tender emotional realism in Anna’s relationship with her father and the mystical imagery of the girl’s fantasy dreamworlds.

caption:
Today I’m inspired by the magic and mystery of Eric A. Kimmel and Trina Schart Hyman’s Iron John. Walter is the youngest son of a king. In his father’s royal menagerie is a wild man covered in matted gray hair, a fearsome being known to all as Iron John. When Walter’s ball flies into the creature’s enclosure, the two of them strike a bargain—the ball for the key to the cage. The young prince, fearing his father’s wrath, asks to go away with Iron John. The two of them live together in the woods for many years, and the boy is tasked with guarding a magical spring, which eventually turns his long, flowing hair to gold. Walter grows to adulthood, and eventually returns to civilization, where he gains employment in the garden of a king. He attends a royal ball, jousts in a royal tournament, and engages a band of robbers in battle, all thanks to clothing and equipment supplied by Iron John. Finally, he marries a young woman who has always loved him despite his rough exterior. Kimmel’s elegant text and Hyman’s regal illustrations make a worthy and engaging fairy tale adaptation.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: this story is adapted from the Brothers Grimm tale “Eisenhans”, literally “Iron Hans”. Since Hans is a diminutive of the German name Johann, the title is often rendered in English as “Iron John”.

Luna is a very unusual girl. She lives above the clouds in what appears to be a floating lighthouse. caption:
In honor of the great Raymond Briggs, here’s a little glimpse of his heartwarming tale The Bear. Tilly, a happy and ordinary child, is asleep in her bedroom. Unbeknownst to her, an unlikely visitor is about to arrive and upend her life entirely. In the middle of the night, a polar bear opens the window, crawls inside, and makes itself at home. Once the girl wakes up, the two make fast friends. They pass a dynamic day together, eating, bathing, and playing. The great beast proves an unpredictable companion, causing Tilly a good deal of stress and worry as she cleans up after it and attempts to explain its presence to her parents—who somehow never do manage to catch a glimpse of it despite its considerable bulk. Finally, the bear slips out Tilly’s window in the night and makes for the wild, departing as quietly and inexplicably as it arrived. With sweetly humorous dialogue and soft colored pencil drawings organized in comic strip format, the book mixes slice-of-life and magic realism in a delicate and truly memorable blend. Rest in peace, Mr. Briggs.

caption:
Colin Thompson muses on humanity’s relationship to the land and environment in his thought-provoking work The Paper Bag Prince. A busy town disposes of its garbage by tossing it in the middle of a nearby valley. Despite the filthy conditions, life manages to thrive in the form of wildflowers, trees, and a few animals. An old man known to everyone as the Paper Bag Prince visits the dump every day, caring for the animals and collecting odd bits of junk in an abandoned railway carriage. In his youth, the location was his beloved home, but he was evicted after his farmhouse burned down. When the city decides to begin incinerating its trash, they return ownership of the site to the Paper Bag Prince, who is overjoyed. A truck driver and crane operator help him place several of the old train cars in a row, and he moves his belongings in at once. Considering himself truly blessed, he settles into a happy life wit his animal companions. Thompson’s straightforward text, along with his illustrations boasting intricate borders and a wealth of fascinating details, forms a simple but powerful parable of the sanctity of nature.

caption:
Lately I’ve been itching to do another Fairy Tale Theme Week—specifically another Sequel Week—specifically Hansel and Gretel. Let’s begin.

Here is an adaptation written and illustrated by Susan Jeffers, who has hewn closely to the text of the Brothers Grimm. The art comprises fine-line pen drawn over a detailed pencil sketch (which was then erased) and colored with ink and dyes. Fine hatching and intricate pebbled patterns create delicate natural textures. Jeffers, picking up on clues left by the Brothers Grimm, links the witch to the children’s stepmother by giving her an eerily similar outfit—a ruffled bonnet, a purple dress with a white apron and ruffled collar, black shoes, and a shawl with an identical pink floral pattern.

An observation: This is the 1980 edition of he book. The 2011 edition features the same text with a few deletions (confusingly, credited to author Amy Ehrlich, whose name was nowhere to be found in the original). More strikingly, the illustrations have been altered for the reissue—the witch’s facial features have been altered, evidently to make her less frightening, as has fence of gingerbread children. A few of the more chilling vignettes have been omitted entirely. This subtle bowdlerization is perplexing in a tale that so thoroughly dwells in the emotions of fear and despair. On principle, I have chosen to present the original.

caption:
May you draw on the power of Hansel and Gretel to push your greatest obstacles into the fire and let them burn away to ash. For today’s adaptation, I have Joan Walsh Anglund’s Nibble Nibble Mousekin. Alternating between black and white and full color art, Anglund puts a distinctive stamp on the tale. The two young children here are rendered as doll-like cherubs with dot eyes and blank faces. They meet their diametric opposite in the two antagonists—their stepmother and the witch, both charismatic figures with bony frames, pointy noses, and wicked, smirking expressions.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: The unusual title here draws from a specific passage in the Brothers Grimm tale. As Hansel and Gretel feast on the house of sweets, they hear a voice from within call out, “knuper, knuper, kneischen,/wer knupert an meinem Häuschen?” This rhyme translates into English literally as, “Nibble, nibble, munch,/Who is nibbling at my house?” However, most retellings today render the phrase: “Nibble, nibble, like a mouse,/Who is nibbling at my house?” This idiomatic and irresistibly rhymed translation is the work of Lucy Crane, who published a volume of the Grimms’ tales illustrated by her brother, celebrated artist Walter Crane, in 1882.

I now present @neilhimself’s powerful retelling of the story, accompanied by the art of @lorenzomattotti. caption:
In honor of the remarkable Dennis Nolan, here is the engaging story of a ragtag group of travelers striking bravely out into the unknown: Hunters of the Great Forest. Seven tiny humans leave their little village with great fanfare and trek off through the wilderness on an important expedition. Each member of the team carries a different item: a walking stick, a telescope, a magnifying glass, a spear, a knapsack, a bedroll, and a mysterious map that leads them on a path over large rocks and past towering trees. Each animal they pass (a snail, a dragonfly, a toad, a blue jay, a chipmunk) represents a strange new curiosity or a danger narrowly escaped. Finally, they arrive at their quarry: a campfire with a bag of marshmallows lying on the ground, waiting to be toasted. They carry a marshmallow back to their community, divide it happily among their brethren, and eat it as they share stories of their great journey. Nolan imbues his wordless adventure with action, intrigue, humor, and heart. Lacking visible mouths, the little wanderers convey emotion through body language in the appealing illustrations, executed in pen and ink, watercolor, and colored pencil on watercolor board. Rest in peace, Mr. Nolan.

The book of the day is The Legend of Sea Glass by Trinka Hakes Noble and Doris Ettlinger. The story opens in a time when humans believe the world is flat and therefore remain on land for fear of sailing too close to the edge and falling off. A pod of mermaids lives in peace, exploring the magnificent ocean depths and occasionally rising to the surface to bask in the sunshine. From this fateful moment on, stories of the lovely beings’ existence begin to spread, and people lose their fear of the sea. When sailors inevitably perish on the water, the mermaids weep beautiful tears, which the ocean magically preserved as sea glass. Noble’s eloquent text and Ettlinger’s colorful illustrations come together for a fanciful and endearing etiology.

caption:
Imagine being beckoned into a strange land, not by a magical invitation but by the theft of something very precious to you. This is the driving force behind the mysterious wordless adventure of @sgraegin’s Little Fox in the Forest. A young girl learns that her class will be having Show-and-Tell, and her teacher prompts the students to bring in something old and treasured. She chooses her beloved stuffed fox. Out on the playground, however, the toy fox is stolen by a real fox, an anthropomorphic creature who promptly runs off into the trees. The girl gives chase, followed closely by a boy from her class, and the two soon enter a neighborhood of busy streets and bustling shops, all populated by the forest animals. When she finally reaches the little fox’s home she finds her quarry unexpectedly sympathetic. A trade is made, and human and fox contentedly part ways. Through comic-style panels created in pencil, watercolor, and ink and colored digitally, Graegin presents a whirlwind trip into a delightful parallel world. Fascinatingly, the young girl’s daily life in the real world is depicted in desaturated blues and grays; the little fox introduces a contrasting spot of orange, and his anthropomorphic neighbors boast a wide range of rich hues.

caption:
For a with a compelling emotional core shrouded in a cosmic riddle, look no further than Mượn Thị Văn and April Chu’s In a Village by the Sea. The viewpoint of the story moves continuously inward, shifting its perspective ever smaller. We begin with a house, then move to the kitchen, then the stove, a woman cooking, a child beside her, a hole in the floor, a cricket, and even a miraculously tiny seascape the cricket is painting. However, in a truly mind-bending turn of events, the story pushes ahead into the cricket’s art, where a little boat navigates a rough, stormy sea. The sailor on this boat is none other than the husband of the woman cooking in the kitchen of the little house. What has happened? Is the cricket somehow able to produce a detailed representation of the outside world? Is the universe nested inside itself, a path of infinite recursion? These questions are for the reader to answer…or simply to ponder. The rich shading and dramatic angles of Chu’s illustrations complement Van’s simple and eloquent text.

A sobering work of tragic beauty awaits you in The Feral Child by Eric Sundell and Charles Mikolaycak. It is the end of summer. Eighteen-year-old Aaron journeys out into the forest to seek his baby sister Katrina, carried away by wolves when he was only three. Sundell’s magnificent text alternates forms, beginning as an epic prose poem and shifting into lyrical songs and dramatic dialogue when characters meet and interact. caption:
Rafe Martin and Kimberly Bulcken Root spin a delightful yarn in their comical adventure The Storytelling Princess. When a well-read prince hears that his parents have found him a bride, he declares he will only marry her if she can tell him a tale whose ending he does not already know. His father the king proclaims a large reward for anyone who meets the criterion. In a realm far away across the ocean, a princess is told that her parents have made a match for her, and she retorts that she would rather be washed overboard at sea than have someone else arrange her marriage. As fate would have it, her royal ship is caught in a storm that very night and she is indeed swept into the ocean. After washing up on land with only a chest of sailor’s clothes, she disguises herself as a young man and accepts the challenge to surprise the bookish prince, who is confident that he has heard enough stories to predict any ending. The princess cleverly relates the account of her own hazardous voyage, drawing it out for days and days before finally taking off her sailor’s outfit and revealing that protagonist and storyteller are one and the same. At that exact moment, her parents arrive and the whole truth emerges: the prince and the princess were arranged to be married from the very start. Martin’s cleverly circuitous narrative is well complemented by Root’s pencil-and-watercolor illustrations.

caption:
Did you ever feel left out as a child? Awkward? Isolated? Perhaps you imagined a wild place where your outsider status would be a boon rather then a hindrance. Lee Nordling and Bruce Zick give us a glimpse of just such a marvelous location in The Bramble. A young boy, excluded from a group game of tag, spots a strange anthropomorphic animal and follows it through a thicket into a mysterious forested realm. There he encounters a clan of strange beasts menaced by an eldritch wave of sentient slime that threatens to devour everything in its path. After participating in the creatures’ ritual bonfire dance, he faces off against the monstrous ooze and dispatches it for good. In the end, he returns to the familiar world with a newfound confidence and poise. Nordling conveys his original tale in a nearly wordless format, the only text consisting of periodic variations on the phrase “Tag. You’re it!” Zick’s illustrations are presented in comic-style panels with limited color palette—sepia for the scenes set in mundane reality, green for the magical woodland, and purple for the dark, roiling wave.

David Wiesner’s Hurricane depicts a dramatic weather event from the viewpoint of two children eager to explore the paths of their creative play. One night, a family receives a storm warning. David, George, and their mother and father set about making safety preparations for a hurricane to pass overhead. In the morning, the boys discover that one of two giant elm trees in their yard has blown down. Immediately they begin to use the fallen trunk as a prop in their imaginary adventures: safaris with elephants and leopards, ocean voyages through octopus-ridden waters, and space flights to alien planets. Eventually the tree, having landed on their neighbor’s lawn, is finally cut and removed. George and David are heartbroken, but news of another storm leaves them hoping for the other elm to fall and become a new nexus of play. With an appealing story and illustrations, Wiesner taps into children’s universal attraction to worlds of pretend.

caption:
Today I’ve been combing through this merry adaptation of Nikolai Gogol’s short story Sorotchintzy Fair, adapted by Countess Sybil Schönfeldt, translated from German by Daniel Reynolds, and illustrated by Gennadij Spirin. The narrative centers on a young woman named Paraska, out riding with her father and stepmother. When the three of them visit the Fair at Sorotchintzy, Paraska meets a beautiful young man in a white coat and wishes to take him as her betrothed. Though her father is willing, her stepmother frowns on the match. Soon afterward, the father is disturbed by tales of a herd of demonic swine conjured by the Devil to torment the townspeople who mislaid his Red Coat. Hoodwinked by the thought of this monster and by a staged accusation of theft, he eventually agrees to the match between his daughter and the fine young man. The structure of this abridgment remains largely faithful to the original, with a few changes here and there for propriety (a Jew is changed to an innkeeper). Spirin’s marvelous paintings provide a lively air of old world charm, with fragments of occult imagery peeking in at the edges.

Robert spends a frustrating day visiting his Uncle Ed, Aunt Margo, and their four rambunctious sons. caption:
Jay Williams and @frisohenstra invite you to a delightfully anarchic good time with The Wicked Tricks of Tyl Uilenspiegel. The book takes place in various cities across the Netherlands. Tyl Uilenspiegel, an incorrigible prankster, arouses the ire of the citizenry wherever he goes. He often makes restitution by turning his rapier-sharp wit on the invading Spanish forces, swindling the occupiers and delivering the ill-gotten gains to the Dutch folk. In the four stories contained in this volume, Tyl brings down a Spanish-held stronghold by walking a tightrope, incapacitates a Spanish governor with a ball of taffy, humiliates a Dutch plutocrat to satisfy a wager with Prince William of Orange, and feeds a hungry town at Christmas by stuffing an entire banquet into Spanish cannons. Williams ably evokes Tyl’s roguish humor and devil-may-care attitude, while Henstra illustrates the mischief and mayhem with hatching and bright colors.

No matter where in the world they live, people from all cultures have always been able to look up at the night sky and see the stars. caption:
Today I present Kathy-Jo Wargin and Anne Yvonne Gilbert’s elegant version of The Frog Prince. A princess promises a frog that he may be her companion if he retrieves her precious golden ball from the bottom of a well. Though she tries to avoid making good on her end of the bargain, her father the king commands her to welcome the little amphibian into the castle. Finally, forced to allow the frog into her bedchamber, she loses her temper and throws him against the wall, only to see him transform into a prince. Wargin’s faithful adaptation of the Grimms’ language is well complemented by Gilbert’s refined drawings.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: the Brothers Grimm originally titled this tale “Der Froschkönig oder der eiserne Heinrich”, which translates to “The Frog King or Iron Heinrich”. Fascinatingly, in the first edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen, the Grimms included a similar tale called “Der Froschprinz” (“The Frog Prince”). Nothing remains of that other tale except the title and the detail (mentioned once by Wargin on the first page and then utterly forgotten) of the princess having two older sisters.

Elvira Woodruff and Stephen Gammell concoct a quirky original tale of homesickness and magic realism in The Wing Shop. Matthew does not like his family’s new home on Finley Street. He wishes for nothing more than the ability to return to his house on Main Street, where everything is familiar. caption:
Today I am delighted to present the first chapter in a trilogy that I consider the premiere wordless picture book achievement of the past decade: @storybreathing’s Journey. Unable to hook her family’s attention, a girl sits at home, bored and alone. Suddenly she spots something bright red. Is it a crayon? A marker? A piece of chalk? No matter. She picks it up, makes a door on her bedroom wall, passes through, and suddenly finds herself in an alternate universe, a thrilling fantasy world of high action and adventure. She travels across the mysterious landscape from an ethereal forest hung with glowing lanterns to a grand castle crisscrossed by locks and canals to a massive and imposing airship above the clouds to a city of domes and minarets to a desert under a starry sky. All the while, she uses her drawing implement to create handy vehicles—a rowboat, a hot air balloon, a flying carpet. Finally, she returns to her own familiar world, only to discover that she may not be as alone as she thinks. With an impressive range of techniques—digital modeling as a base, then pen and ink, watercolor, and gouache—Becker invites the reader into a timeless and uniquely marvelous adventure.

Here is a deep dive into part two of a truly epic wordless trilogy. Quest by @storybreathing both continues the story begun in the previous book Journey and adds subtle layers of complexity to the mythology of the fantasy world. The girl and the boy, having grasped the magic of the red and purple pencils—or are they pastels?—take shelter from the rain under a bridge, accompanied by their trusty purple bird companion. Suddenly, a door opens and a king emerges to gift them with a bandolier, a third color implement (orange), and a wondrous map. After the king is seized by enemy soldiers, the two young friends travel across hitherto unseen regions of the supernatural realm, collecting other drawing tools as they go: a yellow one from a sunken city, a green one from a jungle tower, and a blue one from a mountain shrine. Once the bandolier is full, the bird grabs it and flies off to send a miraculous rainbow streaking across the sky, preserving the kingdom in its hour of need. At last, the boy and girl return to the world they know, content in their achievement. With a dazzling array of techniques—digital modeling as a base, then pen and ink, watercolor, and gouache—Becker thrillingly expands the scope of his sweeping visual work.

caption:
When’s my next Fairy Tale Theme Week going to be, you ask? Right now—starting today, I’m featuring seven different versions of Aladdin!

First up, The Tale of Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp, an adaptation by Eric A. Kimmel and Ju-Hong Chen. Kimmel’s text brings energy and warmth to the tale, and Chen’s illustrations shine with bright colors and swirling impasto.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Aladdin is perhaps the most famous story from the Middle Eastern folktale collection One Thousand and One Nights, which dates from around the eighth or the ninth century of the Common Era. However, as Kimmel explains in an Author’s Note, it’s authenticity remains in question. No known manuscripts of Aladdin exist before Antoine Galland’s translation of the collection into French. In 1709, Galland heard the tale in Paris from Syrian storyteller Antun Yusuf Hanna Diyab, whom he did not credit in his publication the following year. Before that, the narrative’s origins lie shrouded in mystery.

caption:
Grahame Baker-Smith creates a haunting portrait of longing and loss in his enchanting Farther. Narrated by a young boy, the story takes place on rocky cliff by the sea. His father, an inventor, struggles for many years to build wings and soar into the air. Consumed by the dream, he works doggedly for many years, sometimes slipping so far away from reality that he seems to forget the boy entirely. Eventually, the father is called away to war and does not return. Once grown, the son is visited by the same dream; he perfects his father’s work and learns to fly. Having finally become a father himself, the young man wonders whether his own son will carry on the family legacy and turn his eyes to the heavens. Through spare text and gripping digital illustrations, Baker-Smith etches magic realism into a coming-of-age tale exploring the indelible bond between father and son.

Mosel’s lively text is well matched by Lent’s vivid illustrations, especially of the monstrous oni and their eerie green huts.

caption:
Odds Bodkin and Gennady Spirin weave a haunting tale of love and sorrow in The Crane Wife. One stormy night, a sailmaker named Osamu discovers an injured crane outside his door. He nurses it back to health until it is strong enough to fly away. Soon afterward, a mysterious woman arrives at his home. She introduces herself as Yukiko, but beyond her name she reveals nothing of herself. The two grow to love each other and live together as husband and wife. To earn money, Yukiko weaves a magic sail, but insists on working behind a screen, extracting Osamu’s promise never to look at her as she works. When the money from the first sail runs out, Yukiko reluctantly weaves a second, warning that the process is physically draining. When a rich trader offers a lifetime of gold, Osamu rashly demands a third sail. Moreover, he impatiently breaks his vow and looks behind the screen, only to see that Yukiko is none other than the wounded crane, weaving its feathers on the loom. Bodkin’s elegant adaptation of this Japanese folktale pairs beautifully with Spirin’s illustrations, inspired by traditional Japanese art.

caption:
Robin Muller crafts a tale of high drama and enchantment in The Sorcerer’s apprentice. Read on and you’ll encounter dark forests, royal intrigue, and tomes of the most eldritch lore. An orphan named Robin sets out to make his way in the world. When a mysterious man indicates he will only employ someone who can neither read nor write, the youth pretends to be illiterate. His new master soon turns out to be a wicked sorcerer and brother to the king, with designs on the throne of the kingdom. After the court turns down his offer to succeed his late brother as monarch, the magician begins concocting a foul spell of dark nightmares to take revenge. Robin must study the man’s evil grimoires in secret in order to stop his master’s diabolical plan once and for all. With a powerful voice and dramatic illustrations, Muller creates a bold original tale shot through with folkloric motifs and imagery.

caption:
Halloween approaches. A time when lights flicker in the darkness, thumps and bumps echo in the night, and the rich smoke of mystery pervades the autumn air. For the third year in a row, I will be posting a week of Halloween books, this time with the visual theme of pumpkins and jack-o’-lanterns.

Here is Linda Williams and Megan Lloyd’s The Little Old Lady Who Was Not Afraid of Anything. The protagonist, having gone out to the woods to collect herbs and spices, nuts and seeds, finds herself menaced by a sequence of mysteriously animate objects: a pair of shoes, a pair of pants, a shirt, a hat and a pair of gloves, and a big pumpkin head. These items chase her all the way back to her house, where she finally confronts them. The pumpkin head admits that they simply wanted to scare her. The little old lady makes a helpful suggestion, and by the next day the pumpkin and the articles of clothing have assembled themselves into an amiable scarecrow. Assigning a catchy onomatopoeia to each whimsical apparition, Williams creates an irresistible cumulative story; Lloyd provides charming illustrations for an elementally simple and uniquely memorable combination.

Halloween inches closer, and this week of seven pumpkin books continues with The Magic Pumpkin, written by Bill Martin Jr. and John Archambault and illustrated by Robert J. Lee. The chill in the air in the days before Halloween has me curling up under a nice, warm blanket and reading Fall by Chris Odgers. Young Harvey is devastated to be missing a piece of himself. His disguised friends Jack and Sarah arrive at his door, excited to celebrate All Hallow’s Eve. However, the search proves more difficult than expected, and it does not come to fruition…until the arrival of a mysterious voice from the clouds. The three sons of the sultan of India, Prince Husayn, Prince Ali, and Prince Ahmad, grow up alongside their late uncle’s daughter, Princess Nur-al Nihar. A queen with no children falls afoul of a troupe of hobgoblins, who demand to be given one of a set of twins she will bear. caption:
It’s time for another Fairy Tale Theme Week. Rather than one specific tale type, will center on a character. And what a character! The wild witch of the woods in Russian folklore herself…welcome, one and all, to Baba Yaga Week.

Let’s get things started with this Baba Yaga book by Katya Arnold. An elderly couple, longing for a child, wrap a wooden log in a blanket and place it in a cradle. The next morning, they discover that the log has turned into a baby boy, whom they name Tishka. When he is older, Tishka’s mother warns him to beware of the evil witch Baba Yaga. Sure enough, Baba Yaga soon kidnaps him and takes him to her hut. After tricking her into devouring her own daughter, Tishka must use all his wits to escape the witch’s vengeful clutches. Arnold draws inspiration from tradition Russian lubok prints in her bold-colored, thick-lined illustrations.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Baba Yaga features in countless tales from Russia and many other countries in Eastern Europe. “Baba” means “grandmother”; “Yaga” (accent on the second syllable in Russian but on the first syllable in several other cultures) is a bit more mysterious, but it seems to come from the root words for “terrible” or “wicked”. This particular narrative is adapted from a Russian story called Tereshichka.

A bit of personal history: Katya Arnold was my art teacher when I was a child!

Young Olga is ordered to go her stepmother’s sister’s house in the forest and bring back a needle and thread. Unfortunately, as the girl well knows, this sister is none other than Baba Yaga, and the house in the woods is the witch’s strange hut that walks on chicken legs. A note for folklore enthusiasts: This book adapts one of the best-known Baba Yaga tales. One main difference—here, the father simply drives his wife away when he discovers her contemptible treatment of his daughter. In the original story, he becomes so angry that he shoots her.

caption:
Listen for the scratching of chicken feet through the trees as we continue through our sequence of seven Baba Yaga books, today contemplating Jane Yolen and Vladimir Vagin’s The Flying Witch. This story, unusually, is set recognizably in the twentieth century. A young girl falls off the back of her father’s turnip truck and into the clutches of Baba Yaga. The clever father tails Baba Yaga in his truck, but inside the old hag’s hut his daughter has cleverly replaced herself on the menu with a delicious root vegetable stew. Yolen’s warm text and Vagin’s cheerful illustrations go neatly in hand.

caption:
In the realm of the witch, we may see strange sights: a fence of skulls and bones, talking animals, and riders of day, night, and sun. Next up in our Seven Books of Baba Yaga is a fascinating version written by Margaret Yatsevitch Phinney and illustrated by Lydian Green. The text is largely set in rhyming couplets, with refrains in a form akin to a limerick. The art mines an eerie atmosphere from soft, muted earth tones.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: In this story, Baba Yaga has a helper, a skeletal servant named Kosshchei Bez Smertnyi. Transliterations of course vary, but the name is often rendered in English as Koschei the Deathless (“Bez Smertnyi” literally means “without death”), as the character has extricated his death from his body in physical form. With a mythos all his own, he is typically an unambiguous villain, in contrast to Baba Yaga’s mercurial moods.

caption:
We must now flee the darkness and the terror, tossing enchanted obstacles over our shoulders as we hear the grind of mortar and pestle close behind. Today brings another entry in Baba Yaga Week. Hiawyn Oram and Ruth Brown create a bold retelling with Baba Yaga and the Wise Doll. Unusually, the story opens from the witch’s perspective. A young girl named Too Nice is exiled by her sisters, Horrid and Very Horrid, who drive her into the forest to retrieve one of Baba Yaga’s toads. Too Nice leaves, with only her beloved doll for company. After she is taken in as the witch’s servant, the doll completes a series of difficult tasks for her—cleaning a mountain of dishes, sorting a pile of dirt and poppyseeds, and answering a challenging riddle. In the end, one of the old hag’s toads devours the two wicked sisters, leaving Too Nice to thrive on her own. Oram’s entertaining narrative meshes well with Brown’s dramatic and eerily glamorous depiction of Baba Yaga.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This story is an adaptation of “Vasilisa the Beautiful”, a tale collected by by Aleksandr Nikolaevich Afanas’ev in Narodnye Russki Skazki, published between 1855 and 1863.

caption:
Emerging from the wild woods, we will surely find ourselves bathed in the safety of hearth and home. To cap off this Week of Baba Yaga, let us marvel at the ferocious beauty that Marianna Mayer and Kinuko Y. Craft have rendered on the pages of their adaptation of Baba Yaga and Vasilisa the Brave. The book centers on a young girl plagued by misery. Vasilisa’s parents are both dead, and she lives at the mercy of her stepmother and stepsisters. The stepmother, envious of Vasilisa’s beauty, waits until their candle burns out one night and then sends the girl into the forest to bring back a new light from the house of Baba Yaga. The brave heroine must travel through the darkness, past riders of day, night, and sun, to the witch’s hut on chicken legs. Baba Yaga, impressed with Vasilisa’s fortitude does indeed give her in the light—in the form of a magical skull whose fiery eyes burn the stepmother and stepsisters to ashes. Mayer’s elegant text and Craft’s resplendent paintings do honor to the myth and mystery of Baba Yaga.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: No one knows the exact provenance of Baba Yaga tales. Though the earliest reference to her name comes from the eighteenth century, some scholars theorize a connection to ancient Slavic gods. Whatever her origin, one thing is clear—the world will not soon forget the wonder and dark power of Baba Yaga.

caption:
For those of you eagerly looking ahead to the arrival of winter, I’ve got something you’ll surely enjoy. In the tender and touching When Will the Snow Trees Grow? Ben Shecter creates a loving exploration of friendship and seasonal change. The book centers on a boy and his beloved bear companion. At the outset of the story, the child asks when the snow trees will grow. In response, the bear provides soothing, poetic descriptions of the transition into winter. The two friends enjoy a bevy of autumnal experiences, including pumpkin picking, gathering firewood, curling up under quilts, drinking hot cupcake, and witnessing the first flakes of snow. In a poignant final illustration, the boy watches as the bear leaves to hibernate for the winter. Shecter creates a cozy blend of text and illustration.

caption:
When you start getting drowsy and waves of sleep begin to wash over you, what words or phrases come to mind? Sometimes I think of beloved verses from childhood. To that end, here is Eugene W. Field’s poem Wynken, Blynken, and Nod, with illustrations by Giselle Potter. Three small sailors ride in a wooden shoe through the night sky. Ultimately, the three are revealed to be sleepily closing eyes and a nodding head, while the shoe is a trundle bed, ready for a young one to lie down for the night. Potter’s fanciful art serves as a lovely complement to Field’s gentle rhymes.

Picture a monster under your bed that emerges only because it wants to be your friend. Beatrice Modaressi demonstrates the power of courage and friendship with her quirky story The Beastly Visits. Newton is a monster who dwells in an underground burrow. In the house above lives a boy named Miles. A secret tunnel leads from the burrow up to a trapdoor beneath Miles’s bed. Modaressi’s whimsical narrative and illustrations treat her subjects with tenderness and charm.

caption:
Rotate this book sideways, putting its spine at the top edge, and flip the pages upward to read the enchanting story of The Lighthouse of Souls by Ariel A. Almada and @zuzannacelej. The narrative centers on a profound relationship between two loving family members. As Leo’s ninth birthday draws to a close, he and his grandpa head out to the seaside cliffs where an d lighthouse stands. Together, they make the long climb to the top of the tower. Leo watches as his grandpa turns on the beacon. The old man uses the light in multiple creative ways: first to create shadow puppetry, then to send a Morse code signal, and finally to project slides onto a backdrop of billowing smoke clouds from his pipe. On the way home, he explains that many in the community watch the sky for these special messages each night. He then presents his grandson with a unique birthday gift—Leo will now have the responsibility of working the lighthouse and casting the shadows for all to see. Almada’s text, translated from Spanish by Jon Brokenbrow depicts a night filled with imaginative possibilities, while Celej contributes an inviting collection of delicate, earth-toned watercolor paintings.

caption:
A gem of poignant sadness is Maurice Sendak’s Dear Mili. A young girl’s quiet life with her mother is shattered by the arrival of a terrible war. The mother tells her to hide herself and sends her off into the forest. The girl wanders for a long time, uncertain of her future. Finally, she comes upon an old man dwelling in a little house in the woods. This man, who is later revealed to be Saint Joseph, cares for her and gives her shelter. She also spends time with a child who looks just like her—a guardian angel in human form. After three days, she returns to her village only to find that everything has changed and her mother is now an old woman. Each day in the forest, it emerges, was really ten years. Sendak’s illustrations endow the narrative with an even mix of tranquility and wonder.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: As the book’s front matter explains, this tale was discovered in 1983 in a letter written to a little girl by Wilhelm Grimm.
