caption:
Imagine a happening as marvelous as contact between our world and an extraterrestrial life form. Now imagine it happens right under your nose and you miss it entirely. How could this be? David Wiesner’s hilarious Mr. Wuffles! shows one possible scenario. The alien explorers here are a squadron of five minuscule beings who arrive in a metallic flying saucer. They are soon menaced by a common house cat, a formidable predator with the undignified name “Mr. Wuffles”. The tiny team of explorers discovers an insect community—consisting of three ants and a ladybug—whose cave-painting-style wall art tells of countless battles with the terrifying feline beast. The tiny heroes must work together to return to evade the deadly clutches of Mr. Wuffles and return the crew to their spacecraft in one piece. Wiesner conveys the story through a mostly-wordless narrative, the only dialogue coming from the human owner, oblivious to the science-fictional goings-on. The aliens themselves populate their speech bubbles with impenetrable geometric glyphs. Watercolor and India ink in comic-style panels bring the delightful action sequences to life.

caption:
If you’ve ever wished for the experience of slipping off among the trees and having a brush with something dark, dangerous, and altogether otherworldly, you can’t go wrong with Barry Moser’s haunting version of The Magic Wood, a poem by Henry Treece. A child meets a mysterious man in the forest who immediately appears entertaining yet unsettling. He can catch a lark and draw a dragon in the air, yet both his eyes are glass and his teeth can be seen through the back of his head. Cleverly, the child provides a false name and ultimately says a prayer to ward off the man’s eldritch influence. Interspersed with the quatrains is the nerve-jangling refrain: “The wood is full of shining eyes,/The wood is full of creeping feet,/The wood is full of tiny cries;/You must not go to the wood at night!” Just who—or what is this man? We may never know. Moser’s art outlines the eerie encounter in dramatic hues of teal and shadowy black.

caption:
Katherine Paterson and Leo and Diane Dillon bring us today’s entry: The Tale of the Mandarin Ducks. A proud district lord rides out with his hunting party. Along their way, the group happens by a lake. When he spies a pair of mandarin ducks, the lord immediately covets the male for his brilliant plumage and orders him captured. The beautiful drake is brought back to the lord’s house and shown off in a cage, against the advice of Shozo, the good-natured chief steward. When a compassionate kitchen maid named Yasuko secretly frees the poor bird, Shozo is falsely blamed. The two fall in love, and the lord accuses them of conspiracy and sentences them both to death. Fortunately, Yasuko and Shozo are freed by the timely intervention of a pair of messengers claiming to be emissaries of the emperor. These messengers are ultimately revealed to be the mandarin ducks in disguise, acting out of gratitude to the kindly couple. Paterson’s elegant narrative is accompanied by the Dillons’ dramatic illustrations, based on eighteenth-century Japanese woodcuts.

caption:
Do things ever seem like they’ve just gone completely wrong and it’s all your fault? It can be hard to remember that moments like this happen to everyone, and harder still to look ahead and recognize that the situation can likely be fixed. It’s all too easy to feel alone, trapped, utterly miserable. Fortunately, there is always @ioana.hobai’s A Whale of a Mistake to guide us through our times of trouble. This inventive and socially insightful book is structured as a second-person narrative, confronting readers with the stark reality of their own human limitations. Meanwhile, the illustrations complement the text with images of a child being unceremoniously whisked out to sea by an enormous whale, an apt visual metaphor for the perceived immensity of a single, glaring blunder. Ultimately, the young protagonist learns to accept the ubiquity and transience of mistakes and bids the whale, now manageably small, a fond farewell. Hobai’s sensitive writing and glowing, jewel-toned art (a combination of ink, watercolor, and acrylic) provide a sober yet uplifting modern allegory.

caption:
Have a chuckle at The Bremen Town Musicians, retold and illustrated by Janet Stevens. A donkey, a dog, a cat, and a rooster, all unloved by their masters, decide to go away together. They plan to form a band and entertain at the town of Bremen. Their journey, however, is derailed when they come across a house of robbers. The plucky travelers clamber onto one another’s shoulders in order to peer inside; they topple forward, crash through the window (sending the hoodlums fleeing), and proceed to enjoy the food left on the table. When one brigand sneaks back in the night to surveil the hideout, he is beset by the animals in the dark. He flees in panic, and reports to his compatriots that the house is filled with vengeful monsters. With loose lines and large scrawls of color, Stevens brings a playful energy to her retelling.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This story is adapted from “Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten”, a tale from Kinder- und Hausmärchen by the Brothers Grimm

caption:
What does happiness mean to you? Where does it come from? Are you content to let it find you, or do you believe you must actively seek it out? Let us consider these questions as we flip through Juliette Saumande and Eric Puybaret’s In Search of Happiness. Young Alexander lives with his grandfather In the town of Prudence, where the people are never upset because they fervently avoid risk. The boy dreams of leaving this timid community and striking out on his own. He attempts to follow a bird named Paradiso who is heading for the Land of Happiness, but he quickly becomes lost. He visits the Isle of Treats, the Gorge of the Spoiled Ones, the Glacier of the Frozen Ones, the Valley of the Delighted, and many other marvelous locales. Upon returning home, Alexander finally realizes that the mythical Land of Happiness exists wherever people are happy. Satisfied at last, he invites his grandfather to join him on a new adventure to parts unknown. Saumande’s text, translated from French by Andrew Weller, rings with allegorical power. Puybaret’s smooth-textured illustrations conjure up strange and beautiful vistas not soon forgotten.

caption:
Another Theme Week is now underway—and this time I’ll be exploring seven different versions of Snow White!

First up, an adaptation written and illustrated by Charles Santore. The plot remains scrupulously faithful to its fairy-tale origins, from the queen’s three attempts to kill Snow White to her ultimate fate dancing herself to death at the young princess’s wedding. Santore fills his art with resplendent imagery, including a wealth of period-appropriate renaissance costumes and decor.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: “Sneewittchen”, or “Little Snow-White”, first appeared in Jakob and Wilhelm Grimm’s collection Kinder- und Hausmärchen in 1812. In the original edition of the tale, the murderous queen is in fact Snow White’s mother. However, in later versions, the Grimms altered the text, with the first queen dying and the king remarrying. Santore inserts a few changes of his own—the huntsman here brings back an animal’s heart as proof that he has carried out her execution (in the fairy tale the queen demands her lungs and liver) and the dancing shoes kill the queen with magic (in the original tale, they are made of iron and heated in a fire before they are forced onto the queen’s feet).

Making my way through the dark wilderness, I have another entry in this Snow White Theme Week for you: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs by Wanda Gág. The story here is adapted faithfully from the German of the Brothers Grimm. Gág’s trademark black and white illustrations lend the proceedings a quaint, old-world atmosphere.

caption:
In an endless slumber, there must surely be some measure of peace. But not so for the ill-fated heroine of @anajuan_art’s Snowhite, a darkly modern update of the Brothers Grimm tale. Lady Hawthorn pricks her finger on a hatpin, and the drop of blood on the snow drives her desire for a daughter. But, soon after the birth of little Snowhite, her mother dies. Her father, Lord Hawthorn, eventually remarries, but he too soon passes away. The new Lady Hawthorn is a vain woman who oppresses her stepdaughter and eventually banishes her. The young ingenue begins working at the “Lilly and Putt”, an inn owned by the seven Penny Brothers. In disguise, her stepmother offers her a drug that puts her into a waking trance. The tale ends with Snowhite’s captivity and assault in the home of the unscrupulous Mr. Prince—no happiness or comfort to be found. Juan’s text, rendered on each page in both Italian (translated by Antonella Lami) and English (translated by Bill Dodd), presents the uniquely modern horrors in a spare, unflinching tone. Her dramatic grayscale art accords the landscape a ghostly dread.

Awaken, friends, and return to the world of love, laughter, and light. To conclude Snow White Week, I am thrilled to present this marvelous edition by Paul Heins and Trina Schart Hyman. Heins remains deeply faithful to the German text of the Brothers Grimm, creating the perfect base for the flowing lines and bright colors of Hyman’s lyrical work. caption:
Sharon King-Chai’s Starbird gives us an original fairy tale of beauty, wonder, greed, sorrow, and understanding. When the wealthy and powerful Moon King learns that he is to have a daughter, he wishes to give her an extraordinary gift. He therefore traps Starbird, a legendary creature with a beautiful voice. As the princess grows older, she detects a note of sadness in her pet’s nightly song. Filled with pity, she frees the captive animal. Starbird roams here and there about the land in search of his home, but the Moon King, with his cold, piercing gaze, hunts him down once more. As the wondrous bird wastes away in a cage, only the princess’s voice can reach her father and sway his heart towards mercy. King-Chai weaves themes of love and kindness together with magical imagery. Her cool-toned, flat-style multimedia illustrations, creates through a combination of paint, ink, leaves, potatoes, feathers, collage, and digital technique, gleam with silver foil stamping.

caption:
Eric A. Kimmel and Robert Rayevsky present a tale of wit and romance in Bernal and Florinda. The story begins in Seville. A young man named Bernal, possessed of only a field swarming with grasshoppers, is in love with Florinda, daughter of the greedy, arrogant mayor Don Garcilaso. When the pompous official learns that his daughter is being wooed by a man of such little means, he angrily forbids the match. Bernal then cleverly embarks upon a series of trades—a sack of grasshoppers for a goose, the goose for a load of charcoal, the charcoal for fine candles, the candles for a disguise that enables him to orchestrate a false accusation of murder against Don Garcilaso. The mayor frantically promises the mysterious stranger his daughter’s hand in marriage—only to learn that he has been hoodwinked. Kimmel, writing an original story in the tradition of a Spanish picaresque, employs a clever, winning narrative voice. Rayevsky’s thick-lined art, pen and ink with watercolor, portrays characters with comically theatrical poses and expressions.

You won’t know whether to laugh or shudder as you turn the pages of Grandpa’s Ghost Stories by James Flora. A young boy listens to a storm raging outside. One particularly loud clap of thunder gives him a jolt of fear and sends him scurrying onto his grandfather’s lap. To calm his nerves, Grandpa begins telling him ghost stories—perhaps three tales, each flowing directly into the next, or perhaps a single narrative split into three episodes. Flora creates one ghoulish image after another—a bag of bones in an old shack, a witch’s cave filled with slimy creatures, and an eerie ghost in a house of mud and blood. Both the writing and the art treat the macabre spectacles with a starling blend of humor and horror.

The new queen, long having nursed a grudge against her nieces and nephews, turns them into four swans. caption:
Today I have been contemplating Mordicai Gerstein’s mystical and deeply moving The Mountains of Tibet. The story follows the cycle of a human life from childhood, through adulthood, to old age and into the afterlife itself. A man lives and dies in a small Tibetan village. After his death, a mysterious entity speaks to him, offering him first the option to be reincarnated and then a series of further choices homing in on a place of birth—from galaxy to planet to nation to family. As much as the wide array of unfamiliar options dazzles him, the man ultimately chooses to be born in the same village where he spent his previous life—this time as a girl. Gerstein pairs his simple yet thought-provoking story, inspired by readings of the Tibetan Book of the Dead, with cosmic watercolor and gouache illustrations reminiscent of luminous mandalas.

caption:
The book of the day is Jay Williams and Mercer Mayer’s Everyone Knows What a Dragon Looks Like. A messenger arrives at the city of Wu and tells the Mandarin that Wild Horsemen are on their way, bringing war and destruction. The court and all the citizens begin praying to the Great Cloud Dragon for aid. The next day, a little old man in simple attire arrives in the city, claiming to be a dragon. He is quickly dismissed by the Mandarin and his councilors. Each official reasons that dragons must look like him, and therefore the shabby old stranger cannot be a dragon. Only a young boy named Han, a city gate-sweeper, treats the visitor respectfully by offering him food, drink, and hospitality. For Han’s sake, the old man dispatches the Wild Horsemen and saves the city. Williams crafts an elegant and exciting tale, while Mayer’s illustrations provide grandeur and spectacle.

caption:
When you have bad dreams, do you ever wish they could simply be sucked away by an outside force, leaving you in a peaceful slumber? If so, you’ll enjoy The Dream Eater by Christian Garrison and Diane Goode. Yukio awakens from a terrible nightmare in which he is being chased by a three-headed demon riding a dragon with twenty eyes. He soon learns that everyone in his small community is experiencing troubled sleep. His father dreams he has planted bamboo instead of rice. His mother dreams of being frozen by the winter snow. His grandfather dreams he is a fish caught in a net. Danjuro the samurai dreams the village is under attack by an infernal army. Outside the village, Yukio spots a strange animal drowning in the river and pulls it to safety. The unusual creature identifies itself as a Baku—an eater of dreams. Struck by inspiration, Yukio leads the Baku back towards his home, and the beast devours the nightmares of everyone it encounters. Garrison’s simple text is well complemented by Goode’s elaborate artwork.

caption:
Today at sundown, Hanukkah begins. In recognition of a holiday I grew up celebrating with my family, I am turning to an old childhood favorite. Eric A. Kimmel and Trina Schart Hyman present a thrillingly entertaining yarn in Hershel and the Hanukkah Goblins. In this tale of outlandish monsters, patience and cleverness trump brute force every time. Hershel of Ostropol arrives in a little town on the first night of Hanukkah, dismayed to find the houses dark and quiet. A foul band of goblins has driven the villagers out of the synagogue and forbidden dreidels, menorahs, and all other forms of Hanukkah celebration. Hershel bravely agrees to spend eight nights in the little temple and take on the creatures one by one. He bests the goblins with a succession of simple tricks—an egg that looks like a stone, a jar of pickles, a game of dreidel with unfair rules. Finally, he takes on the king of the goblins, a demonic, looming shadow that threatens to destroy him utterly. However, keeping his faith and his brains about him, Hershel outwits his foe; light defeats the power of darkness. Kimmel’s writing draws the reader expertly into the action, while Hyman’s grotesque goblin horde elicits grins and gasps in equal measure.

caption:
Come and make your way into a wasteland of lost hopes and shattered dreams with Glenda Millard and @stephenmichaelking’s post-apocalyptic The Duck and the Darklings. Peterboy lives with his Grandpapa in a hole in the ground. Up above lies the land of Dark, an empty, ruined place where nothing grows, nothing thrives, and all is gloom. One day, on a foraging trip, Peterboy comes across Idaduck. He takes the invalid bird home and nurses her back to health. Grandpapa tells her stories about the beautiful world of his youth. Finally, the community bands together to help Idaduck fly away, a symbol of possibility for a better future. Millard leavens the morose setting with delightful invented words and fanciful imagery, including “Only when the heavenlies were deepest indigo”, “Yellowly, yellowly shone the sun”, and “The velvet wind whispered.” With pen, brush, ink, and digital digital compilation, King creates a marvelous visual landscape of thick lines, wild shapes, and lively speckles.

caption:
If the goal is perfection, what happens to those who cannot measure up? Flawed beings with bulges, blotches, and blemishes have as much intrinsic worth as anyone else—and this is the thesis of @thefanbrothers’ charming original tale The Barnabus Project. Deep under the city, below a shop that proudly advertises genetically engineered Perfect Pets, lies a secret laboratory where scientists conduct shadowy experiments to produce cuddly and appealing little animals. Failed Projects are stored in bell jars and left on shelves to gather dust. One of these discarded creatures is Barnabus, a half-mouse, half-elephant who dreams of seeing the world outside. After being marked for recycling, the unlikely hero breaks free of his prison, releases his friends, and mounts a daring escape…with the help of an eldritch beast from the facility’s nethermost sub-basement. @terryfanillustration and @ericfanillustration collaborate for the first time with their brother @devin.fan.art, and the resulting story is told with entertaining narrative voice and a rich, cinematic combination of graphite and digital art.

caption:
Today is the winter solstice: the first day of winter. With the turning of the season, I’m contemplating Winter Waits, an allegorical tale by Lynn Plourde and Greg Couch. Winter, the youngest child of Mother Earth and Father Time, wakes up. Having been asleep for so long, he is brimming with energy. Father Time promises to come play, but first he must finish his work, and his son is left alone for hours and hours. When Winter makes a marvelous snowflake as a gift, Father Time, deeply touched, finally puts aside his work and the two share a tender romp across the sky. Plourde unfurls her original story in rhyming quatrains, while Couch illustrates the mythical proceedings in acrylic and colored pencil on museum board.

caption:
Darkness must surely be one of the few truly universal fears. In the absence of light, we grow acutely aware of our inability to see. Adult rationality succumbs to childhood terror; modern humanity regresses to primordial wildness. Distilling this stark emotion, @porliniers has created What There Is Before There Is Anything There, an offbeat and eerie look at an all-too-familiar phobias. Each night at bedtime a young boy is faced with a recurring fright—bizarre little creatures begin floating down from above. One by one they come, some standing ominously beside him, some perching on the bed itself, until he is completely surrounded. Then, the final horror—the ceiling itself melts away to reveal a sentient, shapeless void with black, branchlike tendrils stretching out to ensnare him. The sinister presence then speaks, identifying itself only as “what there is before there is anything there.” Who among us would not flee, as the boy does, to the warmth and safety of their parents’ bedroom? With simple, foreboding text (translated from Spanish by Elisa Amado) and thick-lined, cross-hatched art, Liniers conjures up a creeping nightmare—and steadfastly refuses to banish it with the comfort of a happy ending.

caption:
Imagine that birds, insects, and other animals were originally created without wings and subsequently had to be completed. This odd thought is the premise of The Little Wing Giver, a whimsical tale written by Jacques Taravant and illustrated by @peter.sis.art. A boy lives at the beginning of creation, when all animals in the world are newly made. Since no creatures have yet been given wings, the boy (known only as Little Wing Giver) travels all over the earth handing them out to birds, insects, and even windmills. One day the wind, angered by these gifts, blows the boy’s basket of wings into the ocean. Even so, he still manages to help a caterpillar transform into a butterfly by giving it wings made of poppy petals. Finally, exhausted and utterly spent by his endless quest, the boy rises into the sky and is transformed into an angel. Taravant creates a gentle and imaginative etiological tale, while Sís contributes his signature pale-colored ethereal art.

caption:
Tonight is Christmas Eve. If your path has taken you out into the bitter chill, perhaps I can provide you some measure of warmth with a look at the solemn and heartfelt Through the Mickle Woods, written by Valiska Gregory and illustrated Barry Moser. The queen is dead, and a pall has settled over the castle. During the period of mourning, Michael, a young orphan and ward of the castle, reveals a letter containing the queen’s ring and her last will. The king must take the boy to deliver the ring to a mysterious bear who lives in the dark and mickle woods. Reluctantly, the grieving monarch agrees to honor his wife’s request. After receiving the ring, the bear tells three stories, teaching tales with great symbolic resonance. The parables warn against grasping for easy answers, shying away from risk, and trying to separate the bad from the good in life. Finally, young Michael and the king return to the castle as the morningtide bells begin to peal, hope for the future within their souls. Gregory fills her narrative with beauty and pathos, each moment crafted to inform the king’s journey from despair to acceptance. With paintings of ink, watercolor, and gouache, Moser gives readers glimpses at the world of the story in stately tableaux. For all of you traveling through sorrow and cold, I wish a safe passage and good warmth at journey’s end.

caption:
Trip, trap, trip, trap…that’s the sound of hooves crossing over a wooden bridge, and of course an eternal reminder of The Three Billy Goats Gruff, adapted and illustrated by Marcia Brown. Three goat brothers wish to go up to a meadow to make themselves fat feasting on all the luscious grass. Unfortunately, to get there, they must cross a bridge under which lives a foul, ugly troll. The monster challenges first the smallest, then the middle-sized, and finally the largest billy goat. The biggest makes short work of the troll, and the three brothers delight in the beauty and abundance of the lovely meadow. Brown’s lively text, at every turn faithful to the original tale, is well matched by her loose, jangly drawings and bright, bold colors.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Brown’s source is the original Norwegian fairy tale collected by by Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe in their collection Norske Folkeeventyr, published in 1843 and 1844. Unlike many modern authors, Brown retains the biggest billy goat’s shockingly graphic retort to the troll’s threat: "Well, come along! I've got two spears,/And I'll poke your eyeballs out at your ears;/I've got besides two curling-stones,/And I'll crush you to bits, body and bones." She also cheerfully illustrates the ensuing clash in which the goat fulfills his violent promise.

caption:
Chris Conover fashions an epic tale of bravery and enchantment in The Wizard’s Daughter. In need of a living, young Boots finds himself in the employ of an evil wizard who holds the entire realm of the North in his malevolent grasp. He serves his new master for three years, each spent in the form of a different animal—a hare, a raven, and a fish. During the third year, he discovers the wizard’s daughter trapped in a glass palace at the bottom of the sea. Together they formulate a plan to outwit the tyrannical mage and free the land from his control once and for all. With her energetic writing and bright illustrations, Conover creates a deeply entertaining fairy tale adaptation. Fascinating visual details include the wizard himself, sporting a nose ring, three scaly limbs, and one cloven hoof, and a hag in his retinue with a candle sprouting out of her neck to replace her head, which she carries under her arm.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Though the subtitle of the book is “A Viking Legend”, the front matter identifies the source as “The Wizard’s Daughter”, a tale collected by Danish folklorist Svend Grundtvig. Though some English translators have used this title, the original Danish story features a troll, rather than a wizard.

caption:
I am reveling in the action and adventure of Aaron Shepard and Pauline Ellison’s Master Maid. A young man named Leif is known for being headstrong and contrary. Therefore, when warned not to go and work for a fearsome troll, he does just that. Leif is given a series of impossible tasks and told that the punishment for failure is death. Fortunately, he survives thanks to the grace and good will of a young woman also in the wicked creature’s employ, known only as the Master Maid. Leif and the Master Maid flee together, leaving behind a series of magical obstacles to foil the troll and hinder his advance, and ultimately escape with their lives. Shepard’s narrative sparkles, enhanced by high stakes and charm throughout. Ellison’s irresistible art makes use of a glowing color palette and memorable character design, particularly in the final chase sequence involving the troll’s three magical hench-beasts—Forest Chewer, Mountain Cruncher, and Water Sucker.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This story is based on a tale collected by Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe in Norske Folkeeventyr, published in 1843 and 1844. Shepard omits the second half of the narrative, in which the young hero falls under a mysterious curse and forgets his love altogether. The Master Maid is obliged to use her wits and magical powers to break the spell, meting out comedic violence to a series of overeager suitors along the way.

caption:
Come journey with me into the frosty dark through the pages of Phyllis Root and @marygrandpre’s Lucia and the Light. The story opens in a little cottage at the foot of a mountain in the Far North. Lucia lives with her mother, her baby brother, a brown cow, and white cat. One day, the light disappears, and the family is left without warmth. The young girl sets off on skis with her cat nestled inside the hood of her coat for company. At the mountain’s icy top, a wicked pack of trolls has hidden the sun in a bundle of rags to shield themselves from its rays. Lucia cleverly evades the hungry monsters and, with the help of her cat, uncovers the sun, which turns the trolls to stone. From then on, light fills the sky, warmth returns to the air, and the family is safe. Root draws inspiration from Scandinavian traditions celebrating Lucia of Syracuse, also known as Saint Lucy, for her dramatic adventure tale. GrandPré supplies thrilling pastel art with contrasting tones of chill blue and glowing yellow.

caption:
Greetings to all, perched as we are on the precipice of a new year. Now is a time of change and excitement leavened with a subtle melancholy, for the birth of the new heralds the death of the old. One personal change in store for me in the year ahead is the end of these daily posts. Yes, I will be stopping my book reviews in 2023. But not right away! See tomorrow’s post for more details…

Jane Yolen and John Wallner explore the passage of time and the cycle of the year in Ring of Earth. A series of four sweeping poems explores the movements and sensations of creatures representing the seasons—the weasel for winter, the spring peeper for spring, the dragonfly for summer, and the goose for autumn. Yolen composes lyrical verse with subtly different rhyme schemes and metric patterns for each animal, and Wallner supplies breathtaking watercolor images of nature. My wish for you on this New Year’s Eve is a fitting and joyous close to the cycle of wonder you have experienced this year.

If aliens were arriving and planning to explore our world, what would they need to know? @sophieblackall begins with this powerful guiding question in her sweeping and thought-provoking work If You Come to Earth. The text serves as a primer for extraterrestrial visitors to our planet. A boy in a bright red Phrygian cap introduces facets of natural science and human culture all around the globe. Bodies, emotions, clothing, transportation, animals, plants, and manufactured objects are all examined with simple clarity and warmth as part of our lived experience. Inspired by her travels to Rwanda, India, Bhutan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and other countries, Blackall marries thoughtful text with delicate ink-and-watercolor art to create a simultaneously epic and intimate whole. I wish you a future full of bright hope and possibility in the year to come.

caption:
Amanda Loverseed presents an energetic narrative of adventure and magic in The Thunder King, an adaptation of a Peruvian folktale. Twin brothers Tantay and Illanti care deeply for each other and hate to be separated. One day, their mother assigns them different chores, which requires them to separate. Then, disaster strikes—Thunder, the King of the Skies, whisks Tantay into the sky and whirls him away. Illanti must journey to Thunder’s palace and rescue his beloved brother. With the help of the strong and kindly Condor, the twins escape the clutches of the wicked sky god and return safely home. With entertaining text and dynamic illustrations, Loverseed crafts a story of danger and excitement.

Eve Bunting and Charles Mikolaycak’s The Man Who Could Call Down Owls offers a clear and irresistible hook in its title. What you may not expect, however, is the beauty, wildness, and danger you’ll encounter by the story’s conclusion. In a little village, a man is revered for his affinity with owls. Everyone gathers in the dark to watch as the majestic birds swoop down and perch on him, a young boy named Con the most eager among them. During the day, Con apprentices himself to the man, learning about a wide array of different species. One day, however, a mysterious stranger arrives who covets the man’s power. The next night, the man is gone, and it soon becomes clear that the stranger, now in possession of the man’s cloak, his feathered hat, and his willow wand, has committed a terrible crime. When the owls arrive this time, however, they attack the villain, ripping at his flesh with their talons and driving him away into the forest. Afterward, Con takes up the mantle of his late mentor, calling down the owls and treating them with gentleness and respect. Bunting’s dark story and Mikolaycak’s gripping monochromatic art combine for a quietly powerful experience.

If you’re in the mood for a thrilling folktale, I highly recommend @yangsook.choi’s The Sun Girl and the Moon Boy. A woman sets out for the market, leaving her daughter and son alone at home. On her way home, she is menaced by a ravenous tiger, who soon devours her. The beast then makes his way to the mother’s house and employs disguise and trickery to fool the children into letting him in. The girl and the boy climb a tree to evade the ferocious predator, who soon claws his way up to catch them. Unable to retreat further, the young siblings grab onto a magical rope, which pulls them up into the sky, where they become the sun and the moon; their mother, already waiting for them in the heavens, turns into the stars. Choi’s gripping storyline is enhanced by her dramatic compositions, in which the characters display a stunning depth of emotion.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This story is Choi’s adaptation of a traditional Korean tale which she heard many times in her youth.

caption:
Anthony Browne creates a striking tale of childhood fears and emotions with his cryptic book Into the Forest. After hearing a terrible noise in the night, a young boy awakens to find his father gone. The next day, his mother asks him to take a cake to his sick grandmother, but warns him not to take the shortcut through the forest. The boy, however, does not listen, and embarks on the path through the woods. Along the way he encounters children evoking the narratives of Jack and the Beanstalk, The Three Bears, and Hansel and Gretel; he himself finds a red coat and puts it on, emphasizing the ongoing parallel to Little Red Riding Hood. Finally, he arrives at his destination to discover his grandmother, recuperating in the company of his father. The boy and his father return home and the family is reunited. The mystery of the opening tumult and the father’s disappearance, however, remains open to interpretation. Employing the powerful visual metaphor of a fairy tale world, Browne augments his simple first-person narrative with pencil-and-watercolor illustrations in which key objects stand out in color against stark black and white backgrounds.

A textual connection: The Hansel and Gretel that appear in this book bear a strong resemblance to the characters as illustrated in Browne’s own adaptation of the tale.

caption:
Is it our loved ones we see before us, or a feral impostor? If our senses can be deceived, how are we to tell the difference? Ed Young layers these and other unsettling questions throughout his unforgettable Lon Po Po, our next entry in Little Red Riding Hood Week Two. A woman goes to visit her mother. She bids goodbye to her three daughters, Shang, Tao, and Paotze, planning to return the next day. The sisters are therefore surprised to hear a knock at the door. The visitor claims to be their Po Po, or grandmother…but is she really? In the dark, they cannot see her face. The newcomer is, in fact, a wicked wolf, and the young girls must band together and use their wits as well as their strength to put a stop to his monstrous appetites. Young writes with a masterful voice, and his paintings, split into vertical sections that evoke traditional Chinese panel art, cleverly incorporates the wolf’s face into everyday objects and the landscape itself.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: As indicated in the book’s subtitle, this tale is a variant of Little Red Riding Hood from China. The back matter indicates that it was translated from a collection of Chinese folktales.

caption:
The fate of planet Earth is a deep concern for us all, and the gravest predictions warn that we are headed for environmental catastrophe. What more sobering alarm call than to look back at the present from the perspective of an irreparably damaged future? Colin Thompson’s The Tower to the Sun allows us to do just that. The richest man in the world tells his grandson about the old days, the days before the atmosphere was choked by a thick, yellow smog. Wishing to see the sun in the clear blue sky, the boy suggests building a colossal tower. The old man pours his vast resources into the project, which drags on for decades—long enough for the grandson to grow up and have children of his own. Finally, the tower is complete. The top breaches the clouds, finally allowing the man and his family to glimpse the sun. In the solemn conclusion, the world’s entire population forms a line, all of them waiting to make the unfathomable climb. Thompson pairs the dire warning at the story’s core with his trademark detail-saturated art, stripping away the noise and clutter for the startlingly serene image of the clear blue sky.

A point of interest: One illustration of the monumental structure is an unmistakable homage to Pieter Breugel the Elder’s painting The Tower of Babel.

caption:
Barbara Cooney presents a merry version of an old tale in The Little Juggler. To earn a living, young orphan Barnaby performs in the town square, local inns, and castle courts. A nimble and graceful entertainer, he leaps, dances, sings, and juggles, all to his audiences’ great delight. One winter, a brotherhood of monks takes him in and gives him food and shelter in their abbey. He watches them express their religious worship through writing, art, and music and feels ashamed that he has no similar gift to offer. Barnaby soon begins expressing his devotion to the Virgin Mary in the only way he knows how: by performing. Each night in a little chapel, he juggles and tumbles before the altar in secret, an unorthodox but reverential act of prayer. One day, another monk discovers Barnaby’s hidden activities. He and the abbot himself witness the Virgin Mary descend to thank the little juggler after he has fallen asleep. Thus, they come to understand the holiness of the boy’s actions and recognize him as a saint. With eloquent text and stately black and white illustrations accented with bright fields of red, green, and blue, Cooney celebrates gentleness and compassion as qualities of true nobility.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Cooney’s source material is a medieval French legend, which has inspired adaptations into numerous media, including books, films, and even an opera.

caption:
For today, have a fairy tale retelling with sparks of wonder and enchantment: Rafe Martin and Vladyana Langer Krykorka’s The Twelve Months. Young Marushka’s parents have died. She lives with her wicked aunt and cousin, who force her to perform all the menial household chores. One day in midwinter, the two women order her to go and gather a bunch of violets. Without much hope, Marushka reluctantly heads out into the snow. However, instead of freezing to death, she climbs up to a mountain peak, where she encounters a circle of mystical beings gathered around a fire—twelve brothers who represent the months of the year. The benevolent figures take pity on her and melt the snow to reveal a meadow filled with violets, which Marushka takes back home. Unsatisfied, her cruel relatives continue to make outlandish demands in the following days, instructing her to bring first strawberries and then apples. Vexed by her continuing success, they go out to the mountaintop where the twelve months sit. However, their rudeness displeases the frosty deities, and they are never heard from again. Martin’s lively writing and Krykorka’s energetic, scratchy illustrations make for a rousing adaptation.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This story is a variant of “The Kind and the Unkind Girls”, a plot found the world over. The front matter identifies it as a Slavic tale.

caption:
What do you do to relax during stormy weather? Do you make a nice, warm cup of tea? Listen to the rain? Perhaps you curl up with a good ghost story? Take a look at One Stormy Night by Ruth Brown, a faintly eerie original tale whose simple narrative contains a bit more than meets the eye. A little white dog prowls around outside a manor house on the lonely moor. Each animal it encounters—a black cat, a gray mare, a white owl—seems to react with shock and fear. Once dawn breaks, we finally learn why the other beasts are so perturbed: the dog the dog enters a lonely chapel, jumps up onto an old knight’s tomb, and rejoins its master as a statue. Brown’s spare text and evocative illustrations all build cleverly towards the reveal of the jocund little creature as an undead spirit out for a stroll.

caption:
Let Maurice Sendak whisk you away on a bizarre journey into lands thrilling and inscrutable. You won’t find these places on any map. You simply have to begin your excursion turned the wrong way around, as does the protagonist of the marvelous Outside Over There. Ida leads a lonely life, her father away at sea, her mother in the arbor watching endlessly for his return. Thus, the girl is tasked with watching over her baby sister. One fateful day, when she is not watching as carefully as she should be, the infant is stolen by goblins and replaced by a changeling made of dripping ice. Ida resolves to go and rescue her sister, but she makes a mistake: she climbs backwards out her window, which lands her in a strange place called Outside Over There. When she finally locates the goblins, she discovers that they have the appearance of squalling babies. Fortunately, she plays a tune on her horn that causes the little imps to dance so quickly that they churn themselves into a stream and flow away, leaving behind the true human baby. Ida picks up her sister and returns safely home. Sendak’s quiet text is by turns sinister and reassuring, while his masterful paintings take readers on an uncanny odyssey.

caption:
@sandradieckmann’s The Dog That Ate the World is by turns thrilling, bleak, and heartwarming. A group of animals resides in a peaceful valley. They spend their days in harmony until the arrival of a menacing dog, who starts to devour everything in sight. No plan the animals devise—playing soothing music, talking to the dog, building inventive decoys—is effective. The dog swallows them all. The terrible beast consumes forests, mountains, and finally the sun itself. And then something unexpected happens: the dog is left in a barren void. Having swallowed the world, it becomes the world, and the animals within can live in happiness once more. Dieckmann’s compelling original story and warm-hued art lead to a serene ending that meets conflict with a gentle and philosophical solution.

Today I’m basking in the charm of Hortense and the Shadow, co-created by Natalia and Lauren O’Hara, also known as @oharasisters. The story begins in a dark wood filled with wolves and softly falling snow. A young girl named Hortense lives in a large and well-appointed manor house. She has but one complaint—she hates her shadow. It follows her around everywhere, imitating her every movement and scaring her with its eerie shapes. So vexed is she by the troublesome shadow that she slams a window on it and shuts it out of her life completely. Now, all is quiet and peaceful. With Natalia’s delicious phrasing (“Through the dark and wolfish woods”) and Lauren’s elegant pastel color palette, the O’Hara Sisters have fashioned an original tale replete with wildness, drama, and heart.

caption:
Today I’ve been enjoying the fairy tale magic of Sherry Meidell’s The Devil with the Three Golden Hairs. When the king overhears that the newborn son of a peasant is destined to marry his daughter, he throws the baby into a nearby river. Fortunately, a miller rescues the infant and raises him as his own child. Years later, the king discovers the boy alive and bids him carry a letter to the queen that would have him put to death upon arrival at the royal palace. However, a band of robbers reads the message while the young man is asleep, takes pity on him, and replaces it with instructions that he is to be married to the princess. When the king returns to the palace, he is furious to see that the prophecy has come to pass. He demands that his new son-in-law go to hell and bring back three golden hairs from the head of the devil himself. The clever lad succeeds in this quest with help from the devil’s wily grandmother; along the way he solves the mysteries plaguing two troubled villages and a beleaguered ferryman. As for the king, his cruelty is met with a just reward. Meidell’s winning text and expressive illustrations make for a winning experience.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This book is adapted from a story of the same name collected by the Brothers Grimm.

caption:
The book of the day is Wilhelmina Harper and William Wiesner’s The Gunniwolf. A young girl lives with her mother near a dense jungle. Somewhere among the trees, the mother warns, lurks the Gunniwolf, a fearsome predator to be avoided at all costs. When the girl is left home alone one day, she recklessly ventures into the jungle. For a time, all is well—she picks flowers and sings a cheerful tune. Soon enough, however, she meets the Gunniwolf. She cannot outrun the dangerous beast, but she can soothe it with her song and escape while it sleeps. Harper employs an enigmatic vocabulary, with unforgettable turns of phrase such as, “Sing that guten, sweeten song again!” and “Away he ran: hunker-cha, hunker-cha, hunker-cha”. Wiesner’s hatched line art, colored solely with reds and greens, depicts the eponymous creature as a mischievous fox-hyena hybrid with lion-cut fur and a shag hairdo.

Mary K. Whittington and Sue Ellen Brown whip up a tale of magic and heart in Winter’s Child. The narrative rings with allegorical power and beauty, anchored by a deep emotional core. caption:
Have a look with me through Charlotte Huck and Anita Lobel’s delightful Princess Furball. A king’s daughter is chagrined to learn that her hand in marriage has been promised to an ogre in exchange for fifty wagons of silver. The clever young woman insists on a few bridal gifts: a dress as golden as the sun, another as silvery as the moon, a third as glittering as the stars, and a coat made up of fur from every animal in the kingdom. To her shock, her father successfully produced these gifts. She decides that her only recourse is to run away, and one snowy night she absconds from her home. The princess is eventually taken in by the young king of a neighboring land. By day, she works in the kitchens, nicknamed “Furball” and believed by everyone to be a pauper; by night, she attends the royal ball in her shining gowns, a figure of mystery and radiance. When the besotted king finally discovers that his alluring guest and his lowly kitchen maid are one and the same, he marries her and all is well. Huck’s rollicking text pairs wonderfully with Lobel’s lively art.

caption:
What if an otherworldly newcomer upended your life? You might be confused, frightened, angry…but this entity might simply be misunderstood. Perhaps a bit of grace and understanding would change everything. @levi_pinfold explores just such a scenario in his elegant and expressive Greenling. Mr. Barleycorn comes across a green baby inside an enormous blossom nestled in a culvert. He brings it home and, much to Mrs. Barleycorn’s chagrin, keeps it. The vegetable-infant hybrid brings about strange phenomena: fruits and flowers begin appearing all over the couple’s house. Mrs. Barleycorn, shaken by the unexpected growth, begins to lose patience with her husband. The plants spread outward, throttling a nearby railroad and earning the wrath of the community. However, Mrs. Barleycorn quickly jumps in to defend their peculiar ward. The people eat the wondrous fruit and are placated. The little green child eventually disappears, leaving the Barleycorns to look to the future and wonder what sort of miracle they might find growing on their land next spring. With elliptical text in common meter and pensive mixed-media illustrations in a muted color palette, Pinfold spins an understated tale of fear, mystery, and miracles.

If gentle rhythm and rhyme relaxes you, you’ll surely love Wynken, Blynken, and Nod, a renowned poem by Eugene Field with illustrations by Johanna Westerman. caption:
Barbara Lehman presents a mystical, wordless adventure that begins with the turn of a page in her endlessly fascinating The Red Book. A young girl is waking through the snowy streets of her city on the way to school. She notices a small red book lying in the snow, picks it up, and takes it with her. Later, in the warmth of her classroom, she opens it and looks at the pages. One of the illustrations appears to zoom in from high overhead to show a boy on a tropical beach. He finds an identical red book lying in the sand, picks it up, and opens it. Incredibly, his book shows him the girl in her classroom while hers shows him on the beach, creating a loop of infinite recursion. Later, the girl mounts a daring journey to find the boy by floating away on a bunch of balloons. To her chagrin, the book slips out of her hand. The boy sees it fall to the ground and begins to lose hope. However, the girl finds her way to his island after all, and they embrace happily. Meanwhile, another boy finds the dropped red book and rides off on his bicycle, perhaps to begin a new adventure. Through bright, expressive cartoon-style illustrations, Lehman injects her high-concept paranormal premise with energy and heart.

caption:
Barbara Lehman expands and deepens a wordless slice of speculative fiction with Red Again, the sequel to her lightly magical The Red Book. The story begins where its predecessor left off: with a boy finding the red book dropped by the girl. He brings it to his house and, high up in a little cupola, begins flipping through the pages. Simultaneously, another child in a fishing boat near a tropical island discovers a red book floating in the water. The two readers discover that they can see each other through the pages of their books, and they eventually come together in person. However, the real shock comes with the story’s mind-bending conclusion: the boy lets the red book fall into the snow…where it is discovered by the girl from the previous story, somehow at the start of her adventure. This revelation ties the duology, already infused with an inscrutable spatial magic, into a bizarre time loop. Lehman’s cheerful flat-style art belies a complex treatise on friendship, connection, and helical chronology.

caption:
Robert D. San Souci and Stephen T. Johnson combine their talents to produce a frightening yet alluring tale—The Snow Wife. One night in a little hut in the middle of a blizzard, apprentice woodcutter Minokichi witnesses the death of his old mentor at the hands of a pale, ghostly woman, whose body ends in a wisp of smoke where legs ought to be. The specter agrees to spare the young man’s life in exchange for his promise never to reveal the supernatural occurrence to anyone. Months later, he meets a young woman named Yuki and falls in love. The two of them marry, raise three children and live together for years in happiness. However, one evening after Minokichi carelessly lets slip the story of the woman in the snow, Yuki reveals that she herself is the entity and vanishes. The despondent woodcutter must make a dangerous pilgrimage to the Wind God on the peak of of Bitter Mountain to retain his lost love. San Souci, inspired by numerous Japanese tales of yuki-onna, the Snow Woman, crafts an adventure of drama, danger, and lost love, well matched by Johnson’s illustrations, a thrilling blend of watercolor and pastel art.

caption:
What if your mundane routine were upended by the arrival of someone completely unexpected? @marlafrazee creates a quietly charming and deeply human character study in The Farmer and the Clown. The wordless book opens on a wide, lonely plain. A dour farmer, in the midst of tilling the soil, sees a train go by in the distance…and someone falls off the back. He makes his way over to the tracks and discovers a child in white clown makeup. The two return to the farmer’s house, where they gradually form a close bond. By the time the train returns with the clown’s relieved family, the new friends find it difficult to say goodbye. As parting gifts, they trade hats. Unbeknownst to the farmer, however, he has gained more than a new piece of headwear—at the close of the story, a circus monkey has hopped off the train and is following him home. Frazee’s black pencil and gouache illustrations depict the subtle evolution of the relationship between the title characters from uncertainty to trust to loving friendship. The farmer’s long white beard and black pants and the clown’s Pierrot-style ruff and pointed cap make for a delightful visual contrast.

caption:
How do you adapt when the peaceful order of your everyday life is shattered by an inherently chaotic interloper? @marlafrazee’s wordless trilogy continues with The Farmer and the Monkey. Picking up immediately after the conclusion of the previous book, the story opens with the farmer returning home followed by the circus train’s lovable, mischievous pet monkey. Having bid a tender goodbye to his friend the young clown, the farmer is in no mood for jiggery-pokery. At first he orders the frenetic creature out of his house, but a sudden snowfall brings him a change of heart. He cares for the monkey as best he can, over the strenuous objections of his farm animals. When the circus train returns once more, the farmer sends his new friend off with a snare drum and a fully packed picnic basket for the road. As in The Farmer and the Clown, Frazee underscores the contrast between the title characters—the farmer remains a curmudgeonly figure, while the monkey brims with manic energy.

caption:
Where do you go when your everyday life is tied to one place but your heart is leading somewhere else altogether? Here is the conclusion to a gentle and heartfelt wordless trilogy by @marlafrazee: The Farmer and the Circus. The story serves as a sequel to both The Farmer and the Clown and The Farmer and the Monkey. The young child, having returned to his circus family, rejects clownish attire and dons a pair of black overalls, much like his beloved farmer. The monkey returns from the farm, and the two develop a delightful juggling act. Later, the circus starts putting down stakes. When the farmer arrives to see the show, the young clown and the monkey are overjoyed to see him. They perform their act for him and the clown’s mother, and the charmed adults begin to fall in love. Eventually, all four leave the circus and move into the farmhouse together, a loving found family unit. As in the previous two titles in the trilogy, Frazee ably conveys the action through a mix of vignettes, full-bleed illustrations, and her signature repeated-figure motion sequences.

caption:
On a dark night, when I’m in the mood for a good shiver, I crack open Joanna and Paul Galdone’s The Tailypo, quite possibly the scariest ever put into picture book form. An old man lives out in a cabin in the wilderness with only his dogs for company. One night, when the hunt has turned up precious little meat, a strange animal with a long bushy tail creeps into the cabin. The man chops off the tail, cooks it in his pot, eats it, and goes to bed happy. In the middle of the night, he hears the creature scratching around outside and calling relentlessly for its missing tail. He repeatedly sets his dogs on the thing, but it cannot be driven away. Finally, it creeps into the house and appears by the side of the bed. Though the man denies having eaten the tail, the infernal thing proceeds to scratch him to pieces, destroying the cabin for good measure. Joanna Galdone’s eerie narrative makes ruthlessly effective use of the refrain: “Tailypo, tailypo,/all I want is my tailypo.” Paul Galdone depicts the monster as a dark, furry blob staring at the old man with wide, yellow eyes. Together, the daughter-father team execute a riveting, nightmarish ghost story, coldly and utterly devoid of the comfort of a happy ending.

First up, come bask in the gleam and glow of Brad Kessler and Robert Van Nutt’s adaptation. A young archer Ivan and his Horse of Power find a golden feather in the forest, dropped by the legendary Firebird. Against the horse’s dire warnings, Ivan brings it to his employer, the czar, who quickly commands him to capture the Firebird itself. When Ivan succeeds at that task, he is promptly sent to the Land of Never, where he is to retrieve the Princess Vasilisa to be the wicked ruler’s bride. caption:
At the halfway point of Firebird Week, I’m perusing @ruthsandersonart’s The Golden Mare, the Firebird, and the Magic Ring. After finding a bright, glowing feather, earnest young huntsman Alexi is pressed into service by the wicked Tsar. If he values his life, he is to capture the legendary Firebird and bring it back for the monarch’s viewing pleasure. When he succeeds, the Tsar commands him to locate Yelena the Fair, a renowned beauty who sails on the Lake of the Sun. Rather than marry the black-hearted ruler, however, Yelena tricks him into jumping into a cauldron which she claims contains the Water of Youth. Indeed, the water makes the Tsar young again: he transforms into a baby. Alexi and Yelena take the infant as their own child and rule the kingdom together. caption:
Continuing with my new Firebird Week, Neil Philip and Isabel Brent create a dazzling adventure in The Golden Bird. A young prince must discover who is eating the precious apples of his father, the king. So begins a tale of magic and danger—the prince retrieves a golden bird, a golden horse, and a beautiful princess, all with the help of a clever fox. caption:
Onward and onward, Firebird Week, and now I present Gilly Martin the Fox, a delightful collaboration between Mollie Hunter and Dennis McDermott. A witch has placed a terrible curse upon the Prince of Alban. He must retrieve the Blue Falcon from the Giant with Five Heads. However, he can only get the bird in exchange for the White Glave of Light, which is owned by the Seven Big Women of Jura. The women will only give up their precious sword in trade for the Bay Filly of the King of Erin, and the King of Erin wants the hand of the daughter of the King of Lochlann in marriage. With the help of the clever fox Gilly Martin, the prince retrieves these magic items, defeats the fearsome witch, and breaks the wicked spell. In an unusual format, Hunter chooses to tell the story from the perspective of the wily fox, beginning with the first encounter between the animal and the prince and including the start of the prince’s quest as backstory. McDermott’s illustrations (an oil painting on the cover, watercolor and ink in the interior) convey action, scale, and wonder.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: As mentioned in the front matter, this book was adapted from a Scottish story called “Mac Iain Direach” (in English, “Son of John the Upright”), published in 1860 by John Francis Campbell in Popular Tales of the West Highlands. The story was adapted by Andrew Lang and Leonora Blanche Alleyne for the Orange Fairy Book in 1906; this version was called “How Ian Direach got the Blue Falcon”. This tale is a variant of “Tsarevich Ivan, the Firebird, and the Gray Wolf”, with the Blue Falcon taking the place of the Firebird.

caption:
Opposites fascinate us. The dichotomy of two contrasting forces or entities holds deep symbolic resonance for the human mind. This power serves as a foundation for the whimsy and grace of Kerstin Hau and Julie Völk’s The Dark and the Light. The story centers on the border between two realms. Shaggy dwells on the shadowy side of the line, while Sparkle basks in the sun. Though they fear the unknown, each nurtures a secret curiosity to cross over and see what is on the other side. Soon enough, they meet and become friends, with Sparkle leading Shaggy gently over the dividing band of blue-gray to explore the bright zone. When her house is destroyed, Sparkle comes to live on the dark side. By the time they are ready to return to the light, she herself is afraid, and Shaggy provides her with the same courage she instilled in him. Ultimately, the two friends move back and forth between the worlds, maintaining a happy home on each side of the line. Hau provides a thought-provoking text (translated from German by David Henry Wilson), replete with such lovely details as a parasol to protect from the light, a flashlight to brighten the dark, and fur that gradually shifts color to match a change in environment. Völk’s illustrations employ cyanotype, a natural printing technique that yields the vivid blue pervading the book.

Alan Marks spins an otherworldly yarn in the magical and mystical Childe Roland. A gaggle of children is playing near a church. From @angelamcallisterbooks and Grahame Baker-Smith comes a lyrical tale of friendship, wonder, and seasons personified: Winter’s Child. Tom lives in a little house with his mother and his Nana. Winter has been dragging on unusually long, and everything all around is frosty and chill. Tom revels in the snow blanketing the landscape, though his grandmother, old and in frail condition, cannot bear the cold. Soon, he meets a pale boy who becomes his new playmate out in the frosted world, and the two meet every day for bouts of icy revelry. When Nana’s health begins to suffer, Tom cannot hide his concern for her. The pale boy finally reveals his secret: he is Winter’s Child, and as long as he stays away from home spring will be held at bay. Now, however, he does his duty and returns to his family, thus allowing the world to burst into bloom and saving the life of Tom’s beloved Nana. McAllister’s elegant text infuses mystical allegory with genuine emotion and heart; Baker-Smith’s compelling digital art gleams with bright white, swirling silver, and shivery blue.

caption:
Patricia C. McKissack and Leo and Diane Dillon craft a stunning work of magical realism in Never Forgotten. The story is set in eighteenth-century Mali. After his wife dies, a Mende blacksmith named Dinga vows to raise their newborn son on his own. To help him with the task, he invokes the four elements—Earth Mother, Fire Woman, Water Maiden, and Wind Spirit. The boy grows up happy and carefree, apprenticed to his father. One day, tragedy strikes: Musafa is kidnapped and sold into slavery. The elements are able to follow and bring back reports of the terrible things they have witnessed, but they can do nothing to intervene. Dinga is devastated. Years later, Wind Spirit returns with the news that Musafa is alive and working as a blacksmith in Charleston, providing his father a small morsel of comfort, though the two will never be reunited. McKissack’s text, in the form of elegiac prose poems, takes an unflinching look at the horrors of the slave trade. In their masterful acrylic and watercolor art, the Dillons never allow the beauty of the supernatural imagery to palliate the nightmarish truth of history.

caption:
Fever Dream is an unsettling little slice of science fiction horror by Ray Bradbury with illustrations by Darrel Anderson. Charles has been sick in bed for three days, with a doctor looking in on him. The frightened boy confides that a strange feeling has come over him. His right hand, he says, no longer belongs to him. It has changed, somehow, into something else. The doctor dismisses his concern as nothing more than a fever dream and gives him a pill. Soon, however, Charles perceives the same transformation taking place in the rest of his body—his other hand, his legs, and eventually his torso. In terror, he begins to suspect that the disease inside him is taking over his body, infecting and replacing him cell by cell until nothing is left. Nobody believes him—not the doctor, not his parents. Suddenly, however, Charles makes a miraculous recovery. And he begins expressing a sinister desire to come into physical contact with as many people and animals as possible. Is this really Charles? Or is it something else entirely, some unknowable entity that has emerged from within and now wishes to propagate? Anderson’s eerie illustrations complement Bradbury’s sinister and subtly apocalyptic tale.

caption:
Is there any such thing as objectivity? That is, when you look at a thing and I look at that thing, do we see the same thing? @brendan_wenzel’s They All Saw a Cat takes a marvelous deep dive into these deceptively deep questions. The story, stripped down to the utmost simplicity, shifts perspectives constantly from page to page. A cat takes a walk, passing by numerous animals as it goes. Each creature perceives the cat differently—the dog sees a miserable, slinking wretch; the mouse sees a hulking, taloned fiend; the fly sees a mosaic of spots; the snake sees a glowing heat signature; the bat sees a splash of echolocated texture. Wenzel pairs his quietly philosophical writing with vividly expressive art executed in a variety of media, including colored pencils, oil pastels, acrylic paint, watercolor, charcoal, marker, and digital technique. Finally, the cat comes upon its own reflection, and here Wenzel leaves readers with the most arcane question of all: what does it see when it looks at itself?

Saunders’ uplifting text and Ottley’s fantastical illustrations come together for a gripping story of magic realism, culminating in the delightful reveal, on the final page, that the amazing vehicle is a metaphor for a very different kind of freedom machine: a book.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This story was first collected by Robert Chambers in his 1858 book Popular Rhymes of Scotland. White puts her own stamp on the plot by changing the baby to a young girl called Kate, naming the pig “Grumphie”, and having the mysterious green fairy travel in a whirlwind that makes the sound “Whuppity! Whuppity!”—perhaps explaining her distinctive name.

caption:
Here, smack-dab in the middle of Name of the Helper Week, husband-and-wife team Harve and Margot Zemach have provided the entertainment with their lively adaptation of Duffy and the Devil. A rich squire sees a young lady being thrown out by her own mother, who claims she does not a lick of work to help out around the house. The daughter claims to be able to spin and knit wonderfully, and so the squire brings her home with him. However, the maiden, Duffy, was lying, and so is forced to engage the help of a little man with a long tail, who willingly makes clothing for her. Thanks to the wonderful craftsmanship of these garments, the squire makes Duffy his wife. However, the mysterious little being soon names his price: he threatens to take the young woman away with him unless she can guess his name. Then, a stroke of luck—the squire, out on a hunt, accidentally falls down a hole into a den of witches, and amid the wild revelries he overhears the creature’s name: Tarraway. Harve Zemach (real name Harvey Fischtrom) constructs a delightfully energetic story, enhanced by Margot Zemach’s loose line and rich color.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: In the oral story, collected by Robert Hunt in Popular Romances of the West of England; or, The Drolls, Traditions, and Superstitions of Old Cornwall (1871), the devil’s name is Terrytop. Reasons for the change are unclear.

caption:
From Evaline Ness comes our next Name of the Helper book: Tom Tit Tot. A despondent mother sits outside her house, devastated that her daughter has greedily eaten up five pies. Overheard by a passing king, the embarrassed woman claims that she was singing about the girl’s having spun five skeins. The king immediately insists upon marrying the daughter, with the proviso that she spin for him. Unable to spin, the trapped girl agrees to the help of a dark imp who soon threatens to take her away unless she can guess his name. Only by happenstance does the king himself overhear the little creature’s name: Tom Tit Tot. Ness hews close to the language of the original tale, pairing her text with energetic woodcut illustrations.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This story was first published by Joseph Jacobs in his 1890 collection English Fairy Tales.

caption:
Name of the Helper Week moves from England to America with Barry Moser’s Tucker Pfeffercorn. An old miner named Jefferson Tadlock invents a story that a local woman can spin cotton into gold. Unfortunately, he is overheard by Hezakiah Sweatt, a wealthy and greedy landowner. The subject of Tadlock’s farfetched claim is Bessie Grace Kinzalow, a widow with a young daughter. The villainous Sweatt demands that Bessie Grace make good on Tadlock’s claim, holding her child hostage. A bizarre little man offers to perform the task for her, and she rashly promises him whatever he wants as a reward. Later on, the stranger names his price: Bessie Grace’s daughter. The mother begs and pleads, and finally gets him to agree to forgive the debt if she can guess his name. Fortunately, she successfully tracks him down in a cemetery at night and overhears his name: Tucker Pfeffercorn. When she triumphantly confronts him with his name, the little man is so angry that he bounces up to the ceiling and berates her while upside down. Moser pairs a text full of folk whimsy with paintings rich in expressive color.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Though American “Name of the Helper” folk variants do exist, this narrative is a direct adaptation of the Brothers Grimm tale “Rumpelstiltskin”, reimagined by Moser in the American South.

caption:
To conclude Name of the Helper Week, let us examine Virginia Hamilton and Leo and Diane Dillon’s The Girl Who Spun Gold. Young Quashiba must live up to her mother’s lie—that she can spin a whole field of golden thread. The king will marry her if she can achieve the task, but he will leave her locked up if she cannot. In comes a tiny, shadow my man who offers to spin the gold for her. In return, if she cannot guess his name, he will make her tiny like him and carry her off. Only by a happy accident does the king overhear his name: Lit’mahn Bittyun. Confronted with his true name, the weird creature pops into a million flecks and scatters on the wind. Hamilton creates an energetic retelling, full of appealing details and turns of phrase. Fascinatingly, she reveals the little man’s name from the beginning of the narrative, leaving readers one step ahead of Quashiba. The Dillons provide lush illustrations executed in acrylic on acetate, followed by applications of gold paint (for the gold in the images) and gold leaf (for the borders).

A note for folklore enthusiasts: In the back matter, Hamilton lists her source as “Mr. Titman”, from an 1899 collection of Caribbean folklore by Pamela Coleman Smith.

caption:
Step through a seemingly ordinary doorway into an entirely new reality with @bottomshelfbks and @dsantat’s Lift. Young Iris loves to push the button when her family rides in their building’s elevator, considering it an important job. One day, disaster strikes: her little brother presses the button instead. Even worse, their parents praise him for it. Later, Iris finds a discarded elevator button set in a wall plate and tapes it up in her bedroom. To her surprise, the button transforms her closet door into a portal leading to far-off lands. Finally, it would seem, she has a means to escape her pesky younger sibling. But she soon realizes that a good adventure is far more fun with a sidekick in tow. Lê’s warm-hearted story and Santat’s irresistible art blend perfectly together in comic-style panels interspersed with full-bleed illustrations revealing each marvelous new destination.

caption:
The Spring equinox has come ‘round again, and I am celebrating with a reading of The Search for Spring, a pensive and poetic work by Moira Miller and Ian Deuchar. A boy who lives on his family’s farm wishes to know where Spring goes once Summer arrives. Since his mother and father cannot tell him, he sets out into the world to find out. Days, weeks, months, and years slip away; through brushes with wisdom, violence, and hardship, he can never quite seem to find Spring. He grows from a boy into a young man, endlessly seeking the answer to his mystical question. Then, he arrives at a familiar little farmhouse in a broad valley—he has come home again. Moreover, Spring is there waiting for him. But, his mother wonders, where has her little boy gone? Miller’s through-provoking allegory pairs beautifully with Deuchar’s delicate paintings.

caption:
Let married co-creators @laurenmillsart and Dennis Nolan beckon you into a world of gossamer magic in their book Fairy Wings. Fia the fairy is a laughingstock among her sisters, for she was born without wings. One day she meets a fairy boy named Kip and mends his torn wing; he in turn invites her to the May Dance, where all the eligible young fairy girls will be competing for the affections of Prince Hyacinth. Fia’s sisters cruelly mock her and nearly succeed at convincing her to stay home. At the dance, it turns out that Prince Hyacinth and Kip are one and the same. However, disaster soon strikes: a wicked troll kidnaps all the fairies but Fia, plotting to steal their wings for himself. With the help of her devoted friends Rat, Frog, and Crow, the wingless fairy rescues her people and turns the greedy troll to stone. The delightful text by Mills offers enchantment and suspense, while the wondrous graphite and watercolor art, a collaboration between Mills and Nolan, unlocks an irresistible fantasy realm.

caption:
You’ll shiver indeed at The Bone Man, a frightening story by Laura Simms and Michael McCurdy. Young Nulwee and his grandmother live in a drought-stricken land. The last survivors of their tribe, they eke out a meager existence by gathering berries. One day, the boy accidentally awakens an ancient evil: Kokolimalayas, the Bone Man. Nulwee must hone his skill with a bow and arrow to defeat the enormous skeletal monster and restore peace to the land around him. Simms weaves a chilling narrative, enhanced by McCurdy’s eerie illustrations.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: As noted in the back matter, the tale of the Bone Man was first recorded by Jeremiah Curtin in 1900; Simms consulted with members of the Salish, Acoma Pueblo, and Chippewa Cree tribes in preparation for writing the text.

caption:
Truthfully, I’m not sure what this book is about. If it’s a simple plot with easily digested characters and themes you want, look elsewhere. But if an elliptical slice of introspection’s what you’re after, give yourself over to Etienne Delessert’s Ashes, Ashes. The narrator of this impenetrable tale passes from the mundane world into a strange wilderness at the behest of three pale men. Others soon arrive in the mystical land, and the wanderers build a house together. After reveling in the sensory marvels of nature, the protagonist soon feels the call of the journey once more and departs, either to return home or to move on to parts unknown. Delessert weaves together his expressive text and lightly surreal art in pursuit of mood and tone. Rejecting easy interpretation, the work is wholly experimental and strangely beautiful.

caption:
Eric A. Kimmel and Charles Mikolaycak present a delightful adaptation of an old tale in the aptly and pithily titled Bearhead. A man and a woman discover a baby abandoned in the forest. To their surprise, the child has the head of a bear. The woman therefore bestows on him the first name that comes into her mind—Bearhead—and they raise the child as their own son. Years later, the husband is summoned into the service of a local witch named Madame Hexaba. Bearhead goes in his father’s place. He proceeds to take the witch’s commands literally, clearing away her dinner table by throwing it out the window and guarding the door of her treasure house by ripping it off its hinges. Eventually, he receives a long overdue rent payment from the witch’s goblin tenant and makes his old parents rich. Kimmel’s narrative shines with understated humor, and Mikolaycak’s illustrations (created with watercolor and colored pencil) provide plenty of warm and engaging detail.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Kimmel’s source, as he mentions in the front matter, is “Ivanko the Bear’s Son”, a Russian folktale with variants and related narratives around the world.

caption:
Have you ever felt seen? Supported? Empowered? Has the world ever seemed to get brighter with the presence of a friend? What do you do when these new possibilities open before you? I pondered these and many other questions while reading I Get Loud, @d.ouimet’s sequel to I Go Quiet. A young girl’s lonely life in a sprawling city is interrupted by the presence of a child her own age. They form a tight friendship through flying kites, fishing, and swimming. When rising floodwaters force the entire population to abandon their homes, the two girls are separated. On distant shores, they reunite and prepare to face a new life together. Through a spare first-person narrative, combined with intriguing illustrations in a muted color palette, Ouimet makes a triumphant statement on the vital importance of companionship and community.

caption:
Come let @fredericlement whisk you away to a world of wonder and enchantment in the pages of The Merchant of Marvels and the Peddler of Dreams. The book takes the form of an extended monologue from one character to another. The Peddler of Dreams makes a pitch, describing his many wares to the Merchant of Marvels (who never replies, only listens). Contained in the vast collection are objects of delight and mystery, thimbles and flowers and eggs and bones and locks of hair. References to fairy tales and children’s literature abound: we are shown the broken end of Pinocchio’s nose, two whiskers belonging to Puss-in-Boots, Thumbelina’s cradle, Captain Nemo’s cap, Snow White’s powder pot, the splinter from Sleeping Beauty’s finger, a marble made by Merlin, and seven peals of Cinderella’s laughter, among other curios. Clément’s text, originally published in French as “Magasin Zinzin ou Aux Merveilles d’Alys”, echoes with old-world romance. His multimedia art appears as colorful spot illustrations woven into the text. The effect is as if we are delving into an antique treasure trove, flipping through the pages of an arcane catalogue presented by the Peddler of Dreams himself.

The book of the day is Shadow by @christopher.lucy and @chaosego. A young girl moves to a new house. There, she discovers Shadow, a friend who plays with her to her heart’s content. Her mother all too often seems to be distracted, overworked, exhausted, and she cannot see the mysterious being. Christopher’s subtle, introspective writing and Suvorova’s richly textured digital art combine for an intriguing meditation on loneliness, change, and understanding.

caption:
Marianna Mayer and Winslow Pels collaborate on a handsome adaptation of the Brothers Grimm tale Iron John. A young prince named Hans frees a wild man from a cage in his father’s courtyard. Fearing punishment, he flees to the forest. The wild man becomes his guardian and eventually helps him win a fierce battle and a challenging tournament for the hand of a princess. Mayer crafts an elegant text, while Pels employs large-scale compositions that evoke the flattened perspective of medieval art.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Mayer keeps the architecture of the plot contained in the story included by Brothers Grimm in the sixth edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen (1850). Into that structure she weaves numerous additional details. For example, the young prince is now named Hans (taken from the Grimms’ title “Iron Hans”). Instead of a king under a magic spell, the wild man is now a guise of the wizard Merlin himself.
