caption:
Imagine that you can’t sleep, so you look out the window and see a pack of friendly animals getting together for a midnight snack. You have just imagined yourself in the realm of Night Lunch, a cozy collaboration between @ericfanillustration and @dena.seiferling. In the middle of the night, as a full moon hangs in the air, a hungry group of nocturnal animals gathers on a brightly lit city street. With a clip-clop of hooves and a thinking bell, the night lunch cart rolls in. A gentle owl cooks tasty food to order: fried eggs for the moths, sausages and peppers for the bats, puddings for the possums. When the crowd has dispersed, a timid little mouse remains to sweep the gutter. The owl generously opens the door of the cart, and the two share a feast of tea and cakes before the first light of morning creeps over the horizon. Fan’s minimalist text unfolds like quiet poetry; Seiferling’s digital art boasts soft textures and a rich, dreamy palette of reds, browns, and purples.

caption:
Wind Child by Shirley Rousseau Murphy and the Dillons is a lyrical tale of  wildness and freedom. Resshie is the daughter of a mortal woman and the east wind. When she comes of age, she leaves her village and earns a living by weaving marvelous, stormy cloth. Her otherworldly fabric delights all who see it, and she does not want for buyers. Lonely in her daily existence, Resshie resolves to find a husband. She fashions a human out of rushes and vines and names him Summer, but he soon withers and fades away like the season itself. Then she creates a man out of wool and names him Ormond, but he dries out and crumbles. Then she traps a mortal hunter named Clay, but he yearns for his freedom, and she lets him go. One day, a mysterious prince arrives at Resshie’s cottage, having heard of her skill and artistry. The young woman proposes a wager: she will create a tapestry that shows the noble youth’s true likeness, and in return he will offer his hand in marriage. With her marvelous weaving, she reveals her suitor as an elemental being, and two of them take to the skies in glorious union. Murphy’s text rings with wondrous descriptive language. Married collaborators Leo and Diane Dillon provide a lush palette of silvery blues and greens that evokes the wind itself. Their son Lee Dillon interprets the story and characters through sculptures, photographed and reproduced on each page.

caption:
There’s something special about taking time to connect with plants, to experience the tranquility of forests and fields. @shawnharri5 creates a lyrical exploration of the world of flora in Have You Ever Seen a Flower? A young girl takes a car trip out of the city into the countryside, where she finds herself surrounded by the bright, blooming expanse of nature. caption:
Nearing the end of my thousand picture book posts, I cannot help but squeeze in one last Fairy Tale Theme Week. This one is devoted to my very favorite tale type, in which a determined heroine must save her lover from a magical curse—The Search for the Lost Husband.

First up, László Gál supplies a handsome adaptation of East of the Sun & West of the Moon. A young girl agrees to marry a mysterious white bear in exchange for a gift of enormous wealth for her family. When she discovers that he is a human man under a terrible curse, she must follow him across the world to a castle east of the sun and west of the moon and rescue him from the clutches of a pack of hideous trolls. Gál’s elegant retelling and delightful drawings create an air of wonder and enchantment.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This tale comes from Norske Folkeeventyr, originally published in 1841 by Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe.

caption:
With a broken vow and a beastly transformation upon our heads, let us examine D. J. MacHale and Vivienne Flesher’s East of the Sun, West of the Moon. MacHale’s engaging story is well matched by the hazy colors of Flesher’s expressionistic art, which lend a moody palette to the proceedings.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: MacHale’s text adapts Asbjørnsen and Moe’s tale closely, except for the ending. In the original plot, the young woman must trade her treasures to the troll princess in order to be allowed inside her bewitched lover’s room at night. MacHale has the maiden break the spell simply by crying over the young prince’s tallow-stained nightshirt.

caption:
The gifts we collect along the way will aid us on our journey. Here in the very heart of Search for the Lost Husband Week, I am shifting from East of the Sun, West of the Moon adaptations to other variants. Tanya Robyn Batt and @nicolettececcoli create an appealing folkloric blend in The Princess and the White Bear King. A princess dreams of a golden crown, which she later discovers in the possession of a white bear. She becomes his wife but soon loses him to a terrible curse when she looks upon his true form by candlelight in their bedchamber. She must follow him in a difficult quest, traversing strange lands, climbing a glass mountain with iron claws on her hands and feet, and outwitting a shrewd troll queen. Batt’s engaging prose and Ceccoli’s stylized illustrations bring the tale ably to life.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: In the back matter, Batt provides a detailed description of her influences, listing “East of the Sun, West of the Moon”, “The Black Bull of Norroway”, and “White Bear King Valemon” as sources. In fact, the bulk of the plot—the opening dream, the three gifts (tablecloth, cup, and scissors), the blacksmith’s family, the iron claws, the troll queen’s test to see whether the prince is truly sleeping—is drawn directly from “White Bear King Valemon”, with the other two tales providing minimal additional material.

caption:
Arriving in strange lands, we must keep our wits about us. Here, for your comfort and pleasure, is daughter-and-mother team Marie Charlotte and Kinuko Y. Craft’s sumptuous retelling of the tale of Cupid and Psyche. The story opens in Ancient Greece, with a king, a queen, and their three daughters. The youngest princess, Psyche, is so beautiful that people begin to suspect she is an incarnation of Venus. When the goddess herself hears this rumor, she is deeply offended. She commands her son Cupid to avenge the insult, but Cupid accidentally scratches himself with his own arrow of desire and falls in love with Psyche. Later, on the advice of the Oracle of Delphi, Psyche goes to the top of a mountain and is wed to a mysterious suitor who will not reveal his face. Her sisters eventually convince her to look at him as he sleeps. To her surprise, it is Cupid himself. The god flees, and Venus sets Psyche three tasks to win back her husband: sorting a mound of grain into separate piles, gathering golden fleece from a flock of fiery rams, and retrieving a box from Proserpina, queen of the underworld. Once Psyche completes these errands, she is made immortal and she a Cupid are never again parted. Marie Craft’s compelling language and Kinuko Craft’s extraordinary oil-over-watercolor paintings combine for a magnificent whole.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: The myth of Cupid and Psyche was originally recorded in The Golden Ass, a book written by the Roman author Apuleius in the first century of the common era, making it not only the earliest printed variant of the Search for the Lost Husband tale type but also one of the older surviving pieces of folklore in the western world.

caption:
Though we suffer impossible trials, though we sing outside the door of our lost love, will it be enough? Will goodness and courage prevail? The Black Bull of Norroway by Charlotte Huck and Anita Lobel may yet give us hope. A woman with three daughters listens as they imagine their future husbands. The youngest, Peggy Ann, nonchalantly declares that she would be happy to marry the Black Bull of Norroway. When she goes to visit a wise woman down the road, the fearsome creature himself arrives to collect her. He takes her to visit his three royal brothers, and each one gives her a magical piece of fruit. Finally, Peggy Ann pulls a thorn out of the bull’s hoof, which returns him to his human form as the Duke of Norroway. He enters a strange grotto for a fated battle with an entity known as the Guardian of the Glen. Peggy Ann, against the Duke’s orders, jumps up from the rock in excitement at his victory and the two are separated by a fell power. The maiden must serve a blacksmith for seven years, and in return he forges a pair of iron boots that she uses to climb a glassy hill. She exchanges jewelry taken from her marvelous fruit for the chance to sing outside the Duke’s door at night; he eventually awakens and the two are reunited. Huck’s rollicking text and Lobel’s bright illustrations in watercolor and black pen bring the adventure easily to life.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This tale first appeared in print as “The Red Bull of Norroway” in Popular Rhymes of Scotland by Robert Chambers (1842).

caption:
At last we triumph, all spells dispatched, all evil destroyed. As we reunite with our lost loves, let Laurel Long and @jackieogburn supply one last entry in Search for the Lost Husband Week: The Lady and the Lion. A young woman is obliged to marry a lion as penance for her father’s incursion on his castle. The animal soon turns out to be an enchanted prince, but his wife aggravates the curse by allowing him to be struck with a sliver of candlelight. From there, she pursues him all across the world, rescues him from a shapeshifting dragon enchantress, and escapes on the back of a wondrous griffin. The adventurous and uplifting text, co-written by Long and Ogburn, is wonderfully enhanced by Long’s swirling, glowing oil paintings.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: This tale was recorded by the Brothers Grimm in the second volume of the first edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen, published in 1815.

caption:
Today I have for you the provocative and powerful We Are All in the Dumps with Jack and Guy by Maurice Sendak. The text consists of two traditional Mother Goose nursery rhymes back to back—“We Are All in the Dumps”, a nonsense verse with fanciful imagery leavened by a bleak tone, and “Jack and Guy”, a story poem in which violent impulses give way to peace and tenderness. Adding a few expository signs and speech bubbles, Sendak fuses the two rhymes into a single narrative, in which Jack and Guy wander through an eerie, dystopian shantytown filled with homeless and hungry people. Large, anthropomorphic rats menace the population, kidnapping children and kittens and hauling them away in sacks. The enormous white moon looks on in dismay before leaping into action. It lifts Jack and Guy out of the city toward the combination bakery and orphanage where the innocents have been imprisoned and takes the shape of a ferocious cat to help them vanquish the wicked rats. Sendak’s art transforms the nursery rhymes into an incendiary political statement on inequality and apathy, as needed now as ever.

If you’re after a breathtaking fusion of the scientific and the poetic, look no further than Ray Jayawardhana and @raul.colon.7140’s Child of the Universe. At bedtime, a young girl’s father lulls her to sleep with the connections between her own body and the materials of earth and space. caption:
Come and witness a tragedy for the ages, as recounted in Charles Mikolaycak’s Orpheus. Here is a tale full of love, loss, and grief, originating as an Ancient Greek myth, but with a soul that speaks to us across time. Orpheus, a talented musician is wed to his beloved Euridyce, but their happiness is soon spoiled by her untimely death. The devastated young man travels down to the Underworld to beg for her release; the spirit of his fiancée is permitted to follow him, but if he looks at her before they reach the land of the living she will be lost to him forever. As they walk up toward the light, temptation proves too great: Orpheus looks over his shoulder, and Euridyce is whisked back into death. His dreams of a happy life lying in ruins, the ill-fated lover wanders the earth. Eventually, he comes across a pack of revelers, who do not understand why he will not play them a joyous tune. Their anger whips them up into a frenzy, and they tear him limb from limb. Mikolaycak weaves lines from Monteverdi’s 1607 opera L’Orfeo into his poignant text. His illustrations are executed in colored pencil, watercolor, and acrylic on diazo prints made from pencil drawings.

caption:
Let Otfried Preussler and Gennady Spirin whisk you away on an immersive adventure to the ends of the earth and back again—this is The Tale of the Unicorn. Three brothers set off on a quest. Their goal is nothing short of capturing a unicorn, who it is said possesses a horn made of ivory, hooves of pure gold, and a diamond star on its brow. The oldest brother meets an innkeeper’s daughter who cooks wonderful food, marries her straightaway, and settles down. The middle brother happens upon a lump of gold in the desert, buys a fine house in a large city, and settles down. Hans, the youngest brother, travels onward through fire and water, through deepest night and coldest ice. When he at last reaches the unicorn, he stands transfixed, unable to kill the majestic beast. An unknown amount of time passes, and Hans returns to the world he knows, older and wiser than when he left. Preussler crafts a narrative that honors nature, beauty, mystery, and wonder. Spirin contributes a marvelous visual landscape of half-timbered houses, soaring cathedrals, and lonely forests. His unicorn is a triumph, instantly conveying to readers the sheer awe of its otherworldly presence.

caption:
I can’t help but chuckle in amusement even as I shudder in horror when reading George Harland and Rowan Barnes-Murphy’s adaption of a tale recorded by Charles Dickens—Captain Murderer. Good heavens, what a title! Captain Murderer is a gentleman who specializes in marrying wealthy young brides, chopping them up, baking them in pies, and eating them. He even has his teeth filed by the family blacksmith in preparation for satisfying his ghoulish appetites. He eventually makes the mistake of marrying and devouring a lady with a vengeful twin sister. The sister presents herself as an eager bride, but before the villain cooks her and eats her she consumes a deadly poison. In unbearable agony, Captain Murderer swells, turns blue, screams, and explodes. Harland closely adapts Dickens’s text, and Barnes-Murphy contributes delightfully macabre cartoon-style illustrations.

A note for folklore enthusiasts: Dickens included this story in his book The Uncommercial Traveler. Though the plot details differ, the themes of matrimony and cannibalism are reminiscent of the grisly tale The Robber Bridegroom (recorded by the Brothers Grimm) and its variants.

caption:
What would you do at the end of the world? If you were the last surviving member of your civilization, where would you seek shelter? How would you find the strength to keep moving? If you somehow discovered one last act of goodness you could perform, how far would you go to get the job done? These and other weighty questions emerge from a reading of Nonstop, the last work by @tomiungerer. Earth has sunk into desolation. The plants have withered and the animals have perished. The human population has fled to the moon, leaving behind one man, Vasco, who makes his way through the deserted landscapes accompanied only by his shadow. The unfortunate wanderer accepts a letter from a creature named Nothing. Once he locates Nothing’s wife, she charges him with the care of their young child Poco. Vasco and Poco make their way through frigid ice floes, a forest of collapsing metal pipes, and a hazardous factory complex studded with magma pits. Finally, they board a train that takes them out into the wilderness. There, impossibly but undeniably, stands an enormous cake. Vasco and Poco survive inside the bizarre shelter, which contains enough supplies to sustain them for the rest of their lives. Ungerer’s bold text and stark illustrations create a mood of oppressive darkness—leavened gently by the unexpected safe haven at the story’s end.

There’s something magical about a treehouse—halfway between earth and sky, it stands as a symbol for friendship, relaxation, and imaginative play. @carterhiggins and @plaidemily have taken these elements and woven them into the delightful Everything You Need for a Treehouse. For construction, the list contains such sensible items as blueprints, hammers, nails, saws, and hard hats. For furnishing, featured recommendations include a rope swing, a bookshelf, a backpack of snacks, sleeping bags, and flashlights. Both the first page and the last suggest a pair of intangible ingredients: time and looking up. Higgins uses each element of her poetic list as a jumping-off point to explore captivating natural imagery with metaphors such as, “one soldier/in an army of trees”, “you can make your own sky/with spotlights and shadows”, and “the wind keeps them/snug with a rustle/which is a hush you can feel/in your bones”. Hughes contributes lush, delicate-textured illustrations, a seamless combination of graphite and digital technique.

caption:
Gentle Readers, today marks the start of my final ten posts before I reach one thousand book reviews (and go on a little social media hiatus). I decided a long time ago that this last stretch would be devoted to ten truly extraordinary books. I have been curating a special collection for a little while, and I am thrilled to begin sharing it with you now.

Let us begin with a wordless work of art: A Stone for Sascha by @storybreathing. Grieving the loss of a beloved pet, a young girl goes to the beach with her family. In a flashback to the beginning of Earth’s formation, we see a blazing meteor collide with the young planet, depositing a golden ore in the ground. Over millions of years, seismic activity pushes the gleaming mineral to the surface. Humans discover the stone, and it is transformed by every civilization that touches it: a sacred monolith for an ancient tribe, an Egyptian obelisk, a brick in the chest of a Buddhist statue, the keystone in the arch of a Chinese bridge, a dragon statue in a jungle shrine. The treasure is eventually lost in the depths of the ocean, where it is tossed, ground smooth, and polished by the shifting currents. Finally, in the present day, the young girl discovers the stone in the shallows, where it brings her a morsel of comfort as she sits alone beneath the sweeping sky. Becker’s enthralling digital illustrations provide a stunning glimpse of Big History, taking an epic perspective and distilling it down to a beautiful kernel of humanistic truth.

caption:
Welcome back, Gentle Readers, to my Final Ten Books, the counting down of ten magical reviews to conclude my thousand picture books. Andrew Matthews and Justin Todd offer a poignant, emotionally rich creation myth: The Jar of the Sun. A young boy lives with his parents in a strange, untamed landscape. His every whim is their command. When he calls for ice, they collect it from a mountain peak; when he wants fire, they retrieve it from a volcano. After he demands light, his parents trap the sun in a jar, snare the moon in a web, and throw the stars into a bowl of water. Exhausted by the effort, they grow old and crumble into dust. The boy, desperate to escape his newfound loneliness, treks across the land until he hears a quiet song emerging from the lips of a girl sleeping on top of a mountain. To wake her, he releases the stars, the moon, and finally the sun. Matthews takes what could have been a simple morality tale and expands it into an unexpected cosmogony, a fanciful beginning to a universe born out of flawed human emotion, concluding with the enigmatic, unforgettable line, “And everything began.” Todd’s richly colored drawings create deep appeal and anchor the mysterious setting to reality.

For this next entry in my Final Ten Books, Gentle Readers, I have Kiyo Tanaka’s The Little One. On her way home one day, a young girl spies a shadowy little creature perched on a wall. She begins to see it again and again, and finally she decides to follow it. The mysterious entity leads her through a hole in a wall, past a blooming garden, and into a little house. The combination of Tanaka’s thoughtful writing (translated from Japanese by David Boyd) and her understated black and white art provides a lulling, introspective journey of the mind. Though it is not stated directly in the text, the child’s dream about her mother delicately suggests a note of loss and grief as the backdrop to the gentle tale.

caption:
Consider, Gentle Readers, that with the passage of time we may find magic and danger echoing from generation to generation. So it goes in @levi_pinfold’s eerie, poetic tale Paradise Sands. The story opens with a young girl and her three brothers driving through the desert to meet their mother. They stop to pick flowers and find their way to a palatial hotel with no one inside. Tugged onward by the string of destiny and an eldritch nursery rhyme, the boys drink water from a pool, eat food from a table, and are soon ensnared by an unearthly power. The Teller, the edifice’s mysterious leonine master, will only release them if their sister can sit at a banquet table for three days without consuming anything. The sister fulfills her end of the bargain, but because she has used a bit of water on some drooping flowers the Teller lays down a curse: her own children will one day find their way to him and repeat the ordeal. Later, the girl realizes that her mother too visited the Teller as a child. How far back in time does this cycle stretch? How long will it continue? What is the nature of the hotel and its sinister magic? Pinfold, with impressionistic writing and stark, muted mixed-media art, leaves the answers up to us.

caption:
Eternal life, Gentle Readers, is a subject that has fascinated human society for generations. Colin Thompson creates a delicate and profound meditation on the subject with How to Live Forever. The tale is set in a library with a thousand rooms containing every book ever written. At night, the books come to life, with characters and objects spilling out of the pages to form a bustling city. A young boy named Peter discovers a lost library card belonging to a book with the alluring title “How to Live Forever”, but the book is not in its proper place on the shelf. Intrigued by the mystery, Peter searches for two years. He finally locates the book in the possession of four ancient sages—envoys of the Ancient Child, a contradictory being frozen in time. The Ancient Child warns him that the book will drive him mad, granting him endless youth but locking him out of the world he knows. After much deliberation, Peter decides not to read it and returns home with his newfound understanding. With a thought-provoking text and his signature illustrations full of minuscule details and visual humor, Thompson offers a stirring treatise on the nature of aging and the human condition.

caption:
Gentle Readers, the time has come. The time for endings, and for new beginnings, and for the silent contemplation that marks the passage. This is a day I have been anticipating for a very long while now—the day of my thousandth book review. I am a bittersweet barrel of emotions right now, but most of all I am feeling a great sense of fulfillment. When I discovered this book many months ago, I knew instantly that it had to be my last. I am proud to end my Final Ten Books (and indeed the entire set of one thousand) with @margolanagan and @rovinacai’s Tintinnabula. Just what is Tintinnabula? In the ancient world, the Latin word referred to sacred bells used in monasteries. Here, it represents a personal paradise, a sanctuary from oppression and destruction. A wanderer in a devastated landscape flees from a great, swirling darkness toward a gentle country where soft rains fall on grassy hills. The figure of a white bird leads onward through lush forests, across still waters, to a glowing silhouette representing the traveler’s self, pure and holy. With this quiet encounter, the tale ends. Lanagan’s text radiates a serene, poetic vitality. Cai’s transcendent illustrations, a combination of pencil and digital coloring, celebrate the glorious triumph of peace and tranquility. Tintinnabula is everything I love about picture books. It is a masterpiece.

*

And so you have it, Gentle Readers. One thousand days. One thousand books. I cannot thank you enough for reading along with me. Now I must rest. But know that I will be back. Until then, safe travels…and happy reading.
